1. ASP.NET Core Fundamentals

1. What is ASP.NET Core?

Interview-Ready Answer

ASP.NET Core is a cross-platform, open-source framework from Microsoft for building modern web applications, REST APIs, MVC applications, and real-time applications. It runs on Windows, Linux, and macOS and provides features like built-in dependency injection, middleware, configuration, logging, and high-performance HTTP handling.

Real-World Example

In a project, I can use ASP.NET Core Web API to expose REST endpoints such as GET /api/products and POST /api/products. The API can run on Windows during development and be deployed to a Linux-based Docker container in production.

2. What is the difference between ASP.NET and ASP.NET Core?

Interview-Ready Answer

ASP.NET is the older web framework primarily associated with the .NET Framework and Windows, whereas ASP.NET Core is the modern, cross-platform framework designed to run on Windows, Linux, and macOS. ASP.NET Core also has a lightweight middleware-based pipeline and built-in dependency injection.

Real-World Example

If an existing application uses ASP.NET MVC 5 on .NET Framework, it may be Windows/IIS dependent. A newer application can use ASP.NET Core and be deployed using Docker on either Windows or Linux.

Key points to remember

ASP.NETASP.NET Core
Older frameworkModern framework
Mainly .NET FrameworkModern .NET
Primarily WindowsCross-platform
Older pipelineMiddleware pipeline
DI not built into the same wayBuilt-in DI
IIS-focused hosting historicallyKestrel + IIS/Nginx/reverse proxy

3. What is the difference between .NET Framework and modern .NET?

Interview-Ready Answer

.NET Framework is the older Windows-focused implementation of .NET, while modern .NET is the cross-platform, unified platform used for building applications today. ASP.NET Core runs on modern .NET and provides cross-platform development, better performance, and modern application patterns.

Real-World Example

If I'm developing a new Web API, I would normally build it using ASP.NET Core on modern .NET rather than creating a new application on the older .NET Framework.

4. Is ASP.NET Core cross-platform?

Interview-Ready Answer

Yes. ASP.NET Core is cross-platform and can run on Windows, Linux, and macOS. This makes it suitable for applications deployed to Linux servers, containers, and cloud environments.

Real-World Example

I can develop an ASP.NET Core API on Windows, package it into a Docker container, and deploy that container to a Linux-based cloud environment without changing the application architecture.

5. What is Kestrel?

Interview-Ready Answer

Kestrel is the cross-platform web server used by ASP.NET Core to receive and process HTTP requests. It's lightweight and high-performance. It can run directly as the web server or behind a reverse proxy such as IIS or Nginx.

Real-World Example

A common production setup can look like:

Client
   ↓
Internet
   ↓
IIS / Nginx
   ↓
Kestrel
   ↓
ASP.NET Core Application
   ↓
Controller

For example, IIS can act as the reverse proxy while Kestrel hosts the ASP.NET Core application.

6. What is the role of IIS in ASP.NET Core?

Interview-Ready Answer

IIS can act as a reverse proxy in front of an ASP.NET Core application. It can handle incoming requests and forward them to the ASP.NET Core application running on Kestrel. It can also provide features such as process management, HTTPS configuration, and integration with the Windows hosting environment.

Real-World Example

If an ASP.NET Core API is deployed on a Windows server, IIS can receive requests from clients and forward them to the application running through Kestrel.

7. What is a reverse proxy?

Interview-Ready Answer

A reverse proxy is a server that receives client requests and forwards them to one or more backend servers. In ASP.NET Core, IIS or Nginx can act as a reverse proxy in front of Kestrel.

Real-World Example

Client
   ↓
Nginx
   ↓
ASP.NET Core API 1
   ↓
Database

The client doesn't directly communicate with the internal application server.

8. What is Program.cs in ASP.NET Core?

Interview-Ready Answer

Program.cs is the main entry point of a modern ASP.NET Core application. It is typically used to configure services, application configuration, middleware, routing, and start the application.

A simplified example:

var builder = WebApplication.CreateBuilder(args);

builder.Services.AddControllers();

var app = builder.Build();

app.UseHttpsRedirection();

app.MapControllers();

app.Run();

Real-World Example

In a Web API project, I can register application services and configure middleware in Program.cs, such as registering controllers, dependency injection services, authentication, authorization, and exception handling.

9. What is WebApplicationBuilder?

Interview-Ready Answer

WebApplicationBuilder is used to configure and build an ASP.NET Core application. It provides access to configuration, logging, hosting, and the dependency injection service collection.

Example:

var builder = WebApplication.CreateBuilder(args);

builder.Services.AddControllers();

Real-World Example

If I need to register an IProductService, I can use the builder's service collection:
builder.Services.AddScoped<IProductService, ProductService>();

10. What is WebApplication?

Interview-Ready Answer

WebApplication represents the configured ASP.NET Core application. After building it, we use it to configure the HTTP request pipeline and map endpoints.

Example:

var app = builder.Build();

app.UseAuthentication();
app.UseAuthorization();

app.MapControllers();

app.Run();

Real-World Example

After registering services with builder.Services, I use the app object to configure middleware and endpoints that process incoming HTTP requests.

11. What does app.Run() do?

Interview-Ready Answer

app.Run() starts the ASP.NET Core application and begins listening for incoming HTTP requests. It effectively starts the application's hosting and request-processing lifecycle.

Real-World Example

Once the application reaches:
app.Run();

the API starts accepting requests such as:

GET /api/products

12. What is the ASP.NET Core Hosting Model?

Interview-Ready Answer

The hosting model is the way an ASP.NET Core application is created, configured, hosted, and run. The application uses a host to manage things like configuration, logging, dependency injection, server lifetime, and application startup.

At a high level:

Host
 ├── Configuration
 ├── Logging
 ├── Dependency Injection
 ├── Web Server
 └── Application

Real-World Example

When my API starts, the host loads configuration, initializes dependency injection, starts Kestrel, and then the application begins processing HTTP requests.

Environment & Configuration

13. What are Development, Staging, and Production environments?

Interview-Ready Answer

ASP.NET Core supports different environments so that application behavior and configuration can change depending on where the application is running. Common environments are Development, Staging, and Production.

For example:

Development
    ↓
Local development

Staging
    ↓
Testing / pre-production

Production
    ↓
Live application

Real-World Example

In Development, I might enable detailed error information, while in Production I would return a controlled error response and log the actual exception internally.

14. How does ASP.NET Core know which environment it is running in?

Interview-Ready Answer

ASP.NET Core uses the ASPNETCORE_ENVIRONMENT environment variable to determine the current environment.

For example:

ASPNETCORE_ENVIRONMENT=Development

or:

ASPNETCORE_ENVIRONMENT=Production

Real-World Example

The same API can run with Development settings on a developer's machine and Production settings after deployment without changing the application code.

15. What is appsettings.json?

Interview-Ready Answer

appsettings.json is a configuration file commonly used by ASP.NET Core applications to store application settings such as connection strings, logging configuration, API settings, and other configurable values.

Example:

{
  "ConnectionStrings": {
    "DefaultConnection": "..."
  },
  "Logging": {
    "LogLevel": {
      "Default": "Information"
    }
  }
}

Real-World Example

Instead of hardcoding a database connection string in C# code, the application can read it from configuration.

16. What is appsettings.Development.json?

Interview-Ready Answer

appsettings.Development.json contains configuration values specific to the Development environment. ASP.NET Core can load it in addition to the base appsettings.json, allowing environment-specific settings.

Real-World Example

appsettings.json
        +
appsettings.Development.json
        ↓
Development configuration

Production can instead use:

appsettings.json
        +
appsettings.Production.json

Important Interview Scenario

17. Explain the startup flow of an ASP.NET Core application.

Interview-Ready Answer

First, the application starts from Program.cs. We create the WebApplicationBuilder, configure services and application settings, and then build the application. After that, we configure the middleware and endpoints using the WebApplication object. Finally, app.Run() starts the application so it can receive HTTP requests.

Real-World Example

Program.cs
    ↓
Create WebApplicationBuilder
    ↓
Load Configuration
    ↓
Register Services / DI
    ↓
Build Application
    ↓
Configure Middleware
    ↓
Map Endpoints
    ↓
app.Run()
    ↓
Kestrel receives request
    ↓
Request Pipeline

This is a very good answer to remember because it connects several ASP.NET Core concepts together.

Don't memorize these as isolated definitions. For interviews, build this mental model:

WebApplicationBuilder

Configuration + Logging + DI
    ↓
builder.Build()

WebApplication

Response

2. ASP.NET Core Request Pipeline

This is one of the highest-priority ASP.NET Core interview topics. Your source also identifies the request pipeline as a core area and places it immediately after ASP.NET Core fundamentals. Pasted text

Microsoft describes the pipeline as a sequence of middleware/request delegates, where each component can process the request, call the next component, or terminate the pipeline. The order matters and the response travels back through middleware in reverse order. Microsoft Learn

1. What is the ASP.NET Core Request Pipeline?

Interview-Ready Answer

The ASP.NET Core request pipeline is a sequence of middleware components that process an HTTP request and generate a response. Each middleware can perform some work, pass the request to the next middleware, or terminate the pipeline.

Real-World Example

Suppose a React application calls:

GET /api/products

The request can flow through:

Client
   ↓
Kestrel
   ↓
Exception Handling
   ↓
HTTPS
   ↓
Routing
   ↓
Authentication
   ↓
Authorization
   ↓
Controller
   ↓
Response
   ↓
Client

So, if authentication fails, the request may never reach the controller.

2. What is Middleware in the Request Pipeline?

Interview-Ready Answer

Middleware is a component that participates in the ASP.NET Core request pipeline. It can inspect or modify the HTTP request and response, perform some processing, and then either call the next middleware or terminate the pipeline.

Real-World Example

A logging middleware can record:

Request started
GET /api/products

Then call the next middleware.

After the request finishes, it can record:

Request completed
Status: 200
Duration: 120 ms

This is one reason middleware is useful for cross-cutting concerns such as logging, exception handling, authentication, and security. Microsoft Learn

3. How does an HTTP request flow through ASP.NET Core?

Interview-Ready Answer

The request first reaches the web server, typically Kestrel. It then passes through the configured middleware pipeline. Middleware can process the request, routing determines the endpoint, authentication and authorization can be applied, and finally the controller or endpoint executes. The response then travels back through the pipeline to the client.

Real-World Example

For:

GET /api/orders/10

A simplified flow is:

Browser / React
      ↓
    Kestrel
      ↓
Exception Middleware
      ↓
Routing
      ↓
Authentication
      ↓
Authorization
      ↓
OrderController
      ↓
OrderService
      ↓
Database
      ↓
Response
      ↓
Client

4. What is HttpContext?

Interview-Ready Answer

HttpContext represents the context of the current HTTP request and response. It provides access to information such as the request, response, headers, user, cookies, session, and other HTTP-related data.

Real-World Example

Inside middleware:

public async Task InvokeAsync(HttpContext context)
{
    var method = context.Request.Method;
    var path = context.Request.Path;

    await _next(context);
}

Here we can inspect the incoming request.

For example:

Method = GET
Path = /api/products

5. What is RequestDelegate?

Interview-Ready Answer

RequestDelegate represents a method that can process an HTTP request. Middleware uses it to represent the next component in the request pipeline.

Conceptually:

public delegate Task RequestDelegate(HttpContext context);

Real-World Example

A custom middleware commonly receives:

private readonly RequestDelegate _next;

Then:

await _next(context);

passes the request to the next component.

6. What happens if middleware calls _next()?

Interview-Ready Answer

Calling _next() passes the request to the next middleware in the pipeline. After the downstream middleware finishes, execution can return to the current middleware, allowing it to perform additional work on the response.

Real-World Example

public async Task InvokeAsync(HttpContext context)
{
    Console.WriteLine("Before");

    await _next(context);

    Console.WriteLine("After");
}

Suppose three middleware components exist:

Middleware 1
Middleware 2
Middleware 3

Execution is conceptually:

M1 Before
   ↓
M2 Before
   ↓
M3
   ↓
M2 After
   ↓
M1 After

This before/after behavior is extremely important to understand. Microsoft explicitly documents that middleware can execute work both before and after the next delegate. Microsoft Learn

7. What happens if middleware does NOT call _next()?

Interview-Ready Answer

If middleware doesn't call _next(), it short-circuits the request pipeline. The downstream middleware won't execute, and the current middleware is responsible for producing the response if necessary.

Real-World Example

Imagine authentication middleware detects an invalid request:

if (!isValid)
{
    context.Response.StatusCode = 401;
    return;
}

await _next(context);

The controller won't execute.

Flow:

Request
   ↓
Authentication Middleware
   ↓
Invalid
   ↓
401 Response
   X
Controller

This is called short-circuiting. Microsoft Learn

8. What is short-circuiting?

Interview-Ready Answer

Short-circuiting means terminating the request pipeline before the request reaches all downstream middleware components.

Real-World Example

Static file middleware can handle a request itself:

GET /images/logo.png

If the static file middleware finds the file, it can return the file directly instead of sending the request through unnecessary downstream processing. Microsoft Learn

9. What is middleware ordering and why is it important?

Interview-Ready Answer

Middleware executes in the order in which it is registered in the application. The order is important because one middleware may depend on another middleware having already processed the request.

For the response, execution generally happens in the reverse order.

Real-World Example

A common security-related sequence is:

app.UseRouting();

app.UseAuthentication();

app.UseAuthorization();

app.MapControllers();

Authentication needs to happen before authorization because authorization needs the authenticated user information.

Microsoft specifically notes that middleware ordering is critical for security, performance, and functionality. Microsoft Learn

10. What is the difference between Use(), Run(), and Map()?

Interview-Ready Answer

Use() adds middleware that can call the next component. Run() adds terminal middleware that doesn't have a next delegate. Map() branches the pipeline based on the request path.

Real-World Example

Use()

app.Use(async (context, next) =>
{
    // Before

    await next();

    // After
});

It can continue the pipeline.

Run()

app.Run(async context =>
{
    await context.Response.WriteAsync("Hello");
});

It terminates the pipeline.

Map()

app.Map("/admin", adminApp =>
{
    adminApp.Run(async context =>
    {
        await context.Response.WriteAsync("Admin");
    });
});

Requests beginning with /admin go into that branch.

Microsoft documents Use, Run, and Map as the mechanisms used to build and branch the request pipeline. Microsoft Learn

11. What is terminal middleware?

Interview-Ready Answer

Terminal middleware is middleware that terminates the request pipeline and doesn't pass the request to another middleware.

Real-World Example

app.Run(async context =>
{
    await context.Response.WriteAsync("Request completed");
});

Since Run() is terminal, middleware registered after it won't execute.

12. Does middleware execute only before the controller?

Interview-Ready Answer

No. Middleware can execute code both before and after the controller or downstream middleware. The code before _next() runs while moving down the pipeline, and the code after _next() runs while the response travels back up.

Real-World Example

public async Task InvokeAsync(HttpContext context)
{
    var start = DateTime.UtcNow;

    await _next(context);

    var duration = DateTime.UtcNow - start;

    Console.WriteLine($"Request took {duration.TotalMilliseconds} ms");
}

This is a common pattern for request-duration logging.

13. Where should exception-handling middleware be placed?

Interview-Ready Answer

Exception-handling middleware should be placed early in the pipeline so that it can catch exceptions thrown by downstream middleware and application components.

Real-World Example

Exception Middleware
        ↓
Authentication
        ↓
Authorization
        ↓
Controller
        ↓
Service
        ↓
Exception

The exception can travel back to the exception-handling middleware, which can log it and return a standardized response.

Microsoft specifically recommends placing exception-handling middleware early so it can catch exceptions from later stages. Microsoft Learn

14. Explain a typical ASP.NET Core middleware order.

Interview-Ready Answer

The exact order depends on the application, but a typical API pipeline includes exception handling, HTTPS redirection, routing, CORS where required, authentication, authorization, and endpoint mapping.

For example:

app.UseExceptionHandler();

app.UseHttpsRedirection();

app.UseRouting();

app.UseCors();

app.UseAuthentication();

app.UseAuthorization();

app.MapControllers();

Real-World Example

For a React + ASP.NET Core API:

React
 ↓
HTTPS
 ↓
Exception Handler
 ↓
Routing
 ↓
CORS
 ↓
Authentication
 ↓
Authorization
 ↓
Controller
 ↓
Service
 ↓
Database

The important point is not to memorize one universal ordering, because middleware requirements vary by application. Instead, understand the dependency between middleware components. Microsoft Learn

15. What is the difference between Middleware and Controller?

Interview-Ready Answer

Middleware works at the HTTP request-pipeline level and can apply to many or all requests. A controller handles a specific endpoint and usually contains API or MVC action methods. Middleware is better for cross-cutting concerns, while controllers coordinate endpoint-specific operations.

Real-World Example

Middleware:

Logging
Exception handling
Authentication
CORS

Controller:

GET /api/products
POST /api/products
DELETE /api/products/{id}

A logging middleware doesn't need to know which controller handles the request.

16. What is the difference between Middleware and Filters?

Interview-Ready Answer

Middleware operates in the general ASP.NET Core HTTP pipeline, while filters operate within the MVC or controller execution pipeline. Middleware is suitable for application-wide HTTP concerns, while filters are useful when behavior needs to be tied specifically to MVC actions or controllers.

Real-World Example

Use middleware for:

Global exception handling
Request logging
Correlation ID
Authentication-related processing

Use filters for:

Action-specific logging
Action validation
MVC authorization
Action execution behavior

We'll study Filters in detail later in the sequence.

17. Can middleware modify the response?

Interview-Ready Answer

Yes. Middleware can inspect or modify the response, including headers, status codes, and sometimes the response body, as long as the response hasn't already started.

Real-World Example

A middleware can add a correlation ID:

context.Response.Headers["X-Correlation-ID"] = correlationId;

await _next(context);

This can help trace a request across multiple services.

18. What happens if you try to modify headers after the response has started?

Interview-Ready Answer

Once the response has started, headers and the status code generally can't be changed. Therefore, middleware should make response-header changes before the response is committed.

Real-World Example

If a controller has already started sending the response body, middleware shouldn't try to change:

context.Response.StatusCode

or add new headers afterward.

This is an important production-level detail because ASP.NET Core documents that changing headers or the status code after the response starts can cause an exception. Microsoft Learn

19. What is the relationship between Routing and Endpoint Mapping?

Interview-Ready Answer

Routing determines which endpoint matches an incoming request. Endpoint mapping registers the application's endpoints, such as controllers. Once an endpoint is selected, ASP.NET Core can execute the corresponding endpoint pipeline.

Real-World Example

app.UseRouting();

app.MapControllers();

For:

GET /api/products/10

routing identifies the appropriate controller action.

20. Explain the complete Request Pipeline in an interview.

This is the most important question from this topic.

Interview-Ready Answer

When an HTTP request reaches the ASP.NET Core application, it is received by the web server, typically Kestrel. The request then passes through the configured middleware pipeline. Middleware can perform cross-cutting operations such as exception handling, logging, CORS, authentication, and authorization. Routing identifies the appropriate endpoint, and then the controller action or endpoint executes. The response then travels back through the pipeline to the client.

Real-World Example

For your typical React + ASP.NET Core Web API application:

React Frontend
      ↓
HTTP Request
      ↓
Kestrel
      ↓
Exception Middleware
      ↓
HTTPS / Other Middleware
      ↓
Routing
      ↓
CORS
      ↓
Authentication
      ↓
Authorization
      ↓
Controller
      ↓
Service
      ↓
EF Core / Dapper
      ↓
SQL Server
      ↓
Controller Response
      ↓
Middleware
      ↓
React

The key mental model is:

REQUEST
   ↓
Middleware 1
   ↓
Middleware 2
   ↓
Middleware 3
   ↓
Routing
   ↓
Endpoint / Controller
   ↓
RESPONSE
   ↑
Middleware 3
   ↑
Middleware 2
   ↑
Middleware 1

The response-side reverse traversal is an important detail to understand, not just memorize. Microsoft Learn

🔥 Top Questions to Master for Interviews

If you're short on time, make these 10 questions absolutely solid:

PriorityQuestion
⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐What is the ASP.NET Core request pipeline?
⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐What is middleware?
⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐Explain the complete request flow.
⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐What happens when _next() is called?
⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐What is short-circuiting?
⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐Why is middleware ordering important?
⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐Use() vs Run() vs Map()
⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐How does exception middleware work?
⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐Middleware vs Controller
⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐Middleware vs Filters

🎯 Senior-level mental model

Don't think of the pipeline as simply:

Request → Controller → Response

Think:

HTTP Request
     ↓
┌─────────────────────┐
│ Middleware Pipeline │
│                     │
│ Exception Handling  │
│ Logging             │
│ Routing             │
│ CORS                │
│ Authentication      │
│ Authorization       │
└─────────┬───────────┘
          ↓
     Controller
          ↓
       Service
          ↓
      Database
          ↓
       Response
          ↑
┌─────────┴───────────┐
│ Middleware Pipeline │
└─────────────────────┘
          ↑
        Client

If you can explain this clearly on a whiteboard, you have the foundation for Middleware, Filters, Authentication/Authorization, MVC lifecycle, Web API, and exception handling—all of which we'll cover later.

Next in our sequence: Topic 3 — Middleware, where we'll go much deeper into custom middleware, execution order, RequestDelegate, InvokeAsync, short-circuiting, middleware lifetime, and the common interview traps.

3. Middleware

This topic is very important for ASP.NET Core interviews, especially around request pipeline, custom middleware, RequestDelegate, InvokeAsync, ordering, short-circuiting, and DI lifetimes.

Microsoft's current documentation describes middleware as components assembled into the request/response pipeline. Convention-based middleware typically has a RequestDelegate constructor parameter and an Invoke/InvokeAsync method receiving HttpContext. Microsoft Learn

We'll follow our agreed format:

Common Question → Interview-Ready Answer → Real-World Example

1. What is Middleware in ASP.NET Core?

Interview-Ready Answer

Middleware is a component in the ASP.NET Core request pipeline that handles HTTP requests and responses.

A middleware can perform some logic, call the next middleware, modify the response, or stop the request from going further.

Real-World Example

For an API request:

Client
  ↓
Logging Middleware
  ↓
Authentication Middleware
  ↓
Authorization Middleware
  ↓
Routing
  ↓
Controller

A logging middleware can record:

Request: GET /api/orders/100
Response: 200
Time: 45ms

2. Why do we use Middleware?

Interview-Ready Answer

Middleware is used for functionality that should be applied across multiple requests or endpoints, such as logging, exception handling, authentication, CORS, security headers, request tracking, and performance monitoring.

Real-World Example

Instead of writing logging code inside every controller:

public IActionResult GetOrders()
{
    // logging
    // business logic
}

we create one logging middleware that automatically logs requests for the entire application.

3. What is the basic structure of Custom Middleware?

Interview-Ready Answer

Convention-based custom middleware normally has a constructor that accepts RequestDelegate and an Invoke or InvokeAsync method that accepts HttpContext and returns a Task. Microsoft Learn

Example

public class LoggingMiddleware
{
    private readonly RequestDelegate _next;

    public LoggingMiddleware(RequestDelegate next)
    {
        _next = next;
    }

    public async Task InvokeAsync(HttpContext context)
    {
        Console.WriteLine("Request started");

        await _next(context);

        Console.WriteLine("Request completed");
    }
}

Real-World Example

This middleware can log every API request before it reaches the controller and log the completion afterward.

4. What is RequestDelegate?

Interview-Ready Answer

RequestDelegate represents the next component in the HTTP request pipeline. It accepts an HttpContext and returns a Task.

Conceptually:

Task RequestDelegate(HttpContext context)

Real-World Example

When we write:

await _next(context);

_next represents the next middleware in the pipeline.

Think:

Middleware A
     ↓
Middleware B
     ↓
Middleware C

Inside A:

await _next(context);

means:

"Pass this request to Middleware B."

5. What is HttpContext?

Interview-Ready Answer

HttpContext represents the current HTTP request and response. It provides access to request information, response information, headers, cookies, user identity, session-related data, and other HTTP features.

Example

public async Task InvokeAsync(HttpContext context)
{
    var method = context.Request.Method;
    var path = context.Request.Path;

    Console.WriteLine($"{method} {path}");

    await _next(context);
}

Real-World Example

For:

GET /api/orders/10

we can access:

context.Request.Method
// GET

context.Request.Path
// /api/orders/10

6. What is the purpose of _next?

Interview-Ready Answer

_next is a RequestDelegate that points to the next middleware in the pipeline. Calling _next(context) allows request processing to continue.

Example

public async Task InvokeAsync(HttpContext context)
{
    Console.WriteLine("Before");

    await _next(context);

    Console.WriteLine("After");
}

If there are three middleware components:

M1 → M2 → M3 → Controller

the execution becomes:

M1 Before
M2 Before
M3 Before
Controller
M3 After
M2 After
M1 After

This is a very common interview question.

7. What happens if Middleware does not call _next()?

Interview-Ready Answer

If middleware doesn't call _next(), it short-circuits the pipeline. The request doesn't continue to the next middleware or endpoint.

Example

public async Task InvokeAsync(HttpContext context)
{
    context.Response.StatusCode = 401;

    await context.Response.WriteAsync("Unauthorized");

    // No _next()
}

Real-World Example

Suppose an API requires a custom API key.

Request
   ↓
API Key Middleware
   ↓
Invalid API Key
   ↓
401 Response

There is no reason to call the controller.

8. What is Short-Circuiting?

Interview-Ready Answer

Short-circuiting means stopping the request pipeline at a middleware instead of passing the request to the next component.

Real-World Example

Imagine:

Request
 ↓
API Key Middleware
 ↓
Invalid Key
 ↓
401 Unauthorized

The request never reaches:

Controller

Typical uses

  • Authentication failure
  • Authorization failure
  • Rate limiting
  • Maintenance mode
  • IP restrictions
  • Request validation

9. What is the difference between Use, Run, and Map?

Interview-Ready Answer

Use adds middleware that can call the next middleware.

Run adds terminal middleware and doesn't provide a next delegate.

Map branches the pipeline based on the request path.

Example

app.Use(async (context, next) =>
{
    Console.WriteLine("Before");

    await next();

    Console.WriteLine("After");
});

Use → can continue.

app.Run(async context =>
{
    await context.Response.WriteAsync("Hello");
});

Run → terminal.

app.Map("/admin", adminApp =>
{
    adminApp.Run(async context =>
    {
        await context.Response.WriteAsync("Admin");
    });
});

Map → creates a branch.

10. What is Terminal Middleware?

Interview-Ready Answer

Terminal middleware is middleware that doesn't call the next component, so it ends request processing.

Example

app.Run(async context =>
{
    await context.Response.WriteAsync("Hello World");
});

There is no:

next()

Real-World Example

A health endpoint could directly return:

Healthy

without continuing through additional application processing.

11. Can Middleware execute code after the Controller?

Interview-Ready Answer

Yes. Middleware can execute code both before and after the next middleware by placing logic before and after await _next(context).

Example

public async Task InvokeAsync(HttpContext context)
{
    // Before controller
    var start = DateTime.UtcNow;

    await _next(context);

    // After controller
    var duration = DateTime.UtcNow - start;

    Console.WriteLine($"Request took {duration.TotalMilliseconds} ms");
}

Real-World Example

This is commonly used for request performance monitoring.

Start Timer
    ↓
Controller
    ↓
Database
    ↓
Response
    ↓
Stop Timer

12. Can Middleware modify the Response?

Interview-Ready Answer

Yes. Middleware can modify response headers, status codes, and other response information as long as the response hasn't already started.

Example

public async Task InvokeAsync(HttpContext context)
{
    context.Response.Headers["X-App-Version"] = "1.0";

    await _next(context);
}

Real-World Example

We can add a custom correlation ID:

X-Correlation-ID: abc123

This helps trace a request across services.

13. Can Middleware modify the response after _next()?

Interview-Ready Answer

Yes, middleware can execute after _next() returns, but response headers or status code cannot be changed once the response has already started.

Example

await _next(context);

// Response may already have started here
context.Response.Headers["X-Test"] = "value";

This can cause problems if the response has already been sent to the client.

Interview Tip

Remember:

Before response starts → headers can be modified.
After response starts → headers/status code generally cannot be changed.

14. Where should Exception Handling Middleware be placed?

Interview-Ready Answer

Exception-handling middleware should be placed early in the pipeline so that it can catch exceptions thrown by downstream middleware, controllers, and other components.

Example

app.UseMiddleware<ExceptionMiddleware>();

app.UseAuthentication();
app.UseAuthorization();

app.MapControllers();

Real-World Example

Suppose:

Exception Middleware
        ↓
Authentication
        ↓
Controller
        ↓
Service
        ↓
Database
        ↓
Exception

The exception travels back up to the exception middleware, which can return a consistent response:

{
    "statusCode": 500,
    "message": "An unexpected error occurred."
}

15. What is Middleware Ordering?

Interview-Ready Answer

Middleware executes in the order in which it is added to the pipeline. Therefore, the order is important because one middleware can depend on another middleware having already executed.

Example

app.UseAuthentication();
app.UseAuthorization();
app.MapControllers();

Authentication needs to establish the user's identity before authorization evaluates permissions.

Interview Tip

Don't just memorize the order.

Understand the dependency:

Authentication
      ↓
Identity established
      ↓
Authorization
      ↓
Access decision

16. How is Middleware registered?

Interview-Ready Answer

Middleware can be registered using built-in methods such as Use, Run, Map, or UseMiddleware<T>().

Custom Middleware

app.UseMiddleware<LoggingMiddleware>();

Real-World Example

In Program.cs:

var builder = WebApplication.CreateBuilder(args);

var app = builder.Build();

app.UseMiddleware<LoggingMiddleware>();

app.MapControllers();

app.Run();

17. Why is Middleware generally considered application-lifetime?

Interview-Ready Answer

Convention-based middleware is constructed at application startup and therefore has application lifetime. Because of this, we need to be careful when injecting scoped services into middleware constructors. Microsoft Learn

This is an important 3+ YOE interview question.

Problem

Suppose:

public LoggingMiddleware(
    RequestDelegate next,
    IMyScopedService service)

Here IMyScopedService is scoped but the middleware itself is constructed for the application's lifetime.

Better approach

Inject the scoped dependency into InvokeAsync:

public async Task InvokeAsync(
    HttpContext context,
    IMyScopedService service)
{
    await _next(context);
}

ASP.NET Core supports resolving additional parameters of InvokeAsync through DI. Microsoft Learn

18. How do you inject a Scoped Service into Middleware?

Interview-Ready Answer

For convention-based middleware, if the dependency is scoped and needs to be resolved per request, inject it into InvokeAsync rather than the middleware constructor.

Example

public class LoggingMiddleware
{
    private readonly RequestDelegate _next;

    public LoggingMiddleware(RequestDelegate next)
    {
        _next = next;
    }

    public async Task InvokeAsync(
        HttpContext context,
        IOrderService orderService)
    {
        // orderService is resolved for this request

        await _next(context);
    }
}

Microsoft specifically documents this pattern for scoped dependencies. Microsoft Learn

19. What is IMiddleware?

Interview-Ready Answer

IMiddleware is an interface-based approach for creating middleware. Unlike conventional middleware, IMiddleware is activated through dependency injection, allowing per-request activation and scoped dependencies in its constructor. Microsoft Learn

Example

public class LoggingMiddleware : IMiddleware
{
    private readonly IOrderService _orderService;

    public LoggingMiddleware(IOrderService orderService)
    {
        _orderService = orderService;
    }

    public async Task InvokeAsync(
        HttpContext context,
        RequestDelegate next)
    {
        await next(context);
    }
}

Registration:

builder.Services.AddScoped<LoggingMiddleware>();

app.UseMiddleware<LoggingMiddleware>();

Interview Difference

Conventional Middleware
        ↓
Constructed at application startup

IMiddleware
        ↓
Activated through DI per request

Microsoft documents IMiddleware as supporting activation per client request and constructor injection of scoped services. Microsoft Learn

20. Conventional Middleware vs IMiddleware

FeatureConventionalIMiddleware
ConstructorRequestDelegateDI-based
ActivationApplication lifetimePer request
Scoped constructor dependencyProblematicSupported
Interface requiredNoYes
RegistrationUseMiddleware<T>()Register with DI + UseMiddleware<T>()

Interview Answer

I would normally use conventional middleware for simple cross-cutting concerns. If I need middleware activation through DI and scoped dependencies in the constructor, I can use IMiddleware.

21. Middleware vs Controller

Interview-Ready Answer

Middleware operates at the HTTP pipeline level and can apply to many or all requests. A controller handles specific application endpoints and generally focuses on HTTP endpoint orchestration.

Example

Middleware
 ├── Logging
 ├── Exception Handling
 ├── Authentication
 └── CORS

Controller
 ├── GetOrders()
 ├── CreateOrder()
 └── UpdateOrder()

Real-World Example

Your ASP.NET Core application may have:

Request
 ↓
Logging Middleware
 ↓
Authentication
 ↓
Authorization
 ↓
OrdersController
 ↓
OrderService
 ↓
EF Core
 ↓
SQL Server

22. Middleware vs Filters

This is extremely important for interviews.

Interview-Ready Answer

Middleware operates in the ASP.NET Core HTTP request pipeline, while filters operate within the MVC/controller pipeline.

Middleware is suitable for application-wide HTTP concerns. Filters are more suitable when behavior is specifically related to MVC actions or controllers.

Example

Middleware:

Exception handling
Logging
Authentication
CORS

Filters:

Action validation
Action-specific logging
Authorization filters
Result processing

Easy way to remember

Middleware → HTTP Pipeline

Filter → MVC Pipeline

23. Can Middleware access the authenticated user?

Interview-Ready Answer

Yes, provided authentication has already run before that middleware. The authenticated user is available through HttpContext.User.

Example

var user = context.User;

var userId = user.FindFirst("sub")?.Value;

Important

Ordering matters.

Authentication
      ↓
Custom Middleware
      ↓
Controller

The custom middleware can access:

context.User

But if it executes before authentication, the expected authenticated identity may not yet be established.

24. Can Middleware return a custom response?

Interview-Ready Answer

Yes. Middleware can set the response status code, headers, and body and then stop the pipeline.

Example

public async Task InvokeAsync(HttpContext context)
{
    if (!context.Request.Headers.ContainsKey("X-API-Key"))
    {
        context.Response.StatusCode = 401;
        await context.Response.WriteAsync("API key required");
        return;
    }

    await _next(context);
}

Real-World Scenario

For an internal API:

Request
 ↓
API Key Middleware
 ↓
Missing API Key
 ↓
401

The controller doesn't execute.

25. How would you create a Logging Middleware?

Interview-Ready Answer

I would capture the request information before calling the next middleware, measure the execution time, call _next, and then log the response status and duration afterward.

Example

public class RequestLoggingMiddleware
{
    private readonly RequestDelegate _next;
    private readonly ILogger<RequestLoggingMiddleware> _logger;

    public RequestLoggingMiddleware(
        RequestDelegate next,
        ILogger<RequestLoggingMiddleware> logger)
    {
        _next = next;
        _logger = logger;
    }

    public async Task InvokeAsync(HttpContext context)
    {
        var start = DateTime.UtcNow;

        _logger.LogInformation(
            "Request started: {Method} {Path}",
            context.Request.Method,
            context.Request.Path);

        await _next(context);

        var duration = DateTime.UtcNow - start;

        _logger.LogInformation(
            "Request completed: {StatusCode} in {Duration}ms",
            context.Response.StatusCode,
            duration.TotalMilliseconds);
    }
}

Real-World Scenario

For your .NET Core + React application, this could help identify APIs that are taking unusually long to respond.

For example:

GET /api/orders
200
1,250 ms

This tells the development team that the endpoint needs investigation.

26. How do you explain Middleware execution order in an interview?

Interview-Ready Answer

Use this exact explanation:

"Middleware executes in the order it's registered on the way into the pipeline, and after calling the next middleware, the remaining code executes in reverse order on the way back."

Example

M1
 ↓
M2
 ↓
M3
 ↓
Controller

Execution:

M1 Before
M2 Before
M3 Before
Controller
M3 After
M2 After
M1 After

This is one of the most important middleware concepts to understand rather than memorize.

27. What are common real-world uses of Middleware?

Interview-Ready Answer

Common uses include exception handling, request logging, authentication, authorization-related processing, CORS, rate limiting, correlation IDs, security headers, performance monitoring, and request/response manipulation.

Real-World Architecture

For a production API:

Request
   ↓
Exception Handling
   ↓
HTTPS
   ↓
Logging / Correlation ID
   ↓
Authentication
   ↓
Authorization
   ↓
Routing
   ↓
Controller
   ↓
Service
   ↓
EF Core
   ↓
SQL Server

28. What are common mistakes with Middleware?

Interview-Ready Answer

The main mistakes I would watch for are:

  1. Incorrect middleware ordering
  1. Forgetting to call _next()
  1. Calling _next() multiple times
  1. Injecting scoped services incorrectly into conventional middleware constructors
  1. Trying to modify response headers after the response has started
  1. Putting expensive operations into globally executed middleware
  1. Using middleware when an MVC filter would be more appropriate

Real-World Example

If authentication is registered after authorization:

Authorization
 ↓
Authentication

authorization may not have the identity information it needs.

⭐ Top Middleware Questions to Master

For your 3+ years / Senior Software Engineer interviews, prioritize these:

🔴 Must Know

  1. What is Middleware?
  1. What is Request Pipeline?
  1. What is RequestDelegate?
  1. What is HttpContext?
  1. How does _next() work?
  1. What happens if _next() isn't called?
  1. What is short-circuiting?
  1. Why does middleware ordering matter?
  1. Use() vs Run() vs Map()
  1. How does middleware execute before and after the controller?
  1. Middleware vs Filters
  1. How do you create custom middleware?
  1. How do you inject scoped services into middleware?
  1. Conventional Middleware vs IMiddleware
  1. Where should exception middleware be placed?

🟡 Senior-Level Follow-ups

  1. What happens when the response has already started?
  1. How does middleware access the authenticated user?
  1. How would you implement request logging middleware?
  1. How would you implement correlation IDs?
  1. How would you implement custom API-key validation middleware?
  1. What middleware should be global vs endpoint-specific?
  1. How can middleware affect performance?
  1. How does IMiddleware activation differ from conventional middleware?

🧠 The Mental Model You Should Remember

Don't memorize 28 separate answers. Understand this:

                HTTP REQUEST
                     │
                     ▼
            ┌─────────────────┐
            │ Middleware 1    │
            │ Before          │
            └────────┬────────┘
                     │
                     ▼
            ┌─────────────────┐
            │ Middleware 2    │
            │ Before          │
            └────────┬────────┘
                     │
                     ▼
            ┌─────────────────┐
            │ Middleware 3    │
            │ Before          │
            └────────┬────────┘
                     │
                     ▼
               Controller
                     │
                     ▼
                 Service
                     │
                     ▼
                EF Core
                     │
                     ▼
                SQL Server
                     │
                     ▼
              HTTP RESPONSE
                     │
                     ▼
            Middleware 3 After
                     │
                     ▼
            Middleware 2 After
                     │
                     ▼
            Middleware 1 After
                     │
                     ▼
                  CLIENT

The key concept is:

Middleware forms the HTTP pipeline. Each middleware can process the request, pass it forward using _next(), process the response on the way back, or short-circuit the pipeline.

Microsoft's documentation also explicitly describes middleware as application-lifetime in the conventional model and recommends method-level injection for scoped per-request dependencies. Microsoft Learn

4. Dependency Injection (DI)

DI is one of the highest-priority ASP.NET Core interview topics. For your experience level, you should be comfortable not only explaining DI, but also discussing lifetimes, constructor injection, captive dependencies, IServiceProvider, scoped services, and real-world architecture.

Microsoft's current .NET documentation defines three primary service lifetimes: Transient, Scoped, and Singleton. In ASP.NET Core web applications, scoped services are normally created once per request, while singleton services are shared for the application's lifetime. Microsoft Learn

1. What is Dependency Injection?

Interview-Ready Answer

Dependency Injection is a design pattern where a class receives the objects it depends on from an external source instead of creating those objects itself.

In ASP.NET Core, the built-in DI container creates and provides these dependencies automatically.

Without DI

public class OrderService
{
    private readonly OrderRepository _repository;

    public OrderService()
    {
        _repository = new OrderRepository();
    }
}

OrderService is tightly coupled to OrderRepository.

With DI

public class OrderService
{
    private readonly IOrderRepository _repository;

    public OrderService(IOrderRepository repository)
    {
        _repository = repository;
    }
}

Registration:

builder.Services.AddScoped<IOrderRepository, OrderRepository>();

Real-World Example

In your .NET application:

Controller
    ↓
IOrderService
    ↓
OrderService
    ↓
IOrderRepository
    ↓
EF Core
    ↓
SQL Server

Each layer receives what it needs instead of creating its dependencies directly.

2. What is the difference between Dependency Injection and Dependency Inversion?

Interview-Ready Answer

Dependency Injection is a technique for providing dependencies to a class. Dependency Inversion is a SOLID principle that says high-level modules should depend on abstractions rather than concrete implementations.

Example

public class OrderService
{
    private readonly IOrderRepository _repository;

    public OrderService(IOrderRepository repository)
    {
        _repository = repository;
    }
}

Here:

  • IOrderRepository → abstraction
  • OrderRepository → implementation
  • DI → provides the implementation

Real-World Example

Today:

IOrderRepository → SQLOrderRepository

Later you could use:

IOrderRepository → DapperOrderRepository

without changing OrderService.

3. What is IoC?

Interview-Ready Answer

IoC, or Inversion of Control, means that the responsibility for creating and managing dependencies is transferred from the application code to an external mechanism such as a DI container.

Easy way to remember

Normally:

Class → creates dependency

With IoC:

DI Container → creates dependency → gives it to Class

Real-World Example

Instead of:

var service = new OrderService(
    new OrderRepository());

ASP.NET Core resolves:

OrderService
    ↓
IOrderRepository
    ↓
OrderRepository

automatically.

4. What is the built-in DI container in ASP.NET Core?

Interview-Ready Answer

ASP.NET Core provides a built-in dependency injection container based on IServiceCollection and IServiceProvider. We register services in IServiceCollection, and the container resolves them when required.

Example

builder.Services.AddScoped<IOrderService, OrderService>();

Later ASP.NET Core can resolve:

public OrdersController(IOrderService orderService)
{
    _orderService = orderService;
}

Real-World Example

Program.cs acts as the main place where application dependencies are registered in modern ASP.NET Core applications.

5. What is IServiceCollection?

Interview-Ready Answer

IServiceCollection is a collection of service registrations. We use it to tell the DI container which abstraction maps to which implementation and what lifetime the service should have.

Example

builder.Services.AddScoped<IOrderService, OrderService>();
builder.Services.AddScoped<IOrderRepository, OrderRepository>();

Conceptually:

IOrderService
      ↓
OrderService
      ↓
Scoped

Microsoft documents IServiceCollection as the collection containing ServiceDescriptor registrations. Microsoft Learn

6. What is IServiceProvider?

Interview-Ready Answer

IServiceProvider is the service locator interface used by the DI system to resolve registered services.

Example:

var service = serviceProvider
    .GetRequiredService<IOrderService>();

However:

In normal application code, I prefer constructor injection instead of manually resolving dependencies through IServiceProvider.

Microsoft similarly recommends requesting dependencies as constructor parameters because this makes classes easier to test. Microsoft Learn

7. What is Constructor Injection?

Interview-Ready Answer

Constructor injection means providing dependencies through the class constructor. It is the most common and preferred form of dependency injection in ASP.NET Core.

Example

public class OrderService
{
    private readonly IOrderRepository _repository;

    public OrderService(IOrderRepository repository)
    {
        _repository = repository;
    }
}

Registration:

builder.Services.AddScoped<IOrderRepository, OrderRepository>();

Real-World Example

Controller:

public class OrdersController : ControllerBase
{
    private readonly IOrderService _service;

    public OrdersController(IOrderService service)
    {
        _service = service;
    }
}

ASP.NET Core automatically supplies IOrderService.

8. What are the types of Dependency Injection?

The commonly discussed forms are:

1. Constructor Injection

public OrderService(IOrderRepository repository)
{
}

2. Method Injection

public void Process(IOrderValidator validator)
{
}

3. Property Injection

public IOrderService OrderService { get; set; }

Interview-Ready Answer

Constructor injection is generally preferred because dependencies are explicit, required dependencies can be enforced, and the class is easier to test.

9. What is AddTransient?

Interview-Ready Answer

AddTransient creates a new service instance every time the service is requested from the container.
builder.Services.AddTransient<IEmailService, EmailService>();

Real-World Example

A lightweight stateless formatter:

Request
 ↓
EmailFormatter instance #1

Another request
 ↓
EmailFormatter instance #2

Each resolution gets a new instance.

Microsoft documents transient services as being created each time they are requested. Microsoft Learn

10. What is AddScoped?

Interview-Ready Answer

AddScoped creates one service instance per scope. In a typical ASP.NET Core web application, that means one instance per HTTP request.
builder.Services.AddScoped<IOrderService, OrderService>();

Example

Within one request:

Controller
    ↓
OrderService → same instance
    ↓
Repository
    ↓
OrderService → same instance

For another request:

Request 2
    ↓
New OrderService instance

Real-World Example

DbContext is registered as scoped by default when using AddDbContext. Microsoft Learn

That's why a typical request might be:

HTTP Request
    ↓
Scoped DbContext
    ↓
Multiple database operations
    ↓
HTTP Response
    ↓
DbContext disposed

11. What is AddSingleton?

Interview-Ready Answer

AddSingleton creates one instance that is reused for the lifetime of the application's service provider.
builder.Services.AddSingleton<ICacheService, CacheService>();

Real-World Example

An application-wide stateless configuration/cache service may be singleton:

Request 1 ─┐
Request 2 ─┼──→ Same CacheService instance
Request 3 ─┘

Singleton services must be designed to be thread-safe when accessed concurrently. Microsoft Learn

12. Explain Transient vs Scoped vs Singleton.

This is a must-know interview question.

LifetimeInstance
TransientNew instance every resolution
ScopedOne instance per scope/request
SingletonOne instance for application lifetime

Interview-Ready Answer

Transient is for lightweight services where I don't need to share the instance. Scoped is commonly used for request-level services such as business services and EF Core DbContext. Singleton is used for application-wide shared services that are thread-safe and don't depend on shorter-lived services.

Memory Trick

Transient → Every time
Scoped    → Every request
Singleton → Entire application

13. Which lifetime would you choose for EF Core DbContext?

Interview-Ready Answer

Normally Scoped, because a DbContext represents a unit of work and should generally be shared across operations within a request rather than across multiple requests.

AddDbContext registers DbContext as scoped by default. Microsoft Learn

Real-World Example

HTTP Request
     ↓
OrderService
     ↓
OrderRepository
     ↓
Same DbContext
     ↓
SQL Server

14. Can a Singleton depend on a Scoped service?

Interview-Ready Answer

No, not directly through constructor injection. A singleton lives longer than a scoped service, so directly capturing a scoped dependency can cause the scoped dependency to effectively behave like a singleton and create incorrect state.

Microsoft's DI scope validation specifically checks for scoped services being injected into singletons. Microsoft Learn

Bad Example

public class CacheService
{
    private readonly OrderDbContext _db;

    public CacheService(OrderDbContext db)
    {
        _db = db;
    }
}
builder.Services.AddSingleton<CacheService>();
builder.Services.AddScoped<OrderDbContext>();

This creates a lifetime mismatch.

15. What is a Captive Dependency?

Interview-Ready Answer

A captive dependency occurs when a long-lived service holds a dependency with a shorter lifetime.

The classic example is:

Singleton
   ↓
Scoped

Example

AddSingleton<A>();
AddScoped<B>();

A → B

A may keep B alive longer than intended.

Interview Tip

Remember:

Longer lifetime depending on shorter lifetime = danger.

16. Can a Scoped service depend on a Singleton?

Interview-Ready Answer

Yes. A scoped service can depend on a singleton because the singleton has a longer lifetime and remains available for the entire lifetime of the scoped service.

Example:

Scoped OrderService
       ↓
Singleton ConfigurationService

This is valid, assuming the singleton is thread-safe and otherwise appropriate.

17. Can a Singleton depend on a Transient service?

Interview-Ready Answer

It can be resolved, but the transient dependency may effectively be captured by the singleton, so its expected transient behavior is lost for that dependency.

Example

Singleton
   ↓
Transient

The transient instance injected into the singleton constructor will remain associated with that singleton rather than being recreated for every later request.

Interview Tip

Don't simply say:

"Singleton cannot depend on transient."

That's too broad.

The important concern is lifetime and state semantics.

18. Why must Singleton services be thread-safe?

Interview-Ready Answer

Because the same singleton instance can be accessed concurrently by many requests or threads.

Example

Imagine:

public class CounterService
{
    private int _count;

    public void Increment()
    {
        _count++;
    }
}

If this is singleton, multiple requests can access _count simultaneously.

Real-World Example

Request 1 ─┐
Request 2 ─┼──→ Same Singleton
Request 3 ─┘

Therefore shared mutable state needs proper synchronization.

Microsoft explicitly recommends thread-safe singleton implementations. Microsoft Learn

19. What is the difference between GetService and GetRequiredService?

Interview-Ready Answer

GetService<T>() returns the service if it exists, otherwise it returns null.

GetRequiredService<T>() throws an exception if the service isn't registered.

Example:

var service = provider.GetService<IOrderService>();

Could return:

null

Whereas:

var service =
    provider.GetRequiredService<IOrderService>();

throws if the service isn't registered.

Interview Tip

For required dependencies:

GetRequiredService<T>() makes the failure explicit.

20. Why is Constructor Injection preferred?

Interview-Ready Answer

Constructor injection makes dependencies explicit, ensures required dependencies are available when the object is created, improves testability, and reduces tight coupling.

Example

public class OrderService
{
    private readonly IOrderRepository _repository;

    public OrderService(IOrderRepository repository)
    {
        _repository = repository;
    }
}

Testing becomes easy:

var mockRepository = new Mock<IOrderRepository>();

var service = new OrderService(
    mockRepository.Object);

This is particularly useful with the xUnit + Moq testing approach you've been preparing.

21. What happens if a dependency isn't registered?

Interview-Ready Answer

If ASP.NET Core tries to construct a class whose required dependency cannot be resolved, dependency resolution fails and an exception is thrown.

Example:

public OrdersController(
    IOrderService orderService)
{
}

But:

builder.Services.AddScoped<IOrderService, OrderService>();

is missing.

The application cannot resolve the controller dependency.

Interview Tip

Say:

"The DI container cannot construct the requested service because its dependency graph cannot be resolved."

That's a stronger interview answer.

22. Can we register a service using only its implementation?

Yes.

builder.Services.AddScoped<OrderService>();

This registers:

OrderService → OrderService

You can also map an abstraction:

builder.Services.AddScoped<IOrderService, OrderService>();

Microsoft documents both forms. Microsoft Learn

23. What is Factory-based Service Registration?

Interview-Ready Answer

Factory registration allows us to control how a service is created, including using configuration or other resolved dependencies.

Example:

builder.Services.AddSingleton<IEmailService>(sp =>
{
    var configuration =
        sp.GetRequiredService<IConfiguration>();

    var connectionString =
        configuration["EmailConnection"];

    return new EmailService(connectionString);
});

Real-World Example

If an implementation needs a value from configuration during creation, a factory registration can be useful.

24. Can we register multiple implementations of the same interface?

Yes.

builder.Services.AddScoped<INotificationService, EmailNotification>();
builder.Services.AddScoped<INotificationService, SmsNotification>();

Then:

public NotificationManager(
    IEnumerable<INotificationService> services)
{
}

can receive all registered implementations.

Microsoft documents resolving multiple registrations through IEnumerable<T>. Microsoft Learn

Real-World Example

INotificationService
       ├── Email
       ├── SMS
       └── Push

This is useful when the application needs to execute multiple notification strategies.

25. What happens when the same service is registered multiple times?

Interview-Ready Answer

For a single service resolution, the last registration generally wins. If we resolve IEnumerable<T>, we can obtain all registered implementations.

Example:

services.AddScoped<IMessageService, EmailService>();
services.AddScoped<IMessageService, SmsService>();

Then:

IMessageService service

resolves the last registration, while:

IEnumerable<IMessageService>

contains both registrations. Microsoft Learn

26. What is IServiceScopeFactory?

Interview-Ready Answer

IServiceScopeFactory is used to explicitly create a dependency-injection scope. It's particularly useful when a long-lived service, such as a background service, needs to work with scoped dependencies.

Example

using var scope =
    scopeFactory.CreateScope();

var orderService =
    scope.ServiceProvider
        .GetRequiredService<IOrderService>();

Real-World Scenario

Suppose:

BackgroundService
       ↓
Needs OrderService
       ↓
OrderService uses DbContext

BackgroundService is effectively long-lived, while DbContext is scoped.

So we create a scope:

BackgroundService
       ↓
CreateScope()
       ↓
Scoped OrderService
       ↓
Scoped DbContext

Microsoft explicitly documents IServiceScopeFactory.CreateScope() as the way to create an explicit scope when a singleton needs scoped work. Microsoft Learn

27. What is IServiceProvider vs IServiceScopeFactory?

Interview-Ready Answer

IServiceProvider resolves services, while IServiceScopeFactory creates a new DI scope.

Conceptually:

IServiceScopeFactory
        ↓
CreateScope()
        ↓
IServiceProvider
        ↓
GetRequiredService<T>()

Real-World Example

Background processing:

using var scope = _scopeFactory.CreateScope();

var service =
    scope.ServiceProvider
         .GetRequiredService<IOrderService>();

28. What is Service Locator and why should we avoid it?

Interview-Ready Answer

Service Locator means a class explicitly asks a service provider for its dependencies instead of declaring them as constructor dependencies. It hides the class's dependencies and makes testing and understanding the class harder.

Example:

public class OrderService
{
    public void Process(IServiceProvider provider)
    {
        var repository =
            provider.GetRequiredService<IOrderRepository>();
    }
}

Prefer:

public class OrderService
{
    private readonly IOrderRepository _repository;

    public OrderService(IOrderRepository repository)
    {
        _repository = repository;
    }
}

Interview Tip

Say:

"I use constructor injection for normal dependencies and IServiceProvider/scopes only when there is a specific infrastructure requirement."

29. What is DI scope in ASP.NET Core?

Interview-Ready Answer

ASP.NET Core normally creates a DI scope for each HTTP request. Scoped services resolved during that request use the same scoped instance.

Conceptually:

Request 1
   ↓
Scope 1
   ↓
Scoped Service A

Request 2
   ↓
Scope 2
   ↓
New Scoped Service A

Real-World Example

For an API:

GET /api/orders
      ↓
Request Scope
      ↓
OrderService
      ↓
DbContext
      ↓
Response
      ↓
Scope disposed

Microsoft documents that the framework creates a scope per request and exposes scoped services through HttpContext.RequestServices. Microsoft Learn

30. What are some common DI mistakes?

Interview-Ready Answer

The main mistakes I would watch for are:

  1. Injecting a scoped service into a singleton
  1. Using singleton for state that should be request-specific
  1. Making singleton services non-thread-safe
  1. Excessive constructor dependencies
  1. Manually creating dependencies using new
  1. Using IServiceProvider everywhere
  1. Creating unnecessary scopes
  1. Registering the wrong lifetime
  1. Putting database contexts in inappropriate lifetimes

Real-World Example

Bad:

public class OrderService
{
    private readonly OrderRepository _repository =
        new OrderRepository();
}

Better:

public class OrderService
{
    private readonly IOrderRepository _repository;

    public OrderService(IOrderRepository repository)
    {
        _repository = repository;
    }
}

31. What is a "Dependency Graph"?

Interview-Ready Answer

A dependency graph represents how services depend on each other and how the DI container resolves the complete chain.

For example:

OrdersController
       ↓
IOrderService
       ↓
OrderService
       ↓
IOrderRepository
       ↓
OrderRepository
       ↓
AppDbContext

The DI container resolves this graph when creating the controller.

Real-World Example

Your typical .NET application can look like:

React
  ↓
ASP.NET Core API
  ↓
Controller
  ↓
Service
  ↓
Repository
  ↓
EF Core
  ↓
SQL Server

DI connects these layers without tightly coupling them.

32. What is Constructor Injection vs IServiceProvider?

Constructor InjectionIServiceProvider
Dependencies are explicitDependencies are hidden
Easier to testHarder to test
Preferred for normal dependenciesUseful for special scenarios
Compile-time visibilityRuntime resolution
Less service-locator behaviorCan become Service Locator

Interview Answer

I prefer constructor injection for normal application dependencies. I use IServiceProvider only when dynamic or scoped resolution is genuinely required.

33. What is the "too many dependencies" problem?

Interview-Ready Answer

If a class has a very large number of constructor dependencies, it can indicate that the class has too many responsibilities and may violate the Single Responsibility Principle.

Example:

public OrderService(
    IRepository repository,
    ILogger logger,
    IEmailService email,
    IPaymentService payment,
    ICache cache,
    IReportService report,
    IAuditService audit,
    ...)

This may indicate the class needs to be broken into smaller responsibilities.

Microsoft also notes that many injected dependencies can be a sign that a class has too many responsibilities. Microsoft Learn

34. Explain DI using a real ASP.NET Core architecture.

This is a great Senior-level interview answer.

Interview-Ready Answer

In my ASP.NET Core applications, I typically use constructor injection across the layers. Controllers depend on service abstractions, services depend on repository abstractions, and repositories use EF Core or Dapper for data access. I register these dependencies in Program.cs with appropriate lifetimes. For request-specific components I generally use Scoped, lightweight stateless components can be Transient, and shared thread-safe infrastructure can be Singleton.

Example

builder.Services.AddScoped<IOrderService, OrderService>();

builder.Services.AddScoped<IOrderRepository, OrderRepository>();

builder.Services.AddScoped<IDbConnectionFactory,
                           DbConnectionFactory>();

Then:

OrdersController
       ↓
IOrderService
       ↓
OrderService
       ↓
IOrderRepository
       ↓
OrderRepository
       ↓
EF Core / Dapper
       ↓
SQL Server

That's the kind of explanation that demonstrates practical DI experience, rather than only knowing definitions.

5. Dependency Injection Lifetimes in Depth

Now we go deeper into the three DI lifetimes because this is where interviewers usually move from basic DI questions to practical scenarios.

The official .NET guidance defines Transient, Scoped, and Singleton lifetimes. In ASP.NET Core web applications, Scoped normally means one instance per request, and EF Core's AddDbContext registers DbContext as Scoped by default. Microsoft Learn

1. What are the three DI lifetimes?

Interview-Ready Answer

ASP.NET Core provides three main service lifetimes: Transient, Scoped, and Singleton.

Transient creates a new instance whenever the service is resolved, Scoped creates one instance per scope, usually per HTTP request, and Singleton uses the same instance for the application's service-provider lifetime.

Example

builder.Services.AddTransient<IEmailService, EmailService>();

builder.Services.AddScoped<IOrderService, OrderService>();

builder.Services.AddSingleton<ICacheService, CacheService>();

Easy memory trick

Transient → Every resolution
Scoped    → Every request/scope
Singleton → Entire application
``` :chatgpt-content-reference{index="1"}


---

# 2. What exactly does "per request" mean for Scoped?

### Interview-Ready Answer

> In a typical ASP.NET Core web application, each HTTP request has its own DI scope. A scoped service is created once within that scope and reused whenever it is requested during that request.

### Example

Request 1:

```text
GET /api/orders
       ↓
Request Scope #1
       ↓
OrderService #1

Request 2:

GET /api/orders
       ↓
Request Scope #2
       ↓
OrderService #2

So:

Same request      → Same scoped instance
Different request → Different scoped instance
``` :chatgpt-content-reference{index="2"}


---

# 3. What happens if I request a Scoped service twice in the same request?

### Interview-Ready Answer

> The DI container returns the same scoped instance within that scope.

Example:

```csharp
var service1 =
    provider.GetRequiredService<IOrderService>();

var service2 =
    provider.GetRequiredService<IOrderService>();

If IOrderService is scoped:

service1 ─┐
          ├── Same instance
service2 ─┘

Real-World Example

A controller and another service may both depend on the same scoped DbContext.

Controller
     ↓
DbContext #123
     ↑
Repository

They can participate in the same request-level unit of work.

4. What happens with Transient?

Interview-Ready Answer

Every time a transient service is resolved, the DI container creates a new instance.

Example:

builder.Services.AddTransient<IReportService, ReportService>();

Then:

Resolve #1 → ReportService #1
Resolve #2 → ReportService #2
Resolve #3 → ReportService #3

Even within the same request, separate resolutions can produce separate instances. Microsoft Learn

Real-World Example

A small stateless formatter:

public class CurrencyFormatter : ICurrencyFormatter
{
    public string Format(decimal amount)
    {
        return amount.ToString("C");
    }
}

doesn't need to maintain state between resolutions.

5. What happens with Singleton?

Interview-Ready Answer

A singleton service is created once and the same instance is reused for subsequent resolutions from that service provider.

Example:

builder.Services.AddSingleton<ICacheService, CacheService>();

Conceptually:

Request 1 ─┐
Request 2 ─┼──→ CacheService #1
Request 3 ─┘

Singleton services can be accessed concurrently, so they must be designed to be thread-safe. Microsoft Learn

6. Give me a practical comparison of all three.

Interview-Ready Answer

Suppose we register:

AddTransient<IService, Service>();
AddScoped<IService, Service>();
AddSingleton<IService, Service>();

For two requests:

                 Request 1       Request 2

Transient       Instance A      Instance D
Scoped          Instance B      Instance E
Singleton       Instance C      Instance C

The key point

Transient → changes every resolution
Scoped    → same within scope, changes between scopes
Singleton → same throughout the service-provider lifetime

7. Which lifetime should I normally use for business services?

Interview-Ready Answer

In a typical ASP.NET Core Web API, I generally use Scoped for business services because they often participate in request-level operations and may depend on scoped services such as DbContext.

Example:

builder.Services.AddScoped<IOrderService, OrderService>();

Real-World Architecture

Controller
    ↓
Scoped OrderService
    ↓
Scoped OrderRepository
    ↓
Scoped DbContext

This is a common request-level dependency chain.

8. Why is DbContext usually Scoped?

Interview-Ready Answer

DbContext is normally scoped because database operations in a web application are usually associated with a single request and unit of work. AddDbContext registers it as Scoped by default. Microsoft Learn

Real-World Example

POST /api/orders
       ↓
OrderService
       ↓
OrderRepository
       ↓
DbContext
       ↓
SQL Server
       ↓
Response
       ↓
Request scope ends
       ↓
DbContext disposed

9. Why shouldn't DbContext be Singleton?

Interview-Ready Answer

DbContext is not intended to be shared across unrelated requests. Making it Singleton can cause incorrect state sharing and concurrency problems.

Bad design

builder.Services.AddSingleton<AppDbContext>();

Better

builder.Services.AddDbContext<AppDbContext>();

which is Scoped by default. Microsoft Learn

Interview Tip

If asked:

"Should DbContext be Singleton?"

Answer directly:

No, normally it should be Scoped in ASP.NET Core web applications.

10. Can a Transient service depend on a Scoped service?

Interview-Ready Answer

Yes. A transient service can depend on a scoped service. The transient instance will use the scoped dependency from the current scope.

Example:

Transient OrderValidator
        ↓
Scoped DbContext

This is valid as long as the transient is resolved within an active scope.

Microsoft's DI guidance allows scoped services to be resolved from transient services. Microsoft Learn

11. Can a Scoped service depend on a Singleton?

Interview-Ready Answer

Yes. A scoped service can depend on a singleton because the singleton has a longer lifetime.

Example:

Scoped OrderService
       ↓
Singleton AppConfiguration

The singleton must still be thread-safe and appropriate to share across requests. Microsoft Learn

12. Can a Singleton depend on a Scoped service?

Interview-Ready Answer

Not directly through constructor injection. A singleton lives longer than a scoped service, so capturing a scoped dependency in the singleton can promote that dependency beyond its intended lifetime.

Example:

❌ Singleton
      ↓
   Scoped DbContext

This is one of the most important lifetime interview questions.

Microsoft's scope validation specifically checks for scoped services injected into singletons. Microsoft Learn

13. What is a Captive Dependency?

Interview-Ready Answer

A captive dependency occurs when a longer-lived service holds a shorter-lived dependency, causing the shorter-lived dependency to effectively live longer than intended.

Classic example:

Singleton
    ↓
Scoped

Example

builder.Services.AddSingleton<OrderManager>();
builder.Services.AddScoped<AppDbContext>();

If:

public OrderManager(AppDbContext db)
{
    _db = db;
}

then the singleton captures the scoped DbContext.

Interview phrase

"The dependency is captive because its lifetime is shorter than the lifetime of the object holding it."

14. What happens if a Singleton resolves a Scoped service from the root provider?

Interview-Ready Answer

The scoped service can effectively become root-scoped, meaning it behaves like a singleton and isn't recreated for each request. This can cause incorrect state and lifetime problems.

Microsoft explicitly warns against resolving scoped services directly from a singleton or root provider. Microsoft Learn

Bad

public class MySingleton
{
    public MySingleton(IServiceProvider provider)
    {
        var service =
            provider.GetRequiredService<MyScopedService>();
    }
}

Better

Create an explicit scope when the scenario genuinely requires it.

15. How do you solve Singleton → Scoped dependency?

Interview-Ready Answer

If a singleton genuinely needs to perform scoped work, I create an explicit scope using IServiceScopeFactory, resolve the scoped service from that scope, and dispose the scope when the work is complete.

Example:

public class MyWorker
{
    private readonly IServiceScopeFactory _scopeFactory;

    public MyWorker(IServiceScopeFactory scopeFactory)
    {
        _scopeFactory = scopeFactory;
    }

    public void Process()
    {
        using var scope = _scopeFactory.CreateScope();

        var service =
            scope.ServiceProvider
                  .GetRequiredService<IOrderService>();

        service.ProcessOrders();
    }
}

Flow

Singleton Worker
       ↓
CreateScope()
       ↓
Scoped OrderService
       ↓
Scoped DbContext
       ↓
Dispose Scope

This is the standard approach documented by Microsoft. Microsoft Learn

16. Why is this especially important in BackgroundService?

Interview-Ready Answer

BackgroundService is long-lived, while services such as DbContext are normally Scoped. Therefore, a background service should create a scope before resolving scoped dependencies.

Microsoft specifically recommends injecting IServiceScopeFactory into hosted/background services and creating a scope for scoped work. Microsoft Learn

Example

public class OrderWorker : BackgroundService
{
    private readonly IServiceScopeFactory _scopeFactory;

    public OrderWorker(IServiceScopeFactory scopeFactory)
    {
        _scopeFactory = scopeFactory;
    }

    protected override async Task ExecuteAsync(
        CancellationToken stoppingToken)
    {
        while (!stoppingToken.IsCancellationRequested)
        {
            using var scope =
                _scopeFactory.CreateScope();

            var service =
                scope.ServiceProvider
                     .GetRequiredService<IOrderService>();

            await service.ProcessOrdersAsync();

            await Task.Delay(5000, stoppingToken);
        }
    }
}

Interview Explanation

"Because the BackgroundService is long-lived, I don't inject the scoped service directly. I create a scope for each unit of background work."

That's a very strong Senior-level answer.

17. What is Scope Validation?

Interview-Ready Answer

Scope validation checks for incorrect DI lifetime usage, such as resolving scoped services from the root provider or injecting scoped services into singletons.

In development, the default service provider performs these checks when building the host. Microsoft Learn

Example Problem

Singleton
    ↓
Scoped Service

Scope validation can identify this configuration problem.

Interview Tip

If asked:

"How can you detect captive dependencies?"

Say:

"Enable or use DI scope validation; ASP.NET Core performs scope validation in development by default in the relevant host-building scenarios."

18. Are Scoped services always tied specifically to HTTP requests?

Interview-Ready Answer

No. Scoped means one instance per DI scope. In an ASP.NET Core web application, the framework normally creates a scope per HTTP request, but we can also explicitly create scopes ourselves.

Example

HTTP request:

Request
  ↓
Scope

Background processing:

BackgroundService
  ↓
CreateScope()
  ↓
Scope

This distinction is important.

Scoped ≠ HTTP request by definition.

It's:

Scoped = one instance per DI scope.

In web applications, the common scope happens to be the request scope. Microsoft Learn

19. What happens when a request ends?

Interview-Ready Answer

When the request scope ends, scoped services created within that scope are disposed by the DI container if they implement IDisposable or IAsyncDisposable.

Example

HTTP Request
     ↓
Create Scope
     ↓
DbContext
     ↓
Repository
     ↓
Response
     ↓
Scope Ends
     ↓
Disposable scoped services disposed

The container manages disposal of services it creates. Microsoft Learn

20. Who disposes DI-created services?

Interview-Ready Answer
