  1. Designing production-ready REST APIs

🧠 30-Second Interview Revision

If the interviewer says:

"Explain REST API design."

You can say:

"REST is an architectural style for designing APIs around resources. I use resource-oriented URLs and standard HTTP methods such as GET, POST, PUT, PATCH and DELETE. GET is generally used for retrieval, POST for creating or processing, PUT for replacing a resource, PATCH for partial updates, and DELETE for removal. I also make sure the API is stateless, uses appropriate HTTP status codes, validates requests, uses DTOs, and handles authentication, authorization, errors and versioning appropriately. In ASP.NET Core, I typically implement this through controllers, services and EF Core or Dapper for data access."

That is a strong 3+ years .NET developer answer without sounding overly theoretical. RFC Editor

12. DTOs (Data Transfer Objects)

🔴 Must Master for ASP.NET Core/Web API interviews

DTOs are extremely common in interviews because they connect API design, security, model binding, EF Core, separation of concerns, and over-posting.

Microsoft's ASP.NET Core guidance specifically recommends using a subset of the model—such as a DTO/input model/view model—to control what clients can send and receive, prevent over-posting, hide properties, reduce payloads, and flatten object graphs. Microsoft Learn

1. What is a DTO?

Interview-Ready Answer

DTO stands for Data Transfer Object. It is a simple object used to transfer data between different layers or between the API and client. It contains only the properties that are required for a particular operation.

For example, instead of exposing our EF Core entity directly:

public class Product
{
    public int Id { get; set; }
    public string Name { get; set; }
    public decimal Price { get; set; }
    public decimal CostPrice { get; set; }
    public string InternalCode { get; set; }
}

We can expose:

public class ProductDto
{
    public int Id { get; set; }
    public string Name { get; set; }
    public decimal Price { get; set; }
}

The client doesn't need to know about CostPrice or InternalCode.

2. Why do we use DTOs?

🔴 Very common

Interview-Ready Answer

I mainly use DTOs for:

  1. Security
  1. Preventing over-posting
  1. Controlling the API contract
  1. Hiding internal properties
  1. Reducing response payload
  1. Separating database entities from API models
  1. Different request and response requirements

Microsoft's ASP.NET Core documentation specifically identifies preventing over-posting, hiding properties, reducing payload size, and flattening nested object graphs as DTO use cases. Microsoft Learn

Real-World Scenario

Suppose my database entity contains:

User
├── Id
├── Name
├── Email
├── PasswordHash
├── Salary
├── IsAdmin
└── CreatedDate

I should not simply return the entity to React.

Instead:

User Entity
     ↓
UserResponseDto
     ↓
React
public class UserResponseDto
{
    public int Id { get; set; }
    public string Name { get; set; }
    public string Email { get; set; }
}

3. DTO vs Entity

🔴 Must Know

Interview-Ready Answer

An Entity represents the application's/database business data, while a DTO represents the data we want to transfer across an API or application boundary.

Entity

public class Product
{
    public int Id { get; set; }
    public string Name { get; set; }
    public decimal Price { get; set; }

    public decimal CostPrice { get; set; }

    public Category Category { get; set; }
}

DTO

public class ProductDto
{
    public int Id { get; set; }
    public string Name { get; set; }
    public decimal Price { get; set; }
}

Mental Model

Database
   ↓
Entity
   ↓
Mapping
   ↓
DTO
   ↓
API Response
   ↓
React

4. Why shouldn't we directly expose EF Core entities?

🔴 Very common interview question

Interview-Ready Answer

"I avoid directly exposing EF Core entities because the entity represents the persistence/business model, while the API has its own contract. Exposing entities can unintentionally expose internal properties, create over-posting risks, tightly couple the API to the database model, and cause issues with complex object graphs."

Microsoft's controller-based Web API tutorial demonstrates using DTOs instead of exposing the complete entity and explicitly highlights over-posting protection. Microsoft Learn

5. What is over-posting?

🔴 Extremely important

Interview-Ready Answer

Over-posting occurs when a client sends properties that the API didn't intend to allow the client to modify, and those properties get bound to the model.

Suppose:

public class User
{
    public int Id { get; set; }
    public string Name { get; set; }
    public bool IsAdmin { get; set; }
}

You expect:

{
    "name": "Saurabh"
}

But a malicious client sends:

{
    "name": "Saurabh",
    "isAdmin": true
}

If the API blindly binds and updates the entity, it could modify a property that the client shouldn't control.

DTO solution

public class UpdateUserDto
{
    public string Name { get; set; }
}

Now:

Client
  ↓
UpdateUserDto
  ↓
Service
  ↓
User Entity

The client can't directly control IsAdmin through this DTO.

Microsoft explicitly identifies DTOs as a way to prevent over-posting. Microsoft Learn

6. What are Request DTOs and Response DTOs?

Interview-Ready Answer

I commonly separate DTOs based on their purpose.

Request DTO

Used when the client sends data:

public class CreateProductRequest
{
    public string Name { get; set; }
    public decimal Price { get; set; }
}

Response DTO

Used when the API returns data:

public class ProductResponse
{
    public int Id { get; set; }
    public string Name { get; set; }
    public decimal Price { get; set; }
}

Flow

React
 ↓
CreateProductRequest
 ↓
Controller
 ↓
Service
 ↓
Product Entity
 ↓
Database

And:

Database
 ↓
Product Entity
 ↓
ProductResponse
 ↓
Controller
 ↓
React

7. Why have separate Create and Update DTOs?

Interview-Ready Answer

Because the properties required for creating and updating a resource can be different.

For example:

public class CreateProductRequest
{
    public string Name { get; set; }
    public decimal Price { get; set; }
}

But update might allow:

public class UpdateProductRequest
{
    public string Name { get; set; }
    public decimal Price { get; set; }
    public int Stock { get; set; }
}

The database-generated Id doesn't belong in the create request.

8. Should DTO contain the database ID?

Interview-Ready Answer

It depends on the operation.

For a response:

public class ProductResponseDto
{
    public int Id { get; set; }
    public string Name { get; set; }
}

makes sense.

For creation:

public class CreateProductRequest
{
    public string Name { get; set; }
}

There is usually no need for the client to provide the database-generated ID.

9. What is the difference between Model, Entity and DTO?

Interview-Ready Answer

These terms can overlap depending on the architecture, so I clarify them by responsibility:

TypePurpose
EntityRepresents persisted/domain data
DTOTransfers data between boundaries
Request DTORepresents client input
Response DTORepresents API output
ViewModelRepresents data required by a UI/view

For a clean Web API architecture:

Client
  ↓
Request DTO
  ↓
Controller
  ↓
Service
  ↓
Entity
  ↓
Database

and:

Database
  ↓
Entity
  ↓
Service
  ↓
Response DTO
  ↓
Client

10. Where should DTOs be located?

Interview-Ready Answer

It depends on the architecture.

For a simple application:

MyApi
├── Controllers
├── DTOs
├── Services
├── Models
└── Data

For a larger application:

Application
├── DTOs
├── Interfaces
└── Services

Domain
└── Entities

Infrastructure
├── EF Core
└── Repositories

API
└── Controllers

In Clean Architecture, DTOs can belong to the application/core side when they represent application-level contracts. Microsoft's architecture guidance describes DTOs as types that can be defined in the Application Core when needed for operations that shouldn't depend on UI or infrastructure. Microsoft Learn

11. How do you map Entity to DTO?

There are two common approaches.

Manual mapping

var dto = new ProductResponseDto
{
    Id = product.Id,
    Name = product.Name,
    Price = product.Price
};

Mapping library

For example, a mapping library can configure:

Product → ProductResponseDto

and automate repetitive mappings.

Interview Answer

"For a small number of mappings, manual mapping is simple and explicit. For larger applications with many repetitive mappings, a mapping library can reduce boilerplate. I still prefer explicit mapping where the transformation contains business-specific logic."

12. AutoMapper vs Manual Mapping

🔴 Common senior-level question

Interview-Ready Answer

Manual mapping

var dto = new ProductDto
{
    Id = product.Id,
    Name = product.Name,
    Price = product.Price
};

Advantages:

  • Explicit
  • Easy to debug
  • No mapping configuration
  • Good for complex transformations

Disadvantages:

  • More boilerplate
  • Repetitive for many DTOs

AutoMapper / mapping library

Advantages:

  • Less repetitive code
  • Useful for many straightforward mappings

Disadvantages:

  • Configuration can become difficult to understand
  • Mapping behavior can be less obvious
  • Debugging complex mappings can take more effort

Good interview answer

"I don't consider AutoMapper mandatory. For simple or critical mappings, manual mapping is very clear. For large applications with many straightforward mappings, a mapping library can reduce boilerplate."

13. Can we use LINQ projection instead of mapping after querying?

🔴 Very useful with EF Core

Yes.

Instead of:

Database
 ↓
Entity
 ↓
Memory
 ↓
DTO

we can project directly:

var products = await _context.Products
    .Select(p => new ProductResponseDto
    {
        Id = p.Id,
        Name = p.Name,
        Price = p.Price
    })
    .ToListAsync();

Why is this useful?

The database can retrieve only the required columns instead of loading the entire entity.

Conceptually:

SELECT Id, Name, Price
FROM Products

rather than:

SELECT *
FROM Products

This can reduce data transferred and unnecessary entity materialization.

14. Why is DTO projection useful for performance?

Interview-Ready Answer

"DTO projection allows me to retrieve only the fields required by the API instead of loading the complete entity and its related data."

For example:

.Select(p => new ProductDto
{
    Id = p.Id,
    Name = p.Name,
    Price = p.Price
})

is preferable to loading a large entity graph when the API only needs three fields.

15. What is a nested DTO?

Interview-Ready Answer

A nested DTO contains another DTO as a property.

For example:

public class OrderDto
{
    public int Id { get; set; }
    public decimal Total { get; set; }

    public CustomerDto Customer { get; set; }
}
public class CustomerDto
{
    public int Id { get; set; }
    public string Name { get; set; }
}

Response:

{
    "id": 1001,
    "total": 5000,
    "customer": {
        "id": 10,
        "name": "Saurabh"
    }
}

DTOs can also be used to flatten object graphs when that representation is more convenient for clients. Microsoft Learn

16. What is the problem with returning nested entities directly?

Interview-Ready Answer

It can create:

  • Large response payloads
  • Unnecessary data
  • Circular reference problems
  • Tight coupling
  • Accidental exposure of internal properties

For example:

Order
 ↓
Customer
 ↓
Orders
 ↓
Customer
 ↓
Orders

A DTO lets us control exactly what gets returned.

17. Should validation be placed on DTOs?

Interview-Ready Answer

Yes, request DTOs are a good place for input validation rules.

For example:

public class CreateProductRequest
{
    [Required]
    public string Name { get; set; }

    [Range(1, 1000000)]
    public decimal Price { get; set; }
}

Then with [ApiController], invalid model state can automatically result in a client error response for validation failures.

This keeps the API input contract explicit.

18. DTO vs ViewModel

Interview-Ready Answer

They are related but have different common purposes.

DTO:

Used primarily to transfer data between application boundaries.

ViewModel:

Usually represents the data required by a particular UI/view.

For example:

API
 ↓
ProductResponseDto
 ↓
React

Whereas in MVC:

Controller
 ↓
ProductViewModel
 ↓
Razor View

The terminology can overlap in some applications, so I focus on the object's responsibility rather than the name alone.

19. Can DTO contain business logic?

Interview-Ready Answer

Generally, DTOs should remain simple data-carrying objects.

For example, this is good:

public class ProductDto
{
    public int Id { get; set; }
    public string Name { get; set; }
    public decimal Price { get; set; }
}

I wouldn't put business operations such as:

CalculateDiscount()
ProcessPayment()
ApproveOrder()

inside a DTO.

Those responsibilities belong in the appropriate service/domain layer.

20. Can DTO inherit from Entity?

Interview-Ready Answer

Technically, C# allows it, but I generally avoid using inheritance between DTOs and persistence entities.

For example, I wouldn't normally do:

public class ProductDto : Product
{
}

because it creates coupling between the API contract and the persistence/domain model.

Instead:

Product Entity

ProductDto

remain separate types.

21. What happens if the API returns an Entity instead of a DTO?

Interview-Ready Answer

It can work technically, but it can create several problems:

Database Entity
      ↓
JSON Serializer
      ↓
Client

Potential issues include:

  • Internal properties exposed
  • Over-posting risks when used for input
  • Large object graphs
  • Circular references
  • API/database coupling
  • Difficult API evolution

That's why I generally use DTOs at the API boundary.

22. How would you implement POST using DTO?

Interview-Ready Answer

A clean implementation looks like:

[HttpPost]
public async Task<ActionResult<ProductDto>> Create(
    CreateProductRequest request)
{
    var product = new Product
    {
        Name = request.Name,
        Price = request.Price
    };

    await _productService.CreateAsync(product);

    var response = new ProductDto
    {
        Id = product.Id,
        Name = product.Name,
        Price = product.Price
    };

    return CreatedAtAction(
        nameof(GetById),
        new { id = product.Id },
        response);
}

Flow

React
 ↓
CreateProductRequest
 ↓
Controller
 ↓
Service
 ↓
Product Entity
 ↓
EF Core
 ↓
SQL Server

Microsoft's controller-based Web API example follows the same general pattern: accept a DTO, map it to the entity, save it, and return a DTO through CreatedAtAction. Microsoft Learn

23. How would you implement PUT using DTO?

Interview-Ready Answer

[HttpPut("{id}")]
public async Task<IActionResult> Update(
    int id,
    UpdateProductRequest request)
{
    var product = await _context.Products.FindAsync(id);

    if (product == null)
        return NotFound();

    product.Name = request.Name;
    product.Price = request.Price;

    await _context.SaveChangesAsync();

    return NoContent();
}

Notice that the client controls only the properties defined in:

UpdateProductRequest

rather than the complete entity.

Microsoft's Web API tutorial similarly maps only the permitted DTO properties onto the entity during update. Microsoft Learn

24. What is the difference between Entity → DTO and DTO → Entity?

Interview-Ready Answer

Entity → DTO

Usually used for response:

Product Entity
      ↓
ProductResponseDto
      ↓
Client

DTO → Entity

Usually used for create/update:

CreateProductRequest
      ↓
Product Entity
      ↓
Database

The mappings don't necessarily need to be symmetrical.

25. Can one DTO be used for GET, POST and PUT?

Interview-Ready Answer

Technically yes, but I generally prefer separate DTOs when the operations have different requirements.

For example:

CreateProductRequest
UpdateProductRequest
ProductResponse

This makes the API contract clearer and prevents clients from controlling fields that belong only to responses or internal state.

26. Why shouldn't a response DTO contain PasswordHash?

Interview-Ready Answer

Because PasswordHash is an internal security-sensitive property and should never be part of a normal user response.

Instead:

public class UserResponseDto
{
    public int Id { get; set; }
    public string Name { get; set; }
    public string Email { get; set; }
}

This is another example of why DTOs provide a security boundary.

27. What is DTO flattening?

Interview-Ready Answer

Suppose the entities are:

Order
 └── Customer
      ├── Id
      └── Name

Instead of returning:

{
    "id": 100,
    "customer": {
        "id": 10,
        "name": "Saurabh"
    }
}

we might return:

{
    "orderId": 100,
    "customerId": 10,
    "customerName": "Saurabh"
}

This is called flattening.

It can make the API response simpler for the client. Microsoft also lists flattening object graphs as one use of DTOs. Microsoft Learn

28. DTOs and API versioning

🔴 Senior-level

Interview-Ready Answer

DTOs help us evolve an API contract independently from our database model.

For example:

v1
ProductResponseV1

v2
ProductResponseV2

The underlying entity can remain:

Product Entity

while the external representation changes.

This is especially useful when multiple clients depend on different versions of an API.

29. DTOs in Clean Architecture

Interview-Ready Answer

A common architecture is:

                API
                 │
        Request/Response DTOs
                 │
                 ▼
            Application
                 │
          Business Logic
                 │
                 ▼
             Domain
                 │
                 ▼
         Infrastructure
                 │
             EF Core
                 │
                 ▼
           SQL Server

The important principle is:

The API contract shouldn't be tightly coupled to the database schema.

DTOs help create that boundary.

Microsoft's architecture guidance describes DTOs as types that can be used in the Application Core without depending on UI or infrastructure. Microsoft Learn

30. What would you use in your .NET project?

Interview-Ready Answer — tailored to you

"In my .NET Core Web API projects, I would use separate request and response DTOs rather than exposing EF Core entities directly. For example, a CreateAuditRequest would contain only the fields required to create an audit, while an AuditResponseDto would contain only the information the React frontend needs. The controller receives the DTO, the service handles the business logic, and EF Core or Dapper works with the database entities. This gives us better security, prevents over-posting, keeps the API contract independent from the database model, and helps control the response payload."

That answer ties together your .NET Core + React + SQL Server + EF Core/Dapper experience.

🔥 DTO Interview Priority

🔴 Must Master

  1. Why do we need DTOs?
  1. DTO vs Entity
  1. Why not expose EF Core entities?
  1. What is over-posting?
  1. How do DTOs prevent over-posting?
  1. Request DTO vs Response DTO
  1. Create DTO vs Update DTO
  1. Entity → DTO
  1. DTO → Entity
  1. DTO validation
  1. Manual mapping
  1. AutoMapper vs manual mapping
  1. LINQ projection
  1. DTO security benefits

🟡 Senior-Level

  1. Nested DTOs
  1. DTO flattening
  1. DTO vs ViewModel
  1. DTO and Clean Architecture
  1. DTO and API versioning
  1. DTO performance
  1. DTO inheritance
  1. Mapping large object graphs
  1. Projection vs materialization
  1. DTO design for backward compatibility

🧠 30-Second Interview Answer

If the interviewer asks:

"Why do you use DTOs?"

Say:

"I use DTOs to define a clear API contract instead of exposing my database entities directly. They help prevent over-posting, hide internal or sensitive properties, reduce response payloads, and keep the API contract independent from the database model. I usually use separate request and response DTOs and map between DTOs and entities in the service or application layer. With EF Core, I can also project directly into DTOs so that only the required columns are retrieved."

That is the core DTO answer you should memorize.

13. Authentication in ASP.NET Core

🔴 Must Master

For your interviews, authentication is one of the highest-priority ASP.NET Core security topics. You should be able to clearly explain:

Authentication
     ↓
JWT
     ↓
Claims
     ↓
Authentication Scheme
     ↓
Middleware
     ↓
[Authorize]
     ↓
Authorization

Microsoft defines authentication as determining a user's identity, while authorization determines whether that identity has access to a resource. ASP.NET Core authentication uses authentication schemes and handlers, with UseAuthentication() adding the authentication middleware to the pipeline. Microsoft Learn

1. What is Authentication?

Interview-Ready Answer

Authentication is the process of verifying who the user or client is.

For example:

Username + Password
        ↓
Identity Provider
        ↓
User authenticated
        ↓
Access Token / Cookie

The API can then identify the caller.

Real-World Scenario

A user logs into your React application:

React
  ↓
Login API
  ↓
Identity Provider
  ↓
Access Token
  ↓
React

The token is then sent when calling protected APIs.

2. Authentication vs Authorization

🔴 Extremely common interview question

Interview-Ready Answer

Authentication answers "Who are you?" while authorization answers "What are you allowed to do?"

Example:

Authentication:
Is this user Saurabh?
        ↓
YES

Authorization:
Can Saurabh delete this product?
        ↓
Depends on role/permission

Microsoft explicitly distinguishes the two this way: authentication determines identity, while authorization determines access. Microsoft Learn

Easy way to remember

Authentication → Identity
Authorization  → Permission

3. How does authentication work in ASP.NET Core?

Interview-Ready Answer

At a high level:

HTTP Request
     ↓
Authentication Middleware
     ↓
Authentication Handler
     ↓
Validate Credentials/Token
     ↓
Create ClaimsPrincipal
     ↓
HttpContext.User
     ↓
Authorization
     ↓
Controller

ASP.NET Core authentication handlers perform authentication-related work and construct the user's identity. Microsoft Learn

4. What is an Authentication Scheme?

🔴 Important

Interview-Ready Answer

An authentication scheme identifies which authentication handler should be used to authenticate a request.

Examples:

Cookies
Bearer
JWT

For example:

builder.Services
    .AddAuthentication(JwtBearerDefaults.AuthenticationScheme)
    .AddJwtBearer();

Here:

Bearer
  ↓
JwtBearerHandler

ASP.NET Core schemes associate a name with an authentication handler and its configuration. Microsoft Learn

5. What is AddAuthentication()?

Interview-Ready Answer

AddAuthentication() registers/configures authentication services and can specify the default authentication scheme.

For JWT:

builder.Services
    .AddAuthentication(JwtBearerDefaults.AuthenticationScheme)
    .AddJwtBearer(options =>
    {
        // JWT configuration
    });

The default scheme tells ASP.NET Core which authentication handler should be used when a specific scheme isn't explicitly requested. Microsoft Learn

6. What is AddJwtBearer()?

Interview-Ready Answer

AddJwtBearer() configures JWT Bearer authentication for an API.

Typical setup:

builder.Services
    .AddAuthentication(JwtBearerDefaults.AuthenticationScheme)
    .AddJwtBearer(options =>
    {
        options.Authority = "https://identity-server";
        options.Audience = "my-api";
    });

ASP.NET Core uses the JWT bearer handler to validate the bearer token and establish the user's identity. Microsoft Learn

7. What is JWT?

🔴 Must Master

Interview-Ready Answer

JWT stands for JSON Web Token. It is a compact token format commonly used to carry claims between parties. In API authentication, a client sends an access token in the Authorization header using the Bearer scheme.

Example:

Authorization: Bearer eyJhbGciOi...

The API validates the token before allowing access to protected endpoints. Microsoft Learn

8. What are the three parts of a JWT?

A JWT typically has:

Header.Payload.Signature

Example:

xxxxx.yyyyy.zzzzz

Header

Contains information such as:

{
  "alg": "RS256",
  "typ": "JWT"
}

Payload

Contains claims:

{
  "sub": "123",
  "name": "Saurabh",
  "role": "Admin"
}

Signature

Used to verify that the token hasn't been tampered with and that it was issued by the trusted signer.

9. Is JWT encrypted?

🔴 Common trick question

Interview-Ready Answer

A JWT is not necessarily encrypted. A signed JWT provides integrity and authenticity, but its payload is generally readable by anyone who possesses the token.

Therefore, don't put secrets such as:

Password
Credit card number
Private keys

inside a normal JWT payload.

For bearer access tokens, the API should validate the signature and relevant claims rather than assuming that the payload is confidential. Microsoft Learn

10. What is the difference between signing and encryption?

Interview-Ready Answer

Signing provides:

Integrity
+
Authenticity

It helps determine whether the token was modified and whether it was signed by the trusted issuer.

Encryption provides:

Confidentiality

It prevents unauthorized parties from reading the protected content.

So:

Signed JWT
→ Can detect tampering

Encrypted token
→ Can protect confidentiality

11. What is a claim?

🔴 Must Master

Interview-Ready Answer

A claim is a piece of information about the authenticated identity.

Examples:

sub = 123
name = Saurabh
email = user@example.com
role = Admin

Claims are used by ASP.NET Core authorization to make access decisions. Microsoft Learn

12. What is ClaimsPrincipal?

Interview-Ready Answer

ClaimsPrincipal represents the current authenticated user.

In ASP.NET Core you can access it through:

HttpContext.User

For example:

var userName = User.Identity?.Name;

or:

var userId = User.FindFirst("sub")?.Value;

Authentication creates the identity/claims information that becomes available to authorization through ClaimsPrincipal. Microsoft Learn

13. What is HttpContext.User?

Interview-Ready Answer

HttpContext.User contains the current request's ClaimsPrincipal.

For example:

var user = HttpContext.User;

var userId = user.FindFirst("sub")?.Value;
var role = user.FindFirst("role")?.Value;

This information is populated as part of authentication.

14. What is Bearer Authentication?

Interview-Ready Answer

Bearer authentication means the client sends an access token in the HTTP Authorization header:

Authorization: Bearer <access-token>

ASP.NET Core's JWT bearer handler validates the token and establishes the user's identity. Microsoft Learn

Real-World Flow

React
  ↓
Authorization: Bearer JWT
  ↓
ASP.NET Core
  ↓
JwtBearerHandler
  ↓
Validate Token
  ↓
ClaimsPrincipal
  ↓
[Authorize]
  ↓
Controller

15. What is UseAuthentication()?

🔴 Important

Interview-Ready Answer

UseAuthentication() adds authentication middleware to the ASP.NET Core request pipeline. It allows the configured authentication handlers to authenticate requests and establish the current user.

Example:

app.UseAuthentication();
app.UseAuthorization();

Authentication should run before authorization so that authorization has an authenticated identity to evaluate. Microsoft Learn

16. Why must UseAuthentication() come before UseAuthorization()?

🔴 Very common

Interview-Ready Answer

Because authorization needs to know who the current user is.

Correct:

app.UseAuthentication();
app.UseAuthorization();

Conceptually:

Request
 ↓
Authentication
 ↓
HttpContext.User
 ↓
Authorization
 ↓
Controller

If authorization runs before authentication has established the identity, protected endpoints cannot be evaluated correctly.

17. Where do UseAuthentication() and UseAuthorization() go?

For controller APIs using endpoint routing, the typical order is:

app.UseRouting();

app.UseAuthentication();

app.UseAuthorization();

app.MapControllers();

Microsoft's guidance requires authentication before middleware that depends on authenticated users; with endpoint routing, authentication is placed after routing and before endpoint execution. Microsoft Learn

Mental Model

UseRouting
    ↓
UseAuthentication
    ↓
UseAuthorization
    ↓
MapControllers

18. Does AddAuthentication() automatically protect all endpoints?

🔴 Trick question

Interview-Ready Answer

No. Configuring authentication doesn't automatically require authentication for every endpoint.

You normally explicitly require authorization:

[Authorize]
public class ProductsController : ControllerBase
{
}

ASP.NET Core also supports a fallback authorization policy when you want authenticated access to be required by default. Microsoft Learn

19. What is [Authorize]?

Interview-Ready Answer

[Authorize] indicates that an endpoint requires an authenticated user and/or a matching authorization policy.

Example:

[Authorize]
[HttpGet]
public IActionResult GetProducts()
{
    return Ok();
}

If the request isn't authenticated, the authorization system triggers the authentication challenge.

For JWT bearer authentication, this normally results in 401 Unauthorized. Microsoft Learn

20. What is [AllowAnonymous]?

Interview-Ready Answer

[AllowAnonymous] allows an endpoint to be accessed without authentication even when authorization is otherwise applied.

Typical example:

[AllowAnonymous]
[HttpPost("login")]
public IActionResult Login(LoginRequest request)
{
    // authenticate user
}

Because users obviously need a way to obtain credentials/token before accessing protected endpoints.

21. What happens when a JWT is invalid?

Interview-Ready Answer

The JWT bearer handler validates the token.

Validation can include:

Signature
Issuer
Audience
Expiration

If validation fails, the request isn't successfully authenticated and a protected endpoint will generally result in:

401 Unauthorized

Microsoft specifically calls out signature, issuer, audience, and expiration validation for JWT bearer APIs. Microsoft Learn

22. What are Issuer and Audience?

🔴 Common JWT question

Issuer

iss identifies who issued the token.

Example:

https://identity.example.com

Audience

aud identifies who the token is intended for.

Example:

my-product-api

The API should validate these values against what it expects. Microsoft Learn

Simple analogy

Issuer   → Who issued this?
Audience → Who is this token for?

23. What is token expiration?

Interview-Ready Answer

A JWT access token normally has an expiration claim such as:

{
    "exp": 1790000000
}

After expiration, the API should reject the token.

This limits how long a stolen or leaked access token can remain usable.

Microsoft includes token expiration among the JWT values that should be validated. Microsoft Learn

24. What happens when the JWT expires?

Interview-Ready Answer

The API rejects the expired access token.

Typically:

Expired JWT
    ↓
Authentication fails
    ↓
401 Unauthorized

The client application may then obtain a new access token using an appropriate authentication flow.

25. What is a Refresh Token?

Interview-Ready Answer

A refresh token is used to obtain a new access token without requiring the user to authenticate interactively again.

Conceptually:

Access Token
Short lifetime
     ↓ expires

Refresh Token
Longer lifetime
     ↓
New Access Token

Microsoft notes that refresh tokens can be used to refresh a UI application without requiring the user to re-authenticate. Microsoft Learn

26. Access Token vs Refresh Token

Access TokenRefresh Token
Used to access APIsUsed to obtain new access token
Usually shorter lifetimeUsually longer lifetime
Sent to resource APISent to authorization/token service
Contains authorization information/claimsUsed primarily for token renewal

Interview Line

"I treat access tokens as short-lived credentials for API access and refresh tokens as credentials for obtaining new access tokens."

27. JWT vs Cookie Authentication

🔴 Very common

JWT Bearer

Client
 ↓
Authorization: Bearer JWT
 ↓
API

Common for:

React SPA
Mobile apps
APIs
Microservices

Cookie

Browser
 ↓
Cookie
 ↓
Web Application

Common for traditional server-rendered web applications.

ASP.NET Core supports both cookie and JWT bearer authentication as separate authentication schemes. Microsoft Learn

28. Why is JWT commonly used for Web APIs?

Interview-Ready Answer

"JWT bearer authentication works well for APIs because the client can send an access token with each request, and the API can validate it without relying on a server-side session for the user's identity."

It also works naturally across:

React
Mobile
Multiple APIs
Microservices

But I wouldn't say JWT is automatically better than cookies; the appropriate approach depends on the application architecture and authentication system.

29. What is the complete JWT authentication flow?

🔴 Must be able to draw this in an interview

                    LOGIN
                      │
                      ▼
                  React App
                      │
                      ▼
              Identity Provider
                      │
                      ▼
                 Access Token
                      │
                      ▼
                  React App
                      │
                      │ Authorization:
                      │ Bearer <JWT>
                      ▼
              ASP.NET Core API
                      │
                      ▼
           Authentication Middleware
                      │
                      ▼
             JWT Bearer Handler
                      │
              ┌───────┴────────┐
              │                │
           Valid             Invalid
              │                │
              ▼                ▼
       ClaimsPrincipal       401
              │
              ▼
       Authorization
              │
       ┌──────┴──────┐
       │             │
     Allowed       Denied
       │             │
       ▼             ▼
 Controller          403

This is one of the most useful diagrams to memorize.

30. What is the difference between 401 and 403?

🔴 Must Master

401 Unauthorized

Authentication failed or isn't present.

Examples:

No token
Expired token
Invalid signature
Wrong issuer
Wrong audience

403 Forbidden

The caller is authenticated, but doesn't have permission.

Example:

JWT valid
Role = Employee
Endpoint requires Admin
       ↓
403

Microsoft's JWT guidance explicitly distinguishes invalid/failed authentication (401) from insufficient permissions (403). Microsoft Learn

31. What is Role-Based Authorization?

Interview-Ready Answer

Role-based authorization restricts access according to roles.

Example:

[Authorize(Roles = "Admin")]
[HttpDelete("{id}")]
public IActionResult Delete(int id)
{
    return NoContent();
}

The JWT can contain role information, which ASP.NET Core can use for authorization. Microsoft Learn

Example

Admin
Manager
Employee
DELETE Product
    ↓
Admin only

32. What is Claims-Based Authorization?

Interview-Ready Answer

Instead of checking only roles, we can use individual claims.

For example:

department = Finance
permission = Product.Delete
country = IN

Then authorization policies can make decisions based on those claims.

This provides more granular control than simply checking:

Role = Admin

33. Role-Based vs Claims-Based Authorization

Interview-Ready Answer

Role-Based

Role = Admin

Simple and suitable when access is primarily organized around roles.

Claims-Based

Permission = Product.Delete

More granular and useful when permissions don't map cleanly to broad roles.

Example

Admin
   ↓
All permissions

Manager
   ↓
Product.Read
Product.Update

Employee
   ↓
Product.Read

34. What is Policy-Based Authorization?

🔴 Senior-level

Interview-Ready Answer

Policy-based authorization allows us to define reusable authorization rules called policies and apply them to endpoints.

Example:

builder.Services.AddAuthorization(options =>
{
    options.AddPolicy("CanDeleteProduct", policy =>
        policy.RequireClaim("permission", "Product.Delete"));
});

Then:

[Authorize(Policy = "CanDeleteProduct")]
[HttpDelete("{id}")]
public IActionResult Delete(int id)
{
    return NoContent();
}

ASP.NET Core provides a richer policy-based authorization model in which requirements and handlers evaluate the user's claims. Microsoft Learn

35. Authentication vs Authorization Middleware

Interview-Ready Answer

UseAuthentication()
        ↓
Establishes identity
        ↓
HttpContext.User
        ↓
UseAuthorization()
        ↓
Checks access
        ↓
Controller

So:

Authentication → Who are you?
Authorization  → Are you allowed?

36. What is an Authentication Handler?

Interview-Ready Answer

An authentication handler contains the logic for a particular authentication scheme.

Examples:

CookieAuthenticationHandler
JwtBearerHandler

For JWT:

Bearer Scheme
      ↓
JwtBearerHandler
      ↓
Validate JWT
      ↓
Create ClaimsPrincipal

ASP.NET Core's JWT package provides the JwtBearerHandler for JWT bearer authentication. Microsoft Learn

37. What is Challenge vs Forbid?

🔴 Good senior interview question

Challenge

Means:

"You haven't successfully authenticated."

For JWT bearer:

401 Unauthorized

Forbid

Means:

"You are authenticated, but you aren't allowed to access this resource."

For JWT bearer:

403 Forbidden

ASP.NET Core authentication schemes define both challenge and forbid behavior; the JWT bearer scheme normally responds with 401 for a challenge and 403 for forbid. Microsoft Learn

38. Can ASP.NET Core have multiple authentication schemes?

Interview-Ready Answer

Yes.

For example:

builder.Services
    .AddAuthentication()
    .AddCookie()
    .AddJwtBearer();

Then an endpoint can specify which scheme it requires:

[Authorize(
    AuthenticationSchemes =
        JwtBearerDefaults.AuthenticationScheme)]

ASP.NET Core supports multiple schemes and allows authorization policies/attributes to select the appropriate scheme. Microsoft Learn

39. What is the difference between ID Token and Access Token?

🔴 Important for modern authentication interviews

Interview-Ready Answer

An ID token tells the client about the authenticated user's identity. An access token is intended to authorize access to a protected resource/API.

A key interview point:

You should not use an ID token as an API access token.

Microsoft's current JWT guidance explicitly states that ID tokens should not be used to access APIs. Microsoft Learn

40. How would you explain authentication in your project?

Tailored Interview Answer

"In a typical .NET Core Web API architecture, I would use JWT bearer authentication. The client obtains an access token from the identity provider and sends it in the Authorization header as a Bearer token. ASP.NET Core's JWT bearer handler validates the token, including its signature, issuer, audience and expiration, and creates the user's ClaimsPrincipal. Then the authorization middleware evaluates the user's roles or claims against the endpoint's authorization requirements. If authentication fails, the API returns 401, and if the user is authenticated but doesn't have permission, it returns 403."

This is a strong answer because it connects:

JWT
 ↓
Authentication
 ↓
Claims
 ↓
Authorization
 ↓
ASP.NET Core Middleware
 ↓
Controller

and directly reflects the concepts Microsoft documents for ASP.NET Core authentication and JWT bearer APIs. Microsoft Learn

🔥 Authentication — Interview Priority

  1. JWT
  1. JWT structure
  1. Is JWT encrypted?
  1. Claims
  1. ClaimsPrincipal
  1. Bearer authentication
  1. AddAuthentication()
  1. AddJwtBearer()
  1. UseAuthentication()
  1. UseAuthorization()

  1. [AllowAnonymous]
  1. 401 vs 403
  1. Issuer
  1. Audience
  1. Token expiration
  1. Access token
  1. Refresh token

  1. Claims-based authorization
  1. Policy-based authorization

🟡 Senior-Level

  1. Authentication schemes

  1. Global authentication/fallback policy
  1. Custom authorization policies
  1. Claims transformation

🧠 The 60-Second Answer to Memorize

If the interviewer asks:

"Explain authentication and authorization in ASP.NET Core."

Say:

"Authentication is the process of identifying the caller, while authorization determines whether that authenticated caller has permission to access a resource. In a typical ASP.NET Core Web API, I can use JWT bearer authentication. The client sends an access token in the Authorization header. The JWT bearer handler validates the token's signature, issuer, audience and expiration, and creates a ClaimsPrincipal that is available through HttpContext.User. Then UseAuthorization and the [Authorize] attribute evaluate whether the user satisfies the required role, claim or policy. If authentication fails, we generally return 401, and if the user is authenticated but doesn't have sufficient permission, we return 403." Microsoft Learn

14. JWT Authentication in Depth

🔴 Must Master for ASP.NET Core interviews

Now we'll go one level deeper than the previous authentication topic. For a 3+ year .NET interview, you should be comfortable explaining not only what JWT is, but also how ASP.NET Core validates it, what TokenValidationParameters do, how claims are created, and what happens when validation fails.

Microsoft's current ASP.NET Core guidance recommends fully validating JWT bearer access tokens, including their signature, issuer, audience, and expiration. Microsoft Learn

1. What is the complete JWT authentication flow?

Interview-Ready Answer

User
 ↓
React Application
 ↓
Identity Provider
 ↓
Login / Authentication
 ↓
Access Token (JWT)
 ↓
React
 ↓
Authorization: Bearer <JWT>
 ↓
ASP.NET Core API
 ↓
JwtBearerHandler
 ↓
Validate JWT
 ↓
ClaimsPrincipal
 ↓
Authorization
 ↓
Controller

The important distinction is:

Authentication
      ↓
"Who is this?"

Authorization
      ↓
"Can this user perform this operation?"

ASP.NET Core's JWT bearer handler validates the token and extracts identity information from its claims. Microsoft Learn

2. What are the three parts of a JWT?

A JWT normally has:

Header.Payload.Signature

For example:

eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9
.
eyJzdWIiOiIxMjMifQ
.
SflKxwRJSMeKKF2QT4f...

Header

Contains metadata such as:

{
  "alg": "RS256",
  "typ": "JWT"
}

Payload

Contains claims:

{
  "sub": "123",
  "name": "Saurabh",
  "role": "Admin",
  "aud": "my-api",
  "iss": "https://identity.example.com",
  "exp": 1790000000
}

Signature

Used to verify the token's integrity and establish trust in its issuer.

3. What is the JWT Header?

Interview-Ready Answer

The header contains metadata about the token.

Common fields include:

{
  "alg": "RS256",
  "typ": "JWT"
}

alg indicates the signing algorithm.

typ identifies the token type.

Interview Tip

Don't say:

"The header encrypts the JWT."

It doesn't.

4. What is the JWT Payload?

Interview-Ready Answer

The payload contains claims about the subject or token.

Example:

{
  "sub": "123",
  "name": "Saurabh",
  "role": "Admin",
  "aud": "product-api",
  "iss": "https://identity.example.com",
  "exp": 1790000000
}

The payload is not a safe place for secrets merely because it's inside a JWT.

5. Is the JWT payload encrypted?

🔴 Trick question

Interview-Ready Answer

Not necessarily. A normal signed JWT is encoded and signed, not encrypted.

Therefore, don't put sensitive information such as:

Password
Password hash
Credit card information
Private keys

into a normal JWT payload.

Microsoft's current guidance also distinguishes access tokens from confidential data and notes that access tokens can have different formats and may be encrypted, so an API/client should not assume every access token is simply a readable JWT. Microsoft Learn

6. What is the JWT Signature?

Interview-Ready Answer

The signature allows the receiver to verify that:

  1. The token was signed by a trusted issuer.
  1. The token hasn't been modified.

Conceptually:

Header
 +
Payload
 +
Secret/private key
      ↓
Signature

The API verifies the signature using the appropriate cryptographic key.

7. What is the difference between symmetric and asymmetric signing?

🔴 Important

Symmetric

The same secret is used for signing and validation.

Example:

Issuer
  ↓
Shared Secret
  ↓
Sign JWT

API:

API
 ↓
Same Secret
 ↓
Validate JWT

A common example is:

HS256

Asymmetric

A private key signs the token, while a corresponding public key verifies it.

Private Key
    ↓
Issuer signs
    ↓
JWT
    ↓
Public Key
    ↓
API validates

Examples include:

RS256
ES256

Interview Answer

"Symmetric signing uses one shared secret for signing and validation, while asymmetric signing uses a private key to sign and a public key to validate. Asymmetric signing is commonly useful when many APIs need to validate tokens issued by a centralized identity provider."

8. What is iss?

Interview-Ready Answer

iss means issuer.

It identifies who issued the token.

Example:

{
  "iss": "https://identity.example.com"
}

The API should validate that the issuer matches the trusted issuer it expects. Microsoft lists issuer validation as one of the required JWT validation checks. Microsoft Learn

9. What is aud?

Interview-Ready Answer

aud means audience.

It identifies the intended recipient/resource for the token.

Example:

{
  "aud": "product-api"
}

If a token was issued for:

order-api

it shouldn't automatically be accepted by:

payment-api

The API should validate the expected audience. Microsoft Learn

10. What is exp?

Interview-Ready Answer

exp means expiration time.

Example:

{
  "exp": 1790000000
}

Once the token expires, the API should reject it.

Token expiration is one of the validation checks Microsoft recommends for JWT bearer APIs. Microsoft Learn

11. What is nbf?

Interview-Ready Answer

nbf means Not Before.

It indicates the time before which the token should not be accepted.

Conceptually:

Current Time
     ↓
nbf
     ↓
Token becomes valid

This helps prevent a token from being used before its intended validity period.

12. What is iat?

Interview-Ready Answer

iat means Issued At.

It represents when the token was issued.

Example:

{
  "iat": 1789990000
}

It can be useful when reasoning about token age and security policies.

13. What is sub?

Interview-Ready Answer

sub means subject.

It normally identifies the subject associated with the token.

Example:

{
  "sub": "12345"
}

In an application, this could represent the user's unique identifier.

14. What is jti?

Interview-Ready Answer

jti means JWT ID.

It provides a unique identifier for the token.

Example:

{
  "jti": "7f8e9d..."
}

It can be useful for scenarios such as token tracking or revocation systems.

Microsoft lists jti among claims required for OAuth 2.0 access tokens in its current JWT bearer guidance. Microsoft Learn

15. What is client_id?

Interview-Ready Answer

client_id identifies the OAuth client/application that requested the access token.

For example:

React Application
      ↓
Client ID
      ↓
Identity Provider

The exact claims present depend on the identity provider and token profile.

Microsoft's current guidance lists client_id among claims required for OAuth 2.0 access tokens. Microsoft Learn

16. What does ASP.NET Core validate in a JWT?

🔴 Very important

You should remember these four:

1. Signature
2. Issuer
3. Audience
4. Expiration

Microsoft explicitly recommends fully validating these values for JWT bearer APIs. Microsoft Learn

Interview Answer

"When my ASP.NET Core API receives a JWT bearer token, I validate its signature to establish integrity and trust, validate the issuer and audience to make sure the token came from the expected authority and is intended for my API, and validate its lifetime so expired tokens aren't accepted."

17. What is TokenValidationParameters?

🔴 Very common .NET question

Interview-Ready Answer

TokenValidationParameters allows us to explicitly configure how a token should be validated.

For example:

options.TokenValidationParameters =
    new TokenValidationParameters
    {
        ValidateIssuer = true,
        ValidateAudience = true,
        ValidateIssuerSigningKey = true,
        ValidateLifetime = true
    };

Microsoft's JWT bearer documentation shows explicit configuration using TokenValidationParameters, including issuer, audience, and signing-key validation. Microsoft Learn

18. Explain the important TokenValidationParameters

ValidateIssuer

ValidateIssuer = true

Checks whether the token's issuer is trusted.

ValidateAudience

ValidateAudience = true

Checks whether the token is intended for this API.

ValidateIssuerSigningKey

ValidateIssuerSigningKey = true

Ensures the signing key is validated.

ValidateLifetime

ValidateLifetime = true

Checks whether the token is still within its valid lifetime.

19. What is ValidIssuer?

Interview-Ready Answer

It specifies the issuer that the API trusts.

Example:

ValidIssuer = "https://identity.example.com"

Then:

JWT iss
   ↓
https://identity.example.com
   ↓
Matches expected issuer
   ↓
Valid

20. What is ValidAudience?

Interview-Ready Answer

It specifies the audience that the API expects.

ValidAudience = "product-api";

If:

{
  "aud": "payment-api"
}

is presented to product-api, validation should fail if the configured audience doesn't match.

21. What is Authority in AddJwtBearer()?

🔴 Important

Interview-Ready Answer

Authority identifies the trusted identity provider/authorization server.

For example:

builder.Services
    .AddAuthentication(JwtBearerDefaults.AuthenticationScheme)
    .AddJwtBearer(options =>
    {
        options.Authority =
            "https://identity.example.com";

        options.Audience = "product-api";
    });

The authority can provide metadata used by the JWT bearer handler, including information needed to validate tokens.

Microsoft recommends using standard identity/OAuth/OIDC mechanisms rather than inventing a custom token-issuing flow. Microsoft Learn

22. Authority vs Audience

This is a very common interview question.

Authority

Who do I trust to issue tokens?

Audience

Which API is this token intended for?

Think:

Authority
    ↓
Identity Provider
    ↓
issues token
    ↓
Audience
    ↓
My API

23. What does AddJwtBearer() do?

Interview-Ready Answer

It registers/configures JWT bearer authentication.

Example:

builder.Services
    .AddAuthentication(
        JwtBearerDefaults.AuthenticationScheme)
    .AddJwtBearer(options =>
    {
        options.Authority =
            "https://identity.example.com";

        options.Audience =
            "product-api";
    });

The Microsoft.AspNetCore.Authentication.JwtBearer package provides the JWT bearer handler used to authenticate requests. Microsoft Learn

24. What is JwtBearerDefaults.AuthenticationScheme?

Interview-Ready Answer

It represents the standard authentication scheme name:

Bearer

So:

.AddAuthentication(
    JwtBearerDefaults.AuthenticationScheme)

essentially tells ASP.NET Core:

Use the JWT Bearer authentication scheme by default.

25. What happens internally when a request contains a JWT?

Suppose:

GET /api/products
Authorization: Bearer eyJ...

Flow

HTTP Request
     ↓
UseAuthentication()
     ↓
Bearer Authentication Scheme
     ↓
JwtBearerHandler
     ↓
Extract Bearer Token
     ↓
Validate Token
     ↓
Validate Signature
     ↓
Validate Issuer
     ↓
Validate Audience
     ↓
Validate Lifetime
     ↓
Create ClaimsPrincipal
     ↓
HttpContext.User
     ↓
UseAuthorization()
     ↓
[Authorize]
     ↓
Controller

This is the most important JWT flow to understand.

26. What happens if the JWT signature is invalid?

Interview-Ready Answer

Authentication fails.

For a protected API endpoint, the request will generally receive:

401 Unauthorized

because the API cannot trust the token.

Microsoft specifically lists an invalid signature as a reason for a 401 response. Microsoft Learn

27. What happens if the JWT audience is wrong?

Example:

{
  "aud": "payment-api"
}

But our API expects:

product-api

Result

Token validation fails:

Authentication failure
        ↓
401 Unauthorized

Microsoft specifically includes incorrect audience values among the conditions that result in a 401. Microsoft Learn

28. What happens if the JWT is expired?

Flow

JWT
 ↓
exp = yesterday
 ↓
Lifetime validation fails
 ↓
Authentication fails
 ↓
401 Unauthorized

The API should not accept an expired access token. Microsoft Learn

29. What happens if the JWT is valid but the user isn't an Admin?

This is different.

JWT
 ↓
Valid
 ↓
Authentication succeeds
 ↓
role = Employee
 ↓
Endpoint requires Admin
 ↓
Authorization fails
 ↓
403 Forbidden

Key distinction

Invalid token → 401
Valid token + insufficient permission → 403

Microsoft's current guidance makes this distinction explicitly. Microsoft Learn

30. How do you configure JWT authentication in ASP.NET Core?

A simplified example:

using Microsoft.AspNetCore.Authentication.JwtBearer;

var builder = WebApplication.CreateBuilder(args);

builder.Services
    .AddAuthentication(JwtBearerDefaults.AuthenticationScheme)
    .AddJwtBearer(options =>
    {
        options.Authority =
            "https://identity.example.com";

        options.Audience =
            "product-api";
    });

builder.Services.AddAuthorization();

builder.Services.AddControllers();

var app = builder.Build();

app.UseRouting();

app.UseAuthentication();

app.UseAuthorization();

app.MapControllers();

app.Run();

This follows the standard ASP.NET Core JWT bearer configuration model. Microsoft Learn

31. How would you configure explicit token validation?

For an interview, you should understand this pattern:

builder.Services
    .AddAuthentication(JwtBearerDefaults.AuthenticationScheme)
    .AddJwtBearer(options =>
    {
        options.TokenValidationParameters =
            new TokenValidationParameters
            {
                ValidateIssuer = true,
                ValidateAudience = true,
                ValidateIssuerSigningKey = true,
                ValidateLifetime = true,

                ValidIssuer =
                    "https://identity.example.com",

                ValidAudience =
                    "product-api"
            };
    });

The exact configuration depends on your token issuer. Microsoft recommends using the identity provider's standard metadata/default configuration when possible rather than unnecessarily overriding defaults. Microsoft Learn

32. What is MapInboundClaims?

Interview-Ready Answer

MapInboundClaims controls whether claims from an incoming token are mapped to different claim types by the JWT bearer handler.

Example:

options.MapInboundClaims = false;

This can be useful when you want to work with the token's claim names directly.

The current JwtBearerOptions documentation states that the default is true. Microsoft Learn

Interview Tip

You don't need to memorize the implementation details. Just understand:

It controls inbound claim mapping.

33. What is signing-key rotation?

🔴 Senior-level

Identity providers may periodically rotate their signing keys.

For example:

Old Key
   ↓
Token A

New Key
   ↓
Token B

The API needs access to the current trusted signing keys.

ASP.NET Core's JWT bearer options support metadata refresh, including automatic refresh when an issuer signing key isn't found. Microsoft Learn

Interview Answer

"In production, I wouldn't hard-code a single signing key if the identity provider publishes signing keys through standard metadata. The API should support key rotation so tokens signed with a newly rotated trusted key can continue to validate."

34. Why shouldn't we create our own JWT tokens in production?

🔴 Important security question

Interview-Ready Answer

"For production authentication, I prefer a standards-based identity provider using OAuth 2.0/OpenID Connect rather than implementing my own token issuance and authentication system."

Microsoft's current guidance explicitly recommends using established OAuth/OpenID Connect standards and warns against creating custom access-token flows for production. Microsoft Learn

Examples include identity platforms such as:

Microsoft Entra ID
Auth0
Okta
Keycloak

depending on the application's architecture.

35. Should the React application decode and trust an access token?

Interview-Ready Answer

No. The client should not treat decoding a token as proof that the token is valid or that the API will accept it.

The API is responsible for validating the access token.

Microsoft's current guidance goes further: access tokens are intended for the API/resource, and a UI application shouldn't open or interpret them as though they were intended for the UI. Microsoft Learn

36. Access Token vs ID Token

🔴 Very important

Access Token

Client
  ↓
Access Token
  ↓
API

Used to access protected APIs.

ID Token

Identity Provider
       ↓
ID Token
       ↓
Client

Used by the client to obtain information about the authenticated identity.

Critical Interview Point

An ID token should not be sent to an API as an access token.

Microsoft explicitly states that ID tokens should never be used to access APIs. Microsoft Learn

37. What is an access token's scope?

Interview-Ready Answer

A scope represents the permissions requested/granted for an access token.

Example:

Product.Read
Product.Write
Order.Read

The API can use scopes/claims as part of authorization decisions.

Conceptually:

Token
 ├── Product.Read
 └── Product.Write

Then:

GET /products
     ↓
Product.Read ✓

while an operation requiring a permission not present in the token would be denied.

38. What is delegated authorization?

Interview-Ready Answer

Delegated authorization means:

An application accesses a resource/API on behalf of a user, using the user's delegated permissions.

For example:

User
 ↓
React
 ↓
API A
 ↓
API B

API A may need a delegated access token to call API B on behalf of the user.

Microsoft's current JWT guidance distinguishes delegated user access tokens from application access tokens and recommends delegated tokens when a user is involved in downstream API access. Microsoft Learn

39. Application token vs delegated user token

Application access token

Represents:

Application → API

There isn't necessarily a user involved.

Delegated access token

Represents:

User
 ↓
Application
 ↓
API

The API can make decisions based on the user's delegated permissions.

40. What security practices should you follow with JWT?

🔴 Senior interview question

Interview-Ready Answer

I would focus on:

  1. Use HTTPS.
  1. Validate signature.
  1. Validate issuer.
  1. Validate audience.
  1. Validate expiration/lifetime.
  1. Use short-lived access tokens where appropriate.
  1. Protect refresh tokens carefully.
  1. Don't put sensitive information in readable JWT payloads.
  1. Don't accept tokens from untrusted issuers.
  1. Use standard OAuth/OIDC flows instead of custom authentication.
  1. Protect signing keys/secrets.
  1. Handle token revocation/rotation requirements appropriately.

Microsoft explicitly recommends full JWT validation and standards-based token issuance. Microsoft Learn

41. What if a JWT is stolen?

Interview-Ready Answer

A bearer access token can generally be used by whoever possesses it until it expires or is otherwise invalidated.

Therefore:

HTTPS
+
Short token lifetime
+
Secure token handling
+
Proper validation
+
Refresh-token protection

are important security controls.

For higher-security scenarios, sender-constrained tokens such as DPoP or mutual TLS can bind token usage to proof of possession rather than relying solely on possession of the bearer token. Microsoft documents these as options for sender-constrained access tokens. Microsoft Learn

42. What is RequireHttpsMetadata?

Interview-Ready Answer

RequireHttpsMetadata controls whether the JWT bearer handler requires HTTPS for the authority/metadata address.

The current ASP.NET Core documentation says its default is true and recommends disabling it only in development environments. Microsoft Learn

So I would not normally do this in production:

options.RequireHttpsMetadata = false;

43. What is SaveToken?

Interview-Ready Answer

SaveToken controls whether the bearer token is stored in AuthenticationProperties after successful authentication.

Example:

options.SaveToken = true;

But I wouldn't enable token storage automatically without a concrete requirement because access tokens are sensitive credentials.

The current JwtBearerOptions documentation describes SaveToken as controlling whether the bearer token is stored in authentication properties. Microsoft Learn

44. Can an API accept tokens from multiple issuers?

Interview-Ready Answer

Yes.

There are multiple approaches, including:

Separate authentication schemes

or:

AddPolicyScheme

to select an authentication scheme based on token information.

Microsoft documents multiple schemes as one approach for supporting multiple token issuers. Microsoft Learn

45. What is the difference between JWT and OAuth 2.0?

🔴 Very common conceptual question

Interview-Ready Answer

JWT is a token format. OAuth 2.0 is an authorization framework.

Think:

OAuth 2.0
   ↓
Defines authorization flows
   ↓
Can issue access tokens

JWT:

JWT
 ↓
One possible token format

So saying:

"JWT is an authentication protocol"

is inaccurate.

46. JWT vs OAuth 2.0 vs OpenID Connect

Interview-Ready Answer

A simple way to remember:

JWT
→ Token format

OAuth 2.0
→ Authorization framework

OpenID Connect
→ Authentication/identity layer built on OAuth 2.0

Interview Tip

If an interviewer asks:

"We use JWT, so are we using OAuth?"

Don't automatically say yes.

JWT and OAuth solve different problems.

47. What happens when [Authorize] is used?

Suppose:

[Authorize]
[HttpGet("products")]
public IActionResult GetProducts()
{
    return Ok();
}

Request flow:

Request
 ↓
Authentication
 ↓
JWT validated
 ↓
ClaimsPrincipal created
 ↓
Authorization
 ↓
[Authorize]
 ↓
Access granted
 ↓
Controller

If authentication fails:

401

If authenticated but authorization fails:

403

48. How would you explain JWT authentication in your project?

Interview-Ready Answer

"In a .NET Core Web API, I would configure JWT bearer authentication using AddAuthentication and AddJwtBearer. The client sends an access token in the Authorization header. The JWT bearer handler validates the token's signature, issuer, audience and lifetime. After successful validation, ASP.NET Core creates the ClaimsPrincipal and exposes it through HttpContext.User. Then authorization policies or roles determine whether the user can access a particular endpoint. This keeps authentication and authorization separate and allows us to secure our REST APIs."

This is a strong answer for your .NET Core + React + SQL Server interview profile.

🔥 JWT — Interview Priority

🔴 Must Master

  1. What is JWT?
  1. JWT structure
  1. Header
  1. Payload
  1. Signature
  1. Is JWT encrypted?

  1. iss

  1. Audience validation

🧠 60-Second JWT Answer

If the interviewer asks:

"Explain how JWT authentication works in ASP.NET Core."

Say:

"The client first obtains an access token from an identity provider. It then sends that token to the ASP.NET Core API using the Authorization header with the Bearer scheme. ASP.NET Core's JWT bearer handler extracts and validates the token. The important validations include the signature, issuer, audience and expiration. If validation succeeds, ASP.NET Core creates a ClaimsPrincipal and makes it available through HttpContext.User. The authorization middleware then evaluates roles, claims or policies for the endpoint. If the token is invalid or missing for a protected endpoint, we generally get 401, while a valid authenticated user without sufficient permissions gets 403." Microsoft Learn

Your mental model

                JWT AUTHENTICATION
                       │
                       ▼
              Authorization Header
              Bearer <access-token>
                       │
                       ▼
              JwtBearerHandler
                       │
              ┌────────┴────────┐
              ▼                 ▼
        Token Validation      Invalid
              │                 │
      ┌───────┼────────┐        ▼
      ▼       ▼        ▼       401
 Signature Issuer  Audience
              │
          Expiration
              │
              ▼
       ClaimsPrincipal
              │
              ▼
       HttpContext.User
              │
              ▼
        Authorization
              │
       ┌──────┴──────┐
       ▼             ▼
     Allowed       Denied
       │             │
       ▼             ▼
 Controller          403

Microsoft Learn — Configure JWT bearer authentication in ASP.NET Core

15. Authorization in ASP.NET Core

This is very high priority for interviews because it naturally follows JWT Authentication. In ASP.NET Core, authorization determines what an authenticated user is allowed to do. It is separate from authentication and can be implemented using roles, claims, policies, and resource-based authorization. Microsoft Learn

🔴 Priority

Must Master

  1. Authentication vs Authorization
  1. [Authorize]
  1. [AllowAnonymous]
  1. Roles
  1. Claims
  1. Role-based vs Claims-based authorization
  1. Policy-based authorization
  1. AddAuthorization / AddAuthorizationBuilder
  1. RequireRole
  1. RequireClaim
  1. Authorization requirements
  1. Authorization handlers
  1. 401 vs 403
  1. Global authorization / fallback policy

Senior-level

15. IAuthorizationService

16. Resource-based authorization

17. Custom authorization handlers

18. context.Succeed() / context.Fail()

19. Multiple requirements/policies

20. Permission-based authorization design

1. What is Authorization?

Interview Question

What is authorization in ASP.NET Core?

Interview-Ready Answer

Authorization determines whether an authenticated user has permission to access a particular resource or perform a particular operation.

For example:

User → Can view products?       YES
User → Can create products?     YES
User → Can delete products?     NO

Authentication answers:

Who are you?

Authorization answers:

What are you allowed to do?

ASP.NET Core provides role-based and policy-based authorization models. Microsoft Learn

2. Authentication vs Authorization

AuthenticationAuthorization
Identifies the userDetermines permissions
"Who are you?""What can you do?"
Happens firstDepends on authenticated identity
JWT/cookie/etc.Roles/claims/policies
Creates ClaimsPrincipalEvaluates that user's permissions

Example

React
  ↓
Login
  ↓
Identity Provider
  ↓
JWT Access Token
  ↓
ASP.NET Core
  ↓
Authentication
  ↓
Who is this user?
  ↓
Authorization
  ↓
Can this user access this endpoint?

3. What is [Authorize]?

[Authorize] protects a controller or action.

[Authorize]
[ApiController]
[Route("api/products")]
public class ProductsController : ControllerBase
{
    [HttpGet]
    public IActionResult GetProducts()
    {
        return Ok();
    }
}

The endpoint requires an authenticated user.

Important

Just configuring authentication does not automatically protect every endpoint. Authorization must be applied through [Authorize], policies, endpoint configuration, or a global/fallback policy. Microsoft Learn

4. What is [AllowAnonymous]?

It allows an endpoint to be accessed without authentication even when authorization is applied more broadly.

[AllowAnonymous]
[HttpPost("login")]
public IActionResult Login(LoginRequest request)
{
    // Authenticate user
    return Ok();
}

Typical examples:

POST /api/auth/login       → Anonymous
POST /api/auth/register   → Anonymous

GET /api/products         → Authenticated
POST /api/products         → Authenticated
DELETE /api/products/10   → Authorized Admin

5. What is Role-Based Authorization?

Roles represent groups of users with predefined permissions.

Example:

Admin
Manager
Employee
Customer

You can protect an endpoint like this:

[Authorize(Roles = "Admin")]
[HttpDelete("{id}")]
public IActionResult DeleteProduct(int id)
{
    return NoContent();
}

Only users belonging to the Admin role can access it.

ASP.NET Core exposes role membership through ClaimsPrincipal.IsInRole. Microsoft Learn

6. Multiple Roles

You can specify multiple roles:

[Authorize(Roles = "Admin,Manager")]

This means:

Admin OR Manager

But if you apply separate [Authorize] attributes:

[Authorize(Roles = "Admin")]
[Authorize(Roles = "Manager")]

both requirements must be satisfied:

Admin AND Manager

This distinction is a common interview question. Microsoft Learn

7. What are Claims?

A claim is a name-value pair associated with an identity.

Example JWT claims:

sub = 12345
email = saurabh@example.com
role = Admin
department = Finance
employeeId = E102

In ASP.NET Core:

User.Claims

can be used to inspect claims.

You can also access a specific claim:

var employeeId = User.FindFirst("employeeId")?.Value;

Microsoft describes claims as information about the subject that can then be evaluated during authorization. Microsoft Learn

8. Role vs Claim

This is important.

Role

Represents a broad category of permissions.

Role = Admin
Role = Manager
Role = Employee

Claim

Represents additional information about the user/application/device.

Department = Finance
EmployeeId = E102
Permission = Product.Delete
Region = India

Think:

Role
 ↓
Broad access category

Claim
 ↓
Specific information/attribute

9. Claims-Based Authorization

Suppose your application has:

Department = Finance

You could create a policy requiring that claim.

builder.Services.AddAuthorizationBuilder()
    .AddPolicy("FinanceOnly", policy =>
        policy.RequireClaim("Department", "Finance"));

Then:

[Authorize(Policy = "FinanceOnly")]
[HttpGet("salary")]
public IActionResult GetSalary()
{
    return Ok();
}

The user must have:

Department = Finance

ASP.NET Core supports claim requirements through authorization policies. Microsoft Learn

10. What is Policy-Based Authorization?

🔴 Very important

A policy is a named collection of authorization requirements.

For example:

Policy: CanManageProducts

Requirements:
    Role = Admin
    Permission = Product.Manage

You define it:

builder.Services.AddAuthorizationBuilder()
    .AddPolicy("CanManageProducts", policy =>
    {
        policy.RequireRole("Admin");
        policy.RequireClaim("Permission", "Product.Manage");
    });

Then:

[Authorize(Policy = "CanManageProducts")]
[HttpPost]
public IActionResult CreateProduct(ProductDto product)
{
    return Ok();
}

A policy can contain one or more requirements, which are evaluated by authorization handlers. Microsoft Learn

11. Why use Policies instead of Roles?

Suppose you have:

Admin
Manager
SeniorManager
ProductOwner

If you put role checks everywhere:

[Authorize(Roles = "Admin,Manager,SeniorManager")]

your authorization logic can become difficult to maintain.

Instead:

CanManageProducts
CanDeleteProducts
CanApproveOrders
CanViewReports

Then your application checks permissions/policies, rather than spreading role names throughout controllers.

Example:

[Authorize(Policy = "CanDeleteProducts")]

This makes authorization rules more centralized and reusable.

12. What is an Authorization Requirement?

A requirement represents a rule that must be satisfied.

public class MinimumAgeRequirement : IAuthorizationRequirement
{
    public int MinimumAge { get; }

    public MinimumAgeRequirement(int minimumAge)
    {
        MinimumAge = minimumAge;
    }
}

The requirement describes the rule.

The handler determines whether the rule is satisfied.

Requirement
     ↓
"What rule needs to be satisfied?"

Handler
     ↓
"Is this rule satisfied for this user?"

Microsoft's authorization model uses IAuthorizationRequirement and IAuthorizationHandler as the core building blocks for policy-based authorization. Microsoft Learn

13. What is an Authorization Handler?

An authorization handler evaluates a requirement.

Example:

public class MinimumAgeHandler
    : AuthorizationHandler<MinimumAgeRequirement>
{
    protected override Task HandleRequirementAsync(
        AuthorizationHandlerContext context,
        MinimumAgeRequirement requirement)
    {
        var ageClaim = context.User.FindFirst("Age");

        if (ageClaim != null &&
            int.Parse(ageClaim.Value) >= requirement.MinimumAge)
        {
            context.Succeed(requirement);
        }

        return Task.CompletedTask;
    }
}

The important method is:

context.Succeed(requirement);

It tells ASP.NET Core:

This requirement has been satisfied.

A handler can also explicitly call:

context.Fail();

to indicate failure. Microsoft Learn

14. Requirement vs Handler

This is a common Senior interview question.

Requirement

Defines what needs to be true.

MinimumAge >= 18

Handler

Defines how to check it.

Read Age claim
↓
Convert to integer
↓
Check >= 18
↓
Succeed

So:

Policy
   ↓
Requirement
   ↓
Handler
   ↓
Authorization decision

15. How do you register a custom handler?

builder.Services.AddSingleton<
    IAuthorizationHandler,
    MinimumAgeHandler>();

ASP.NET Core supports registering authorization handlers with the dependency injection container. Microsoft Learn

16. What is IAuthorizationService?

IAuthorizationService allows you to perform authorization checks programmatically.

Example:

var result = await _authorizationService
    .AuthorizeAsync(
        User,
        document,
        "EditPolicy");

Then:

if (result.Succeeded)
{
    // User is authorized
}

This becomes particularly important for resource-based authorization. Microsoft Learn

17. What is Resource-Based Authorization?

🔴 Senior-level question

Sometimes authorization depends not only on the user but also on the specific resource.

Example:

Document #100
Owner = Saurabh

You might have this rule:

A user can edit a document only if they are the document owner.

You can't simply say:

[Authorize]

because the authorization decision depends on the actual document.

The flow becomes:

Request
 ↓
Load Document
 ↓
Who is the current user?
 ↓
Who owns the document?
 ↓
Authorization check
 ↓
Allow / Deny

ASP.NET Core provides IAuthorizationService for this kind of imperative/resource-based authorization. Microsoft Learn

18. Why can't [Authorize] alone handle resource ownership?

Consider:

PUT /api/documents/123

Before the authorization decision, you need to know:

Document 123
     ↓
OwnerId = 500

Then compare:

CurrentUserId = 500
OwnerId       = 500
                 ↓
               ALLOW

Because attribute authorization occurs before the action loads the resource, resource-based authorization generally requires an explicit authorization check after the resource is available. Microsoft Learn

19. 401 Unauthorized vs 403 Forbidden

🔴 Must Master

401

Authentication failed or the user isn't authenticated.

No token
Invalid token
Expired token
Invalid signature

Conceptually:

"Who are you?"
→ I can't authenticate you.

403

The user is authenticated but doesn't have sufficient permission.

JWT valid
User = Employee
Endpoint requires = Admin

Therefore:

401 → Authentication problem

403 → Authorization problem

20. Complete Authorization Flow

This connects everything you've studied so far:

React Application
       ↓
Authorization: Bearer <JWT>
       ↓
ASP.NET Core Middleware
       ↓
Authentication
       ↓
JWT validation
       ↓
ClaimsPrincipal created
       ↓
Authorization
       ↓
[Authorize]
       ↓
Role / Claim / Policy evaluation
       ↓
   ┌───────────────┐
   │               │
  Fail            Pass
   │               │
  403              ↓
               Controller
                   ↓
                Service
                   ↓
             EF Core/Dapper
                   ↓
              SQL Server

For an unauthenticated request to a protected endpoint, authentication can result in 401; an authenticated user who fails authorization generally gets 403.

21. Global Authorization

Instead of putting:

[Authorize]

on every controller, ASP.NET Core can be configured with a fallback policy requiring authenticated users by default. Microsoft specifically documents fallback policies for requiring authentication globally. Microsoft Learn

Conceptually:

Every endpoint
      ↓
Requires authentication
      ↓
Except explicitly anonymous endpoints

Then:

[AllowAnonymous]

can be used for endpoints such as:

/login
/register
/health

depending on the application's security design.

22. What is Permission-Based Authorization?

For a larger product, I would avoid building the entire authorization model around roles.

For example:

Roles

Admin
Manager
Employee

could map to:

Permissions

Product.Read
Product.Create
Product.Update
Product.Delete

Order.Read
Order.Approve
Order.Cancel

Report.Read
Report.Export

Then:

Admin
 ├── Product.*
 ├── Order.*
 └── Report.*

Manager
 ├── Product.Read
 ├── Product.Update
 ├── Order.Read
 └── Order.Approve

Employee
 ├── Product.Read
 └── Order.Read

This gives you more granular authorization.

A policy can then represent the required permission.

23. Real-World Scenario — Your .NET + React Application

Imagine your application has:

React
   ↓
ASP.NET Core Web API
   ↓
JWT Authentication
   ↓
Authorization
   ↓
Product Service
   ↓
EF Core
   ↓
SQL Server

Suppose the JWT contains:

{
  "sub": "123",
  "role": "Manager",
  "permission": "Product.Update"
}

Your API:

[Authorize(Policy = "CanUpdateProduct")]
[HttpPut("{id}")]
public async Task<IActionResult> UpdateProduct(
    int id,
    UpdateProductDto dto)
{
    await _productService.UpdateAsync(id, dto);

    return NoContent();
}

Policy:

builder.Services.AddAuthorizationBuilder()
    .AddPolicy("CanUpdateProduct", policy =>
    {
        policy.RequireClaim(
            "permission",
            "Product.Update");
    });

Flow:

React
 ↓
PUT /api/products/10
 ↓
Bearer JWT
 ↓
JWT validated
 ↓
ClaimsPrincipal
 ↓
CanUpdateProduct policy
 ↓
permission = Product.Update
 ↓
PASS
 ↓
Controller
 ↓
ProductService
 ↓
EF Core
 ↓
SQL Server

If the user doesn't have the permission:

JWT valid
      ↓
Authentication SUCCESS
      ↓
Authorization FAILED
      ↓
403 Forbidden

24. Common Interview Trap

Question:

If the JWT is valid, can the user access every API?

Answer:

No.

A valid JWT proves that the token is valid and identifies the authenticated principal. Authorization still determines whether that principal has permission to access a particular endpoint or resource.

Valid JWT
   ≠
Permission for everything

25. Common Interview Trap — Role vs Policy

Question:

When would you use roles versus policies?

Good answer:

I use roles when authorization is relatively simple and based on broad user categories such as Admin or Manager. For more complex or granular authorization, I prefer policies because policies can combine roles, claims, custom requirements and handlers. For resource-specific rules, such as allowing a user to edit only their own document, I would use resource-based authorization.

Before moving to the next topic, make sure you can answer these without looking at notes:

  1. What is authorization?
