  1. Explain the complete JWT → Authorization → Controller flow.

🎯 60-Second Interview Answer

If the interviewer asks:

"Explain authorization in ASP.NET Core."

Say:

Authorization determines whether an authenticated user has permission to access a resource or perform an operation. In ASP.NET Core, I can implement authorization using roles, claims, policies, and resource-based authorization. [Authorize] is used to protect controllers or actions. For simple scenarios, I can use roles such as Admin or Manager. For more complex authorization, I prefer policies that can combine claims, roles and custom requirements. A requirement defines the rule, and an authorization handler evaluates whether that rule is satisfied. For resource-based authorization, such as allowing a user to edit only their own document, I can use IAuthorizationService after loading the resource. If authentication fails, we typically get 401, whereas an authenticated user without sufficient permissions gets 403. Microsoft Learn

Your mental model

AUTHENTICATION
"WHO ARE YOU?"
       ↓
JWT
       ↓
ClaimsPrincipal
       ↓
AUTHORIZATION
"WHAT CAN YOU DO?"
       ↓
 ┌─────┬───────┬────────┐
Role  Claim   Policy  Resource
                 ↓
             Requirement
                 ↓
               Handler
                 ↓
             ALLOW / DENY

This is the core authorization model you should be comfortable explaining in a Senior .NET interview.

16. Exception Handling in ASP.NET Core

🔴 Very high priority for .NET interviews. You should be able to explain both how exceptions flow through the middleware pipeline and how you design centralized exception handling for production APIs.

Priority

Must Master

  1. Exception handling in ASP.NET Core
  1. try-catch
  1. Exception middleware
  1. UseExceptionHandler
  1. Developer exception page
  1. Global exception handling
  1. ProblemDetails
  1. HTTP status codes for exceptions
  1. Custom exception middleware
  1. Logging exceptions
  1. throw vs throw ex
  1. Custom exceptions

Senior-level

13. Exception handling middleware vs filters

14. IExceptionHandler

15. AddExceptionHandler

16. Exception-to-status-code mapping

17. Production vs development behavior

18. Correlation/request IDs

19. Avoiding sensitive information in error responses

20. Consistent API error contracts

1. What is Exception Handling?

Exception handling is the mechanism used to handle unexpected errors during application execution without crashing the entire request.

Example:

React
   ↓
ASP.NET Core API
   ↓
Controller
   ↓
Service
   ↓
Database
   ↓
Exception

Instead of exposing:

System.NullReferenceException...
SQL exception...
Stack trace...

the API should generally return a controlled response such as:

{
  "title": "An unexpected error occurred.",
  "status": 500
}

2. What happens when an exception occurs?

Suppose:

[HttpGet("{id}")]
public async Task<IActionResult> GetProduct(int id)
{
    var product = await _service.GetProductAsync(id);

    return Ok(product);
}

And the service throws:

throw new Exception("Database failure");

The exception travels back through the call stack.

If nothing handles it:

Request
  ↓
Middleware
  ↓
Controller
  ↓
Service
  ↓
Exception
  ↑
Controller
  ↑
Middleware

Ultimately ASP.NET Core can return a 500 response.

3. What is try-catch?

The most basic exception-handling mechanism is:

try
{
    var product = await service.GetProductAsync(id);
}
catch (Exception ex)
{
    // Handle exception
}

You can catch specific exceptions:

try
{
    // operation
}
catch (SqlException ex)
{
    // database-related problem
}
catch (Exception ex)
{
    // unexpected problem
}

Interview point

Don't blindly put try-catch around every controller action.

For example, this:

try
{
    return Ok(await _service.GetAsync(id));
}
catch (Exception ex)
{
    return StatusCode(500);
}

repeated across 50 controllers creates duplicated code.

That's why centralized exception handling is preferred.

4. What is Global Exception Handling?

Instead of handling exceptions separately in every controller:

Controller 1 → try/catch
Controller 2 → try/catch
Controller 3 → try/catch
Controller 4 → try/catch

we can handle them centrally:

                 ┌─ Controller
Request → Middleware ─ Service
                 └─ Repository
                    ↓
                 Exception
                    ↓
          Global Exception Handler
                    ↓
              HTTP Response

This gives us:

  • consistent error responses
  • centralized logging
  • less duplicate code
  • easier maintenance
  • better security

5. What is UseExceptionHandler()?

ASP.NET Core provides exception-handling middleware.

if (!app.Environment.IsDevelopment())
{
    app.UseExceptionHandler("/Error");
}

It catches exceptions that occur later in the pipeline and allows the application to produce an appropriate response.

For APIs, you can combine centralized exception handling with ProblemDetails.

6. Developer Exception Page

During development, ASP.NET Core provides detailed exception information using:

app.UseDeveloperExceptionPage();

Modern ASP.NET Core applications commonly configure this through the development environment.

The developer exception page can show:

Exception type
Message
Stack trace
Source code information

This is useful during development.

🔴 Important

Do not expose detailed exception information to production users.

Otherwise you may leak:

Database details
Internal class names
File paths
Stack traces
Connection information
Implementation details

7. Development vs Production

A common design is:

Development
    ↓
Detailed exception information

Production
    ↓
Generic error response
    ↓
Detailed error logged internally

Example:

Development:
500
"NullReferenceException at ProductService.cs:line 45"

Production:
500
"An unexpected error occurred."

The client doesn't need your internal stack trace.

8. What is ProblemDetails?

🔴 Must Master

ProblemDetails provides a standardized structure for describing HTTP API errors.

A response can look like:

{
  "type": "https://example.com/errors/product-not-found",
  "title": "Product not found",
  "status": 404,
  "detail": "The requested product does not exist.",
  "instance": "/api/products/100"
}

This gives your APIs a consistent error contract.

Instead of different controllers returning:

{ "error": "Not found" }

and:

{ "message": "Product doesn't exist" }

you can standardize the format.

9. Why use ProblemDetails?

Imagine your React application consumes 20 APIs.

Without a standard:

API 1 → error
API 2 → message
API 3 → errors
API 4 → validationErrors

The frontend needs special handling for every API.

With a consistent ProblemDetails contract:

title
status
detail
instance
errors

the frontend can handle errors consistently.

10. What is IExceptionHandler?

🔴 Senior-level ASP.NET Core question

Modern ASP.NET Core provides IExceptionHandler for implementing centralized exception handling.

Conceptually:

public class GlobalExceptionHandler : IExceptionHandler
{
    public async ValueTask<bool> TryHandleAsync(
        HttpContext httpContext,
        Exception exception,
        CancellationToken cancellationToken)
    {
        // log exception

        httpContext.Response.StatusCode = 500;

        await httpContext.Response.WriteAsJsonAsync(
            new
            {
                title = "An unexpected error occurred.",
                status = 500
            },
            cancellationToken);

        return true;
    }
}

Then register it:

builder.Services.AddExceptionHandler<GlobalExceptionHandler>();

and enable exception handling:

app.UseExceptionHandler();

This gives you a centralized and DI-friendly way to handle exceptions.

11. Why use IExceptionHandler?

Instead of creating custom exception middleware yourself:

Custom middleware
       ↓
catch Exception
       ↓
map response

you can use the built-in exception-handler abstraction.

Benefits include:

  • centralized handling
  • dependency injection
  • reusable handlers
  • cleaner Program.cs
  • consistent API responses
  • easier testing

12. How should exceptions map to HTTP status codes?

A practical mapping:

Exception / SituationHTTP Status
Validation failure400
Authentication failure401
Authorization failure403
Resource not found404
Conflict409
Unexpected server exception500

For example:

Product doesn't exist
        ↓
ProductNotFoundException
        ↓
404 Not Found

while:

Unexpected database/system failure
        ↓
500 Internal Server Error

13. Should every exception return 500?

No.

Some exceptions represent expected application conditions.

For example:

throw new ProductNotFoundException(id);

can be translated into:

404 Not Found

Whereas an unexpected exception should generally result in:

500 Internal Server Error

The important design principle is:

Don't expose internal exception details; translate known application exceptions into appropriate HTTP responses.

14. Custom Exceptions

You can create domain/application-specific exceptions.

public class ProductNotFoundException : Exception
{
    public ProductNotFoundException(int productId)
        : base($"Product {productId} was not found.")
    {
    }
}

Then your centralized handler can recognize it:

ProductNotFoundException
        ↓
404

Another example:

public class ProductConflictException : Exception
{
    public ProductConflictException(string message)
        : base(message)
    {
    }
}

could map to:

409 Conflict

15. Exception Middleware vs Exception Handler

This is an important Senior-level distinction.

Custom Exception Middleware

You implement the middleware yourself:

Request
 ↓
try
{
    await _next(context);
}
catch(Exception ex)
{
    // handle
}

Example:

public async Task InvokeAsync(HttpContext context)
{
    try
    {
        await _next(context);
    }
    catch (Exception ex)
    {
        // log
        // create response
    }
}

IExceptionHandler

ASP.NET Core provides a built-in abstraction:

Exception
   ↓
IExceptionHandler
   ↓
Response

For a new ASP.NET Core application, the built-in exception handling infrastructure is generally preferable unless you have a specific reason to implement custom middleware.

16. Where should Exception Handling Middleware be placed?

🔴 Very important

Exception handling should be early in the middleware pipeline so it can catch exceptions thrown by later middleware and endpoints.

Conceptually:

app.UseExceptionHandler();

app.UseHttpsRedirection();

app.UseAuthentication();

app.UseAuthorization();

app.MapControllers();

Think:

Exception Handler
       ↓
Other Middleware
       ↓
Authentication
       ↓
Authorization
       ↓
Controller
       ↓
Service
       ↓
Exception
       ↑
Exception Handler catches it

17. Why should exception handling be early?

Suppose:

Exception Handler
      ↓
Authentication
      ↓
Authorization
      ↓
Controller
      ↓
Service
      ↓
Exception

The exception travels back up until the exception handler catches it.

If your exception handler is placed after the component that throws the exception, it may not be able to handle that exception.

This is the same middleware ordering principle you studied earlier.

18. throw vs throw ex

🔴 Common C# interview question

Consider:

catch (Exception ex)
{
    throw;
}

versus:

catch (Exception ex)
{
    throw ex;
}

Prefer:

throw;

because it preserves the original stack trace.

throw ex; resets the stack-trace origin to the current throw location, making debugging harder.

Interview answer

When rethrowing the current exception, I use throw rather than throw ex because throw preserves the original stack trace.

19. Should we catch Exception everywhere?

Generally, no.

Avoid:

try
{
    // everything
}
catch (Exception)
{
    return null;
}

This can hide bugs.

Instead:

Known/expected exception
        ↓
Handle intentionally

Unexpected exception
        ↓
Centralized handler
        ↓
Log + generic response

20. Exception Logging

When an unexpected exception occurs, log it internally.

Example:

_logger.LogError(
    exception,
    "Error while processing product {ProductId}",
    productId);

The log can contain useful diagnostic information:

Timestamp
Request ID
User ID
Endpoint
Exception
Stack trace
Product ID

But don't put sensitive internal details into the API response.

21. Exception Handling + Logging

A production flow should look like:

Request
   ↓
Controller
   ↓
Service
   ↓
Exception
   ↓
Global Exception Handler
   ├── Log exception
   ├── Determine status code
   ├── Create ProblemDetails
   └── Return response

Example response:

{
  "title": "An unexpected error occurred.",
  "status": 500
}

Internal logs:

ERROR
RequestId: abc123
Endpoint: GET /api/products/10
Exception: SqlException
StackTrace: ...

22. What about Validation Errors?

Validation failures are usually not unexpected exceptions.

For example:

{
  "name": "",
  "price": -10
}

should normally be handled through model validation and return:

400 Bad Request

rather than:

throw Exception

This distinction is important:

Invalid user input
       ↓
Validation
       ↓
400

Unexpected application failure
       ↓
Exception handler
       ↓
500

23. Exception Handling Architecture

For your typical stack:

React
  ↓
ASP.NET Core API
  ↓
Exception Handler Middleware
  ↓
Authentication
  ↓
Authorization
  ↓
Controller
  ↓
Service
  ↓
EF Core / Dapper
  ↓
SQL Server

Example:

SQL Server unavailable
        ↓
EF Core throws
        ↓
Service doesn't swallow it
        ↓
Controller doesn't duplicate try/catch
        ↓
Global exception handler
        ↓
Log detailed exception
        ↓
Return generic ProblemDetails
        ↓
HTTP 500

That's a strong production architecture answer.

You should be able to answer these:

  1. What happens when an exception occurs in a controller?
  1. Why use global exception handling?

  1. What is the Developer Exception Page?

  1. What is ProblemDetails?
  1. Why use ProblemDetails for APIs?
  1. What is IExceptionHandler?

  1. How do validation errors differ from exceptions?

🎯 60-Second Interview Answer

In ASP.NET Core, I prefer centralized exception handling rather than putting try-catch blocks in every controller. I can use the built-in exception handling middleware and IExceptionHandler to catch unhandled exceptions centrally. The handler logs the detailed exception internally, maps known application exceptions such as a resource-not-found exception to appropriate status codes like 404, and returns a consistent ProblemDetails response. For unexpected exceptions, I generally return a generic 500 response without exposing stack traces or internal implementation details. I also make sure exception handling is placed early in the middleware pipeline so it can catch exceptions from downstream middleware and controllers.

Mental model

Exception Handling
       │
       ├── Development → Detailed diagnostics
       │
       └── Production
              ↓
       Global Exception Handler
              ↓
        Log detailed error
              ↓
       Map known exception
              ↓
          ProblemDetails
              ↓
        HTTP status code

17. Logging in ASP.NET Core

🔴 Very high priority for .NET interviews. Logging is closely connected with the exception-handling topic we just covered, especially in production systems.

Priority

Must Master

  1. ILogger
  1. ILogger<T>
  1. Log levels
  1. LogInformation, LogWarning, LogError, etc.
  1. Structured logging
  1. Logging providers
  1. appsettings.json logging configuration
  1. Logging in controllers/services
  1. Exception logging
  1. Logging best practices

Senior-level

11. Logging scopes

12. Correlation/request IDs

13. Centralized logging

14. Sensitive-data protection

15. Performance considerations

16. Application Insights / external logging systems

17. Distributed tracing vs logging

18. Production logging strategy

1. What is Logging?

Logging means recording information about what is happening inside an application.

For example:

Application started
User authenticated
Product requested
Database operation completed
Unexpected exception occurred

In a production application, logs help us:

  • troubleshoot failures
  • understand application behavior
  • monitor problems
  • investigate incidents
  • diagnose performance issues
  • trace requests

2. What is ILogger?

🔴 Must know

ILogger is the main logging abstraction provided by .NET.

Example:

public class ProductService
{
    private readonly ILogger<ProductService> _logger;

    public ProductService(ILogger<ProductService> logger)
    {
        _logger = logger;
    }
}

Then:

_logger.LogInformation("Getting product {ProductId}", productId);

The important idea is:

Application Code
      ↓
    ILogger
      ↓
 Logging Provider
      ↓
Console / File / Cloud / Centralized system

Your application doesn't need to directly depend on a specific logging destination.

3. Why use ILogger<T>?

Instead of:

ILogger

we commonly inject:

ILogger<ProductService>

The generic type identifies the category of the logger.

public class ProductService
{
    private readonly ILogger<ProductService> _logger;
}

The category is typically based on the fully qualified class name.

This makes it easier to identify where a log originated.

4. What are Log Levels?

🔴 Very common interview question

.NET provides standard log levels:

Trace
Debug
Information
Warning
Error
Critical
None

Think of them from least to most severe:

Trace
  ↓
Debug
  ↓
Information
  ↓
Warning
  ↓
Error
  ↓
Critical

5. Trace

Used for extremely detailed diagnostic information.

_logger.LogTrace(
    "Entering GetProduct method with ID {ProductId}",
    productId);

Useful when debugging very detailed execution flows.

Usually you don't enable large amounts of Trace logging in production.

6. Debug

Used for development/debugging information.

_logger.LogDebug(
    "Fetching product from database: {ProductId}",
    productId);

Example:

Cache miss
Calling service
Query execution started

7. Information

🔴 Common application-level logging.

_logger.LogInformation(
    "Product {ProductId} retrieved successfully",
    productId);

Examples:

Application started
Order created
Payment completed
User logged in

8. Warning

Used when something unusual happened but the application can continue.

_logger.LogWarning(
    "Product {ProductId} was not found",
    productId);

Other examples:

Cache unavailable
Retry attempt 2
Configuration missing optional value
API response slower than expected

A warning does not necessarily mean the application failed.

9. Error

Used when an operation failed.

_logger.LogError(
    exception,
    "Failed to retrieve product {ProductId}",
    productId);

This is particularly important for exceptions.

Notice that we pass the exception separately:

_logger.LogError(exception, "...");

This allows the logging system to capture exception information and stack trace.

10. Critical

Used for severe failures that may require immediate attention.

_logger.LogCritical(
    exception,
    "Database connection is unavailable");

Examples:

Application cannot start
Critical infrastructure failure
Major dependency unavailable

11. Log Level Cheat Sheet

LevelTypical Use
TraceVery detailed diagnostics
DebugDevelopment/debugging
InformationNormal application events
WarningUnexpected but recoverable
ErrorOperation failed
CriticalSevere application failure

Interview shortcut

Information = normal event, Warning = unusual situation, Error = operation failed, Critical = severe failure.

12. How do you log an exception?

Suppose:

try
{
    await _repository.GetProductAsync(id);
}
catch (Exception ex)
{
    _logger.LogError(
        ex,
        "Error while retrieving product {ProductId}",
        id);

    throw;
}

The important part is:

_logger.LogError(ex, "...");

rather than only:

_logger.LogError(ex.Message);

Because the exception object contains valuable diagnostic information such as its stack trace.

13. What is Structured Logging?

🔴 Very important for Senior interviews

Instead of:

_logger.LogInformation(
    $"Product {productId} retrieved");

prefer:

_logger.LogInformation(
    "Product {ProductId} retrieved",
    productId);

Here:

{ProductId}

is a structured property.

The logging system can store:

Message:
Product 100 retrieved

ProductId:
100

rather than treating everything as one unstructured string.

14. Why is Structured Logging Better?

Imagine you have millions of logs.

With structured data, a centralized logging system can query:

ProductId = 100

or:

OrderId = 5001
UserId = 123

This is much easier than searching arbitrary text.

For example:

_logger.LogInformation(
    "Order {OrderId} created by user {UserId}",
    orderId,
    userId);

The logging system can understand:

OrderId = 5001
UserId = 123

15. Structured Logging vs String Interpolation

Avoid:

_logger.LogInformation(
    $"User {userId} created order {orderId}");

Prefer:

_logger.LogInformation(
    "User {UserId} created order {OrderId}",
    userId,
    orderId);

The second approach preserves structured properties.

Interview answer

I prefer structured logging because important values are captured as named properties, which makes logs easier to search, filter, aggregate and analyze in centralized logging systems.

16. What are Logging Providers?

A logging provider determines where logs are written.

Examples include:

Console
Debug
EventSource
EventLog
Azure Application Insights
Third-party logging systems

Conceptually:

ILogger
   ↓
Logging Provider
   ↓
Destination

Your application code can continue using:

ILogger

without being tightly coupled to a specific destination.

17. Console Logging

During development, you might see:

info: ProductService[0]
      Product 100 retrieved

ASP.NET Core commonly has console logging configured by default in templates.

For local development:

Application
    ↓
ILogger
    ↓
Console

18. How is Logging Configured?

Logging configuration can be placed in:

appsettings.json

Example:

{
  "Logging": {
    "LogLevel": {
      "Default": "Information",
      "Microsoft.AspNetCore": "Warning"
    }
  }
}

This means:

Application logs → Information+
ASP.NET Core logs → Warning+

You can have environment-specific configuration:

appsettings.json
appsettings.Development.json
appsettings.Production.json

19. Why configure different levels for different categories?

ASP.NET Core itself can generate a large number of logs.

You may want:

Your application → Information
Framework logs   → Warning

instead of producing huge amounts of framework diagnostic data.

For example:

{
  "Logging": {
    "LogLevel": {
      "Default": "Information",
      "Microsoft": "Warning",
      "Microsoft.AspNetCore": "Warning"
    }
  }
}

This helps control log volume.

20. How do you inject ILogger into a controller?

[ApiController]
[Route("api/products")]
public class ProductsController : ControllerBase
{
    private readonly ILogger<ProductsController> _logger;

    public ProductsController(
        ILogger<ProductsController> logger)
    {
        _logger = logger;
    }

    [HttpGet("{id}")]
    public async Task<IActionResult> GetProduct(int id)
    {
        _logger.LogInformation(
            "Getting product {ProductId}",
            id);

        return Ok();
    }
}

Because ILogger<T> is available through ASP.NET Core's dependency injection system, you can inject it directly.

21. Should logging be in Controller or Service?

Both can log, but logging should have a purpose.

For example:

Controller

Request received
Endpoint invoked

Service

Business operation
Important business decision
External service call

Repository

Important data-access diagnostics

Avoid logging the same event at every layer.

Otherwise:

Controller → log
Service → log
Repository → log
Database → log

can produce noisy duplicate logs.

22. What is a Logging Scope?

🔴 Senior-level

A logging scope allows you to attach contextual information to multiple log messages.

Example:

using (_logger.BeginScope(
    new Dictionary<string, object>
    {
        ["OrderId"] = orderId
    }))
{
    _logger.LogInformation("Creating order");

    _logger.LogInformation("Validating order");

    _logger.LogInformation("Saving order");
}

Conceptually:

Scope:
OrderId = 5001

    ↓
Creating order
OrderId = 5001

    ↓
Validating order
OrderId = 5001

    ↓
Saving order
OrderId = 5001

This is useful for correlating related logs.

23. What is a Correlation ID?

🔴 Very important for distributed systems

Suppose your request travels through:

React
 ↓
API Gateway
 ↓
Order API
 ↓
Payment Service
 ↓
Notification Service

If something fails, you need to determine:

Which request caused these logs?

A correlation/request ID can be propagated:

CorrelationId = ABC123

Then every service logs:

ABC123

You can search centralized logs for:

ABC123

and reconstruct the request flow.

24. Logging vs Distributed Tracing

Senior interviewers may ask this.

Logging

Records events:

Order created
Payment failed
Database query failed

Distributed tracing

Tracks a request across services:

Request
 ↓
API
 ↓
Payment Service
 ↓
Database

with timing information.

Think:

Logging
"What happened?"

Tracing
"How did this request travel through the system and how long did each step take?"

Modern observability often combines:

Logs
+
Metrics
+
Traces

25. What Should You Never Log?

🔴 Security question

Avoid logging sensitive information such as:

Passwords
Access tokens
Refresh tokens
API keys
Connection strings
Credit-card information
Sensitive personal data

For example, don't do:

_logger.LogInformation(
    "Authorization header: {Token}",
    token);

Logging is useful, but logs themselves must be treated as sensitive production data.

26. Logging and Exception Handling Together

This is the architecture you should explain in interviews:

Request
   ↓
ASP.NET Core Middleware
   ↓
Controller
   ↓
Service
   ↓
Exception
   ↓
Global Exception Handler
   ↓
ILogger.LogError()
   ↓
Centralized Logging System
   ↓
ProblemDetails
   ↓
Client

Example:

_logger.LogError(
    exception,
    "Failed to process order {OrderId}",
    orderId);

Then return:

{
  "title": "An unexpected error occurred.",
  "status": 500
}

The client receives a safe response.

The operations team receives detailed diagnostic information in logs.

27. What is the difference between Logging and Exception Handling?

🔴 Common interview question.

Exception Handling

Determines:

What should the application do when an exception occurs?

For example:

Exception
 ↓
Catch
 ↓
Return 500

Logging

Determines:

What information should we record about application behavior or failures?
Exception
 ↓
Log details

They often work together, but they solve different problems.

28. Production Logging Strategy

For your .NET full-stack application, a practical design could be:

React
   ↓
ASP.NET Core API
   ↓
ILogger
   ↓
Structured Logs
   ↓
Centralized Logging
   ↓
Monitoring / Alerting

For an exception:

Exception
   ↓
IExceptionHandler
   ├── LogError(exception)
   ├── Correlation ID
   ├── Map status code
   └── ProblemDetails

This gives:

Client
 ↓
Safe API error

Operations Team
 ↓
Detailed logs

29. Real-World Scenario

Imagine your application processes:

10,000+ transactions/day

A customer reports:

"My order failed."

You have a correlation ID:

RequestId = 7f91abc

Your logs might show:

INFO  Order request received
      OrderId=5001
      RequestId=7f91abc

INFO  Payment service called
      OrderId=5001
      RequestId=7f91abc

ERROR Payment service failed
      OrderId=5001
      RequestId=7f91abc
      Exception=TimeoutException

Now you can trace the failure without reproducing the problem locally.

That's the practical value of production logging.

Make sure you can answer these:

  1. What is ILogger?

🎯 60-Second Interview Answer

ASP.NET Core provides the ILogger abstraction for application logging. I normally inject ILogger<T> into controllers or services and use appropriate log levels such as Information, Warning, Error and Critical. For production applications, I prefer structured logging, where values such as OrderId, UserId or RequestId are captured as named properties rather than concatenated into strings. I also use centralized exception handling with ILogger.LogError() to record detailed exceptions while returning safe error responses to clients. In distributed systems, correlation IDs and logging scopes help connect related log entries across a request. I also make sure sensitive information such as passwords, tokens and API keys is never written to logs.

Mental Model

Application
    ↓
ILogger<T>
    ↓
Structured Logging
    ↓
Log Levels
    ↓
Logging Provider
    ↓
Centralized Logging
    ↓
Search / Monitoring / Alerting

18. Async/Await in ASP.NET Core

🔴 Extremely important for .NET interviews. Since you already have async/await experience, interviewers may go beyond syntax and ask about thread blocking, I/O vs CPU work, Task, Task<T>, Task.WhenAll, cancellation, Task.Run, and common async mistakes.

Microsoft recommends asynchronous APIs for I/O-bound work such as database and network operations because they avoid blocking Thread Pool threads and improve ASP.NET Core scalability. Microsoft Learn

🔴 Priority

Must Master

  1. What is asynchronous programming?
  1. async and await
  1. Task vs Task<T>
  1. How await works
  1. Synchronous vs asynchronous execution
  1. I/O-bound vs CPU-bound
  1. Why async is important in ASP.NET Core
  1. Task.Run
  1. Task.WhenAll
  1. Task.WhenAny
  1. CancellationToken
  1. async void
  1. .Result / .Wait() problems
  1. Async all the way
  1. Exception handling with async

Senior-level

  1. Thread Pool and async
  1. SynchronizationContext
  1. ConfigureAwait(false)
  1. Parallel async operations
  1. Cancellation propagation
  1. Request cancellation in ASP.NET Core
  1. Fire-and-forget problems
  1. Async database operations
  1. Async HttpClient
  1. Async performance/scalability

1. What is Asynchronous Programming?

Asynchronous programming allows your application to start an operation and not block the current thread while waiting for the operation to complete.

For example:

API
 ↓
SQL Server query
 ↓
Waiting...

With synchronous code:

Thread
 ↓
SQL query
 ↓
BLOCKED waiting for SQL
 ↓
Result

With asynchronous code:

Thread
 ↓
Start SQL query
 ↓
Thread is available for other work
 ↓
SQL completes
 ↓
Continue processing

That's especially valuable in ASP.NET Core because the server can handle many concurrent requests without tying up a Thread Pool thread while I/O is pending. Microsoft Learn

2. What is async?

The async keyword tells C# that a method can use await and normally returns a task representing its asynchronous operation.

Example:

public async Task<Product> GetProductAsync(int id)
{
    var product = await _dbContext.Products.FindAsync(id);

    return product;
}

Here:

async
 ↓
Method can use await
 ↓
Returns Task / Task<T>

But remember:

async itself does not create a new thread.

Microsoft explicitly notes that async/await doesn't automatically create additional threads. Microsoft Learn

3. What is await?

await asynchronously waits for a task to complete.

var product = await GetProductAsync(id);

Conceptually:

Call GetProductAsync()
        ↓
Task returned
        ↓
Is it complete?
   ↙          ↘
 Yes           No
 ↓             ↓
Continue       Yield control
               ↓
          Other work can run
               ↓
          Task completes
               ↓
          Continue method

The important point:

await does not block the current thread while an incomplete asynchronous operation is running. Microsoft Learn

4. What is Task?

Task represents an asynchronous operation that doesn't return a value.

public async Task SaveProductAsync(Product product)
{
    await _dbContext.SaveChangesAsync();
}

Think:

Task
 ↓
Operation will complete
 ↓
No result value

Example:

await SaveProductAsync(product);

5. What is Task<T>?

Task<T> represents an asynchronous operation that eventually produces a value.

public async Task<Product> GetProductAsync(int id)
{
    return await _dbContext.Products
        .FindAsync(id);
}

Think:

Task<T>
   ↓
Async operation
   ↓
Result of type T

For example:

Task<Product>
Task<List<Product>>
Task<int>
Task<string>

6. Task vs Task<T>

TypeMeaning
TaskAsync operation without result
Task<T>Async operation returning T

Example:

Task SaveAsync();

versus:

Task<Product> GetProductAsync();

7. Why is async important in ASP.NET Core?

Imagine your API receives:

1,000 requests

Each request performs a database call.

With synchronous blocking:

Request
 ↓
Thread
 ↓
DB call
 ↓
Thread BLOCKED

With asynchronous database access:

Request
 ↓
Thread
 ↓
Start DB operation
 ↓
Thread released
 ↓
DB completes
 ↓
Continue

This improves the server's ability to handle concurrent I/O-bound requests.

Microsoft specifically recommends making controller actions and the entire call chain asynchronous when asynchronous APIs are available. Microsoft Learn

8. I/O-Bound vs CPU-Bound

🔴 Very important

I/O-bound

The application is waiting for an external resource.

Examples:

SQL Server
REST API
File system
Network
Cloud service

Example:

var product = await _dbContext.Products
    .FirstOrDefaultAsync(x => x.Id == id);

Use asynchronous APIs.

CPU-bound

The processor itself is doing expensive computation.

Examples:

Large image processing
Complex mathematical calculation
Large data transformation
Machine-learning computation

For CPU-bound work, Task.Run may be appropriate when you intentionally want to move the computation to a Thread Pool thread. Microsoft Learn

9. Should you use Task.Run for database calls?

🔴 Common interview trap

Generally:

No.

Don't do:

var result = await Task.Run(() =>
    _repository.GetProducts());

if GetProducts() is a synchronous database call.

You're simply moving blocking work to another Thread Pool thread.

Instead, use the database provider's asynchronous API:

var result = await _repository.GetProductsAsync();

ASP.NET Core guidance specifically recommends not using Task.Run to make synchronous APIs artificially asynchronous. Microsoft Learn

10. When should you use Task.Run?

For CPU-bound work where moving computation to a Thread Pool thread is appropriate.

Example:

var result = await Task.Run(() =>
{
    return PerformExpensiveCalculation();
});

But don't automatically use it just because a method is asynchronous.

Remember:

I/O-bound
 → async API + await

CPU-bound
 → potentially Task.Run
``` :chatgpt-content-reference{index="7"}


---

# 11. What happens internally when you use `await`?

Consider:

```csharp
public async Task<Product> GetProductAsync(int id)
{
    var product = await _repository.GetProductAsync(id);

    return product;
}

Conceptually:

Method starts
    ↓
Call database
    ↓
Task returned
    ↓
await
    ↓
If incomplete:
    method yields
    ↓
caller gets control
    ↓
database completes
    ↓
continuation resumes
    ↓
return Product

The compiler transforms async methods into a state machine that tracks where execution should continue. The important interview-level point is that await allows the method to suspend without synchronously blocking the thread. Microsoft Learn

12. Does async create a new thread?

❌ No.

This is one of the most common interview questions.

Wrong:

async creates a new thread.

Correct:

async/await provides a non-blocking programming model. It doesn't inherently create a new thread. For I/O-bound operations, the thread can return to the Thread Pool while the I/O operation is pending. Microsoft Learn

13. What is Task.WhenAll()?

🔴 Must Master

Suppose you have three independent API calls:

var products = await GetProductsAsync();
var orders = await GetOrdersAsync();
var customers = await GetCustomersAsync();

This executes them sequentially.

If they're independent, you can start them together:

var productsTask = GetProductsAsync();
var ordersTask = GetOrdersAsync();
var customersTask = GetCustomersAsync();

await Task.WhenAll(
    productsTask,
    ordersTask,
    customersTask);

Then:

var products = await productsTask;
var orders = await ordersTask;
var customers = await customersTask;

Conceptually:

Sequential:

A → B → C


WhenAll:

A ────────┐
B ────────┼──→ All complete
C ────────┘

Task.WhenAll is useful when operations are independent and can safely run concurrently. Microsoft documents it as the asynchronous equivalent of waiting for all operations to complete. Microsoft Learn

14. Task.WhenAll() Example in Your Stack

Suppose a dashboard needs:

Product API
Order API
Notification API

Instead of:

var products = await _productService.GetAsync();
var orders = await _orderService.GetAsync();
var notifications = await _notificationService.GetAsync();

you can do:

var productsTask = _productService.GetAsync();
var ordersTask = _orderService.GetAsync();
var notificationsTask = _notificationService.GetAsync();

await Task.WhenAll(
    productsTask,
    ordersTask,
    notificationsTask);

var products = await productsTask;
var orders = await ordersTask;
var notifications = await notificationsTask;

This can reduce total waiting time when the operations are independent.

15. When should you NOT use Task.WhenAll?

If operations depend on each other.

For example:

Create Order
    ↓
Get Order ID
    ↓
Create Payment

You can't meaningfully run them concurrently because:

Payment requires OrderId

So:

var order = await CreateOrderAsync();

var payment = await CreatePaymentAsync(order.Id);

Sequential execution is correct here.

16. What is Task.WhenAny()?

Task.WhenAny() completes when the first supplied task completes.

Example:

var task1 = CallServer1Async();
var task2 = CallServer2Async();

var completedTask =
    await Task.WhenAny(task1, task2);

Conceptually:

Server 1 ────────────────
Server 2 ────────→ DONE
                    ↓
                WhenAny

Useful scenarios include:

  • timeout patterns
  • racing independent services
  • taking the first available result

Microsoft documents Task.WhenAny as the asynchronous counterpart to waiting for any task to complete. Microsoft Learn

17. What is CancellationToken?

🔴 Extremely important

CancellationToken allows an operation to receive a request to cancel.

Example:

public async Task<List<Product>> GetProductsAsync(
    CancellationToken cancellationToken)
{
    return await _dbContext.Products
        .ToListAsync(cancellationToken);
}

Then the token can be passed through the call chain:

Controller
   ↓
Service
   ↓
Repository
   ↓
EF Core
   ↓
SQL Server

This is called cancellation propagation.

.NET uses cooperative cancellation: the code performing the operation needs to observe the token and stop appropriately. Microsoft Learn

18. Why is CancellationToken useful in ASP.NET Core?

Suppose a user sends:

GET /api/products

and then closes the browser.

Continuing expensive work unnecessarily may waste resources.

You can propagate cancellation:

[HttpGet]
public async Task<IActionResult> GetProducts(
    CancellationToken cancellationToken)
{
    var products = await _service
        .GetProductsAsync(cancellationToken);

    return Ok(products);
}

Then:

public async Task<List<Product>> GetProductsAsync(
    CancellationToken cancellationToken)
{
    return await _dbContext.Products
        .ToListAsync(cancellationToken);
}

The cancellation token reaches the database operation.

19. What is Cooperative Cancellation?

Cancellation isn't necessarily:

"Kill the thread immediately."

Instead:

Cancellation requested
       ↓
Operation checks token
       ↓
Operation stops safely

Example:

cancellationToken.ThrowIfCancellationRequested();

Or pass it to an API that understands cancellation:

await httpClient.GetAsync(
    url,
    cancellationToken);

The operation decides how to respond to the cancellation request. Microsoft Learn

20. What happens when cancellation occurs?

A cancellable task commonly results in:

OperationCanceledException

or:

TaskCanceledException

The important conceptual distinction is:

Cancellation
    ≠
Application failure

Cancellation usually means the caller no longer wants the operation to continue.

21. What is async void?

🔴 Interview trap

Avoid:

public async void ProcessAsync()
{
    await DoSomethingAsync();
}

For normal application/service/controller code, prefer:

public async Task ProcessAsync()
{
    await DoSomethingAsync();
}

or:

public async Task<Product> GetProductAsync()
{
    return await GetAsync();
}

Why?

Task allows the caller to:

  • await completion
  • observe exceptions
  • compose operations
  • test the method

Microsoft specifically recommends avoiding async void except for event-handler scenarios. Microsoft Learn

22. Why is async void dangerous in ASP.NET Core?

Consider:

[HttpGet]
public async void Get()
{
    await Task.Delay(1000);

    // response work
}

ASP.NET Core expects a Task so it knows when the request has completed.

Correct:

[HttpGet]
public async Task Get()
{
    await Task.Delay(1000);
}

Microsoft's ASP.NET Core guidance specifically warns against async void because the HTTP request can complete before the asynchronous work finishes. Microsoft Learn

23. What happens with .Result?

Avoid:

var result = GetProductAsync().Result;

This synchronously blocks waiting for the task.

Similarly:

GetProductAsync().Wait();

can block a Thread Pool thread and, in some environments, contribute to deadlocks.

ASP.NET Core guidance explicitly recommends avoiding blocking calls such as .Result and .Wait(). Microsoft Learn

Prefer:

var result = await GetProductAsync();

24. What is "Async All the Way"?

🔴 Very common Senior question

Suppose:

Controller
 ↓
Service
 ↓
Repository
 ↓
Database

If the database operation is asynchronous, don't do:

Controller async
Service sync
Repository sync
Database async

Prefer:

Controller async
      ↓
Service async
      ↓
Repository async
      ↓
Database async

Example:

public async Task<IActionResult> GetProduct(int id)
{
    var product = await _service.GetProductAsync(id);

    return Ok(product);
}
public async Task<Product> GetProductAsync(int id)
{
    return await _repository.GetProductAsync(id);
}
public async Task<Product> GetProductAsync(int id)
{
    return await _dbContext.Products
        .FirstOrDefaultAsync(x => x.Id == id);
}

This allows asynchronous behavior to propagate through the call stack. Microsoft Learn

25. Async Exception Handling

You can use normal try-catch with asynchronous code:

try
{
    var product = await _service.GetProductAsync(id);
}
catch (Exception ex)
{
    _logger.LogError(
        ex,
        "Error getting product {ProductId}",
        id);

    throw;
}

The exception from the awaited task can be observed by the try-catch.

In a production API, however, you would generally let your centralized exception handler handle unexpected exceptions rather than duplicating this pattern in every controller.

26. What is ConfigureAwait(false)?

🔴 Senior-level

ConfigureAwait(false) tells the awaiter not to capture the current synchronization context for the continuation.

Example:

var result = await SomeOperationAsync()
    .ConfigureAwait(false);

This is particularly relevant in reusable library code.

For modern ASP.NET Core applications, there generally isn't the same classic ASP.NET synchronization-context issue that existed in older ASP.NET, so don't claim that ConfigureAwait(false) is required everywhere in ASP.NET Core.

Interview answer

ConfigureAwait(false) prevents capturing the current synchronization context. It's particularly useful in reusable library code, while in typical ASP.NET Core application code it's not something I blindly add to every await.

27. Async vs Parallelism

Don't confuse them.

Async

Primarily about:

Not blocking while waiting

Parallelism

Primarily about:

Doing multiple pieces of work simultaneously

Example:

Async DB call
    ↓
Waiting without blocking thread

versus:

Task A ──┐
Task B ──┼── concurrent execution
Task C ──┘

Task.WhenAll can coordinate concurrent asynchronous operations, but async itself doesn't automatically mean parallel CPU execution.

28. Async Database Access

For EF Core:

var products = await _dbContext.Products
    .ToListAsync(cancellationToken);

Instead of:

var products = _dbContext.Products
    .ToList();

For your stack, this is especially relevant because your API layer is backed by SQL Server.

Typical flow:

React
 ↓
Controller
 ↓
Service
 ↓
EF Core
 ↓
SQL Server

Make the entire I/O path asynchronous.

29. Async HttpClient

Suppose your API calls another service:

var response = await _httpClient
    .GetAsync(
        "/api/products",
        cancellationToken);

Again:

API
 ↓
HTTP request
 ↓
Wait for remote server
 ↓
Thread not synchronously blocked
 ↓
Response

Network calls are classic I/O-bound operations. Microsoft Learn

30. Fire-and-Forget — Why is it Dangerous?

Avoid:

_ = SomeAsyncOperation();

when you need guaranteed completion or error handling.

For example:

public IActionResult CreateOrder()
{
    _ = SendEmailAsync();

    return Ok();
}

Potential problem:

Request finishes
     ↓
Background operation still running
     ↓
Exception?
Request scope disposed?
Application shutdown?

ASP.NET Core recommends using hosted/background services for reliable background work rather than casually launching fire-and-forget work from request code. Microsoft Learn

For your stack, if sending an email can happen asynchronously after an order is created, a queue such as your AWS SQS workflow is often a better architectural approach.

31. Complete Real-World Example

Your application:

React
 ↓
ASP.NET Core
 ↓
ProductController
 ↓
ProductService
 ↓
EF Core
 ↓
SQL Server

Controller:

[HttpGet("{id}")]
public async Task<ActionResult<ProductDto>> GetProduct(
    int id,
    CancellationToken cancellationToken)
{
    var product = await _productService
        .GetProductAsync(id, cancellationToken);

    if (product == null)
        return NotFound();

    return Ok(product);
}

Service:

public async Task<ProductDto?> GetProductAsync(
    int id,
    CancellationToken cancellationToken)
{
    return await _dbContext.Products
        .Where(x => x.Id == id)
        .Select(x => new ProductDto
        {
            Id = x.Id,
            Name = x.Name
        })
        .FirstOrDefaultAsync(cancellationToken);
}

Flow:

HTTP Request
    ↓
Controller
    ↓
await Service
    ↓
await EF Core
    ↓
SQL Server
    ↓
Database response
    ↓
DTO
    ↓
HTTP Response

During the database wait, the server isn't synchronously blocking a Thread Pool thread.

🔴 32. Common Async Mistakes

❌ Mistake 1

var result = GetDataAsync().Result;

✅

var result = await GetDataAsync();

❌ Mistake 2

GetDataAsync().Wait();

✅

await GetDataAsync();

❌ Mistake 3

public async void GetData()

✅

public async Task GetDataAsync()

❌ Mistake 4

await Task.Run(() => databaseCall());

✅

await databaseCallAsync();

❌ Mistake 5

Sequential independent operations:

await GetAAsync();
await GetBAsync();
await GetCAsync();

Potentially better:

var a = GetAAsync();
var b = GetBAsync();
var c = GetCAsync();

await Task.WhenAll(a, b, c);

when those operations are truly independent.
