A browser may send an HTTP OPTIONS request before the actual request.

This is called a preflight request.

Example:

React
  ↓
OPTIONS /api/products
  ↓
ASP.NET Core
  ↓
CORS validation
  ↓
Allowed
  ↓
POST /api/products

The browser uses the preflight to determine whether the actual cross-origin request is permitted.

13. Why does the browser send OPTIONS?

Suppose React wants to send:

POST /api/orders
Authorization: Bearer ...
Content-Type: application/json

The browser may first ask the server:

OPTIONS /api/orders
Origin: https://myapp.com
Access-Control-Request-Method: POST
Access-Control-Request-Headers: authorization, content-type

The server can respond with appropriate CORS headers.

Conceptually:

Access-Control-Allow-Origin: https://myapp.com
Access-Control-Allow-Methods: POST
Access-Control-Allow-Headers: authorization, content-type

If the CORS policy allows the request, the browser proceeds with the actual request. ASP.NET Core's CORS middleware handles preflight requests according to the configured policy. Microsoft Learn

14. Simple Request vs Preflighted Request

Don't confuse these.

Some cross-origin requests can be sent without a preflight.

Others require a preflight.

A request may trigger preflight because of factors such as:

  • HTTP method
  • request headers
  • content type

For interview purposes:

Simple request
      ↓
Actual request

Preflighted request
      ↓
OPTIONS
      ↓
CORS check
      ↓
Actual request

15. What is Access-Control-Allow-Origin?

This response header tells the browser which origin is allowed.

Example:

Access-Control-Allow-Origin: https://myapp.com

Then the browser can expose the response to that origin if the rest of the CORS requirements are satisfied.

16. What is Access-Control-Allow-Methods?

Example:

Access-Control-Allow-Methods: GET, POST, PUT

It tells the browser which methods are allowed by the CORS policy.

17. What is Access-Control-Allow-Headers?

Example:

Access-Control-Allow-Headers:
Authorization, Content-Type

This controls which request headers can be used in the cross-origin request.

18. What is Access-Control-Expose-Headers?

🔴 Important interview question

By default, browsers don't expose every response header to frontend JavaScript.

Suppose your API returns:

X-Request-ID: abc123

Your React application may need to read it.

Then configure:

policy.WithExposedHeaders("X-Request-ID");

Microsoft documents WithExposedHeaders for making additional response headers available to browser code. Microsoft Learn

19. What are credentials in CORS?

Credentials can include things such as:

  • cookies
  • HTTP authentication information

For a browser request using credentials, the client must opt into sending them, and the server must allow credentials through its CORS policy. Microsoft Learn

Example React:

fetch("https://api.myapp.com/user", {
    credentials: "include"
});

Server:

policy
    .WithOrigins("https://myapp.com")
    .AllowCredentials();

20. Why can't we use AllowAnyOrigin + AllowCredentials?

🔴 Classic interview question

This is invalid/insecure configuration.

Don't do:

policy
    .AllowAnyOrigin()
    .AllowCredentials();

CORS does not allow credentials with a wildcard origin.

Instead:

policy
    .WithOrigins("https://myapp.com")
    .AllowCredentials();

Microsoft explicitly documents that "*" cannot be used as the allowed origin when credentials are allowed. Microsoft Learn

Interview answer

“When credentials are involved, I must specify explicit allowed origins rather than using AllowAnyOrigin. Wildcard origin with credentials is not a valid CORS configuration.”

21. CORS + JWT

Suppose your React application sends:

Authorization: Bearer eyJ...

Your API needs a CORS policy that allows the frontend origin and the required request headers.

For example:

builder.Services.AddCors(options =>
{
    options.AddPolicy("ReactPolicy", policy =>
    {
        policy
            .WithOrigins("https://myapp.com")
            .AllowAnyMethod()
            .AllowAnyHeader();
    });
});

Then:

React
   ↓
Authorization: Bearer JWT
   ↓
CORS
   ↓
Authentication
   ↓
Authorization
   ↓
Controller

CORS and authentication are different concerns.

22. CORS vs Authentication

Very common interview question.

CORS

Answers:

“Is this browser origin allowed to make/access this cross-origin request?”

Authentication

Answers:

“Who is the caller?”

Authorization

Answers:

“Is this authenticated caller allowed to perform this operation?”

Mental model:

CORS
 ↓
Can this browser origin access the API?

Authentication
 ↓
Who are you?

Authorization
 ↓
What are you allowed to do?

23. Where should UseCors() be placed?

With endpoint routing, middleware ordering matters.

A typical API pipeline can look like:

app.UseHttpsRedirection();

app.UseCors("ReactPolicy");

app.UseAuthentication();

app.UseAuthorization();

app.MapControllers();

CORS needs to be positioned appropriately in the middleware pipeline, and Microsoft specifically documents UseCors ordering relative to other middleware such as response caching. Microsoft Learn

For your interview, remember:

UseCors
   ↓
UseAuthentication
   ↓
UseAuthorization
   ↓
MapControllers

24. Can CORS be applied to specific controllers?

Yes.

ASP.NET Core supports [EnableCors].

Example:

[EnableCors("ReactPolicy")]
[ApiController]
[Route("api/[controller]")]
public class ProductsController : ControllerBase
{
}

You can also apply it at action level.

Microsoft documents EnableCorsAttribute as applicable to controllers and methods. Microsoft Learn

25. Global vs endpoint-specific CORS

Global

app.UseCors("ReactPolicy");

Good when most/all API endpoints follow the same policy.

Specific

[EnableCors("AdminPolicy")]

Useful when different endpoints require different CORS behavior.

26. Common CORS error scenario

Suppose React runs at:

http://localhost:3000

API:

https://localhost:7001

You configured:

.WithOrigins("http://localhost:5173")

React calls the API.

Result:

React
 ↓
API
 ↓
Origin doesn't match
 ↓
Browser blocks response

The fix is to configure the actual frontend origin:

.WithOrigins("http://localhost:3000")

27. Why does Postman work but React fail?

🔴 Very common interview/debugging question

Because CORS is primarily a browser security mechanism.

Postman isn't subject to the browser's same-origin policy in the same way.

So:

Postman
   ↓
API
   ↓
Works

while:

React Browser
   ↓
CORS check
   ↓
Blocked

Interview answer

“If an API works from Postman but fails from React, I would check CORS early because the browser enforces cross-origin restrictions while tools such as Postman aren't constrained by the browser's same-origin policy in the same way.”

28. CORS vs CSRF

Don't confuse these.

CORS

Controls whether browser JavaScript can access cross-origin resources.

CSRF

A security attack where a user's browser is tricked into sending an authenticated request to a site.

They are related to browser security but solve different problems.

CORS ≠ CSRF protection

Also, enabling credentials with broad cross-origin access can introduce security risks, which is why Microsoft cautions against overly broad credentialed CORS policies. Microsoft Learn

29. Real-world scenario for YOUR stack

Suppose your production architecture is:

React
https://app.company.com
          │
          │ HTTPS
          ▼
ASP.NET Core API
https://api.company.com
          │
          ▼
       Service
          │
          ▼
      SQL Server

Configure:

builder.Services.AddCors(options =>
{
    options.AddPolicy("FrontendPolicy", policy =>
    {
        policy
            .WithOrigins("https://app.company.com")
            .AllowAnyHeader()
            .AllowAnyMethod();
    });
});

Pipeline:

app.UseHttpsRedirection();

app.UseCors("FrontendPolicy");

app.UseAuthentication();

app.UseAuthorization();

app.MapControllers();

Now:

React
   ↓
Cross-origin request
   ↓
CORS policy
   ↓
Authentication
   ↓
Authorization
   ↓
Controller
   ↓
Service
   ↓
EF Core
   ↓
SQL Server

This is exactly the kind of architecture scenario you can explain in a .NET full-stack interview.

🔥 Top Interview Questions

MUST MASTER

  1. What is CORS?
  1. Why do we need CORS?
  1. What is an origin?
  1. Same-origin vs cross-origin?
  1. How do you configure CORS in ASP.NET Core?
  1. What does WithOrigins() do?
  1. What is AllowAnyOrigin()?
  1. WithOrigins() vs AllowAnyOrigin()?
  1. What does AllowAnyMethod() do?
  1. What does AllowAnyHeader() do?
  1. What is a preflight request?
  1. Why does the browser send an OPTIONS request?
  1. What is Access-Control-Allow-Origin?
  1. What is Access-Control-Allow-Methods?
  1. What is Access-Control-Allow-Headers?
  1. What is Access-Control-Expose-Headers?
  1. What are credentials in CORS?
  1. Why can't AllowAnyOrigin() be combined with AllowCredentials()?
  1. Where should UseCors() be placed?
  1. Can CORS be applied to individual controllers/actions?
  1. Why does Postman work while React fails?
  1. CORS vs authentication?
  1. CORS vs authorization?
  1. CORS vs CSRF?
  1. How would you configure CORS for a React + ASP.NET Core application?

🎯 Strong 60-Second Interview Answer

“CORS stands for Cross-Origin Resource Sharing and is used to control cross-origin browser requests to an API. In my React and ASP.NET Core applications, the frontend and API can run on different origins, so I configure a CORS policy in Program.cs using AddCors and specify the allowed frontend origins, methods and headers. I then enable it with UseCors in the middleware pipeline. For example, I would normally use WithOrigins with the actual React application's production URL rather than allowing every origin. For requests that require preflight, the browser sends an OPTIONS request first and the CORS middleware evaluates the policy. If credentials such as cookies are required, I use AllowCredentials with explicit origins and don't combine it with AllowAnyOrigin. CORS is separate from authentication and authorization: CORS controls browser cross-origin access, authentication identifies the user, and authorization determines permissions.” Microsoft Learn

🧠 Final Cheat Sheet

CORS
│
├── Origin
│   └── Scheme + Host + Port
│
├── Policy
│   ├── WithOrigins()
│   ├── AllowAnyOrigin()
│   ├── AllowAnyMethod()
│   ├── AllowAnyHeader()
│   ├── WithExposedHeaders()
│   └── AllowCredentials()
│
├── Preflight
│   └── OPTIONS
│
└── Middleware
    └── UseCors()

One-line memory trick:

CORS = “Which browser origins are allowed to access my API, and under what HTTP rules?”

27. API Versioning

🔴 Priority: MUST MASTER

API versioning is used when an API evolves while existing clients still need to work.

For example:

Mobile App v1
       ↓
   API v1

React App v2
       ↓
   API v2

The important goal is backward compatibility: existing consumers should continue working while newer consumers can adopt breaking changes.

For ASP.NET Core, API versioning for controllers and Minimal APIs is commonly provided through the Asp.Versioning packages; Microsoft’s current OpenAPI documentation also points to Asp.Versioning.Http for Minimal APIs. Microsoft Learn

1. What is API Versioning?

API versioning means maintaining different contracts/versions of an API so that clients don't break when the API changes.

Example:

/api/v1/products
/api/v2/products

Suppose v1 returns:

{
  "id": 1,
  "name": "Laptop"
}

Later, you need:

{
  "id": 1,
  "name": "Laptop",
  "price": 75000,
  "currency": "INR"
}

If the change is compatible, you may not need a new version.

But if the contract changes in a breaking way, you can introduce:

v2

2. Why do we need API Versioning?

Imagine you have:

100,000 mobile users
20 frontend applications
10 partner integrations

You release a breaking API change.

Without versioning:

Old Client
    ↓
New API
    ↓
❌ Broken

With versioning:

Old Client ──→ API v1
                    │
New Client ──→ API v2

Both can coexist during migration.

Interview answer

“API versioning allows us to evolve an API contract without immediately breaking existing clients. When a breaking change is required, we can introduce a new API version while continuing to support the older version during the migration period.”

3. When should you create a new API version?

🔴 Very important

Not every change requires a new version.

Usually non-breaking

Add a new optional response field
Add a new endpoint
Add a new optional request field

Potentially breaking

Remove a response field
Rename a response field
Change field type
Change endpoint behavior
Change required request field
Change response structure

So:

Non-breaking change
       ↓
Usually same version

Breaking contract change
       ↓
Consider new version

The general principle is to avoid unnecessary version proliferation and only create a new version when compatibility actually requires it.

4. Common API Versioning Strategies

🔴 MUST MASTER

There are four commonly discussed approaches:

API Versioning
│
├── 1. URL Path
│      /api/v1/products
│
├── 2. Query String
│      /api/products?api-version=1.0
│
├── 3. Header
│      X-API-Version: 1.0
│
└── 4. Media Type / Accept Header
       Accept: application/vnd.company.v1+json

5. URL Path Versioning

Probably the easiest to understand.

GET /api/v1/products

and:

GET /api/v2/products

Architecture:

/api/v1/products
       ↓
ProductsController V1


/api/v2/products
       ↓
ProductsController V2

Advantages

  • Very visible
  • Easy to understand
  • Easy to test
  • Easy to document
  • Easy to route

Disadvantage

The version becomes part of the URL.

6. Query String Versioning

Example:

GET /api/products?api-version=1.0

or:

GET /api/products?api-version=2.0

The resource URL remains the same.

Advantage

Simple URL structure.

Disadvantage

The API version is less obvious than URL-path versioning.

7. Header Versioning

The URL remains:

GET /api/products

and version is specified in a header:

X-API-Version: 1.0

Then:

/api/products
       +
X-API-Version: 1.0
       ↓
API v1

Advantage

Clean resource URLs.

Disadvantage

Harder to discover/test because the version isn't visible in the URL.

8. Media Type Versioning

Version can be represented using the Accept header.

For example:

Accept: application/vnd.company.v1+json

Then:

Accept: ...v1+json → API v1
Accept: ...v2+json → API v2

This approach is closely related to HTTP content negotiation.

9. Which versioning approach should you use?

Don't give an absolute answer like:

"URL versioning is always the best."

Instead:

“The choice depends on the organization's API standards and client requirements. URL versioning is straightforward and easy for consumers to understand, while header or media-type versioning keeps the resource URL stable. In an existing organization, I would follow the established API contract rather than introducing a different strategy for one service.”

That's a better senior-level answer.

10. ASP.NET Core API Versioning

For controller-based APIs, the commonly used package is:

Asp.Versioning.Mvc

and related packages provide API versioning support.

Conceptually:

builder.Services.AddApiVersioning(options =>
{
    options.DefaultApiVersion =
        new ApiVersion(1, 0);

    options.AssumeDefaultVersionWhenUnspecified = true;

    options.ReportApiVersions = true;
});

The exact package/API surface depends on the Asp.Versioning package version being used.

11. Versioning a Controller

A controller can specify its API version.

Conceptually:

[ApiController]
[ApiVersion("1.0")]
[Route("api/v{version:apiVersion}/products")]
public class ProductsController : ControllerBase
{
}

Then:

GET /api/v1/products

maps to version 1.

12. Multiple Versions

Suppose:

Products API

v1
v2

You can expose:

/api/v1/products
/api/v2/products

Conceptually:

                Products
                   │
          ┌────────┴────────┐
          ↓                 ↓
        V1 API             V2 API
          ↓                 ↓
      Old contract      New contract

13. Why shouldn't we duplicate all business logic?

This is an important architecture question.

Bad:

ProductsV1Controller
       ↓
V1 Business Logic


ProductsV2Controller
       ↓
V2 Business Logic

You can end up duplicating everything.

Better:

ProductsV1Controller ─┐
                      ├──→ ProductService
ProductsV2Controller ─┘

If the business rules are the same, keep them in shared services/domain logic.

Only the API contract/mapping should differ when necessary.

Interview answer

“I try to keep version-specific concerns at the API boundary. If the underlying business rules are unchanged, both versions can reuse the same service layer, while each controller maps the request and response to its respective DTO contract.”

14. Versioning with DTOs

This is particularly important in your .NET architecture.

Don't expose your EF Core entities directly.

Instead:

Database Entity
       ↓
Service
       ↓
DTO
       ↓
API Version

Example:

V1 DTO

public class ProductV1Dto
{
    public int Id { get; set; }

    public string Name { get; set; }
}

V2 DTO

public class ProductV2Dto
{
    public int Id { get; set; }

    public string Name { get; set; }

    public decimal Price { get; set; }

    public string Currency { get; set; }
}

Then:

Product Entity
      ↓
   Service
   ↙     ↘
V1 DTO   V2 DTO

This protects your database/domain model from becoming tightly coupled to the public API contract.

15. What is backward compatibility?

Backward compatibility means existing clients continue working after the API evolves.

Example:

Existing React App
       ↓
     API v1
       ↓
Still works

New React App
       ↓
     API v2

The old client doesn't have to immediately upgrade.

16. What is breaking change?

A breaking change is a change that can cause an existing client to stop functioning correctly.

Examples:

Before

{
  "id": 1,
  "name": "Laptop"
}

Changing:

"name": "Laptop"

to:

"productName": "Laptop"

can break clients expecting name.

Another example:

Before:
price → decimal

After:
price → object

A client expecting a decimal can fail to deserialize it.

17. What is API deprecation?

Suppose:

v1
v2

You want clients to move to v2.

You can mark v1 as deprecated and communicate:

v1 → deprecated
v2 → current

The lifecycle can be:

v1 Released
   ↓
v2 Released
   ↓
v1 Deprecated
   ↓
Migration period
   ↓
v1 Retired

Important

Deprecation ≠ immediate removal.

You normally give consumers time to migrate.

18. What does ReportApiVersions do?

When API versioning is configured to report versions, responses can include headers describing supported/deprecated API versions.

Conceptually:

api-supported-versions: 1.0, 2.0

This can help clients understand which versions are available.

19. What does DefaultApiVersion mean?

Suppose a client sends:

GET /api/products

without specifying a version.

A default version can be configured.

Conceptually:

options.DefaultApiVersion =
    new ApiVersion(1, 0);

So an unspecified version can resolve to:

v1

depending on the configured versioning behavior.

20. What does AssumeDefaultVersionWhenUnspecified mean?

If enabled:

options.AssumeDefaultVersionWhenUnspecified = true;

then requests that don't specify a version can use the configured default version.

Interview warning

Don't automatically enable this just because it's convenient.

For APIs where explicit versioning is important, requiring consumers to specify a version may be preferable.

21. What happens when an unsupported version is requested?

Suppose only:

v1
v2

exist.

Client requests:

GET /api/v3/products

The API versioning system should reject the request rather than silently pretending that v3 exists.

The exact HTTP response depends on the versioning configuration and request mechanism, but the key interview concept is:

Unsupported version
       ↓
Versioning error
       ↓
Client must use supported version

22. API Versioning + Swagger/OpenAPI

🔴 Important for real projects

If you have:

v1
v2

your API documentation should make the versions discoverable.

For example:

Swagger

Products API v1
Products API v2

This helps frontend developers and external consumers understand which contract they should use.

ASP.NET Core has built-in OpenAPI support, and current Microsoft documentation shows versioned OpenAPI documents can be generated with appropriate versioning tooling. Microsoft Learn

23. API Versioning + React

Suppose you have:

React Application
       ↓
/api/v1/products

Later you release:

React Application v2
       ↓
/api/v2/products

You can migrate gradually:

Old React
    ↓
API v1

New React
    ↓
API v2

This is especially useful when multiple frontend applications don't upgrade simultaneously.

24. API Versioning + Mobile Apps

This is a classic real-world scenario.

Suppose:

Mobile App 1.0 → API v1
Mobile App 2.0 → API v2

Users don't necessarily update their mobile application immediately.

Therefore:

API v1
   ↑
Old mobile users

API v2
   ↑
New mobile users

Removing v1 immediately could break users who haven't upgraded.

This is one of the strongest practical reasons for API versioning.

25. Should every API change create a new version?

No.

This is a very important interview answer.

You should first ask:

Does this change break existing clients?
              │
        ┌─────┴─────┐
        ↓           ↓
       No          Yes
        ↓           ↓
Same version    New version

Avoid creating:

v1
v1.1
v1.2
v1.3
v1.4
...

for every tiny change.

That creates unnecessary maintenance overhead.

26. API Versioning vs .NET Versioning

Don't confuse these.

.NET version

.NET 8
.NET 9
.NET 10

This is the framework/runtime version.

API version

/api/v1
/api/v2

This is your application's public API contract version.

They are completely different concepts.

Microsoft currently lists .NET 10 as an LTS release, but that runtime version has no direct relationship to whether your application's API is v1 or v2. Microsoft Learn

27. API Versioning vs Database Versioning

Again, different concepts.

API Version
    ↓
Public contract

Database Migration
    ↓
Database schema

For example:

API v1
API v2

Database
Products table
Orders table
Customers table

You can have:

API v1 + DB schema v10
API v2 + DB schema v10

The API version doesn't have to equal the database migration version.

28. Real-World Scenario for YOUR Stack

Imagine your application:

React
   ↓
ASP.NET Core Web API
   ↓
Controller
   ↓
Service
   ↓
EF Core
   ↓
SQL Server

Current API:

GET /api/v1/products

V1:

{
  "id": 1,
  "name": "Laptop"
}

Later, product requirements change significantly.

You create:

GET /api/v2/products

V2:

{
  "id": 1,
  "name": "Laptop",
  "price": 75000,
  "currency": "INR"
}

Architecture:

                 ProductService
                 /             \
                /               \
               ↓                 ↓
       ProductV1Dto        ProductV2Dto
              ↓                   ↓
        API /v1/products     API /v2/products

Both versions can reuse:

EF Core
SQL Server
Business logic
Repositories

where appropriate.

🔥 Top Interview Questions

MUST MASTER

  1. What is API versioning?
  1. Why do we need API versioning?
  1. When should you create a new API version?
  1. What is a breaking change?
  1. What is backward compatibility?
  1. What are the API versioning strategies?
  1. URL vs query-string versioning?
  1. Header vs URL versioning?
  1. What is media-type versioning?
  1. How do you implement API versioning in ASP.NET Core?
  1. How do you version a controller?
  1. Can multiple API versions coexist?
  1. How do you handle shared business logic between versions?
  1. Why should version-specific DTOs be used?
  1. What is API deprecation?
  1. What is DefaultApiVersion?
  1. What is AssumeDefaultVersionWhenUnspecified?
  1. What is ReportApiVersions?
  1. What happens when an unsupported version is requested?
  1. How does API versioning work with Swagger/OpenAPI?
  1. Should every API change create a new version?
  1. API versioning vs .NET versioning?
  1. API versioning vs database versioning?
  1. How would you version a React + ASP.NET Core application?
  1. How would you safely retire API v1?

🎯 Strong 60-Second Interview Answer

“API versioning allows us to evolve an API without immediately breaking existing clients. I use it when a change introduces a breaking change to the public API contract. Common approaches include URL-based versioning such as /api/v1/products, query-string versioning, headers, and media-type versioning. In an ASP.NET Core application, I can use the Asp.Versioning packages to define supported API versions and map controllers or endpoints to those versions. I prefer keeping version-specific DTOs at the API boundary while reusing the underlying service and business logic when the rules are unchanged. I also document the different versions through OpenAPI or Swagger and deprecate older versions before eventually removing them. I wouldn't create a new version for every small change; I would first determine whether existing consumers would actually be broken.” Microsoft Learn

🧠 Final Cheat Sheet

API VERSIONING
│
├── Why?
│   └── Protect existing clients
│
├── Common strategies
│   ├── URL
│   │   /api/v1/products
│   │
│   ├── Query
│   │   /api/products?api-version=1
│   │
│   ├── Header
│   │   X-API-Version: 1
│   │
│   └── Media Type
│       application/vnd.company.v1+json
│
├── Breaking change?
│   ├── No → Same version
│   └── Yes → Consider new version
│
├── Architecture
│   ├── V1 Controller → V1 DTO ─┐
│   └── V2 Controller → V2 DTO ─┤
│                                ↓
│                           Shared Service
│                                ↓
│                             EF Core
│                                ↓
│                           SQL Server
│
└── Lifecycle
    v1 → v2 released → v1 deprecated → v1 retired

One-line memory trick:

API versioning = evolve the public contract without breaking existing consumers.

28. Rate Limiting in ASP.NET Core

Rate limiting is a high-priority ASP.NET Core interview topic, especially for backend/product-company interviews.

Microsoft's current ASP.NET Core documentation provides built-in rate-limiting middleware with Fixed Window, Sliding Window, Token Bucket, and Concurrency algorithms. Microsoft Learn

🔴 Priority — Must Master

Focus especially on:

  1. What is rate limiting?
  1. Why do we need rate limiting?
  1. AddRateLimiter()
  1. UseRateLimiter()
  1. Fixed Window
  1. Sliding Window
  1. Token Bucket
  1. Concurrency Limiter
  1. Global vs endpoint-specific policies
  1. Partitioning — per user/IP/API key
  1. 429 Too Many Requests
  1. QueueLimit
  1. OnRejected
  1. Rate limiting vs throttling
  1. Rate limiting vs authentication/authorization
  1. Real-world API scenario

1. What is Rate Limiting?

Rate limiting controls how many requests a client can make within a particular period or how many requests can execute concurrently.

For example:

Maximum 100 requests per minute per user

If the user exceeds the limit:

HTTP 429 Too Many Requests

ASP.NET Core provides rate-limiting middleware specifically for this purpose. Microsoft Learn

Interview answer

"Rate limiting is a mechanism used to control how many requests a client can send to an API within a given time period or how many requests can execute concurrently. It protects APIs from excessive traffic, accidental overload and certain types of abuse. In ASP.NET Core, I can configure rate-limiting policies using AddRateLimiter and apply them globally or to specific endpoints."

2. Why do we need Rate Limiting?

Imagine your API:

POST /api/orders

Normally:

User → 20 requests/minute

But a malicious client sends:

10,000 requests/minute

This could consume:

  • CPU
  • database connections
  • memory
  • Thread Pool resources
  • external API quota
  • network bandwidth

Rate limiting protects the application from excessive request volume. Microsoft also notes that rate limiting can help mitigate certain denial-of-service scenarios, although it should not be treated as a complete DDoS solution. Microsoft Learn

3. How do we configure Rate Limiting?

First register the service:

builder.Services.AddRateLimiter(options =>
{
    options.AddFixedWindowLimiter("api", opt =>
    {
        opt.PermitLimit = 10;
        opt.Window = TimeSpan.FromMinutes(1);
        opt.QueueLimit = 0;
    });
});

Then enable the middleware:

app.UseRateLimiter();

And apply the policy:

app.MapControllers()
   .RequireRateLimiting("api");

Or for a controller/action, you can use:

[EnableRateLimiting("api")]

AddRateLimiter is required in modern ASP.NET Core before using the middleware. Microsoft Learn

4. What is a Fixed Window Limiter?

A Fixed Window divides time into fixed intervals.

Example:

Limit = 10 requests
Window = 1 minute

So:

12:00:00 → 12:00:59
Maximum = 10 requests

12:01:00 → 12:01:59
Maximum = 10 requests

Configuration:

options.AddFixedWindowLimiter("fixed", opt =>
{
    opt.PermitLimit = 10;
    opt.Window = TimeSpan.FromMinutes(1);
});

Microsoft describes the fixed window limiter as resetting the request limit when the configured window expires. Microsoft Learn

Advantage

Simple and easy to understand.

Disadvantage

It can allow bursts around window boundaries.

For example:

12:00:59 → 10 requests
12:01:00 → 10 requests

Potentially:

20 requests within ~2 seconds

5. What is Sliding Window?

A Sliding Window evaluates requests over a continuously moving time window rather than simply resetting everything at a fixed boundary.

Example:

Limit = 100 requests
Window = 1 minute
Segments = 6

The window is divided into smaller segments.

This provides smoother request distribution than a basic fixed window.

ASP.NET Core supports configuring SegmentsPerWindow for the sliding-window limiter. Microsoft Learn

Interview answer

"A sliding window is similar to a fixed window, but the time period is divided into segments and the limiter considers requests across the moving window. It generally provides smoother rate limiting and reduces the boundary burst problem of fixed windows."

6. What is Token Bucket?

Think of a bucket containing tokens.

For example:

Bucket capacity = 100 tokens

Each request consumes one token:

Request → 1 token
Request → 1 token
Request → 1 token

Tokens are periodically replenished.

So:

100 tokens
     ↓
Requests consume tokens
     ↓
Tokens become available again

Configuration:

options.AddTokenBucketLimiter("token", opt =>
{
    opt.TokenLimit = 100;
    opt.TokensPerPeriod = 20;
    opt.ReplenishmentPeriod = TimeSpan.FromSeconds(10);
    opt.AutoReplenishment = true;
});

Microsoft's implementation supports automatic token replenishment or manual replenishment via TryReplenish. Microsoft Learn

Why is it useful?

It allows controlled bursts while still limiting the overall rate.

7. What is Concurrency Limiting?

This is slightly different.

Instead of:

"How many requests per minute?"

it asks:

"How many requests can execute at the same time?"

Example:

Maximum concurrent requests = 20

Suppose:

20 requests → executing
21st request → rejected/queued

When one finishes:

19 requests → executing
New request → allowed

ASP.NET Core's concurrency limiter limits concurrent requests rather than the number of requests over a time period. Microsoft Learn

Real-world use

Suppose you have:

POST /api/generate-report

Each request performs:

SQL queries
+
large data processing
+
PDF generation

You may not want 1,000 requests executing simultaneously.

Instead:

Maximum concurrent report generation = 10

That's a good concurrency-limiter scenario.

8. Fixed Window vs Sliding Window vs Token Bucket vs Concurrency

AlgorithmControlsGood for
Fixed WindowRequests per fixed periodSimple APIs
Sliding WindowRequests across moving periodSmoother limits
Token BucketToken consumption/replenishmentControlled bursts
ConcurrencySimultaneous requestsExpensive operations

Easy memory trick

Fixed     → Fixed time
Sliding   → Moving time
Token     → Bucket of tokens
Concurrency → Requests running now

9. What is a Global Rate Limiter?

A global limiter applies to requests across the application.

Example:

builder.Services.AddRateLimiter(options =>
{
    options.GlobalLimiter =
        PartitionedRateLimiter.Create<HttpContext, string>(
            httpContext =>
                RateLimitPartition.GetFixedWindowLimiter(
                    httpContext.Connection.RemoteIpAddress?.ToString()
                        ?? "unknown",
                    _ => new FixedWindowRateLimiterOptions
                    {
                        PermitLimit = 100,
                        Window = TimeSpan.FromMinutes(1)
                    }));
});

This can be useful when you want a general protection layer.

Microsoft documents GlobalLimiter as applying to all requests; an endpoint-specific limiter can then be evaluated as well. Microsoft Learn

10. What is Endpoint-Specific Rate Limiting?

Instead of limiting everything, you can protect expensive or sensitive endpoints.

For example:

GET /api/products

might allow:

1000 requests/minute

while:

POST /api/orders

might allow:

50 requests/minute

And:

POST /api/login

might allow:

10 requests/minute

Example:

builder.Services.AddRateLimiter(options =>
{
    options.AddFixedWindowLimiter("login", opt =>
    {
        opt.PermitLimit = 10;
        opt.Window = TimeSpan.FromMinutes(1);
    });
});

Then:

[EnableRateLimiting("login")]
[HttpPost("login")]
public IActionResult Login(LoginRequest request)
{
    ...
}

11. What is Rate Limiting Partitioning?

This is an important Senior-level interview question.

Suppose you configure:

100 requests/minute

If it's global, 100 requests might be shared by everyone.

But usually you want:

User A → 100/minute
User B → 100/minute
User C → 100/minute

That's where partitioning comes in.

You can create a separate limiter based on:

User ID
IP address
API key
tenant ID

For example:

Partition Key = UserId

Then:

User 101 → own limit
User 102 → own limit
User 103 → own limit

ASP.NET Core supports custom policies using RateLimitPartition and AddPolicy. Microsoft Learn

12. What happens when the rate limit is exceeded?

Typically the API returns:

429 Too Many Requests

You can configure what happens when a request is rejected through OnRejected.

For example:

builder.Services.AddRateLimiter(options =>
{
    options.RejectionStatusCode = StatusCodes.Status429TooManyRequests;

    options.OnRejected = async (context, token) =>
    {
        await context.HttpContext.Response.WriteAsync(
            "Too many requests.",
            token);
    };
});

Microsoft's samples demonstrate OnRejected and configuring 429 Too Many Requests. Microsoft Learn

13. What is QueueLimit?

Instead of immediately rejecting requests, you can allow some requests to wait.

Example:

options.AddFixedWindowLimiter("api", opt =>
{
    opt.PermitLimit = 10;
    opt.Window = TimeSpan.FromSeconds(10);

    opt.QueueLimit = 5;

    opt.QueueProcessingOrder =
        QueueProcessingOrder.OldestFirst;
});

Meaning:

10 → execute immediately

Next 5 → wait in queue

Next request → rejected

ASP.NET Core supports configurable queue limits and processing order for supported limiters. Microsoft Learn

Important

Don't blindly make the queue very large.

A huge queue can increase:

latency
memory usage
resource pressure

14. Rate Limiting vs Throttling

These terms are often used interchangeably.

Rate limiting

Controls the allowed request rate.

100 requests/minute

Throttling

Usually refers more broadly to deliberately slowing or restricting processing when demand becomes excessive.

For interviews, you can say:

"Rate limiting is a specific mechanism for restricting request rate or concurrency. Throttling is a broader term that can include slowing or restricting processing under high load."

15. Rate Limiting vs Authentication

They solve different problems.

Authentication

Who are you?

Authorization

What are you allowed to do?

Rate Limiting

How many requests are you allowed to make?

Example:

JWT
 ↓
Authentication
 ↓
User identified
 ↓
Authorization
 ↓
User has permission
 ↓
Rate Limiting
 ↓
User hasn't exceeded request limit
 ↓
Controller

They complement each other.

16. Rate Limiting vs Caching

Caching:

Reduce repeated work

Rate limiting:

Reduce excessive requests

Example:

GET /api/products

Caching might prevent repeated database queries.

Rate limiting might prevent:

10,000 requests/minute

from one client.

You can use both.

17. Real-World Scenario — Your React + ASP.NET Core API

Imagine your application:

React
  ↓
ASP.NET Core Web API
  ↓
Service
  ↓
EF Core
  ↓
SQL Server

You have:

POST /api/orders

Each request:

API
 ↓
Business validation
 ↓
SQL Server
 ↓
Payment API
 ↓
Order creation

This is relatively expensive.

You could configure:

Normal API
→ 100 requests/minute/user

Order API
→ 30 requests/minute/user

Report API
→ 10 requests/minute/user

Login API
→ 5 requests/minute/IP

And for report generation:

Concurrency = 5

This protects your:

ASP.NET Core
      ↓
SQL Server
      ↓
External APIs

from excessive load.

18. What would you choose for different scenarios?

Scenario 1 — Simple public API

100 requests/minute

Use:

Fixed Window

Scenario 2 — Need smoother traffic

100 requests/minute

but want to reduce boundary bursts.

Use:

Sliding Window

Scenario 3 — Allow controlled bursts

Use:

Token Bucket

Scenario 4 — Expensive report generation

Only 5 reports executing simultaneously

Use:

Concurrency Limiter

Scenario 5 — Per-user API limit

100 requests/minute/user

Use:

Partitioned rate limiting

19. Where does Rate Limiting fit in the pipeline?

Think:

Client
   ↓
Middleware
   ↓
Rate Limiting
   ↓
Authentication
   ↓
Authorization
   ↓
Routing / Endpoint
   ↓
Controller
   ↓
Service
   ↓
EF Core
   ↓
SQL Server

The exact middleware ordering depends on the scenario. For endpoint-specific rate limiting, Microsoft documents placing UseRateLimiter after routing; for only a global limiter, it can be placed before routing. Microsoft Learn

20. Common Interview Questions

Q1. What is rate limiting?

Rate limiting controls how many requests a client can make within a specific period or how many requests can execute concurrently.

Q2. What status code is generally returned when the limit is exceeded?

429 Too Many Requests.

Q3. What algorithms does ASP.NET Core support?

Fixed Window, Sliding Window, Token Bucket and Concurrency limiting. Microsoft Learn

Q4. What is Fixed Window?

It allows a specified number of requests during a fixed time window and resets the limit when the window expires.

Q5. What is Sliding Window?

It evaluates requests across a moving time window divided into segments, providing smoother limiting than a simple fixed window.

Q6. What is Token Bucket?

Requests consume tokens from a bucket, and tokens are replenished periodically. It is useful when controlled bursts are required.

Q7. What is Concurrency Limiting?

It limits the number of requests executing simultaneously rather than limiting the number of requests during a time period.

Q8. Can rate limiting be applied only to specific endpoints?

Yes. We can define named policies and apply them to specific endpoints or controllers.

Q9. Can rate limiting be applied per user?

Yes. We can partition the limiter using a user ID, API key, IP address or another partition key.

Q10. What is AddRateLimiter()?

It registers and configures ASP.NET Core rate-limiting services and policies.

Q11. What is UseRateLimiter()?

It adds the rate-limiting middleware to the ASP.NET Core request pipeline.

Q12. What is QueueLimit?

It defines how many requests can wait when no permit is immediately available.

Q13. What happens if the queue is full?

The request is rejected according to the configured rejection behavior.

Q14. What is OnRejected?

It allows us to customize behavior when a request is rejected by the rate limiter.

Q15. Is rate limiting a replacement for authentication?

No. Authentication identifies the caller, authorization checks permissions, and rate limiting controls request consumption.

🎯 Strong 60-Second Interview Answer

"Rate limiting is used to control how many requests a client can make to an API within a specific time period or how many requests can execute concurrently. In ASP.NET Core, I can configure rate limiting using AddRateLimiter and enable it with UseRateLimiter. The framework supports Fixed Window, Sliding Window, Token Bucket and Concurrency limiters. For example, I might allow 100 requests per minute per user for normal APIs, while limiting expensive report generation based on concurrency. I can apply policies globally or to specific endpoints, and I can partition limits by user, IP address, API key or tenant. When the limit is exceeded, the API can return 429 Too Many Requests, and I can customize rejection handling using OnRejected. The goal is to protect application resources such as CPU, database connections and downstream services while maintaining predictable API behavior." Microsoft Learn

🧠 Final Mental Model

Remember this:

                 RATE LIMITING
                      │
       ┌──────────────┼──────────────┐
       ↓              ↓              ↓
   Fixed Window   Sliding Window  Token Bucket
       │              │              │
   Fixed period    Moving period   Tokens
       │              │              │
       └──────────────┼──────────────┘
                      ↓
                Concurrency
                      │
             simultaneous work

And:

Client
  ↓
Rate Limiter
  ↓
429 if limit exceeded
  ↓
Authentication
  ↓
Authorization
  ↓
Controller
  ↓
Service
  ↓
EF Core / SQL Server

One-line memory trick:

Rate limiting = control request rate/concurrency → protect resources → return 429 when limits are exceeded.

29. Health Checks in ASP.NET Core

Health Checks are a high-priority production/interview topic, especially for Senior .NET roles.

ASP.NET Core provides built-in health-check infrastructure for exposing endpoints that report application and dependency health. These endpoints can be consumed by load balancers, container orchestrators, monitoring systems, and deployment infrastructure. Microsoft Learn

🔴 Priority — Must Master

Focus especially on:

  1. What are Health Checks?
  1. Why do we need them?
  1. AddHealthChecks()
  1. MapHealthChecks()
  1. IHealthCheck
  1. HealthCheckResult
  1. Healthy / Degraded / Unhealthy
  1. Database health check
  1. Custom health check
  1. Liveness vs Readiness
  1. Health check tags
  1. Multiple health-check endpoints
  1. UseHealthChecks() vs MapHealthChecks()
  1. Health checks with Docker/Kubernetes
  1. Health checks vs monitoring/logging
  1. Real-world API scenario

1. What are Health Checks?

A health check is a mechanism that tells us whether an application or one of its important dependencies is functioning properly.

For example:

GET /health

might check:

Application
   ↓
SQL Server
   ↓
Redis
   ↓
External API

and return an overall status.

ASP.NET Core supports three health states:

Healthy
Degraded
Unhealthy
``` :chatgpt-content-reference{index="1"}


### Interview answer

> "Health checks are used to determine whether an application and its important dependencies are functioning correctly. ASP.NET Core provides built-in health-check services and endpoints that can be consumed by load balancers, container orchestrators, monitoring systems, and deployment infrastructure."

---

# 2. Why do we need Health Checks?

Imagine you have:

```text
React
   ↓
ASP.NET Core API
   ↓
SQL Server

The API process may still be running, but SQL Server could be unavailable.

So:

Application process = running
Database = unavailable

A simple:

ping

isn't enough.

A health check can tell infrastructure:

API instance
     ↓
Database unavailable
     ↓
Unhealthy

A load balancer could then stop routing traffic to that instance, while an orchestrator may restart or otherwise react to an unhealthy container. Microsoft Learn

3. Basic Health Check

The simplest configuration is:

var builder = WebApplication.CreateBuilder(args);

builder.Services.AddHealthChecks();

var app = builder.Build();

app.MapHealthChecks("/healthz");

app.Run();

Now:

GET /healthz

provides a health response.

By default, simply registering AddHealthChecks() without specific dependency checks means the application is considered healthy if it can respond at the health endpoint. Microsoft Learn

4. What is AddHealthChecks()?

This registers the health-check services with dependency injection.

builder.Services.AddHealthChecks();

Think:

AddHealthChecks()
      ↓
Register health-check infrastructure
      ↓
Add individual checks

For example:

builder.Services
    .AddHealthChecks()
    .AddCheck<DatabaseHealthCheck>("database");

5. What is MapHealthChecks()?

It exposes the health checks through an HTTP endpoint.

app.MapHealthChecks("/health");

So:

Browser / Load Balancer / Kubernetes
                ↓
         GET /health
                ↓
       ASP.NET Core Health Checks

Microsoft currently documents MapHealthChecks as the endpoint-routing approach and notes that it allows endpoint-aware middleware such as authorization. Microsoft Learn

6. What is IHealthCheck?

If you need your own custom health check, implement:

IHealthCheck

The important method is:

CheckHealthAsync()

Example:

public class MyHealthCheck : IHealthCheck
{
    public Task<HealthCheckResult> CheckHealthAsync(
        HealthCheckContext context,
        CancellationToken cancellationToken)
    {
        return Task.FromResult(
            HealthCheckResult.Healthy("Application is healthy"));
    }
}

Then register it:

builder.Services
    .AddHealthChecks()
    .AddCheck<MyHealthCheck>("my-check");

ASP.NET Core health checks use IHealthCheck.CheckHealthAsync to produce a HealthCheckResult. Microsoft Learn

7. What is HealthCheckResult?

It represents the result of a health check.

The important statuses are:

Healthy
Degraded
Unhealthy

For example:

return HealthCheckResult.Healthy();

or:

return HealthCheckResult.Degraded(
    "Dependency is slow");

or:

return HealthCheckResult.Unhealthy(
    "Database is unavailable");

A health-check result can also contain a description, exception information, and additional data. Microsoft Learn

8. Healthy vs Degraded vs Unhealthy

This is a common interview question.

Healthy

Everything is working normally.

API       → OK
Database  → OK
Redis     → OK

Degraded

The application can still operate, but something isn't operating normally.

Example:

API       → OK
Database  → OK
Redis     → Slow

You might classify:

Redis → Degraded

Unhealthy

An important component is unavailable or the application cannot operate correctly.

Example:

API       → Running
Database  → DOWN

Result:

Unhealthy

9. Database Health Check

A common real-world requirement is checking SQL Server.

For example:

ASP.NET Core
      ↓
SQL Server

A SQL health check verifies that the database connection is available.

Microsoft's documentation notes that a database probe can use a simple query such as SELECT 1 when a query is actually necessary, and warns against expensive health-check queries that could put additional load on the database. Microsoft Learn

You may see a SQL Server health-check package used like:

builder.Services
    .AddHealthChecks()
    .AddSqlServer(connectionString);

But be aware that the AspNetCore.Diagnostics.HealthChecks library mentioned in Microsoft's documentation is not maintained or supported by Microsoft. Microsoft Learn

That's a useful interview nuance.

10. EF Core Health Check

You may also see health checks for an EF Core DbContext.

Conceptually:

Health Check
     ↓
DbContext
     ↓
SQL Server

This can verify that the application's EF Core database dependency is available.

For your stack, this is particularly relevant because you use:

ASP.NET Core
      ↓
EF Core
      ↓
SQL Server

11. Custom Health Check — Real Example

Suppose your application depends on:

Payment API

You could create:

public class PaymentApiHealthCheck : IHealthCheck
{
    private readonly HttpClient _httpClient;

    public PaymentApiHealthCheck(HttpClient httpClient)
    {
        _httpClient = httpClient;
    }

    public async Task<HealthCheckResult> CheckHealthAsync(
        HealthCheckContext context,
        CancellationToken cancellationToken)
    {
        try
        {
            var response = await _httpClient.GetAsync(
                "/health",
                cancellationToken);

            if (response.IsSuccessStatusCode)
            {
                return HealthCheckResult.Healthy();
            }

            return HealthCheckResult.Unhealthy(
                "Payment API is unavailable.");
        }
        catch (Exception ex)
        {
            return HealthCheckResult.Unhealthy(
                "Payment API check failed.",
                ex);
        }
    }
}

Then:

builder.Services
    .AddHealthChecks()
    .AddCheck<PaymentApiHealthCheck>("payment-api");

12. Liveness vs Readiness

🔥 Very important for Senior interviews.

These two concepts are different.

Liveness

Answers:

"Is the application process alive?"

Example:

GET /health/live

It might only verify that the application itself is running.

Application
     ↓
Alive

Readiness

Answers:

"Is this application instance ready to receive traffic?"

It can check important dependencies.

Application
    ↓
SQL Server
    ↓
Redis
    ↓
External services

If critical dependencies aren't available:

Not Ready

A load balancer/orchestrator can then avoid sending traffic to that instance.

Microsoft specifically documents separate readiness and liveness probes as a health-check scenario. Microsoft Learn

13. Real-World Liveness + Readiness

For example:

/health/live

checks:

Is application running?

while:

/health/ready

checks:

Application
   +
SQL Server
   +
Redis
   +
required dependencies

Architecture:

                    ┌── /health/live
                    │
Load Balancer ──────┤
                    │
                    └── /health/ready
                              ↓
                         ASP.NET Core
                              ↓
                    ┌─────────┴─────────┐
                    ↓                   ↓
                SQL Server           Redis

14. What are Health Check Tags?

Tags allow you to categorize health checks.

Example:

builder.Services
    .AddHealthChecks()
    .AddCheck<DatabaseHealthCheck>(
        "database",
        tags: new[] { "ready" })
    .AddCheck<PaymentApiHealthCheck>(
        "payment-api",
        tags: new[] { "ready" });

Then you can create different endpoints that execute different subsets of checks.

For example:

/health/live

could execute only liveness checks.

And:

/health/ready

could execute readiness checks.

Microsoft documents tags as a way to filter health checks. Microsoft Learn

15. Multiple Health Endpoints

You don't have to expose only one endpoint.

For example:

app.MapHealthChecks("/health");

app.MapHealthChecks("/health/ready");

app.MapHealthChecks("/health/live");

This is useful when different infrastructure components need different information.

Microsoft's current documentation explicitly notes that MapHealthChecks supports mapping multiple health-check endpoints with different routes/configurations. Microsoft Learn

16. UseHealthChecks() vs MapHealthChecks()

🔥 Common interview question.

MapHealthChecks()

Uses endpoint routing:

app.MapHealthChecks("/health");

Advantages:

  • endpoint-aware
  • supports endpoint metadata
  • can use authorization
  • can map multiple endpoints
  • integrates naturally with endpoint routing

UseHealthChecks()

Adds health-check middleware directly into the middleware pipeline.

app.UseHealthChecks("/health");

Microsoft describes the distinction as:

UseHealthChecks
→ middleware pipeline

MapHealthChecks
→ endpoint routing

UseHealthChecks gives you more direct control over where the health-check middleware executes, while MapHealthChecks provides endpoint-aware behavior and finer endpoint configuration. Microsoft Learn

Easy memory

UseHealthChecks()
→ Middleware

MapHealthChecks()
→ Endpoint

17. Health Checks with Docker

Docker can use a health endpoint.

For example:

HEALTHCHECK CMD curl --fail \
    http://localhost:5000/healthz || exit 1

Conceptually:

Docker
   ↓
GET /healthz
   ↓
ASP.NET Core
   ↓
Healthy?

Microsoft documents Docker's HEALTHCHECK directive with an ASP.NET Core health endpoint. Microsoft Learn

18. Health Checks with Kubernetes

In containerized environments, health checks can be used for:

Liveness Probe
Readiness Probe

Conceptually:

Kubernetes
     ↓
/health/live
     ↓
Is container alive?

Kubernetes
     ↓
/health/ready
     ↓
Can this instance receive traffic?

If readiness fails:

Instance
   ↓
Removed from traffic

If liveness continually fails:

Container
   ↓
Potential restart

The exact behavior is controlled by the orchestrator configuration.

Microsoft identifies container orchestrators and load balancers as common consumers of ASP.NET Core health endpoints. Microsoft Learn

19. Health Checks vs Monitoring

They are related but not identical.

Health Check

Answers:

"Is the application/dependency healthy right now?"
GET /health
→ Healthy

Monitoring

Collects and analyzes information over time.

Examples:

CPU
Memory
Request latency
Error rate
Throughput
Database latency

So:

Health Check
     ↓
Current health signal

Monitoring
     ↓
Historical + operational visibility

20. Health Checks vs Logging

Logging

Tells you:

What happened?

Example:

Database connection failed.

Health Check

Tells infrastructure:

Is the service currently healthy?

Example:

Unhealthy

You generally want both.

21. Important Production Rule

Don't make health checks unnecessarily expensive.

Bad:

/health
   ↓
Huge SQL query
   ↓
Multiple external APIs
   ↓
Large data processing

Now every health probe itself creates load.

Better:

/health
   ↓
Fast lightweight checks

For a database query, Microsoft recommends choosing a query that returns quickly, such as SELECT 1, if a query is needed at all. Microsoft Learn

22. Security of Health Endpoints

Don't automatically expose sensitive internal information publicly.

For example, don't return:

{
  "databasePassword": "...",
  "connectionString": "...",
  "internalServer": "..."
}

Health endpoints should expose only the information needed by the intended monitoring infrastructure.

You can also require authorization:

app.MapHealthChecks("/health")
   .RequireAuthorization();

ASP.NET Core supports authorization on MapHealthChecks endpoints. Microsoft Learn

23. Real-World Scenario — Your .NET Full Stack Application

Imagine your application:

React
  ↓
ASP.NET Core Web API
  ↓
Service Layer
  ↓
EF Core
  ↓
SQL Server

And:

Redis
External Payment API
AWS services

You could design:

/health/live

Checks:

Application process

and:

/health/ready

Checks:

SQL Server
Redis
Required external dependency

Then:

Load Balancer
      ↓
/health/ready
      ↓
Healthy?
   /     \
 Yes      No
 ↓         ↓
Traffic   No traffic

This is exactly the kind of production architecture you should be able to explain in a Senior .NET interview.

24. Common Interview Questions

Q1. What are Health Checks?

Health checks determine whether an application or its important dependencies are functioning properly.

Q2. How do you enable health checks?

builder.Services.AddHealthChecks();

app.MapHealthChecks("/health");

Q3. What is IHealthCheck?

An interface used to implement custom health-check logic.

Q4. What does CheckHealthAsync() return?

A HealthCheckResult containing a health status and optional description, exception, and data.

Q5. What are the three health statuses?

Healthy, Degraded and Unhealthy.

Q6. What is liveness?

It indicates whether the application is alive and able to run.

Q7. What is readiness?

It indicates whether the application is ready to receive traffic, usually considering required dependencies.

Q8. Why separate liveness and readiness?

Because an application can be alive but temporarily unable to serve requests correctly. Separating them allows infrastructure to distinguish "restart me" from "don't send traffic to me yet."

Q9. How do you check SQL Server health?

We can register a database health check using an appropriate provider/package or implement a custom IHealthCheck. The check should be lightweight and avoid expensive database operations.

Q10. What is MapHealthChecks()?

It exposes health checks as an endpoint using endpoint routing.

Q11. What is UseHealthChecks()?

It registers health-check handling directly into the middleware pipeline.

Q12. Can we have multiple health endpoints?

Yes. For example, separate liveness and readiness endpoints.

Q13. What are health-check tags?

Tags categorize checks so different endpoints can execute different subsets of health checks.

Q14. Can health checks use dependency injection?

Yes. Health-check implementations can receive dependencies through ASP.NET Core's DI system.

Q15. Should health checks execute expensive operations?

Generally no. Health checks should be lightweight and fast because infrastructure may call them frequently.

🎯 Strong 60-Second Interview Answer

"Health checks are used to determine whether an ASP.NET Core application and its important dependencies are functioning correctly. I can register health-check services using AddHealthChecks and expose endpoints using MapHealthChecks. For example, in a .NET Web API application, I might have a liveness endpoint that verifies the application is running and a readiness endpoint that checks dependencies such as SQL Server or Redis before allowing the instance to receive traffic. Custom checks can be implemented using IHealthCheck, which returns Healthy, Degraded or Unhealthy through HealthCheckResult. Health endpoints can be consumed by load balancers, Docker or Kubernetes and monitoring systems. I keep health checks lightweight and avoid expensive database or external-service operations. I also distinguish health checks from monitoring: health checks provide an immediate health signal, while monitoring gives broader operational visibility." Microsoft Learn

🧠 Final Mental Model

                 HEALTH CHECKS
                       │
          ┌────────────┴────────────┐
          ↓                         ↓
      Liveness                  Readiness
          ↓                         ↓
   Is app alive?             Can it serve traffic?
                                    ↓
                         ┌──────────┼──────────┐
                         ↓          ↓          ↓
                      SQL Server  Redis    External API

And:

ASP.NET Core
     │
     ├── AddHealthChecks()
     │
     ├── AddCheck<T>()
     │
     └── MapHealthChecks()
               ↓
        /health/live
        /health/ready
               ↓
       Healthy / Degraded /
          Unhealthy

One-line memory trick

Health check = "Can this application safely operate right now?"

30. Background Services / BackgroundService in ASP.NET Core

🔥 Very important for Senior .NET interviews.

Background services are used when work needs to happen outside the normal HTTP request-response flow.

Microsoft's current ASP.NET Core documentation describes hosted services as the standard mechanism for implementing background tasks, with IHostedService and the BackgroundService base class being the main abstractions. Microsoft Learn

🔴 Priority — Must Master

Focus especially on:

  1. What is a background service?
  1. IHostedService
  1. BackgroundService
  1. ExecuteAsync()
  1. StartAsync() and StopAsync()
  1. AddHostedService()
  1. CancellationToken
  1. BackgroundService + scoped services
  1. IServiceScopeFactory
  1. Timed background tasks
  1. Queued background tasks
  1. Graceful shutdown
  1. Exception handling
  1. BackgroundService vs Controller
  1. BackgroundService vs Azure Functions / Hangfire
  1. Real-world use cases

1. What is a Background Service?

A background service performs work independently of an incoming HTTP request.

Normally:

React
  ↓
HTTP Request
  ↓
Controller
  ↓
Service
  ↓
Response

But some operations don't need to keep the HTTP request waiting:

Order Created
      ↓
Return 201
      ↓
Background Service
      ↓
Send Email
      ↓
Generate Report
      ↓
Process Notification

Examples:

  • sending emails
  • processing queued messages
  • scheduled jobs
  • cleanup tasks
  • generating reports
  • processing files
  • consuming messages from a queue
  • sending notifications
  • periodic synchronization

ASP.NET Core supports these scenarios through hosted services. Microsoft Learn

2. What is IHostedService?

IHostedService is the basic interface for a service managed by the .NET host.

It has two important methods:

Task StartAsync(CancellationToken cancellationToken);

Task StopAsync(CancellationToken cancellationToken);

Conceptually:

Application starts
       ↓
StartAsync()
       ↓
Background work
       ↓
Application shutting down
       ↓
StopAsync()

Microsoft documents StartAsync and StopAsync as the lifecycle methods managed by the host. Microsoft Learn

3. What is BackgroundService?

BackgroundService is a base class that implements IHostedService and provides a simpler model for long-running background work.

You generally override:

protected override Task ExecuteAsync(
    CancellationToken stoppingToken)

Example:

public class EmailBackgroundService : BackgroundService
{
    protected override async Task ExecuteAsync(
        CancellationToken stoppingToken)
    {
        while (!stoppingToken.IsCancellationRequested)
        {
            // Background work

            await Task.Delay(
                TimeSpan.FromSeconds(10),
                stoppingToken);
        }
    }
}

Microsoft describes BackgroundService as a base class for implementing long-running IHostedService instances. Microsoft Learn

4. How do you register a BackgroundService?

Use:

builder.Services.AddHostedService<EmailBackgroundService>();

Example:

var builder = WebApplication.CreateBuilder(args);

builder.Services.AddHostedService<EmailBackgroundService>();

var app = builder.Build();

app.Run();

The host starts the registered hosted service with the application. Microsoft Learn

5. What is ExecuteAsync()?

ExecuteAsync() contains the main background-work logic.

Example:

protected override async Task ExecuteAsync(
    CancellationToken stoppingToken)
{
    while (!stoppingToken.IsCancellationRequested)
    {
        await ProcessOrders(stoppingToken);

        await Task.Delay(
            TimeSpan.FromMinutes(1),
            stoppingToken);
    }
}

Think:

ExecuteAsync()
      ↓
Run background work
      ↓
Wait
      ↓
Run again
      ↓
Wait
      ↓
...

The CancellationToken tells the service when the host is shutting down.

6. What is the CancellationToken used for?

This is extremely important.

When the application shuts down:

Application
     ↓
Shutdown requested
     ↓
CancellationToken = Cancelled
     ↓
BackgroundService stops

Example:

while (!stoppingToken.IsCancellationRequested)
{
    await ProcessData(stoppingToken);
}

And:

await Task.Delay(
    TimeSpan.FromSeconds(10),
    stoppingToken);

The background service should honor the cancellation token so shutdown can happen gracefully. Microsoft specifically recommends honoring the shutdown token promptly. Microsoft Learn

7. StartAsync() vs ExecuteAsync() vs StopAsync()

🔥 Common interview question.

StartAsync()

Called when the hosted service starts.

Application starts
       ↓
StartAsync()

It should generally contain only short startup work.

ExecuteAsync()

Contains the actual long-running background operation.

Start
 ↓
ExecuteAsync
 ↓
Long-running work

StopAsync()

Called when the application is shutting down.

Shutdown
   ↓
StopAsync()

Easy memory

StartAsync  → Start
ExecuteAsync → Work
StopAsync   → Stop

Microsoft notes that hosted services are started by the host and that long-running work belongs in the background execution path rather than making startup block unnecessarily. Microsoft Learn

8. Important .NET 10 Change

🔥 This is a useful current Senior-level detail.

Starting with .NET 10, all of BackgroundService.ExecuteAsync runs on a background thread, so synchronous code at the beginning of ExecuteAsync no longer blocks other hosted services from starting. Microsoft Learn

If you specifically need synchronous startup work that blocks other hosted services, Microsoft recommends approaches such as overriding StartAsync before calling base.StartAsync, depending on the requirement. Microsoft Learn

For interview purposes:

"In current .NET 10 behavior, ExecuteAsync runs on a background thread. If I need synchronous startup initialization to happen before other hosted services start, I would use the appropriate startup lifecycle method rather than relying on the beginning of ExecuteAsync."

9. Timed Background Service

Suppose you need to run a task every 5 minutes.

public class ReportBackgroundService : BackgroundService
{
    private readonly ILogger<ReportBackgroundService> _logger;

    public ReportBackgroundService(
        ILogger<ReportBackgroundService> logger)
    {
        _logger = logger;
    }

    protected override async Task ExecuteAsync(
        CancellationToken stoppingToken)
    {
        while (!stoppingToken.IsCancellationRequested)
        {
            _logger.LogInformation(
                "Generating reports...");

            await GenerateReports(stoppingToken);

            await Task.Delay(
                TimeSpan.FromMinutes(5),
                stoppingToken);
        }
    }

    private async Task GenerateReports(
        CancellationToken cancellationToken)
    {
        // Report processing
    }
}

This pattern is useful for simple periodic work.

Microsoft's hosted-service guidance includes timed background-task examples. Microsoft Learn

10. Why shouldn't we inject DbContext directly into a BackgroundService?

🔥 Very important interview question.

Suppose:

public class OrderBackgroundService : BackgroundService
{
    private readonly AppDbContext _context;

    public OrderBackgroundService(AppDbContext context)
    {
        _context = context;
    }
}

This is problematic because:

BackgroundService
      ↓
Long-lived

while:

DbContext
      ↓
Scoped

A hosted service does not automatically get a scope. Microsoft explicitly documents that you must create a scope when consuming scoped services from a BackgroundService. Microsoft Learn

11. Correct Way — Create a Scope

Use IServiceScopeFactory or create a scope from the service provider.

Example:

public class OrderBackgroundService : BackgroundService
{
    private readonly IServiceScopeFactory _scopeFactory;

    public OrderBackgroundService(
        IServiceScopeFactory scopeFactory)
    {
        _scopeFactory = scopeFactory;
    }

    protected override async Task ExecuteAsync(
        CancellationToken stoppingToken)
    {
        while (!stoppingToken.IsCancellationRequested)
        {
            using var scope = _scopeFactory.CreateScope();

            var service =
                scope.ServiceProvider
                    .GetRequiredService<IOrderService>();

            await service.ProcessOrders(stoppingToken);

            await Task.Delay(
                TimeSpan.FromMinutes(1),
                stoppingToken);
        }
    }
}

Architecture:

BackgroundService
       ↓
Create Scope
       ↓
IOrderService
       ↓
DbContext
       ↓
SQL Server

Microsoft's current guidance specifically demonstrates creating a scope because no scope is automatically created for a hosted service. Microsoft Learn

12. Why create a new scope for each iteration?

Suppose:

Every minute
   ↓
Process orders

You can create:

Scope 1
  ↓
DbContext 1
  ↓
Dispose

Scope 2
  ↓
DbContext 2
  ↓
Dispose

This prevents a long-running service from holding onto one scoped dependency indefinitely.

A useful mental model:

BackgroundService = long-lived

Scope = short-lived

DbContext = short-lived

13. IServiceScopeFactory vs IServiceProvider

You may see both:

IServiceScopeFactory

and:

IServiceProvider

being used to create scopes.

For example:

using var scope = _scopeFactory.CreateScope();

or:

using var scope = _services.CreateScope();

The important concept isn't the exact mechanism.

The important point is:

Create a DI scope before resolving scoped services from a BackgroundService.

Microsoft's current examples use a service provider to create the scope, while IServiceScopeFactory is also a common explicit pattern. Microsoft Learn

14. BackgroundService + EF Core

For your stack:

BackgroundService
       ↓
IServiceScopeFactory
       ↓
OrderService
       ↓
AppDbContext
       ↓
SQL Server

Example:

public class OrderProcessor : BackgroundService
{
    private readonly IServiceScopeFactory _scopeFactory;

    public OrderProcessor(
        IServiceScopeFactory scopeFactory)
    {
        _scopeFactory = scopeFactory;
    }

    protected override async Task ExecuteAsync(
        CancellationToken stoppingToken)
    {
        while (!stoppingToken.IsCancellationRequested)
        {
            using var scope = _scopeFactory.CreateScope();

            var db =
                scope.ServiceProvider
                    .GetRequiredService<AppDbContext>();

            var orders = await db.Orders
                .Where(x => !x.IsProcessed)
                .ToListAsync(stoppingToken);

            foreach (var order in orders)
            {
                order.IsProcessed = true;
            }

            await db.SaveChangesAsync(stoppingToken);

            await Task.Delay(
                TimeSpan.FromSeconds(30),
                stoppingToken);
        }
    }
}

15. BackgroundService + HttpClient

You can also call external APIs.

For your architecture:

BackgroundService
      ↓
Payment/Notification Service
      ↓
IHttpClientFactory
      ↓
External API

For example:

public class NotificationWorker : BackgroundService
{
    private readonly IHttpClientFactory _httpClientFactory;

    public NotificationWorker(
        IHttpClientFactory httpClientFactory)
    {
        _httpClientFactory = httpClientFactory;
    }

    protected override async Task ExecuteAsync(
        CancellationToken stoppingToken)
    {
        var client =
            _httpClientFactory.CreateClient("NotificationApi");

        while (!stoppingToken.IsCancellationRequested)
        {
            await client.PostAsync(
                "/notifications/process",
                null,
                stoppingToken);

            await Task.Delay(
                TimeSpan.FromMinutes(1),
                stoppingToken);
        }
    }
}

This also demonstrates why propagating the cancellation token matters.

16. Queued Background Tasks

This is a very useful production pattern.

Suppose a user creates an order:

POST /api/orders

You don't want to make the HTTP request wait for:

Email
+
Notification
+
Audit processing

Instead:

POST /api/orders
       ↓
Create Order
       ↓
Queue Background Work
       ↓
Return 201
       ↓
BackgroundService
       ↓
Process Queue

Microsoft's hosted-service guidance includes queued background tasks as a supported pattern. Microsoft Learn

17. Why use a Queue?

Imagine:

1000 orders

Each order needs an email.

Instead of:

Request
 ↓
Save order
 ↓
Send email
 ↓
Wait
 ↓
Return response

you can do:

Request
 ↓
Save order
 ↓
Queue email job
 ↓
Return response

BackgroundService
 ↓
Read queue
 ↓
Send emails

Benefits:

  • faster API response
  • decoupling
  • controlled processing
  • retry possibilities
  • better resource utilization

18. In-Memory Queue vs Message Broker

For simple applications:

ASP.NET Core
     ↓
In-memory queue
     ↓
BackgroundService

But for distributed production systems:

ASP.NET Core
     ↓
Message Broker
     ↓
Background Worker

Examples:

Azure Service Bus
AWS SQS
RabbitMQ
Kafka

Since you have experience with AWS SQS, this is particularly useful for your interviews.

You can explain:

React
 ↓
ASP.NET Core API
 ↓
Save Order
 ↓
Publish Message → SQS
 ↓
Return 201

Background Worker
 ↓
Consume SQS message
 ↓
Process order
 ↓
Send notification

This is generally more resilient than relying only on an in-memory queue because the message broker can provide durable messaging semantics depending on its configuration.

19. BackgroundService vs Controller

🔥 Common interview question.

Controller

Handles:

HTTP request
      ↓
Business logic
      ↓
HTTP response

BackgroundService

Handles:

Long-running/background work
      ↓
No direct HTTP response

Example

Controller:

POST /orders

BackgroundService:

Process pending orders

Easy rule

Controller = request-driven work.
BackgroundService = background/event/scheduled work.

20. BackgroundService vs IHostedService

IHostedService:

Interface

You implement:

StartAsync()
StopAsync()

BackgroundService:

Base class

You generally implement:

ExecuteAsync()

Mental model:

IHostedService
      ↑
BackgroundService

Use BackgroundService when you have a long-running operation and want the framework to handle much of the lifecycle implementation.

21. Graceful Shutdown

Suppose your application is running:

BackgroundService
      ↓
Processing 500 orders

Then deployment starts:

Application shutdown requested

The host signals cancellation:

CancellationToken
      ↓
Cancelled

Your service should stop accepting new work and finish/exit appropriately.

Example:

protected override async Task ExecuteAsync(
    CancellationToken stoppingToken)
{
    while (!stoppingToken.IsCancellationRequested)
    {
        await ProcessWork(stoppingToken);
    }
}

Microsoft documents graceful shutdown through StopAsync, with a cancellation token used to signal when the graceful shutdown period is ending. Microsoft Learn

22. What happens if the BackgroundService throws an exception?

This is an important production concern.

A background service should not silently fail.

Use appropriate:

Logging
+
Exception handling
+
Retry strategy
+
Monitoring

For example:

protected override async Task ExecuteAsync(
    CancellationToken stoppingToken)
{
    while (!stoppingToken.IsCancellationRequested)
    {
        try
        {
            await ProcessOrders(stoppingToken);
        }
        catch (OperationCanceledException)
            when (stoppingToken.IsCancellationRequested)
        {
            break;
        }
        catch (Exception ex)
        {
            _logger.LogError(
                ex,
                "Error processing orders.");

            await Task.Delay(
                TimeSpan.FromSeconds(10),
                stoppingToken);
        }
    }
}

The exact exception strategy depends on whether the failure is transient, permanent, or indicates the service should stop.

23. Should we use Task.Run() inside BackgroundService?

Usually, not just because it's a BackgroundService.

For I/O-bound work:

await db.SaveChangesAsync();

is preferable.

You don't normally need:

await Task.Run(() =>
    db.SaveChanges());

That simply moves synchronous work to a Thread Pool thread.

For your application:

BackgroundService
      ↓
async EF Core
      ↓
SQL Server

is the normal approach.

24. Important Mistake — async void

Avoid:

async void ProcessOrders()
{
}

Prefer:

async Task ProcessOrders()
{
}

Why?

Because Task allows:

  • awaiting
  • exception propagation
  • cancellation propagation
  • lifecycle control

25. BackgroundService + SignalR

This is another nice Senior-level scenario.

Suppose a background process detects:

New notification

It can use:

BackgroundService
      ↓
IHubContext
      ↓
SignalR Hub
      ↓
React clients

Microsoft documents injecting IHubContext into a BackgroundService to send messages from background processing. Microsoft Learn

This maps well to your experience with SignalR real-time notifications.

26. BackgroundService + AWS SQS

A very realistic example for your resume:

React
 ↓
ASP.NET Core API
 ↓
Order Service
 ↓
AWS SQS
 ↓
Background Worker
 ↓
Process Message
 ↓
AWS SNS / Email

The API doesn't need to wait for notification processing.

API
 ↓
SQS
 ↓
201 Created

Then:

BackgroundService
 ↓
Consume SQS
 ↓
Process
 ↓
SNS notification

This is a strong architecture example to discuss in a Senior interview.

27. When should you NOT use BackgroundService?

Don't automatically put every background task inside ASP.NET Core.

For critical workloads requiring:

  • durable job storage
  • complex scheduling
  • retries
  • distributed execution
  • persistence across application restarts
  • advanced monitoring

you may consider dedicated infrastructure such as:

Azure Functions
AWS Lambda
Hangfire
Quartz.NET
Azure Service Bus
AWS SQS
RabbitMQ
Kafka

The right choice depends on workload and operational requirements.

28. BackgroundService Lifecycle

Remember:

Application starts
       ↓
DI creates hosted service
       ↓
StartAsync()
       ↓
ExecuteAsync()
       ↓
Long-running processing
       ↓
Shutdown requested
       ↓
CancellationToken cancelled
       ↓
StopAsync()
       ↓
Dispose

The hosted service is activated at application startup and participates in graceful application shutdown. Microsoft Learn

29. Common Interview Questions

Q1. What is BackgroundService?

BackgroundService is a base class for implementing long-running hosted services in .NET/ASP.NET Core.

Q2. What is IHostedService?

It is the basic interface for services managed by the .NET host and exposes StartAsync and StopAsync.

Q3. How do you register a BackgroundService?

builder.Services.AddHostedService<MyBackgroundService>();

Q4. Which method do you normally override?

ExecuteAsync(CancellationToken)

Q5. Why is CancellationToken important?

It allows the background service to respond to application shutdown and cancel ongoing asynchronous operations.

Q6. Can BackgroundService use scoped services?

Yes, but a hosted service doesn't automatically receive a DI scope. I create a scope and resolve scoped services such as DbContext inside that scope.

Q7. Can we inject DbContext directly?

We should not treat the BackgroundService itself as a request scope. Since DbContext is normally scoped, I create a scope and resolve it inside that scope.

Q8. Why create a new scope?

To correctly manage the lifetime of scoped dependencies and dispose them after the unit of work.

Q9. Difference between BackgroundService and Controller?

Controller handles HTTP requests; BackgroundService handles long-running or scheduled background work.

Q10. Can BackgroundService process queues?

Yes. It can process in-memory queues or consume messages from external brokers such as AWS SQS, Azure Service Bus or RabbitMQ.

Q11. Can BackgroundService use SignalR?

Yes. For example, it can inject IHubContext and send real-time notifications to connected clients. Microsoft Learn

Q12. What happens during application shutdown?

The host signals cancellation, the background service should honor the token, and the host waits for the hosted service to stop gracefully.

Q13. Should you use Task.Run inside BackgroundService?

Not merely to make I/O asynchronous. For I/O operations I prefer native asynchronous APIs such as EF Core async methods or HttpClient async methods.

Q14. What is a common BackgroundService mistake?

Injecting a scoped service such as DbContext directly into a long-lived hosted service instead of creating a scope.

Q15. When would you use a message broker instead?
