34. ASP.NET Core Testing & Unit/Integration Testing

For your 3+ years .NET / ASP.NET Core profile, testing is an important Senior Developer topic. You should be comfortable explaining unit tests, mocks, integration tests, controller/service testing, EF Core testing, API testing, code coverage, and CI/CD test execution.

Microsoft currently distinguishes unit tests, integration tests, and load tests. Unit tests focus on isolated code under your control, while integration tests verify multiple components working together. Microsoft Learn

🔴 Must Master

  1. What is unit testing?
  1. What is integration testing?
  1. Unit vs integration testing
  1. Arrange-Act-Assert
  1. xUnit
  1. [Fact] vs [Theory]
  1. Assertions
  1. Mocking
  1. Moq
  1. Mock vs Stub vs Fake
  1. Testing services
  1. Testing controllers
  1. Testing exceptions
  1. Testing async methods
  1. Testing EF Core
  1. WebApplicationFactory
  1. TestServer
  1. API integration testing
  1. Test database
  1. Code coverage
  1. Test isolation
  1. Testing authentication/authorization
  1. CI/CD test execution
  1. Unit-test best practices

1. What is Unit Testing?

A unit test tests a small, isolated piece of application logic.

Usually:

One class
   ↓
One method
   ↓
Expected behavior

Example:

public decimal CalculateDiscount(decimal price)
{
    return price * 0.10m;
}

Test:

[Fact]
public void CalculateDiscount_Returns10Percent()
{
    var service = new DiscountService();

    var result = service.CalculateDiscount(100);

    Assert.Equal(10, result);
}

The test doesn't need:

  • SQL Server
  • HTTP
  • filesystem
  • Redis
  • external APIs

Microsoft defines unit tests as tests of individual software components/methods and recommends keeping infrastructure concerns outside unit tests. Microsoft Learn

2. What is Integration Testing?

Integration testing verifies that multiple components work together.

For example:

HTTP Request
     ↓
Middleware
     ↓
Routing
     ↓
Controller
     ↓
Service
     ↓
EF Core
     ↓
Database

An integration test can test this flow instead of mocking every layer.

Example

GET /api/products/10

Then verify:

HTTP Status = 200
Response JSON = expected product

Microsoft describes integration tests as testing two or more components working together, often including infrastructure such as databases, filesystems, networking, and the request-response pipeline. Microsoft Learn

3. Unit Test vs Integration Test

Unit TestIntegration Test
Tests isolated componentTests multiple components
Usually mocks dependenciesUses real/integrated components
Very fastUsually slower
No real DB requiredMay use test DB
Easy to run frequentlyMore infrastructure
Tests business logicTests integration behavior

Easy interview answer

Unit tests verify isolated business logic, while integration tests verify that multiple parts of the application work correctly together. Unit tests are faster and usually use mocks or fakes, whereas integration tests use a broader application setup and may involve databases, HTTP pipelines or other infrastructure.

Microsoft specifically recommends using unit tests for routine logic and keeping integration tests focused on important infrastructure scenarios because integration tests require more processing and are slower. Microsoft Learn

4. What is AAA Pattern?

AAA means:

Arrange
Act
Assert

Arrange

Prepare the test.

var service = new ProductService();

Act

Execute the operation.

var result = service.GetProductName(10);

Assert

Verify the result.

Assert.Equal("Laptop", result);

Complete example

[Fact]
public void GetProductName_ReturnsExpectedName()
{
    // Arrange
    var service = new ProductService();

    // Act
    var result = service.GetProductName(10);

    // Assert
    Assert.Equal("Laptop", result);
}

Memory trick

Prepare → Execute → Verify

5. Why do we use xUnit?

xUnit is a popular testing framework for .NET.

Typical test project:

MyApplication
MyApplication.Tests

Example:

public class ProductServiceTests
{
    [Fact]
    public void Test1()
    {
        // test
    }
}

You can execute tests using:

dotnet test

The .NET CLI supports running tests and is suitable for CI/CD automation. Microsoft Learn

6. [Fact] vs [Theory]

[Fact]

Used for a test with a fixed scenario.

[Fact]
public void Add_ReturnsCorrectResult()
{
    Assert.Equal(5, 2 + 3);
}

[Theory]

Used when the same test should run with different inputs.

[Theory]
[InlineData(2, 3, 5)]
[InlineData(5, 5, 10)]
[InlineData(10, 20, 30)]
public void Add_ReturnsCorrectResult(
    int a,
    int b,
    int expected)
{
    var result = a + b;

    Assert.Equal(expected, result);
}

Interview answer

[Fact] is generally used for a single fixed test case, while [Theory] allows the same test logic to execute with multiple sets of input data.

7. What is Mocking?

Suppose your service depends on a repository:

ProductService
      ↓
IProductRepository
      ↓
SQL Server

When unit testing ProductService, you don't necessarily want to access SQL Server.

So you replace the real repository with a mock:

ProductService
      ↓
Mock<IProductRepository>

Now the test controls what the repository returns.

8. Example using Moq

Suppose:

public interface IProductRepository
{
    Task<Product?> GetByIdAsync(int id);
}

Service:

public class ProductService
{
    private readonly IProductRepository _repository;

    public ProductService(IProductRepository repository)
    {
        _repository = repository;
    }

    public async Task<Product?> GetProductAsync(int id)
    {
        return await _repository.GetByIdAsync(id);
    }
}

Test:

[Fact]
public async Task GetProductAsync_ReturnsProduct()
{
    // Arrange
    var mockRepository = new Mock<IProductRepository>();

    mockRepository
        .Setup(x => x.GetByIdAsync(10))
        .ReturnsAsync(new Product
        {
            Id = 10,
            Name = "Laptop"
        });

    var service = new ProductService(
        mockRepository.Object);

    // Act
    var result = await service.GetProductAsync(10);

    // Assert
    Assert.NotNull(result);
    Assert.Equal("Laptop", result!.Name);
}

Here:

Real Repository ❌
SQL Server ❌

Mock Repository ✅

9. Mock vs Stub vs Fake

This is a common conceptual question.

Mock

Used to configure behavior and often verify interactions.

"Was GetByIdAsync called?"

Stub

Provides predetermined data.

"Whenever GetByIdAsync(10) is called, return Product 10."

Fake

A lightweight working implementation.

Example:

InMemoryProductRepository

instead of:

SQLProductRepository

Easy interview answer

A stub mainly provides controlled test data, a mock can also verify interactions, and a fake is a lightweight working implementation used instead of the real dependency.

10. Should we mock everything?

No.

This is an important senior-level point.

Don't write:

Mock Controller
Mock Service
Mock Repository
Mock DbContext
Mock Logger
Mock Configuration
Mock Everything

just to make the test pass.

Mock the dependency that is outside the unit you're testing or whose real implementation would introduce unwanted infrastructure/external behavior.

Better

For:

ProductService

mock:

IProductRepository

and test the actual:

ProductService

11. How do you unit test a Service Layer?

Suppose your architecture is:

Controller
    ↓
ProductService
    ↓
Repository

For a service unit test:

Actual ProductService
        ↓
Mock Repository

You test:

  • business rules
  • validation
  • branching
  • calculations
  • error handling
  • dependency interactions

You don't test SQL Server here.

12. How do you test a Controller?

Suppose:

[HttpGet("{id}")]
public async Task<ActionResult<ProductDto>> Get(int id)
{
    var product = await _service.GetAsync(id);

    if (product == null)
        return NotFound();

    return Ok(product);
}

A controller unit test can mock the service:

Controller
    ↓
Mock ProductService

Test:

Service returns product
       ↓
Expected 200 OK

and:

Service returns null
       ↓
Expected 404 NotFound

Important

You're testing controller behavior—not the service's internal implementation.

13. How do you test exceptions?

Suppose:

public void ProcessOrder()
{
    throw new InvalidOperationException();
}

Test:

[Fact]
public void ProcessOrder_ThrowsException()
{
    var service = new OrderService();

    Assert.Throws<InvalidOperationException>(
        () => service.ProcessOrder());
}

For async:

[Fact]
public async Task ProcessOrderAsync_ThrowsException()
{
    var service = new OrderService();

    await Assert.ThrowsAsync<InvalidOperationException>(
        () => service.ProcessOrderAsync());
}

14. How do you test async methods?

Use async test methods:

[Fact]
public async Task GetProduct_ReturnsProduct()
{
    // Arrange
    ...

    // Act
    var result = await service.GetProductAsync(10);

    // Assert
    Assert.NotNull(result);
}

Avoid:

var result = service.GetProductAsync(10).Result;

The same principle applies to testing as to application code:

Async code should be awaited asynchronously.

15. What is WebApplicationFactory?

This is one of the most important ASP.NET Core integration-testing questions.

WebApplicationFactory<TEntryPoint> helps bootstrap your ASP.NET Core application in a test environment and provides a test server/client for making requests.

Microsoft's current integration-testing documentation uses:

WebApplicationFactory<Program>

to bootstrap the application and create a TestServer/HttpClient. Microsoft Learn

Conceptually:

Test
 ↓
WebApplicationFactory
 ↓
ASP.NET Core Application
 ↓
TestServer
 ↓
HttpClient
 ↓
API Endpoint

16. Example Integration Test

public class ProductApiTests
    : IClassFixture<WebApplicationFactory<Program>>
{
    private readonly HttpClient _client;

    public ProductApiTests(
        WebApplicationFactory<Program> factory)
    {
        _client = factory.CreateClient();
    }

    [Fact]
    public async Task GetProduct_ReturnsSuccess()
    {
        // Act
        var response =
            await _client.GetAsync("/api/products/10");

        // Assert
        response.EnsureSuccessStatusCode();
    }
}

Microsoft's current example follows this same WebApplicationFactory<Program> + CreateClient() approach. Microsoft Learn

17. What is TestServer?

TestServer provides an in-memory test host for ASP.NET Core integration testing.

Think:

Normal:
React
 ↓
Network
 ↓
Kestrel
 ↓
API

Integration test:

Test
 ↓
HttpClient
 ↓
TestServer
 ↓
API

The request can exercise the actual ASP.NET Core application pipeline.

18. What should an ASP.NET Core integration test verify?

For example:

GET /api/products/10

You can verify:

✓ Routing
✓ Middleware
✓ Authentication
✓ Authorization
✓ Controller
✓ Model binding
✓ Service
✓ Repository
✓ Database interaction
✓ HTTP status
✓ Response body

That's why integration tests are broader than unit tests.

19. How do you test a database-dependent API?

You have several options depending on the test's purpose.

Option 1 — Real test database

Integration Test
       ↓
Test SQL Server

Good for realistic database behavior.

Option 2 — SQLite

Useful for lightweight database integration tests.

Option 3 — EF Core InMemory provider

Useful for some basic tests, but it does not behave like a relational SQL Server database.

Microsoft's current integration-testing guidance notes that the EF Core InMemory provider is suitable only for limited/basic testing and recommends SQLite when an in-memory relational database is appropriate. Microsoft Learn

Interview answer

I wouldn't assume EF Core InMemory behaves exactly like SQL Server. For tests where relational database behavior matters, I'd prefer a more representative test database or SQLite where appropriate.

20. How can we replace the production database during integration testing?

With WebApplicationFactory, you can customize the application services used by the test host.

Conceptually:

Production
DbContext → SQL Server

Test
DbContext → Test Database

Microsoft's integration-test documentation specifically demonstrates replacing the application's database registration inside ConfigureServices when customizing WebApplicationFactory. Microsoft Learn

21. What is Test Isolation?

Tests should not depend on another test's state.

Bad:

Test A inserts Product 10
        ↓
Test B expects Product 10

If Test A doesn't run:

Test B fails

Better:

Test A → Arrange own data
Test B → Arrange own data
Test C → Arrange own data

Principle

Each test should be independently executable.

22. What is code coverage?

Code coverage tells you how much of your code is exercised by tests.

Common measurements:

Line coverage
Branch coverage
Method coverage

Example:

Application code
1000 lines

Tests execute
800 lines

Coverage ≈ 80%

But:

80% coverage does not automatically mean 80% quality.

You can have high coverage with weak assertions.

Better principle

Measure coverage, but focus on meaningful behavior and important business scenarios.

23. What should you test?

For your application:

ProductService

test:

✓ Product exists
✓ Product doesn't exist
✓ Invalid input
✓ Business rule
✓ Exception
✓ Dependency failure

For:

ProductController

test:

✓ 200 OK
✓ 404 NotFound
✓ 400 BadRequest
✓ Correct response

For:

Product API

integration test:

✓ Routing
✓ Authentication
✓ Authorization
✓ Database
✓ HTTP response

24. How do you test authentication?

Integration tests are particularly useful here.

For example:

GET /api/admin/users

Test:

No token
   ↓
401

Authenticated normal user:

Valid token
   ↓
No Admin permission
   ↓
403

Admin:

Valid token
+
Admin role
   ↓
200

This verifies the actual authentication/authorization pipeline rather than merely testing controller code in isolation.

Microsoft's integration test guidance includes authentication testing scenarios using test authentication handlers. Microsoft Learn

25. How would you test your real-world API?

Suppose you have:

React
 ↓
ASP.NET Core
 ↓
ProductController
 ↓
ProductService
 ↓
EF Core
 ↓
SQL Server

Unit tests

ProductService
      ↓
Mock Repository

Test:

Business logic

Controller tests

ProductController
      ↓
Mock ProductService

Test:

HTTP result mapping

Integration tests

HttpClient
    ↓
WebApplicationFactory
    ↓
ASP.NET Core
    ↓
Service
    ↓
EF Core
    ↓
Test DB

Test:

Complete request flow

26. What is the testing pyramid?

Think:

                 /\
                /  \
               / E2E\
              /------\
             / Integr.\
            /----------\
           / Unit Tests \
          /--------------\

Generally:

Many unit tests
        ↓
Fewer integration tests
        ↓
Small number of end-to-end tests

Why?

Unit
✓ Fast
✓ Cheap
✓ Isolated

Integration
✓ More realistic
✗ Slower

E2E
✓ Most realistic
✗ Most expensive/fragile

Microsoft similarly recommends keeping integration tests focused because they require more processing than unit tests. Microsoft Learn

27. What is TDD?

TDD = Test-Driven Development

Typical cycle:

Red
 ↓
Write failing test

Green
 ↓
Write minimum code to pass

Refactor
 ↓
Improve code
RED → GREEN → REFACTOR

Microsoft describes TDD as writing the unit test before the code it is intended to verify. Microsoft Learn

You don't need to claim that you use strict TDD if you don't. In interviews, answer based on your actual experience.

28. How do you run tests in CI/CD?

For your Azure DevOps experience:

Developer
    ↓
Git Push
    ↓
Azure DevOps Pipeline
    ↓
Restore
    ↓
Build
    ↓
Unit Tests
    ↓
Integration Tests
    ↓
Code Coverage
    ↓
Deploy

Typical command:

dotnet test

The .NET CLI supports test execution and is designed to work in automated CI/CD workflows. Microsoft Learn

29. What makes a good unit test?

A good test should be:

Fast

milliseconds

Independent

Doesn't depend on another test

Deterministic

Same input → same result

Focused

Tests one behavior

Readable

The test itself should explain the expected behavior.

Stable

Don't make tests depend unnecessarily on:

  • current time
  • random values
  • external APIs
  • production database
  • network.

30. Common testing mistakes

❌ Testing implementation instead of behavior

Bad:

Verify private internal method calls

Better:

Verify observable behavior

❌ Excessive mocking

Mock everything

This can produce tests that don't give much confidence.

❌ Integration tests for every scenario

This makes the suite slow.

Use unit tests for routine business logic and targeted integration tests for important integration behavior. Microsoft Learn

❌ Weak assertions

Bad:

Assert.NotNull(result);

when you should verify:

Assert.Equal("Laptop", result.Name);
Assert.Equal(10, result.Id);

❌ Shared mutable test data

One test changes data that another test depends on.

⭐ Strong 60-Second Interview Answer

"In my ASP.NET Core applications, I use both unit and integration testing. For unit tests, I isolate individual components such as services and use mocks for external dependencies like repositories or external APIs. I generally follow the Arrange, Act and Assert pattern and use xUnit with Moq where mocking is required. For example, when testing a ProductService, I can mock the repository and verify business rules without connecting to SQL Server. For integration testing, I use ASP.NET Core's WebApplicationFactory to bootstrap the application and create an HttpClient, allowing me to test the actual request pipeline, routing, controllers, services and database integration. I keep unit tests fast and numerous, while using focused integration tests for important infrastructure and end-to-end behaviors. I also run the tests through the CI/CD pipeline using dotnet test and monitor meaningful code coverage." Microsoft Learn

🧠 Final Mental Model

ASP.NET Core Testing
│
├── Unit Testing
│   ├── Isolated
│   ├── xUnit
│   ├── AAA
│   ├── Mock
│   └── Moq
│
├── Controller Testing
│   ├── Mock Service
│   └── Verify HTTP Result
│
├── Service Testing
│   ├── Mock Dependencies
│   └── Verify Business Logic
│
├── Integration Testing
│   ├── WebApplicationFactory
│   ├── TestServer
│   ├── HttpClient
│   └── Test Database
│
├── API Testing
│   ├── Authentication
│   ├── Authorization
│   ├── Routing
│   └── HTTP Responses
│
└── CI/CD
    ├── dotnet test
    ├── Coverage
    └── Pipeline

🔥 Remember this

Unit test = Isolate the logic.

Integration test = Verify components work together.

WebApplicationFactory = Test the ASP.NET Core application through HTTP.

Mock = Replace an external dependency.

AAA = Arrange → Act → Assert.

CI/CD = Run tests automatically before deployment.

Next: Topic 35 — ASP.NET Core Clean Architecture.

35. ASP.NET Core Clean Architecture

This is a high-priority Senior .NET interview topic, especially when the interviewer asks:

  • "How do you structure a large ASP.NET Core application?"
  • "How do you separate business logic from infrastructure?"
  • "Explain Clean Architecture."
  • "Why shouldn't your business layer depend directly on EF Core?"
  • "How does Dependency Inversion apply to Clean Architecture?"

Microsoft describes Clean Architecture as an approach where the business/application model is at the center, while infrastructure and UI depend on the core rather than the core depending on infrastructure. Microsoft Learn

🔴 Must Master

  1. What is Clean Architecture?
  1. Why do we need it?
  1. Layers of Clean Architecture
  1. Dependency rule
  1. Dependency Inversion Principle
  1. Domain vs Application layer
  1. Infrastructure layer
  1. Presentation/API layer
  1. Entities
  1. Interfaces
  1. Repository pattern
  1. DTOs
  1. Dependency Injection
  1. Why Application shouldn't depend on Infrastructure
  1. Project references
  1. Testing benefits
  1. Clean Architecture vs 3-tier/N-tier
  1. Clean Architecture vs MVC
  1. Where should business logic go?
  1. Where should EF Core go?
  1. Where should interfaces go?
  1. Where should DTOs go?
  1. Real-world ASP.NET Core structure
  1. Common Clean Architecture mistakes

1. What is Clean Architecture?

Clean Architecture is an architectural approach that separates an application into layers with clearly defined responsibilities and dependency direction.

The key idea is:

Business logic should not depend on implementation details such as databases, frameworks, or external services.

Instead:

Infrastructure
      ↓
Application / Domain Core
      ↑
      │
     API

More precisely, dependencies point toward the inner core.

Microsoft describes the Application Core as having no dependency on other application layers, while UI and Infrastructure depend on the Application Core. Microsoft Learn

2. Why do we need Clean Architecture?

Imagine a large application where everything is inside controllers:

Controller
   ↓
Business Logic
   ↓
EF Core
   ↓
SQL Server
   ↓
Email
   ↓
External API

Eventually controllers become huge:

ProductController.cs
    3000 lines

This creates:

  • tight coupling
  • difficult testing
  • difficult maintenance
  • difficult replacement of infrastructure
  • duplicated business logic
  • unclear responsibilities.

Clean Architecture separates those responsibilities.

3. The Four Main Layers

For your ASP.NET Core application, think:

┌──────────────────────────────┐
│        Presentation          │
│      ASP.NET Core API        │
└──────────────┬───────────────┘
               ↓
┌──────────────────────────────┐
│         Application          │
│ Use Cases / Services / DTOs  │
│ Interfaces                   │
└──────────────┬───────────────┘
               ↓
┌──────────────────────────────┐
│            Domain            │
│ Entities / Business Rules    │
└──────────────────────────────┘

Infrastructure
      ↓
implements Application interfaces

A common project structure is:

MyApp.Domain
MyApp.Application
MyApp.Infrastructure
MyApp.API
MyApp.Tests

Microsoft's guidance similarly describes separate Application Core, Infrastructure, and UI projects for non-trivial applications. Microsoft Learn

4. Domain Layer

The Domain contains the core business model and rules.

Examples:

Entities
Value Objects
Domain Services
Business Rules
Domain Events
Exceptions

For example:

public class Order
{
    public int Id { get; private set; }

    public decimal Total { get; private set; }

    public void ApplyDiscount(decimal percentage)
    {
        if (percentage < 0 || percentage > 50)
            throw new InvalidOperationException(
                "Invalid discount.");

        Total -= Total * percentage / 100;
    }
}

The important point:

This business rule doesn't need to know about SQL Server or ASP.NET Core.

Microsoft's Application Core guidance includes entities, aggregates, domain services, interfaces, specifications, domain events and custom exceptions among the types that belong in the core. Microsoft Learn

5. Application Layer

The Application layer contains application use cases.

For example:

CreateOrder
GetOrder
UpdateOrder
CancelOrder
ApproveOrder

It coordinates the business operation.

Example:

public class CreateOrderService
{
    private readonly IOrderRepository _repository;

    public CreateOrderService(
        IOrderRepository repository)
    {
        _repository = repository;
    }

    public async Task CreateAsync(
        CreateOrderRequest request)
    {
        var order = new Order();

        // Business/application workflow

        await _repository.AddAsync(order);
    }
}

Notice:

Application
     ↓
IOrderRepository

not:

Application
     ↓
OrderRepository
     ↓
EF Core

The Application layer depends on the abstraction, not the implementation.

6. Infrastructure Layer

Infrastructure contains implementation details.

Examples:

EF Core
DbContext
Repositories
Dapper
SQL Server
Redis
AWS
Azure
Email
File System
External APIs

For example:

public class OrderRepository : IOrderRepository
{
    private readonly AppDbContext _context;

    public OrderRepository(AppDbContext context)
    {
        _context = context;
    }

    public async Task AddAsync(Order order)
    {
        await _context.Orders.AddAsync(order);
        await _context.SaveChangesAsync();
    }
}

Here:

OrderRepository
     ↓
EF Core
     ↓
SQL Server

Microsoft specifically places EF Core DbContext, migrations and data-access implementations in the Infrastructure project. Microsoft Learn

7. Presentation/API Layer

This is your ASP.NET Core project.

It contains:

Controllers
Middleware
Filters
API configuration
Authentication
Authorization
Dependency Injection setup
Program.cs

Example:

[ApiController]
[Route("api/orders")]
public class OrdersController : ControllerBase
{
    private readonly IOrderService _service;

    public OrdersController(IOrderService service)
    {
        _service = service;
    }

    [HttpPost]
    public async Task<IActionResult> Create(
        CreateOrderRequest request)
    {
        await _service.CreateAsync(request);

        return Ok();
    }
}

The controller should primarily handle HTTP concerns.

8. The Most Important Rule — Dependency Direction

This is the #1 Clean Architecture interview question.

Wrong

Domain
   ↓
EF Core
   ↓
SQL Server

The business logic is now coupled to infrastructure.

Better

        Domain
          ↑
     Application
          ↑
   Infrastructure

and:

Presentation
      ↓
Application
      ↓
Domain

Infrastructure implements interfaces defined by the inner layers.

Microsoft describes this as dependency inversion: infrastructure and implementation details depend on the Application Core rather than the core depending on them. Microsoft Learn

9. Why use interfaces?

Suppose Application defines:

public interface IOrderRepository
{
    Task<Order?> GetByIdAsync(int id);
}

Infrastructure implements:

public class OrderRepository : IOrderRepository
{
    // EF Core implementation
}

Now Application doesn't care whether the implementation uses:

EF Core
Dapper
SQL
MongoDB
Web API
Mock

The Application layer only knows:

IOrderRepository

That's loose coupling.

10. How does Dependency Injection connect everything?

This is where ASP.NET Core DI becomes important.

Suppose:

Application
IOrderRepository

and:

Infrastructure
OrderRepository

In Program.cs:

builder.Services.AddScoped<
    IOrderRepository,
    OrderRepository>();

Then:

Controller
   ↓
IOrderService
   ↓
IOrderRepository
   ↓
OrderRepository
   ↓
DbContext

At compile time, Application only knows the interface.

At runtime, ASP.NET Core DI supplies the Infrastructure implementation.

Microsoft's ASP.NET Core architecture guidance explicitly describes this runtime wiring through dependency injection. Microsoft Learn

11. Where should EF Core go?

Generally:

Infrastructure
    ↓
EF Core
    ↓
DbContext

Not:

Domain
    ↓
DbContext

and ideally not directly inside business/application logic.

For example:

MyApp.Infrastructure
│
├── Persistence
│   ├── AppDbContext.cs
│   ├── Configurations
│   └── Migrations
│
└── Repositories
    └── OrderRepository.cs

This keeps database implementation details outside the core.

12. Where should business logic go?

This is another common interview question.

❌ Don't put complex business logic in Controller

[HttpPost]
public IActionResult Create(...)
{
    // 100 lines of business rules
}

Better

Controller
    ↓
Application Service / Use Case
    ↓
Domain

For example:

OrdersController
      ↓
CreateOrderHandler
      ↓
Order domain
      ↓
IOrderRepository

The controller handles HTTP.

The application layer coordinates the use case.

The domain owns core business rules.

13. Where should DTOs go?

DTO placement depends on architecture and the type of DTO.

For API-specific request/response DTOs, a common choice is:

Application
   ↓
DTOs

or an API/presentation contract project if those DTOs are strictly transport-specific.

Example:

public class ProductDto
{
    public int Id { get; set; }

    public string Name { get; set; } = "";

    public decimal Price { get; set; }
}

The important architectural rule is:

Don't expose your EF Core entity model directly as your public API contract when that creates unwanted coupling.

14. Entity vs DTO

Entity

Represents domain/business state.

Order
Product
Customer

DTO

Represents data crossing a boundary.

CreateOrderRequest
OrderResponse
ProductDto

Think:

Entity
   ↓
Domain model

DTO
   ↓
Boundary/API contract

15. What happens when React calls your API?

For your stack:

React + TypeScript
        ↓
HTTP
        ↓
ASP.NET Core Controller
        ↓
Application Service
        ↓
Domain Rules
        ↓
Repository Interface
        ↓
Infrastructure Repository
        ↓
EF Core
        ↓
SQL Server

Response:

SQL Server
    ↓
EF Core
    ↓
Repository
    ↓
Application
    ↓
DTO
    ↓
Controller
    ↓
JSON
    ↓
React

This is the architecture you should be able to draw during an interview.

16. Clean Architecture vs 3-Tier Architecture

Very common question.

Traditional 3-tier

Presentation
     ↓
Business Logic
     ↓
Data Access

Typically dependencies flow downward.

Clean Architecture

       Domain
         ↑
    Application
         ↑
 Infrastructure
         ↑
   Presentation

The key difference isn't simply "more layers."

The major difference is dependency direction and protection of the core business logic.

Microsoft notes that traditional layered architectures separate concerns, while Clean Architecture uses dependency inversion so infrastructure depends on the application core. Microsoft Learn

17. Clean Architecture vs MVC

These are not competing alternatives.

MVC

A presentation/application framework pattern:

Model
View
Controller

Clean Architecture

An overall application architecture:

Domain
Application
Infrastructure
Presentation

Your ASP.NET Core controller can still use MVC/Web API concepts inside Clean Architecture.

For example:

Clean Architecture
│
├── Domain
├── Application
├── Infrastructure
└── API
      └── ASP.NET Core Controllers

18. Clean Architecture vs Microservices

Also not the same thing.

Clean Architecture

Concerned primarily with:

Code organization
Dependencies
Separation of concerns
Testability

Microservices

Concerned primarily with:

Service boundaries
Independent deployment
Distributed architecture
Data ownership
Scaling

You can have:

Clean Architecture + Monolith

or:

Clean Architecture + Microservices

Microsoft's architecture guidance explicitly describes Clean Architecture as applicable to monolithic applications, while microservices represent a separate distributed architectural style. Microsoft Learn

19. Example Project Structure

For your .NET application, a practical structure could be:

MyCompany.Product
│
├── MyCompany.Product.API
│   ├── Controllers
│   ├── Middleware
│   ├── Filters
│   ├── Program.cs
│   └── appsettings.json
│
├── MyCompany.Product.Application
│   ├── Interfaces
│   ├── Services
│   ├── DTOs
│   ├── Features
│   └── Validators
│
├── MyCompany.Product.Domain
│   ├── Entities
│   ├── ValueObjects
│   ├── DomainServices
│   ├── Events
│   └── Exceptions
│
├── MyCompany.Product.Infrastructure
│   ├── Persistence
│   │   ├── AppDbContext.cs
│   │   ├── Configurations
│   │   └── Migrations
│   ├── Repositories
│   ├── ExternalServices
│   └── DependencyInjection.cs
│
└── MyCompany.Product.Tests
    ├── Unit
    └── Integration

This goes beyond merely organizing folders: separate projects can enforce clearer boundaries and encapsulation. Microsoft recommends separate libraries for UI, Infrastructure and Application Core in non-trivial applications. Microsoft Learn

20. How does testing benefit from Clean Architecture?

This is a major advantage.

Suppose:

Application
   ↓
IOrderRepository

You can unit test the application without SQL Server:

OrderService
    ↓
Mock IOrderRepository

Therefore:

No database
No network
No external API
        ↓
Fast unit tests

Microsoft specifically notes that because Application Core doesn't depend on Infrastructure, it is easier to unit test in isolation; Infrastructure implementations can instead be covered with integration tests. Microsoft Learn

21. What if tomorrow we replace EF Core with Dapper?

Without good separation:

Business Logic
      ↓
EF Core

You may need to modify business code.

With Clean Architecture:

Application
     ↓
IProductRepository
     ↑
     │
 ┌───┴─────┐
 │         │
EF Core   Dapper

The application contract remains:

IProductRepository

Only Infrastructure changes.

22. Is Repository Pattern mandatory in Clean Architecture?

No.

This is an important nuance.

Clean Architecture requires dependency boundaries and appropriate abstractions, not necessarily a repository around every DbSet.

For simple applications, adding:

Controller
 ↓
Service
 ↓
Repository
 ↓
DbContext

to every operation can create unnecessary abstraction.

For more complex domains, repositories can be useful for encapsulating persistence concerns.

Interview answer

Repository isn't mandatory just because we're using Clean Architecture. I use abstractions where they provide a meaningful boundary, especially around infrastructure or domain-specific persistence behavior. I avoid creating unnecessary pass-through repositories that only wrap EF Core without adding value.

23. What are common Clean Architecture mistakes?

❌ Mistake 1 — Domain depends on EF Core

Domain
 ↓
EF Core

This couples business logic to infrastructure.

❌ Mistake 2 — Controllers contain business logic

Controller
 ↓
1000 lines of business rules

Keep controllers thin.

❌ Mistake 3 — Application directly uses DbContext

Application
 ↓
DbContext

This couples Application to EF Core infrastructure.

❌ Mistake 4 — Everything becomes an interface

Don't create interfaces simply for the sake of creating interfaces.

❌ Mistake 5 — Generic repository everywhere

IGenericRepository<T>

for every entity without meaningful behavior can add abstraction without much benefit.

❌ Mistake 6 — Too many projects

Architecture should reduce complexity, not create unnecessary complexity.

24. Is Clean Architecture always the best choice?

No architecture is automatically appropriate for every application.

For a tiny CRUD API:

One project
Controllers
Services
DbContext

may be completely reasonable.

For a large business application with:

  • complex business rules
  • multiple integrations
  • significant testing requirements
  • multiple teams
  • long-term maintenance

strong architectural boundaries become more valuable.

Microsoft's guidance notes that simple applications can use a single project, while non-trivial applications benefit from logical separation and separate projects. Microsoft Learn

⭐ Strong 60-Second Interview Answer

"Clean Architecture is an approach I use to separate business logic from infrastructure and presentation concerns. I typically structure an ASP.NET Core application into Domain, Application, Infrastructure and API layers. The Domain contains entities and core business rules. The Application layer contains use cases, DTOs and interfaces for infrastructure operations. Infrastructure contains implementations such as EF Core, repositories, SQL Server, external APIs and other integrations. The API layer contains controllers and HTTP-specific concerns. The key principle is dependency inversion: the inner business layers should not depend on infrastructure implementations. For example, the Application layer can define an IProductRepository, while Infrastructure implements it using EF Core. ASP.NET Core dependency injection wires the implementation at runtime. This separation makes the application easier to test, maintain and evolve because infrastructure implementations can be replaced without changing the core business logic." Microsoft Learn

36. SOLID Principles in ASP.NET Core

SOLID is very important for Senior .NET interviews, especially when discussing Clean Architecture, DI, maintainability, testing, and design decisions.

Microsoft's ASP.NET Core guidance explicitly connects DI with loose coupling, testability, and the Dependency Inversion Principle, and notes that classes with too many dependencies can indicate a violation of Single Responsibility Principle. Microsoft Learn

🔴 Priority: MUST MASTER

You should be able to explain these 5 principles with an ASP.NET Core example:

  1. S — Single Responsibility Principle
  1. O — Open/Closed Principle
  1. L — Liskov Substitution Principle
  1. I — Interface Segregation Principle
  1. D — Dependency Inversion Principle

Easy memory trick

S = One responsibility

O = Extend, don't modify

L = Child should replace parent

I = Small interfaces

D = Depend on abstractions

1. Single Responsibility Principle — SRP

Definition

A class should have one responsibility and therefore one primary reason to change.

It doesn't necessarily mean a class can have only one method.

❌ Bad example

public class OrderService
{
    public void CreateOrder(Order order)
    {
        // Create order
    }

    public void SendEmail(Order order)
    {
        // Send email
    }

    public void GenerateInvoice(Order order)
    {
        // Generate invoice
    }

    public void SaveToDatabase(Order order)
    {
        // Save to database
    }
}

This class has multiple responsibilities:

  • Business logic
  • Database access
  • Email
  • Invoice generation

If email requirements change, OrderService changes.

If invoice generation changes, OrderService changes.

If database implementation changes, OrderService changes.

✅ Better design

OrderService
    ↓
OrderRepository

OrderService
    ↓
EmailService

OrderService
    ↓
InvoiceService
public class OrderService
{
    private readonly IOrderRepository _repository;
    private readonly IEmailService _emailService;
    private readonly IInvoiceService _invoiceService;

    public OrderService(
        IOrderRepository repository,
        IEmailService emailService,
        IInvoiceService invoiceService)
    {
        _repository = repository;
        _emailService = emailService;
        _invoiceService = invoiceService;
    }
}

Now each class has a focused responsibility.

Microsoft specifically recommends keeping DI services small, well-factored and testable; having many injected dependencies can be a sign that a class has too many responsibilities. Microsoft Learn

2. Open/Closed Principle — OCP

Definition

Software entities should be open for extension but closed for modification.

Meaning:

  • You should be able to add new behavior
  • Without constantly modifying existing, tested code

❌ Bad example

public class PaymentService
{
    public void Pay(string paymentType)
    {
        if (paymentType == "CreditCard")
        {
            // Credit card payment
        }
        else if (paymentType == "UPI")
        {
            // UPI payment
        }
        else if (paymentType == "PayPal")
        {
            // PayPal payment
        }
    }
}

Suppose tomorrow we add:

ApplePay
GooglePay
Crypto

We keep modifying PaymentService.

✅ Better

Create an abstraction:

public interface IPaymentProcessor
{
    void ProcessPayment(decimal amount);
}

Implement different processors:

public class CreditCardProcessor : IPaymentProcessor
{
    public void ProcessPayment(decimal amount)
    {
        // Credit card payment
    }
}
public class UpiProcessor : IPaymentProcessor
{
    public void ProcessPayment(decimal amount)
    {
        // UPI payment
    }
}

Now adding a new payment method means adding a new implementation.

public class PayPalProcessor : IPaymentProcessor
{
    public void ProcessPayment(decimal amount)
    {
        // PayPal payment
    }
}

The existing payment logic doesn't need to be modified.

ASP.NET Core connection

DI makes this pattern practical because implementations can be registered with the service container. .NET's DI system is designed around abstractions and registered implementations. Microsoft Learn

3. Liskov Substitution Principle — LSP

Definition

Objects of a derived class should be replaceable for objects of the base class without breaking the expected behavior.

In simple words:

If B is a child of A, I should be able to use B wherever A is expected.

Classic bad example

public class Bird
{
    public virtual void Fly()
    {
        Console.WriteLine("Flying");
    }
}
public class Penguin : Bird
{
    public override void Fly()
    {
        throw new NotSupportedException();
    }
}

Now:

Bird bird = new Penguin();

bird.Fly();

The program breaks.

The inheritance relationship is incorrect.

Better design

Separate capabilities:

public abstract class Bird
{
    public abstract void Eat();
}
public interface IFlyingBird
{
    void Fly();
}
public class Eagle : Bird, IFlyingBird
{
    public override void Eat()
    {
    }

    public void Fly()
    {
    }
}
public class Penguin : Bird
{
    public override void Eat()
    {
    }
}

Now we don't force Penguin to implement behavior it doesn't support.

ASP.NET Core example

Suppose:

public interface IFileStorage
{
    void Upload();
    void Download();
    void Delete();
}

If one implementation supports upload but cannot delete, forcing it into this interface can violate LSP/design expectations.

We should rethink the abstraction.

4. Interface Segregation Principle — ISP

Definition

Clients should not be forced to depend on methods they don't use.

In simple words:

Prefer small, focused interfaces instead of one huge interface.

❌ Bad

public interface IUserService
{
    void CreateUser();
    void UpdateUser();
    void DeleteUser();
    void SendEmail();
    void GenerateReport();
    void ExportExcel();
}

A class that only needs user creation now depends on unrelated operations.

✅ Better

Split the interfaces:

public interface IUserCreator
{
    void CreateUser();
}
public interface IUserUpdater
{
    void UpdateUser();
}
public interface IUserDeleter
{
    void DeleteUser();
}
public interface IReportGenerator
{
    void GenerateReport();
}

Now consumers depend only on what they need.

ASP.NET Core example

Instead of:

IApplicationService

with 30 unrelated methods, prefer focused abstractions:

IProductReader
IProductWriter
IProductSearchService
IProductPricingService

when the application's design actually requires those separate responsibilities.

5. Dependency Inversion Principle — DIP

Definition

High-level modules should not depend directly on low-level modules. Both should depend on abstractions.

And:

Abstractions should not depend on implementation details. Implementation details should depend on abstractions.

This is one of the most important SOLID principles for ASP.NET Core.

Microsoft's architecture guidance describes dependency inversion as directing dependencies toward abstractions rather than implementation details, which helps create loosely coupled, testable and maintainable applications. Microsoft Learn

❌ Without DIP

public class OrderService
{
    private readonly SqlOrderRepository _repository;

    public OrderService()
    {
        _repository = new SqlOrderRepository();
    }
}

OrderService directly depends on:

SqlOrderRepository

Now it is tightly coupled to SQL implementation.

Testing becomes harder.

✅ With DIP

Create abstraction:

public interface IOrderRepository
{
    Task<Order?> GetByIdAsync(int id);
}

Implementation:

public class SqlOrderRepository : IOrderRepository
{
    public async Task<Order?> GetByIdAsync(int id)
    {
        // SQL / EF Core
        return null;
    }
}

Service:

public class OrderService
{
    private readonly IOrderRepository _repository;

    public OrderService(IOrderRepository repository)
    {
        _repository = repository;
    }
}

Register:

builder.Services.AddScoped<IOrderRepository, SqlOrderRepository>();

Now:

OrderService
      ↓
IOrderRepository
      ↑
SqlOrderRepository

The service depends on the abstraction.

ASP.NET Core's built-in DI system supports this style by registering interfaces and implementations and injecting the dependency into constructors. Microsoft Learn

SOLID in Your ASP.NET Core Architecture

Think about your typical stack:

React
   ↓
ASP.NET Core Controller
   ↓
Application/Service
   ↓
Repository Interface
   ↓
EF Core / Dapper
   ↓
SQL Server

SOLID can appear throughout this architecture.

SRP

Controller → HTTP handling
Service → Business logic
Repository → Data access

OCP

IPaymentProcessor
       ↑
 ┌─────┼─────────┐
Card   UPI      PayPal

Add a new processor without changing existing processors.

LSP

Implementations of an abstraction should behave according to the abstraction's contract.

ISP

Use focused interfaces:

IProductReader
IProductWriter

instead of one giant interface when appropriate.

DIP

Service
   ↓
IRepository
   ↑
EFRepository

Common Interview Questions

Q1. What is SOLID?

Interview answer:

SOLID is a set of five object-oriented design principles that help us build software that is maintainable, loosely coupled, extensible and testable. The five principles are Single Responsibility, Open/Closed, Liskov Substitution, Interface Segregation and Dependency Inversion. In ASP.NET Core, these principles are commonly applied through services, interfaces, dependency injection and layered architecture.

Q2. Explain SRP with an ASP.NET Core example.

SRP means a class should have one primary responsibility. For example, I wouldn't put database access, email sending, invoice generation and business logic inside one OrderService. I would separate those responsibilities into appropriate services or repositories. This makes the classes easier to test and reduces the impact of changes.

Q3. How does DI help SOLID?

Dependency Injection particularly supports the Dependency Inversion Principle. Instead of a service directly creating a concrete dependency using new, I define an abstraction and inject the required implementation through the constructor. ASP.NET Core's DI container then provides the implementation. This reduces coupling and makes it easier to replace implementations and unit test the service.

Microsoft explicitly recommends avoiding direct instantiation of dependent classes because it couples the code to a particular implementation. Microsoft Learn

Q4. What is the difference between DIP and DI?

Very common interview question.

DIP

Design principle

Depend on abstractions rather than concrete implementations.

DI

Technique used to implement that principle

Provide the required dependency from outside the class.

Example:

DIP:
OrderService → IOrderRepository

DI:
ASP.NET Core → gives OrderService → SqlOrderRepository

So:

DIP is the principle; DI is one way to implement it.

Q5. How does SRP relate to Clean Architecture?

Clean Architecture separates responsibilities into different layers:

Domain
   ↓
Application
   ↓
Infrastructure
   ↓
API

For example:

Controller
→ HTTP responsibility

Service
→ Business/use-case responsibility

Repository
→ Data-access responsibility

DbContext
→ EF Core persistence responsibility

This separation helps avoid large classes with unrelated responsibilities.

Q6. Can a class violate multiple SOLID principles?

Yes.

For example:

public class OrderService
{
    // business logic

    // SQL queries

    // email

    // payment

    // report generation

    // file generation
}

This could violate:

  • SRP — too many responsibilities
  • DIP — if it directly creates concrete dependencies
  • ISP — depending on how its abstractions are designed
  • OCP — if every new behavior requires modifying this class

A single design problem can therefore affect multiple SOLID principles.

🔥 Scenario-Based Interview Question

"Your service class has 15 injected dependencies. What does that tell you?"

Don't simply say:

"That's bad."

A stronger answer:

"A large number of dependencies can be a signal that the class has too many responsibilities. I would review the class and identify groups of related behavior, then extract those responsibilities into focused services where appropriate. For example, if an OrderService handles pricing, payment, notifications and reporting, I might separate those concerns into dedicated services. However, I wouldn't blindly split every dependency; I'd look at the actual responsibilities and cohesion of the class."

Microsoft's ASP.NET Core DI guidance makes essentially this point: many injected dependencies can indicate that a class has too many responsibilities and may need refactoring. Microsoft Learn

🔥 Scenario: SOLID + Your Stack

Imagine your React application calls:

POST /api/orders

Your API has:

[ApiController]
[Route("api/orders")]
public class OrdersController : ControllerBase
{
    private readonly IOrderService _orderService;

    public OrdersController(IOrderService orderService)
    {
        _orderService = orderService;
    }
}

SRP

Controller handles HTTP concerns.

Controller
    ↓
OrderService

DIP

Controller depends on:

IOrderService

not:

OrderService

SRP again

Service handles business rules.

OrderService

doesn't need to directly handle SQL.

DIP

OrderService
     ↓
IOrderRepository
     ↑
EfOrderRepository

OCP

You can introduce:

SqlOrderRepository
CosmosOrderRepository
MockOrderRepository

without changing the service's core contract.

ISP

If necessary:

IOrderReader
IOrderWriter

rather than one enormous repository interface.

🧠 SOLID vs Design Patterns

Don't confuse these.

SOLID

Principles

SRP
OCP
LSP
ISP
DIP

Design Patterns

Reusable design solutions

Factory
Repository
Strategy
Decorator
Singleton
Adapter
Facade
Observer

For example:

Strategy Pattern
      +
OCP
      +
DIP

can be used together.

🎯 Strong 60-Second Interview Answer

"SOLID is a set of five object-oriented design principles that help us build maintainable, loosely coupled and testable applications. SRP means a class should have one primary responsibility. OCP means we should be able to extend behavior without repeatedly modifying existing code. LSP means derived implementations should be safely substitutable for their abstraction. ISP means consumers should not be forced to depend on methods they don't need, so I prefer focused interfaces. DIP means high-level business logic should depend on abstractions rather than concrete infrastructure implementations. In ASP.NET Core, I apply these principles through layered architecture, interfaces and dependency injection. For example, my controller depends on an application service, the service depends on an IRepository, and Infrastructure provides the EF Core implementation. This reduces coupling and makes the application easier to test and evolve."

🧠 Final Mental Model

                 SOLID
                   │
       ┌───────────┼───────────┐
       ↓           ↓           ↓
      SRP         OCP         LSP
   One job     Extend       Safe
              behavior    substitution
       │
       ├──────────────┐
       ↓              ↓
      ISP            DIP
  Small focused   Depend on
   interfaces    abstractions
                      │
                      ↓
                     DI
                      │
                      ↓
              ASP.NET Core

One-line memory trick

SRP = One job | OCP = Extend | LSP = Replace | ISP = Small interfaces | DIP = Abstractions

  1. ISP with large vs focused interfaces

  1. SOLID + Clean Architecture
  1. SOLID + ASP.NET Core DI
  1. 15 dependencies in one service — what would you do?
  1. Repository abstraction + EF Core implementation
  1. Real-world SOLID example from your project

37. CQRS (Command Query Responsibility Segregation)

CQRS is an important Senior .NET / Architecture interview topic, especially when discussing Clean Architecture, DDD, microservices, MediatR, EF Core/Dapper, and scalable APIs.

Microsoft describes CQRS as separating operations that change state (commands) from operations that read state (queries). The separation can be logical within the same application/database; separate read/write databases are an advanced option, not a requirement. Microsoft Learn

🔴 Priority: MUST MASTER

You should know:

  1. What is CQRS?
  1. Command vs Query
  1. CQS vs CQRS
  1. Why use CQRS?
  1. Simple CQRS
  1. CQRS with MediatR
  1. Command Handler
  1. Query Handler
  1. CQRS + Clean Architecture
  1. CQRS + EF Core
  1. CQRS + Dapper
  1. CQRS vs CRUD
  1. CQRS vs Repository
  1. CQRS + Event-driven architecture
  1. CQRS + separate read/write databases
  1. Advantages and disadvantages
  1. When not to use CQRS

1. What is CQRS?

CQRS = Command Query Responsibility Segregation

The main idea is:

Separate operations that change data from operations that read data.

Instead of having one service doing everything:

ProductService
 ├── GetProduct()
 ├── GetProducts()
 ├── CreateProduct()
 ├── UpdateProduct()
 └── DeleteProduct()

we can separate it:

Commands                  Queries
   │                         │
   ↓                         ↓
Write operations         Read operations
   │                         │
   ↓                         ↓
Command Handlers         Query Handlers

Microsoft describes the basic CQRS model as having separate command and query operations/models, while emphasizing that they don't necessarily need separate physical databases. Microsoft Learn

2. Command vs Query

This is the most important CQRS concept.

Command

A command changes application state.

Examples:

CreateOrderCommand
UpdateOrderCommand
CancelOrderCommand
DeleteProductCommand
RegisterUserCommand

Usually:

Command
   ↓
Handler
   ↓
Business Logic
   ↓
Database

Query

A query reads data without changing application state.

Examples:

GetProductByIdQuery
GetOrdersQuery
GetCustomerDetailsQuery
SearchProductsQuery

Usually:

Query
   ↓
Handler
   ↓
Database
   ↓
DTO

Simple rule

Command = Change
Query = Read

3. Example

Suppose you have:

POST /api/products

This changes the database.

Therefore:

CreateProductCommand

For:

GET /api/products/10

we have:

GetProductByIdQuery

So:

POST
 ↓
Command
 ↓
Command Handler
 ↓
Database

and:

GET
 ↓
Query
 ↓
Query Handler
 ↓
Database

4. CQRS vs CQS

Interviewers sometimes ask this.

CQS

Command Query Separation

CQS is primarily a principle at the method/object level:

A method should either change state or return data, but generally shouldn't do both.

For example:

Product GetProduct();

is a query.

And:

void UpdateProduct(Product product);

is a command.

CQRS

CQRS takes this idea further and separates the models/handling paths for commands and queries.

CQS
 ↓
Method-level separation

CQRS
 ↓
Application/architecture-level separation

Microsoft describes CQS as a foundational principle for CQRS. Microsoft Learn

5. Simple CRUD vs CQRS

Traditional CRUD

                 ProductService
                      │
          ┌───────────┴───────────┐
          ↓                       ↓
       Commands                Queries
          │                       │
          └───────────┬───────────┘
                      ↓
                  Repository
                      ↓
                   EF Core
                      ↓
                  SQL Server

Everything goes through the same service/model.

CQRS

                  API
                   │
          ┌────────┴────────┐
          ↓                 ↓
      Commands            Queries
          ↓                 ↓
 Command Handler       Query Handler
          ↓                 ↓
      Write Model       Read Model
          ↓                 ↓
      SQL Server       SQL Server

The read and write paths are separated.

6. Does CQRS require two databases?

❌ No.

This is a common interview trap.

You can have:

Commands ──────┐
               ↓
          SQL Server
               ↑
Queries ───────┘

with one database.

You can also have:

Commands
   ↓
Write DB
   ↓
Events
   ↓
Read DB
   ↑
Queries

with separate databases.

Microsoft's simplified CQRS example uses a single database with two logical models. Microsoft Learn

Therefore:

CQRS does not mean two databases.

Separate read/write databases are an advanced architectural choice.

7. CQRS with ASP.NET Core

A typical architecture can be:

React
  ↓
ASP.NET Core Controller
  ↓
Mediator
  ↓
Command / Query
  ↓
Handler
  ↓
Domain / Application
  ↓
Infrastructure
  ↓
SQL Server

For example:

POST /orders
       ↓
CreateOrderCommand
       ↓
CreateOrderCommandHandler
       ↓
Order Domain
       ↓
Repository
       ↓
EF Core
       ↓
SQL Server

For reading:

GET /orders/100
       ↓
GetOrderQuery
       ↓
GetOrderQueryHandler
       ↓
Dapper / EF Core
       ↓
SQL Server
       ↓
OrderDto

8. Command

A command represents an intention to change state.

Example:

public record CreateProductCommand(
    string Name,
    decimal Price);

It represents:

"Create this product."

It doesn't perform the operation itself.

9. Command Handler

The handler performs the command.

Conceptually:

public class CreateProductCommandHandler
{
    public async Task<int> Handle(
        CreateProductCommand command)
    {
        // Validate business rules

        // Create entity

        // Save to database

        // Return product ID
    }
}

With MediatR-style implementations, command handlers implement an appropriate request-handler interface, and the mediator routes the command to the corresponding handler. Microsoft documents this mediator-based approach for CQRS command pipelines. Microsoft Learn

10. Query

Example:

public record GetProductByIdQuery(int Id);

This represents:

"Give me product 10."

It should not modify application state.

11. Query Handler

public class GetProductByIdQueryHandler
{
    public async Task<ProductDto?> Handle(
        GetProductByIdQuery query)
    {
        // Read database

        // Map to DTO

        // Return result
    }
}

Notice something important:

Query doesn't necessarily need a repository.

For complex read operations, you might directly use Dapper or EF Core projection.

Microsoft's CQRS guidance specifically discusses side queries using SQL/Dapper for flexible read operations. Microsoft Learn

12. CQRS + MediatR

This is a very common interview combination.

Instead of:

public async Task<IActionResult> CreateProduct(...)
{
    // lots of business logic
}

you can have:

[HttpPost]
public async Task<IActionResult> Create(
    CreateProductRequest request)
{
    var result = await _mediator.Send(
        new CreateProductCommand(
            request.Name,
            request.Price));

    return Ok(result);
}

Then:

Controller
    ↓
IMediator
    ↓
CreateProductCommand
    ↓
CreateProductCommandHandler

The controller doesn't need to know which handler performs the operation.

Microsoft's ASP.NET Core architecture guidance notes that the mediator pattern can reduce controller coupling and allow each handler to focus on a specific action/use case. Microsoft Learn

13. Why use MediatR?

MediatR isn't CQRS itself.

This is important.

CQRS

Architectural pattern

MediatR

Mediator implementation/library

You can implement CQRS without MediatR.

For example:

Controller
    ↓
CreateProductCommandHandler

is possible.

Or:

Controller
    ↓
IMediator
    ↓
CreateProductCommandHandler

with a mediator.

Microsoft's documentation describes MediatR as one implementation of the mediator pattern; other approaches are possible. Microsoft Learn

14. CQRS + Clean Architecture

This is particularly relevant to your previous topic.

You can structure the application as:

┌──────────────────────────────┐
│         API / Web            │
│ Controllers                  │
└──────────────┬───────────────┘
               ↓
┌──────────────────────────────┐
│        Application           │
│                              │
│ Commands                     │
│ Command Handlers             │
│ Queries                      │
│ Query Handlers               │
│ DTOs                         │
│ Interfaces                   │
└──────────────┬───────────────┘
               ↓
┌──────────────────────────────┐
│           Domain             │
│                              │
│ Entities                     │
│ Business Rules               │
│ Value Objects                │
└──────────────────────────────┘

               ↑
               │
┌──────────────────────────────┐
│       Infrastructure         │
│                              │
│ EF Core                      │
│ Dapper                       │
│ SQL Server                   │
│ Redis                        │
│ External APIs                │
└──────────────────────────────┘

Microsoft's DDD guidance similarly keeps domain logic independent from infrastructure, with the application layer coordinating use cases and infrastructure handling persistence. Microsoft Learn

15. CQRS + EF Core

You can use EF Core for both sides.

Command

public class CreateProductHandler
{
    private readonly AppDbContext _context;

    public async Task<int> Handle(CreateProductCommand command)
    {
        var product = new Product
        {
            Name = command.Name,
            Price = command.Price
        };

        _context.Products.Add(product);

        await _context.SaveChangesAsync();

        return product.Id;
    }
}

Query

public class GetProductHandler
{
    private readonly AppDbContext _context;

    public async Task<ProductDto?> Handle(int id)
    {
        return await _context.Products
            .AsNoTracking()
            .Where(x => x.Id == id)
            .Select(x => new ProductDto
            {
                Id = x.Id,
                Name = x.Name,
                Price = x.Price
            })
            .FirstOrDefaultAsync();
    }
}

Same database.

Different responsibilities.

16. CQRS + Dapper

This is especially useful for read-heavy systems.

For example:

Command
   ↓
EF Core
   ↓
Domain entities
   ↓
SQL Server

But:

Query
   ↓
Dapper
   ↓
Optimized SQL
   ↓
DTO

Why?

Queries often need:

  • joins
  • aggregations
  • reporting
  • filtering
  • sorting
  • projections

Dapper can be convenient when you want direct SQL control.

Microsoft's CQRS guidance explicitly describes using side queries with SQL/Dapper when flexible read models are useful. Microsoft Learn

17. CQRS + Read Model

Imagine an e-commerce application.

The write model might contain:

Order
Customer
OrderItem
Product
Payment
ShippingAddress

But the UI wants:

OrderNumber
CustomerName
Total
PaymentStatus
ShippingStatus

Instead of loading the entire domain model, the query can return a dedicated:

public class OrderSummaryDto
{
    public int OrderId { get; set; }
    public string CustomerName { get; set; }
    public decimal Total { get; set; }
    public string PaymentStatus { get; set; }
    public string ShippingStatus { get; set; }
}

This is a read model optimized for the query.

18. Advanced CQRS — Separate Databases

For a large system:

                    Commands
                       ↓
                 Write Database
                       ↓
                     Event
                       ↓
                  Event Bus
                       ↓
                 Read Database
                       ↑
                       │
                    Queries

For example:

SQL Server
   ↓
OrderCreated event
   ↓
Message Broker
   ↓
Read Model Processor
   ↓
Read Database

Now reads can be optimized independently.

But there is an important consequence:

Eventual consistency

The read database may not immediately contain the latest write.

For example:

10:00:00 → Order created
10:00:01 → Event processed
10:00:02 → Read model updated

Between those points, a query may temporarily return old data.

Microsoft notes that event-driven CQRS architectures can use eventual consistency between distributed data sources. Microsoft Learn

19. CQRS vs Event Sourcing

Another common interview trap.

They are not the same thing.

CQRS

Separates:

Commands
Queries

Event Sourcing

Stores:

Events

as the source of state/history.

You can have:

CQRS without Event Sourcing

and:

Event Sourcing with or without a full CQRS architecture

Although they are frequently used together in advanced systems.

20. Advantages of CQRS

1. Separation of concerns

Reads ≠ Writes

2. Optimized read models

Queries can be designed specifically for UI/reporting requirements.

3. Independent scaling

In distributed architectures:

Read workload ↑
     ↓
Scale read side

without necessarily scaling the write side identically.

4. Better complex-domain organization

Commands can contain business rules while queries remain focused on retrieval.

5. Easier cross-cutting pipelines

With mediator/handler pipelines, concerns such as:

Validation
Logging
Authorization
Performance measurement
Transactions

can be applied around handlers. Microsoft documents mediator pipeline behaviors as a way to handle such cross-cutting concerns. Microsoft Learn

21. Disadvantages of CQRS

This is very important because interviewers may ask:

"Why wouldn't you use CQRS everywhere?"

Because CQRS adds complexity.

You may introduce:

Commands
Queries
Handlers
DTOs
Validators
Pipeline behaviors
Read models
Events
Message brokers

instead of a simple CRUD service.

For a small application:

Controller
    ↓
Service
    ↓
EF Core

may be perfectly reasonable.

CQRS isn't automatically better.

22. When Should You Use CQRS?

CQRS can make sense when you have:

  • Complex business rules
  • Significant difference between read and write models
  • Read-heavy workloads
  • Complex reporting
  • Different scaling requirements
  • Multiple read models
  • Event-driven architecture
  • DDD-style domain modeling
  • Complex workflows
  • Need for clear use-case boundaries

23. When Should You NOT Use CQRS?

For a simple CRUD application:

Product
Customer
Employee
Category

with straightforward:

Create
Read
Update
Delete

CQRS may introduce unnecessary complexity.

A simpler:

Controller
   ↓
Service
   ↓
EF Core
   ↓
SQL Server

can be easier to maintain.

Interview-ready answer

"I wouldn't introduce CQRS just because it's a popular architecture. For simple CRUD functionality, a conventional service and EF Core approach can be sufficient. I would consider CQRS when the read and write requirements are significantly different, the domain is complex, or we need independently optimized read models or scaling."

24. CQRS vs Repository Pattern

They solve different problems.

Repository

Deals primarily with:

Data access abstraction

Example:

IProductRepository

CQRS

Deals with:

Separation of reads and writes

You can have:

CQRS + Repository

For example:

CreateProductCommand
        ↓
CommandHandler
        ↓
IProductRepository
        ↓
EF Core

while:

GetProductsQuery
        ↓
QueryHandler
        ↓
Dapper
        ↓
SQL Server

Microsoft's persistence guidance also notes that repositories can be used for transactional updates while queries may use separate query mechanisms in a CQRS approach. Microsoft Learn

🔥 Scenario-Based Interview Question

"Your application has 80% read operations and 20% write operations. Would you use CQRS?"

Don't immediately say yes.

A better answer:

"The read/write ratio alone wouldn't automatically make me choose CQRS. I would first look at the complexity of the read models, performance requirements, business rules and scaling needs. If the read side requires complex joins, reporting projections or independent scaling, CQRS could be beneficial. If the application is still straightforward CRUD, I would avoid adding CQRS complexity unnecessarily."

🔥 Scenario: Your React + .NET Application

Suppose your React application has:

Product listing
Product details
Create product
Update product
Delete product

Simple version

React
 ↓
ProductsController
 ↓
ProductService
 ↓
EF Core
 ↓
SQL Server

This may be enough.

Now imagine the product system becomes much more complex:

10 million products
Complex search
Pricing rules
Inventory
Discounts
Recommendations
Reporting
Analytics
Multiple consumers

Now you could evolve toward:

                    React
                      │
             ┌────────┴────────┐
             ↓                 ↓
          Queries           Commands
             ↓                 ↓
       Query Handlers     Command Handlers
             ↓                 ↓
       Read Models        Domain Model
             ↓                 ↓
        Read Store        Write Store

That's where CQRS becomes much more interesting.

🎯 Strong 60-Second Interview Answer

"CQRS stands for Command Query Responsibility Segregation. The basic idea is to separate operations that change state from operations that only read state. Commands such as CreateOrder or UpdateProduct are handled by command handlers, while queries such as GetOrder or SearchProducts are handled by query handlers. CQRS doesn't require separate databases; we can use the same SQL Server database with separate logical read and write models. In a more advanced architecture, we can have separate read and write stores and synchronize them through events, which introduces eventual consistency. In ASP.NET Core, CQRS is often implemented using a mediator such as MediatR, where the controller sends a command or query and the mediator routes it to the appropriate handler. I would use CQRS when the read and write requirements are significantly different, the domain is complex, or we need independently optimized read models. For simple CRUD applications, I would avoid introducing CQRS unnecessarily because it adds architectural complexity."

🧠 Final Mental Model

                    CQRS
                      │
             ┌────────┴────────┐
             ↓                 ↓
         COMMAND             QUERY
             ↓                 ↓
       Changes State       Reads State
             ↓                 ↓
     Command Handler     Query Handler
             ↓                 ↓
       Write Model         Read Model
             ↓                 ↓
       EF Core / DB      EF Core / Dapper

Remember:

Command = Change
Query = Read
CQRS ≠ two databases
MediatR ≠ CQRS
CQRS ≠ Event Sourcing
Simple CRUD doesn't automatically need CQRS

🔴 Interview priority

Must know deeply:

  1. Command vs Query
  1. CQS vs CQRS
  1. CQRS vs CRUD
  1. CQRS with MediatR
  1. Command Handler / Query Handler
  1. CQRS + Clean Architecture
  1. CQRS + EF Core/Dapper
  1. Single DB vs separate DB
  1. Eventual consistency
  1. When to use / not use CQRS

38. Pagination, Filtering & Sorting in ASP.NET Core APIs

This is a very common practical .NET interview topic, especially for Senior Software Engineer roles because it combines API design, EF Core, SQL performance, validation, and frontend requirements.

Microsoft's current EF Core guidance emphasizes limiting result sets, using appropriate indexes, projecting only required columns, and choosing an appropriate pagination strategy. Microsoft Learn

🔴 Priority: MUST MASTER

You should know:

  1. What is pagination?
  1. Why pagination is required
  1. Skip() and Take()
  1. Offset pagination
  1. Keyset/cursor pagination
  1. Filtering
  1. Sorting
  1. Dynamic sorting
  1. Pagination + filtering + sorting together
  1. DTO response design
  1. Total count
  1. Maximum page size
  1. SQL/index performance
  1. Offset vs keyset pagination
  1. Stable/unique ordering
  1. Common API design mistakes

1. What is Pagination?

Pagination means:

Instead of returning thousands or millions of records in one API response, return a limited number of records at a time.

For example:

Database
10,000 products

       ↓

API

Page 1 → 20 products
Page 2 → 20 products
Page 3 → 20 products
...

Without pagination:

GET /api/products

could potentially return thousands of records.

With pagination:

GET /api/products?pageNumber=1&pageSize=20

returns only 20.

Microsoft recommends limiting result-set size because returning all matching rows can increase database, memory, processing, and network costs. Microsoft Learn

2. Basic Pagination

The simplest EF Core approach is:

var products = await _context.Products
    .Skip((pageNumber - 1) * pageSize)
    .Take(pageSize)
    .ToListAsync();

Suppose:

pageNumber = 3
pageSize = 20

Then:

Skip((3 - 1) * 20)
Take(20)

Skip(40)
Take(20)

So:

41 → 60

are returned.

3. Why Do We Use Skip and Take?

Skip()

Specifies how many records to skip.

.Skip(40)

Take()

Specifies how many records to return.

.Take(20)

Together:

.Skip((pageNumber - 1) * pageSize)
.Take(pageSize)

implement traditional page-number pagination.

Microsoft's ASP.NET Core examples use this same Skip/Take approach for server-side paging. Microsoft Learn

4. Basic API Example

Request:

GET /api/products?pageNumber=2&pageSize=20

Controller:

[HttpGet]
public async Task<IActionResult> GetProducts(
    int pageNumber = 1,
    int pageSize = 20)
{
    var products = await _context.Products
        .AsNoTracking()
        .Skip((pageNumber - 1) * pageSize)
        .Take(pageSize)
        .ToListAsync();

    return Ok(products);
}

But this isn't production-ready yet.

Why?

Because the client could send:

?pageNumber=1&pageSize=1000000

We need validation and limits.

5. Page Size Limiting

A common approach:

pageNumber = Math.Max(pageNumber, 1);
pageSize = Math.Clamp(pageSize, 1, 100);

Now:

pageNumber < 1 → 1

pageSize < 1 → 1

pageSize > 100 → 100

So a client cannot accidentally request:

10 million records

in one request.

6. Filtering

Filtering means:

Return only records matching specific conditions.

Example:

GET /api/products?category=Mobile

EF Core:

var query = _context.Products
    .AsNoTracking();

if (!string.IsNullOrEmpty(category))
{
    query = query.Where(x => x.Category == category);
}

You can add multiple filters:

category
minPrice
maxPrice
search
status
createdFrom
createdTo

For example:

GET /api/products
    ?category=Mobile
    &minPrice=10000
    &maxPrice=50000

EF Core uses LINQ expressions such as Where for filtering and translates them through the database provider into database-specific queries such as SQL. Microsoft Learn

7. Searching

Suppose the frontend has:

Search: "iphone"

API:

GET /api/products?search=iphone

Query:

query = query.Where(x =>
    x.Name.Contains(search));

For multiple fields:

query = query.Where(x =>
    x.Name.Contains(search) ||
    x.Description.Contains(search));

For production systems, you should also consider the database's indexing/search capabilities rather than assuming a simple Contains query will always perform well.

8. Sorting

Suppose the frontend wants:

GET /api/products?sortBy=price

Ascending:

query = query.OrderBy(x => x.Price);

Descending:

GET /api/products?sortBy=price&sortOrder=desc
query = query.OrderByDescending(x => x.Price);

9. Dynamic Sorting

A common interview question:

"How do you implement dynamic sorting?"

One simple approach is:

switch (sortBy?.ToLower())
{
    case "name":
        query = sortOrder == "desc"
            ? query.OrderByDescending(x => x.Name)
            : query.OrderBy(x => x.Name);
        break;

    case "price":
        query = sortOrder == "desc"
            ? query.OrderByDescending(x => x.Price)
            : query.OrderBy(x => x.Price);
        break;

    case "created":
        query = sortOrder == "desc"
            ? query.OrderByDescending(x => x.CreatedAt)
            : query.OrderBy(x => x.CreatedAt);
        break;

    default:
        query = query.OrderBy(x => x.Id);
        break;
}

This is safer than blindly accepting arbitrary column names from the client.

10. Why Should We Not Directly Use Client Input as a SQL Column?

Avoid designs like:

ORDER BY {userInput}

without validating the allowed fields.

Instead define an allow-list:

name
price
created
rating

Then map those values to known properties.

This gives you:

  • predictable behavior
  • safer queries
  • controlled API contract
  • easier maintenance

11. Pagination + Filtering + Sorting

This is the real-world pattern you should remember.

Suppose:

GET /api/products
    ?pageNumber=2
    &pageSize=20
    &search=phone
    &category=Mobile
    &sortBy=price
    &sortOrder=desc

Build the query incrementally:

var query = _context.Products
    .AsNoTracking();

if (!string.IsNullOrWhiteSpace(search))
{
    query = query.Where(x =>
        x.Name.Contains(search));
}

if (!string.IsNullOrWhiteSpace(category))
{
    query = query.Where(x =>
        x.Category == category);
}

if (sortBy == "price")
{
    query = sortOrder == "desc"
        ? query.OrderByDescending(x => x.Price)
        : query.OrderBy(x => x.Price);
}

var totalCount = await query.CountAsync();

var products = await query
    .Skip((pageNumber - 1) * pageSize)
    .Take(pageSize)
    .ToListAsync();

The important sequence is:

Filter
   ↓
Sort
   ↓
Count
   ↓
Pagination
   ↓
Execute

12. Why Filter Before Pagination?

Suppose you have:

10,000 products

and only:

500 mobile products

If the user asks for mobile products, you want the database to apply the filter before selecting the requested page.

Conceptually:

Products
   ↓
WHERE Category = 'Mobile'
   ↓
ORDER BY Price
   ↓
OFFSET / LIMIT

rather than retrieving everything into application memory.

13. Why Sorting Before Pagination?

Suppose:

Page 1 = cheapest products

The database needs to establish the ordering before taking the page.

Conceptually:

WHERE
  ↓
ORDER BY
  ↓
OFFSET
  ↓
LIMIT

Otherwise page boundaries wouldn't represent the requested sort order.

14. Response Design

Don't just return:

[
  {},
  {},
  {}
]

A useful paginated API response usually includes metadata.

For example:

{
  "items": [
    {
      "id": 1,
      "name": "iPhone",
      "price": 50000
    }
  ],
  "pageNumber": 1,
  "pageSize": 20,
  "totalCount": 250,
  "totalPages": 13,
  "hasNextPage": true,
  "hasPreviousPage": false
}

Create a generic response model:

public class PagedResult<T>
{
    public List<T> Items { get; set; } = [];
    public int PageNumber { get; set; }
    public int PageSize { get; set; }
    public int TotalCount { get; set; }
    public int TotalPages { get; set; }

    public bool HasNextPage =>
        PageNumber < TotalPages;

    public bool HasPreviousPage =>
        PageNumber > 1;
}

15. Calculating Total Pages

var totalPages =
    (int)Math.Ceiling(
        totalCount / (double)pageSize);

Example:

totalCount = 95
pageSize = 20

Then:

95 / 20 = 4.75

Therefore:

totalPages = 5

16. Complete Practical Example

Here's a clean version you could discuss in an interview:

[HttpGet]
public async Task<ActionResult<PagedResult<ProductDto>>> GetProducts(
    int pageNumber = 1,
    int pageSize = 20,
    string? search = null,
    string? category = null,
    string? sortBy = "name",
    string? sortOrder = "asc",
    CancellationToken cancellationToken = default)
{
    pageNumber = Math.Max(pageNumber, 1);
    pageSize = Math.Clamp(pageSize, 1, 100);

    var query = _context.Products
        .AsNoTracking()
        .AsQueryable();

    // Filtering
    if (!string.IsNullOrWhiteSpace(search))
    {
        query = query.Where(x =>
            x.Name.Contains(search));
    }

    if (!string.IsNullOrWhiteSpace(category))
    {
        query = query.Where(x =>
            x.Category == category);
    }

    // Sorting
    query = sortBy?.ToLower() switch
    {
        "price" => sortOrder == "desc"
            ? query.OrderByDescending(x => x.Price)
            : query.OrderBy(x => x.Price),

        "created" => sortOrder == "desc"
            ? query.OrderByDescending(x => x.CreatedAt)
            : query.OrderBy(x => x.CreatedAt),

        _ => sortOrder == "desc"
            ? query.OrderByDescending(x => x.Name)
            : query.OrderBy(x => x.Name)
    };

    // Count
    var totalCount =
        await query.CountAsync(cancellationToken);

    // Pagination + projection
    var items = await query
        .Skip((pageNumber - 1) * pageSize)
        .Take(pageSize)
        .Select(x => new ProductDto
        {
