🔥 Senior-Level Questions

  1. How do you prevent cascading failures?
  1. How do you prevent retry storms?
  1. How do you design resilience for payment APIs?
  1. How do you handle retries for POST?
  1. How do you combine timeout and retry?
  1. What happens if every service retries independently?
  1. How do you monitor resilience?
  1. What is a dead-letter queue?
  1. How do you make message processing resilient?
  1. How do you design a resilient microservice?

⭐ Strong 60-Second Interview Answer

“Resilience means designing an application so that temporary dependency failures don't cause the entire system to fail. In ASP.NET Core, I typically start with timeouts so downstream calls don't hang indefinitely, then use retries for appropriate transient failures with exponential backoff and jitter. I use circuit breakers when a dependency continues to fail so we stop sending traffic to an unhealthy service and allow it time to recover.

For resource protection, I can use concurrency limits or bulkhead-style isolation, and I use rate limiting where request volume needs to be controlled. For operations that aren't safe to retry, such as payment creation, I combine retries with idempotency rather than blindly retrying the request. For asynchronous workloads, I use queues, retries and dead-letter queues, and make consumers idempotent.

In current .NET, Microsoft.Extensions.Resilience and Microsoft.Extensions.Http.Resilience provide resilience pipelines, including standard HTTP resilience through AddStandardResilienceHandler(). For production, I also monitor retry counts, timeouts, circuit-breaker events, dependency latency and error rates and use distributed tracing to diagnose failures.” Microsoft Learn

🧠 Final Mental Model

Memorize this:

              DOWNSTREAM SERVICE
                     │
              ┌──────┴──────┐
              │             │
           Healthy        Failure
              │             │
              │          Timeout
              │             ↓
              │           Retry
              │             ↓
              │       Exponential Backoff
              │             ↓
              │          Retry again
              │             ↓
              │      ┌──────┴──────┐
              │      │             │
              │   Success       Failure
              │      │             │
              │      │       Circuit Breaker
              │      │             ↓
              │      │           OPEN
              │      │             ↓
              │      │         Wait/Recover
              │      │             ↓
              │      │        HALF-OPEN
              │      │             ↓
              │      │          Test Call
              │      │             ↓
              │      │       CLOSED / OPEN
              └──────┴──────────────────

One-line memory

Timeout limits waiting → Retry handles transient failures → Backoff spaces retries → Jitter prevents retry storms → Circuit Breaker stops repeated failures → Bulkhead limits resource damage → Fallback provides an alternative → Idempotency makes retries safe.

43. Distributed Systems Concepts

This is one of the most important topics for Senior Software Engineer / system-design interviews.

The main idea is:

When your application runs across multiple services, servers, databases, or regions, problems that were easy in a single application become distributed-systems problems.

Microsoft's current architecture guidance emphasizes minimizing coordination, using asynchronous communication where appropriate, accepting eventual consistency when strong consistency isn't required, and explicitly designing for failures and partitions. Microsoft Learn

🔴 Priority — MUST MASTER

Study these in this order:

  1. What is a distributed system?
  1. CAP theorem

1. What is a Distributed System?

A distributed system consists of multiple independent computers/services that communicate over a network and together provide one application or capability.

Simple application

React
  ↓
ASP.NET Core
  ↓
SQL Server

Distributed application

                    React
                      ↓
                 API Gateway
                      ↓
       ┌──────────────┼──────────────┐
       ↓              ↓              ↓
    Order          Payment        Product
    Service        Service        Service
       ↓              ↓              ↓
   Order DB       Payment DB     Product DB

Now you have:

  • Network failures
  • Partial failures
  • Data synchronization
  • Distributed transactions
  • Message duplication
  • Eventual consistency
  • Service discovery
  • Distributed tracing

That's what makes distributed systems difficult.

2. What is a Partial Failure?

This is one of the most important distributed-system concepts.

In a monolith:

Application
     ↓
Everything running

In a distributed system:

Order Service       ✅
Payment Service     ❌
Product Service     ✅

The overall system is partially functioning.

The Order Service may still be healthy while Payment Service is unavailable.

Interview answer

“A partial failure occurs when some components of a distributed system fail while other components continue operating. Distributed systems need to be designed for this because network and service failures are not necessarily all-or-nothing.”

3. CAP Theorem

CAP stands for:

C = Consistency
A = Availability
P = Partition Tolerance

The theorem is about what guarantees a distributed data system can provide when a network partition occurs.

Microsoft's current architecture guidance describes CAP as the trade-off among consistency, availability and partition tolerance, and notes that because partitions are unavoidable in distributed environments, systems have to make a consistency/availability trade-off under partition. Microsoft Learn

4. Consistency

Consistency means that clients see data according to the system's chosen consistency guarantee.

For strong consistency:

Write:
Balance = ₹1000

Read immediately:
Balance = ₹1000

You don't want one replica saying:

₹1000

and another saying:

₹500

when your application's requirement demands the latest committed value.

5. Availability

Availability means the system continues responding to requests.

For example:

Database replica A ❌

Replica B
   ↓
Still responds

The application continues operating.

But there's an important trade-off: returning a response doesn't necessarily mean the response contains the latest globally committed state.

6. Partition Tolerance

A network partition means components cannot communicate reliably.

Server A
   X
   X   Network failure
   X
Server B

Both servers may still be running.

The problem is communication between them.

Important point

In distributed systems, network partitions are considered unavoidable.

Therefore, CAP isn't:

“Choose any two of C, A and P before you build the system.”

The more accurate interview explanation is:

When a partition occurs, a distributed system cannot simultaneously guarantee both strong consistency and availability.

That's a much better Senior-level answer.

7. CAP Example

Suppose:

                Database
              /          \
             A            B

Network partition occurs:

             X X X
            /     \
           A       B

A client writes:

Balance = ₹1000

But B cannot receive the update.

Now you have two choices.

Prefer consistency

Don't allow B to return potentially stale data.

Consistency ↑
Availability ↓

Prefer availability

Allow B to respond using its local state.

Availability ↑
Consistency ↓

The exact trade-off depends on the system's requirements.

8. Strong Consistency vs Eventual Consistency

Strong consistency

After a successful write, subsequent reads observe the new value according to the system's consistency model.

Example:

Write Order = Confirmed
       ↓
Read Order
       ↓
Confirmed

Useful for:

  • Financial balances
  • Inventory constraints
  • Critical transactional operations

Eventual consistency

Different replicas may temporarily contain different values, but if updates stop, the system eventually converges.

Service A → Updated
Service B → Old
Service C → Old

       ↓

Synchronization

       ↓

A → Updated
B → Updated
C → Updated

Event-driven and distributed systems frequently use eventual consistency because avoiding tight coordination can improve scalability and availability. Microsoft Learn

9. Real-World Example of Eventual Consistency

Suppose:

Order Service
     ↓
Order = Confirmed

Then publishes:

OrderConfirmed

Notification Service receives it:

OrderConfirmed
     ↓
Send email

There might be a short delay:

12:00:00 → Order confirmed
12:00:01 → Event published
12:00:02 → Notification processed

During that small interval, different parts of the system don't necessarily reflect exactly the same state.

That's eventual consistency.

10. ACID

You've already encountered ACID with SQL Server.

A = Atomicity
C = Consistency
I = Isolation
D = Durability

Atomicity

All operations succeed or all roll back.

Debit
+
Credit

Both succeed
OR
Both rollback

Consistency

Database moves from one valid state to another.

Isolation

Concurrent transactions don't incorrectly interfere with each other.

Durability

Committed data survives failures.

11. BASE

BASE is commonly discussed for highly distributed systems.

B = Basically Available
S = Soft State
E = Eventually Consistent

The idea is to relax some strong consistency guarantees to improve scalability and availability.

Microsoft's current microservices guidance explicitly contrasts ACID-style transaction handling with BASE-style approaches when data is distributed across independently owned services. Microsoft Learn

Simplified comparison

ACIDBASE
Strong transactional guaranteesRelaxed consistency
Usually centralized transaction boundaryDistributed
Immediate consistencyEventual consistency
Strong coordinationLess coordination
Traditional relational transactionsDistributed/event-driven scenarios

Don't say:

“BASE is always better.”

It depends on business requirements.

12. Why Distributed Transactions Are Difficult

Single database:

BEGIN TRANSACTION

Create Order
Update Inventory
Create Payment Record

COMMIT

Easy.

But with microservices:

Order Service
    ↓
Order DB

Inventory Service
    ↓
Inventory DB

Payment Service
    ↓
Payment DB

You can't simply treat all three independent databases like one local transaction.

Microsoft's current Saga guidance explains that traditional ACID guarantees become much harder across independently managed service databases. Microsoft Learn

13. Two-Phase Commit — 2PC

Two-phase commit is a distributed transaction coordination mechanism.

Phase 1 — Prepare

Coordinator asks:

Order DB       → Ready?
Inventory DB   → Ready?
Payment DB     → Ready?

Each responds:

YES

Phase 2 — Commit

Coordinator says:

COMMIT

All participants commit.

14. Why 2PC Can Be Problematic

Imagine:

Order DB       → YES
Inventory DB   → YES
Payment DB     → YES

Then:

COMMIT

But the coordinator crashes.

Now participants may be waiting for the decision.

This introduces:

  • Coordination overhead
  • Latency
  • Availability concerns
  • Complex failure handling
  • Tight coupling

Therefore, microservices often prefer patterns such as Saga rather than relying on traditional distributed transactions. Microsoft's current microservices guidance identifies Saga as a pattern for maintaining consistency across independently managed data stores. Microsoft Learn

15. Saga Pattern

You've already seen Saga in the previous topic.

Let's connect it to distributed systems.

Suppose:

Create Order
     ↓
Reserve Inventory
     ↓
Process Payment
     ↓
Confirm Order

Each step is its own local transaction.

Order DB
   ↓
Inventory DB
   ↓
Payment DB

If payment fails:

Payment ❌
   ↓
Release Inventory
   ↓
Cancel Order

Those are compensating actions.

A Saga is therefore:

A sequence of local transactions with coordination and compensating actions when later steps fail. Microsoft Learn

16. Saga Choreography

No central coordinator.

Order Service
     │
     │ OrderCreated
     ▼
Inventory Service
     │
     │ InventoryReserved
     ▼
Payment Service
     │
     │ PaymentCompleted
     ▼
Notification Service

Each service reacts to events.

Advantage

Less centralized coordination.

Disadvantage

As the workflow grows, it can become difficult to understand and debug.

Microsoft identifies choreography as useful for simpler workflows but notes that growing workflows can become difficult to track. Microsoft Learn

17. Saga Orchestration

A central orchestrator controls the workflow.

             Order Saga
                 │
       ┌─────────┼─────────┐
       ↓         ↓         ↓
     Order   Inventory   Payment

The orchestrator says:

1. Create order
2. Reserve inventory
3. Process payment
4. Confirm order

If payment fails:

Release inventory
Cancel order

When useful?

Complex workflows with many steps.

Microsoft's current guidance notes that orchestration can make complex workflows easier to understand and evolve, although it introduces coordination logic and an orchestrator component. Microsoft Learn

18. Compensating Transaction

This is not the same as a database rollback.

Suppose:

Inventory reserved

Then payment fails.

You can't necessarily execute:

ROLLBACK

because the inventory transaction has already committed.

Instead:

Reserve Inventory
      ↓
Payment fails
      ↓
Release Inventory

That's a compensating action.

Microsoft's compensating-transaction guidance specifically notes that compensation may not simply restore the exact previous state and can require business-specific rules. Microsoft Learn

19. Important: Compensation isn't always perfect

Suppose:

Payment succeeded
Email failed

Can you "rollback" the payment?

Maybe not.

You might instead:

Payment → SUCCESS
Email → RETRY

This is why distributed systems require business-aware failure handling rather than blindly assuming everything can be rolled back.

20. Idempotency

This is where Topic 39 connects directly.

Suppose a message is delivered twice:

OrderCreated
     ↓
Consumer

First:

OrderCreated → Process

Second:

OrderCreated → Process again ❌

Make the consumer idempotent:

MessageId = ABC123

First:
ABC123 → Process

Second:
ABC123 → Already processed → Ignore

Saga participants should often be designed so retrying operations doesn't create duplicate effects. Microsoft's Saga guidance explicitly calls out idempotence for retryable transactions. Microsoft Learn

21. Message Delivery Semantics

Three terms are important.

At-most-once

Message
 ↓
Process once
 ↓
No retry

Possible outcome:

0 or 1 delivery

You may lose messages.

At-least-once

Message
 ↓
Process
 ↓
Failure before acknowledgement
 ↓
Retry

Possible outcome:

1 or more deliveries

Duplicates are possible.

This is common in message-based systems.

Therefore:

Consumers should be idempotent.

Exactly-once

Sounds ideal:

Process exactly once

But across distributed systems, true end-to-end exactly-once processing is difficult.

Often, systems instead achieve:

At-least-once delivery + idempotent processing = effectively-once business effect.

That's a very useful interview concept.

22. Distributed Lock

Suppose two API instances attempt:

Create same order

simultaneously.

API 1 ──┐
        ├──→ Shared resource
API 2 ──┘

A distributed lock can coordinate access.

Possible technologies:

  • Redis
  • Database-based locks
  • Cloud coordination services

But don't automatically use distributed locks.

They add:

  • Failure scenarios
  • Expiration concerns
  • Deadlock risks
  • Operational complexity

Often, a database unique constraint or optimistic concurrency mechanism is a better solution.

23. Optimistic Concurrency

Suppose two users load:

Product price = ₹100
Version = 5

User A changes:

₹100 → ₹120

Version becomes:

6

User B tries:

₹100 → ₹150

but is still using:

Version = 5

The database can detect:

Expected Version = 5
Actual Version = 6

and reject the update.

This prevents silent overwrites.

24. Why Optimistic Concurrency Is Useful

It's appropriate when:

Conflicts are relatively uncommon

Instead of locking the record for a long time:

User reads
    ↓
Works
    ↓
Updates
    ↓
Check version

If someone changed it meanwhile:

Conflict

The application can ask the user to refresh or resolve the conflict.

25. Leader Election

Sometimes many instances exist:

Worker 1
Worker 2
Worker 3

But only one should perform a particular coordination task.

For example:

Daily settlement job

You don't want all three servers running it simultaneously.

Leader election selects:

Worker 2 = Leader

If Worker 2 fails:

Worker 1 = New Leader

Microsoft's distributed-system design guidance recommends leader election when coordination is necessary, while ensuring the coordinator itself doesn't become a single point of failure. Microsoft Learn

26. Distributed System Failure Types

You should know these:

Network timeout
Network partition
Service crash
Database unavailable
Message duplication
Message loss
Message reordering
Slow dependency
Clock differences
Partial failure
Concurrent updates

These are why distributed systems require more careful design than a simple three-layer application.

27. Event Ordering

Suppose:

Event A: OrderCreated
Event B: OrderCancelled

But consumer receives:

B
A

Now the state can become incorrect.

Solutions can include:

  • Sequence numbers
  • Partitioning by entity key
  • Version numbers
  • Idempotent consumers
  • Event timestamps where appropriate
  • State validation

Don't assume a distributed messaging system automatically gives you global ordering.

28. CAP vs ACID

Very common interview confusion.

CAP

Deals with:

Distributed systems
+
Network partition
+
Consistency/availability trade-off

ACID

Deals with:

Database transactions
+
Atomicity
+
Consistency
+
Isolation
+
Durability

They are not competing definitions of the same thing.

29. CAP vs BASE

Think:

CAP
 ↓
Distributed-system trade-off

BASE
 ↓
Relaxed consistency approach

BASE is often used to describe distributed systems that prioritize availability and eventual consistency.

30. Real-World Architecture

Consider an e-commerce system:

                         React
                           │
                           ▼
                     API Gateway
                           │
             ┌─────────────┼─────────────┐
             ↓             ↓             ↓
          Order          Payment      Inventory
          Service        Service       Service
             │             │             │
             ↓             ↓             ↓

             │
             ▼
          Message Bus
             │
       ┌─────┴──────┐
       ↓            ↓
 Notification    Analytics
 Service          Service

Now think about the distributed-system concerns:

CAP
Consistency
Availability
Eventual consistency
Saga
Idempotency
Retries
Circuit breaker

Message ordering
Observability

31. Production Example

User clicks:

BUY NOW

Flow:

React
 ↓
Order API
 ↓
Create Order
 ↓
OrderCreated event
 ↓
Inventory Service
 ↓
Reserve inventory
 ↓
InventoryReserved
 ↓
Payment Service
 ↓
PaymentCompleted
 ↓
Order Confirmed

If payment fails:

PaymentFailed
     ↓
Release Inventory
     ↓
Cancel Order

PaymentCompleted
PaymentCompleted

the consumer checks:

EventId / IdempotencyKey

and processes the logical event once.

⭐ Strong 60-Second Interview Answer

“A distributed system consists of multiple independent services or nodes communicating over a network, so we have to design for partial failures, network latency and data consistency issues. One important concept is CAP, which explains the trade-off between consistency and availability when a network partition occurs.

For data consistency, I use strong consistency where the business requirement demands it, but for loosely coupled workflows I can use eventual consistency with events or messaging. When a business operation spans multiple services, I avoid assuming that a normal database transaction can cover all services. Instead, I can use the Saga pattern, where each service performs a local transaction and failures are handled using compensating transactions.

Because distributed systems commonly involve retries and at-least-once message delivery, I make operations and consumers idempotent. I also consider optimistic concurrency, ordering, timeouts, retries, circuit breakers, distributed tracing and monitoring. The key principle is to minimize unnecessary coordination while explicitly designing for failures and consistency requirements.” Microsoft Learn

🧠 Final Mental Model

Memorize this:

                 DISTRIBUTED SYSTEM
                         │
          ┌──────────────┼──────────────┐
          ↓              ↓              ↓
      NETWORK         SERVICES        DATA
          │              │              │
     Partitions       Failures      Consistency
     Latency          Timeouts      Replication
     Ordering         Retries       Concurrency
          │              │              │
          └──────────────┼──────────────┘
                         ↓
                  DESIGN PATTERNS
                         │
       ┌─────────────────┼─────────────────┐
       ↓                 ↓                 ↓
     Saga            Eventual          Idempotency
                  Consistency
       │                 │                 │
       ↓                 ↓                 ↓
 Compensation       Events/Queue       Safe Retry
       │
       └─────────────────┬─────────────────┘
                         ↓
                    OBSERVABILITY
                         │
                Logs + Metrics + Traces

One-line memory

Distributed systems = network failures + partial failures + distributed data + consistency trade-offs + coordination problems.

And the most important interview connection to remember is:

Failure
  ↓
Retry
  ↓
Idempotency
  ↓
Eventual Consistency
  ↓
Saga / Compensation
  ↓
Observable Recovery

44. Microservices Architecture in ASP.NET Core

This is an important Senior .NET / Product Company interview topic because it combines ASP.NET Core, APIs, databases, messaging, scalability, and distributed systems.

Microsoft's guidance describes microservices as independently deployable services organized around specific business capabilities/bounded contexts, with each service owning its data. Microsoft Learn

🔴 Priority: MUST MASTER

For interviews, focus especially on:

  1. What is Microservices Architecture?
  1. Monolith vs Microservices
  1. How to identify a Microservice boundary
  1. Bounded Context
  1. Database-per-Service
  1. Service autonomy
  1. Service-to-Service communication
  1. Synchronous vs asynchronous communication
  1. API Gateway
  1. Messaging / Event-driven communication
  1. Shared database vs database-per-service
  1. Distributed transactions
  1. Eventual consistency
  1. Microservices pros and cons
  1. When not to use microservices
  1. Real-world .NET microservices architecture

1. What is Microservices Architecture?

Interview Answer

Microservices architecture is an architectural style where an application is divided into small, independently deployable services, with each service responsible for a specific business capability.

Each service generally:

  • owns its business logic
  • owns its data
  • can be deployed independently
  • can scale independently
  • communicates with other services through APIs or messaging.

For example, an e-commerce application could have:

Order Service
Product Service
Payment Service
Inventory Service
Notification Service
Identity Service

Instead of having one large application containing everything.

Microsoft describes each microservice as implementing an end-to-end business capability within a defined context boundary and being independently deployable. Microsoft Learn

2. Monolith vs Microservices

Monolithic

             ┌──────────────────────┐
             │   Single Application  │
             │                      │
             │ Users                │
             │ Orders               │
             │ Products             │
             │ Payments             │
             │ Notifications        │
             └──────────┬───────────┘
                        │
                  SQL Server

Everything is deployed together.

Microservices

                  API Gateway
                       │
       ┌───────────────┼────────────────┐
       │               │                │
       ▼               ▼                ▼
  Order Service   Product Service  Payment Service
       │               │                │
   Order DB        Product DB        Payment DB

Each service can evolve and deploy independently.

3. What is a Microservice Boundary?

This is one of the most important interview questions.

Question

How do you decide where one microservice ends and another begins?

Answer

I define service boundaries primarily around business capabilities and bounded contexts, rather than simply splitting the application by technical layers.

For example:

E-commerce

Catalog
   ↓
Product Service

Ordering
   ↓
Order Service

Payments
   ↓
Payment Service

Shipping
   ↓
Shipping Service

A good boundary should have:

  • high internal cohesion
  • low coupling with other services
  • clear ownership
  • independent business responsibility
  • minimal communication requirements.

Microsoft's DDD guidance emphasizes cohesion and warns that if two services need to communicate very frequently, they may actually belong within the same boundary. Microsoft Learn

Bad decomposition

UserController Service
ProductController Service
OrderController Service

That's generally technical decomposition.

Better decomposition

Identity
Catalog
Ordering
Payment
Shipping

That's business-oriented decomposition.

4. What is Bounded Context?

A Bounded Context is a clearly defined boundary within which a particular domain model and terminology apply.

For example:

Identity Context
    User

Ordering Context
    Buyer
    Order

Payment Context
    Customer
    Payment

Notice that the concept of a user/customer doesn't necessarily have exactly the same model everywhere.

Microsoft's guidance connects microservice boundaries with DDD bounded contexts. Microsoft Learn

Interview-friendly explanation

"I don't necessarily share the same domain model between microservices. Each bounded context can have its own model optimized for its business responsibility."

5. Database-per-Service

This is another MUST MASTER question.

Question

Should microservices share the same database?

Ideally, each microservice owns its data and other services should not directly access that database.

For example:

Order Service
      │
      ▼
 Order DB


Payment Service
      │
      ▼
 Payment DB


Inventory Service
      │
      ▼
 Inventory DB

Microsoft's cloud-native guidance describes this as database-per-microservice, where each service encapsulates its own data. Microsoft Learn

Why?

Because otherwise:

Order Service ─────┐
Payment Service ───┼──► Shared DB
Inventory Service ─┘

creates strong coupling.

One service could directly modify another service's tables.

That makes independent deployment and schema evolution difficult.

6. Can Different Microservices Use Different Databases?

Yes.

This is commonly called polyglot persistence.

For example:

Order Service
     ↓
SQL Server

Product Service
     ↓
SQL Server

Analytics Service
     ↓
MongoDB

Caching
     ↓
Redis

The important principle isn't that every service must use a different database.

The principle is:

The service owns its data.

You can have:

Order Service → SQL Server
Payment Service → SQL Server

and still have database-per-service if they are separate database instances/databases with independent ownership.

7. How Do Microservices Communicate?

There are two major approaches.

Synchronous

Order Service
      │
      │ HTTP
      ▼
Payment Service
      │
      │ response
      ▼
Order Service

Common technologies:

  • HTTP/REST
  • gRPC

Asynchronous

Order Service
      │
      │ Message
      ▼
Message Broker
      │
      ├────► Payment Service
      │
      └────► Notification Service

Common technologies:

  • RabbitMQ
  • Azure Service Bus
  • Amazon SQS/SNS
  • Kafka

Microsoft's guidance distinguishes synchronous HTTP communication from asynchronous message-based communication and emphasizes minimizing unnecessary synchronous dependencies between services. Microsoft Learn

8. Synchronous vs Asynchronous Communication

SynchronousAsynchronous
HTTP/RESTMessage broker
Caller waitsCaller doesn't wait
SimpleMore complex
Immediate responseEventual processing
Tighter runtime dependencyLooser coupling
Easier to understandBetter for decoupled workflows
Can create service chainsHelps avoid service chains

Example

For:

GET /products/100

HTTP is perfectly reasonable.

But for:

Order Created
   ↓
Send Email

you don't necessarily need:

Order Service
      ↓ HTTP
Notification Service
      ↓
Send Email

Instead:

Order Service
      ↓
OrderCreated Event
      ↓
Message Broker
      ↓
Notification Service

This prevents notification processing from becoming a synchronous dependency of order creation.

9. API Gateway

An API Gateway acts as an entry point between clients and internal microservices.

React
   │
   ▼
API Gateway
   │
   ├──► Order Service
   ├──► Product Service
   ├──► Payment Service
   └──► User Service

Without a gateway:

React
 ├──► Order Service
 ├──► Product Service
 ├──► Payment Service
 └──► User Service

The client becomes tightly coupled to internal services.

Microsoft describes the gateway as a reverse proxy/single entry point that can handle routing and cross-cutting concerns such as authentication, SSL termination and caching. Microsoft Learn

10. What is BFF?

BFF = Backend for Frontend

Instead of one gateway serving every client identically:

                 ┌── Web BFF
React Web ───────┤
                 │
Mobile ──────────┼── Mobile BFF
                 │
Other Client ────┴── Other BFF

Each BFF is optimized for a particular client.

For example:

React Web
    ↓
Web BFF
    ↓
Order + Product + User Services

while:

Mobile App
    ↓
Mobile BFF
    ↓
Order + Product Services

Microsoft's API Gateway guidance discusses BFF as a way to tailor gateway APIs to different client applications. Microsoft Learn

11. What Should an API Gateway Do?

Typical responsibilities:

                API Gateway
                     │
       ┌─────────────┼──────────────┐
       │             │              │
   Routing       Authentication   Rate Limit
       │             │              │
   Caching       SSL/TLS        Logging

Possible responsibilities:

  • request routing
  • authentication
  • authorization-related gateway policies
  • TLS termination
  • rate limiting
  • caching
  • request aggregation
  • logging
  • correlation IDs
  • API version routing

Important

Don't put all business logic into the gateway.

Bad:

Gateway
 ├── Business Rules
 ├── Database Queries
 ├── Payment Logic
 ├── Order Logic
 └── Everything

Then the gateway becomes a new monolith.

Microsoft explicitly warns that an overly centralized gateway can become bloated and tightly coupled to internal services. Microsoft Learn

12. Service-to-Service Communication in ASP.NET Core

Suppose:

OrderService
     ↓
PaymentService

You could use HttpClientFactory:

public class PaymentClient
{
    private readonly HttpClient _httpClient;

    public PaymentClient(HttpClient httpClient)
    {
        _httpClient = httpClient;
    }

    public async Task<PaymentResponse?> ProcessPaymentAsync(
        PaymentRequest request,
        CancellationToken cancellationToken)
    {
        var response = await _httpClient.PostAsJsonAsync(
            "/api/payments",
            request,
            cancellationToken);

        response.EnsureSuccessStatusCode();

        return await response.Content
            .ReadFromJsonAsync<PaymentResponse>(
                cancellationToken);
    }
}

Registration:

builder.Services.AddHttpClient<PaymentClient>(client =>
{
    client.BaseAddress =
        new Uri("https://payment-service");
});

Then:

OrderService
      ↓
PaymentClient
      ↓
HttpClient
      ↓
Payment Service

For production, you'd also consider:

  • timeout
  • retry
  • circuit breaker
  • authentication
  • correlation ID
  • cancellation
  • idempotency

13. Messaging Architecture

A typical asynchronous architecture:

Order Service
      │
      │ OrderCreated
      ▼
┌─────────────────┐
│ Message Broker  │
└────────┬────────┘
         │
    ┌────┴─────┐
    ▼          ▼
Inventory   Notification
 Service       Service

The Order service doesn't need to synchronously call both services.

Microsoft's guidance describes asynchronous messaging as important for propagating changes between microservices and supporting eventual consistency. Microsoft Learn

14. Event vs Command

Command

"Please perform this operation."

Example:

CreateOrder
ProcessPayment
ReserveInventory

Usually directed toward a specific consumer.

Event

"This thing already happened."

Example:

OrderCreated
PaymentCompleted
OrderShipped

Potentially multiple services can consume it.

OrderCreated
      │
      ├──► Inventory
      ├──► Notification
      └──► Analytics

15. Microservices and Eventual Consistency

Because each service owns its database:

Order DB
Payment DB
Inventory DB

we don't normally have one ACID transaction spanning all three databases.

Therefore:

Order Created
      ↓
Payment Processing
      ↓
Inventory Reservation

may temporarily have different states.

This is eventual consistency.

Example:

T1:
Order = Created

T2:
Payment = Pending

T3:
Payment = Completed

T4:
Inventory = Reserved

The system eventually reaches a consistent business state.

16. How Do You Handle Transactions Across Microservices?

This leads to the Saga pattern, which we'll study in detail later.

Example:

Create Order
     ↓
Process Payment
     ↓
Reserve Inventory
     ↓
Ship Order

If inventory fails:

Reserve Inventory ❌
       ↓
Compensate Payment
       ↓
Refund Payment
       ↓
Cancel Order

This is different from:

BEGIN TRANSACTION

Order
Payment
Inventory

COMMIT

because those databases belong to different services.

17. Should Every Application Be Microservices?

No.

This is a very good senior-level interview answer.

Microservices introduce significant complexity:

More services
     ↓
More deployments
     ↓
More networks
     ↓
More failures
     ↓
More monitoring
     ↓
More distributed-data problems

You need to handle:

  • service discovery
  • networking
  • authentication
  • observability
  • distributed tracing
  • retries
  • timeouts
  • message brokers
  • deployment
  • distributed transactions
  • eventual consistency
  • versioning.

For a small application:

ASP.NET Core
     ↓
SQL Server

may be much simpler.

For a large product with independently evolving business capabilities:

API Gateway
    ↓
Order
Product
Payment
Inventory
Notification
Identity

microservices may make sense.

18. Microservices vs Modular Monolith

This is a very important Senior interview question.

Modular Monolith

             ASP.NET Core
                  │
     ┌────────────┼────────────┐
     │            │            │
  Orders       Payments     Products
     │            │            │
     └────────────┼────────────┘
                  ↓
              SQL Server

One deployment, but internally well-separated modules.

Microservices

Order Service ─── Order DB

Payment Service ─ Payment DB

Product Service ─ Product DB

Multiple deployments and processes.

Interview answer

"I wouldn't automatically convert a monolith into microservices. I would first establish clear business boundaries and determine whether independent scaling, deployment, ownership or team autonomy justify the additional distributed-system complexity. A modular monolith can be a good starting architecture when those requirements aren't present."

19. Real-World .NET Architecture

For your stack, imagine an e-commerce system:

                         React
                           │
                           ▼
                     API Gateway
                           │
          ┌────────────────┼────────────────┐
          │                │                │
          ▼                ▼                ▼
     Order API        Product API      Payment API
          │                │                │
          ▼                ▼                ▼
      Order DB        Product DB       Payment DB
          │
          │
          ▼
    Message Broker
          │
     ┌────┴──────────┐
     ▼               ▼
Inventory       Notification
 Service           Service
     │               │
 Inventory DB    AWS SQS/Lambda

Your ASP.NET Core services can internally follow:

Controller
    ↓
Application Service
    ↓
Domain
    ↓
Repository / DbContext
    ↓
Service Database

And cross-service communication can use:

HTTP/gRPC
     OR
Messaging

20. Microservices Interview Questions

🔴 Must know

  1. What are microservices?
  1. Monolith vs microservices?
  1. How do you identify service boundaries?
  1. What is bounded context?
  1. What is database-per-service?
  1. Why shouldn't microservices share databases?
  1. How do microservices communicate?
  1. Synchronous vs asynchronous communication?
  1. What is an API Gateway?
  1. What is BFF?
  1. What is event-driven architecture?
  1. Command vs event?
  1. What is eventual consistency?
  1. How do you handle distributed transactions?
  1. What is Saga?
  1. How do you handle service failure?
  1. How do you make microservices resilient?
  1. How do you monitor microservices?
  1. How do you secure microservices?
  1. When should you NOT use microservices?

🎯 Strong 60-Second Interview Answer

"Microservices architecture is an approach where an application is divided into independently deployable services, with each service responsible for a specific business capability or bounded context. Each service owns its business logic and data, which helps teams deploy and scale services independently.

For example, in an e-commerce system I could have Order, Product, Payment, Inventory and Notification services, each with its own database. Clients can communicate through an API Gateway, while services can communicate through synchronous HTTP when an immediate response is required or asynchronous messaging for decoupled workflows.

Because each service owns its data, distributed transactions become more complex, so we may use eventual consistency and patterns such as Saga for cross-service workflows. I also consider resilience patterns such as timeouts, retries, circuit breakers and idempotency.

I wouldn't introduce microservices just because the application is large. I would first establish clear business boundaries and determine whether independent deployment, scaling and ownership justify the additional distributed-system complexity."

🧠 Final Mental Model

Remember this:

                 MICROSERVICES
                      │
        ┌─────────────┼─────────────┐
        ▼             ▼             ▼
   Business        Own Data     Independent
   Boundary        / DB         Deployment
        │
        ▼
   Communication
      /     \
   HTTP    Messaging
     │         │
 Sync        Async
     │         │
     └────┬────┘
          ▼
    Eventual Consistency
          │
          ▼
        Saga
          │
          ▼
   Distributed System

One-line memory trick

Microservice = Business capability + bounded context + own data + independent deployment + controlled communication.

45. Service-to-Service Communication in ASP.NET Core

For microservices, services need to communicate with each other. The main choices are:

Service-to-Service Communication
│
├── 1. HTTP/REST
├── 2. gRPC
├── 3. Messaging
│   ├── Queue
│   └── Pub/Sub / Events
├── 4. Service Discovery
├── 5. Authentication between services
├── 6. Timeouts & Cancellation
├── 7. Retry / Circuit Breaker
└── 8. Idempotency

Microsoft's current .NET guidance supports IHttpClientFactory for centrally configured HTTP clients and gRPC client-factory integration for managed gRPC clients. Microsoft Learn

🔴 Priority: MUST MASTER

For interviews, focus heavily on:

  1. How microservices communicate
  1. REST vs gRPC vs Messaging
  1. Synchronous vs asynchronous communication
  1. IHttpClientFactory
  1. Typed HttpClient
  1. DelegatingHandler
  1. gRPC
  1. Service discovery
  1. Timeout and CancellationToken
  1. Retry and Circuit Breaker
  1. Authentication between services
  1. Correlation ID
  1. Idempotency
  1. When to use REST vs gRPC vs messaging

1. How Do Microservices Communicate?

There are three major approaches:

1. HTTP/REST

Order Service
      │
      │ HTTP
      ▼
Payment Service

2. gRPC

Order Service
      │
      │ gRPC
      ▼
Payment Service

3. Messaging

Order Service
      │
      │ Event
      ▼
Message Broker
      │
      ▼
Payment Service

The first two are generally request/response communication.

Messaging is generally asynchronous.

2. Synchronous Communication

The caller waits for the response.

Order Service
      │
      │ ProcessPayment()
      ▼
Payment Service
      │
      │ PaymentResult
      ▼
Order Service

Example:

POST /payments

The Order service needs to know immediately whether the payment request succeeded.

Advantages

  • Simple programming model
  • Immediate response
  • Easy to understand
  • Good for queries and operations requiring immediate results

Disadvantages

  • Runtime dependency
  • Network latency
  • Service failure can affect caller
  • Can create long chains

For example:

Order
 ↓
Payment
 ↓
Inventory
 ↓
Shipping
 ↓
Notification

Now one request depends on five services.

That's dangerous from a reliability perspective.

3. Asynchronous Communication

The caller sends a message and doesn't need to wait for the consumer to finish.

Order Service
      │
      │ OrderCreated
      ▼
 Message Broker
      │
      ├────► Inventory Service
      │
      ├────► Notification Service
      │
      └────► Analytics Service

Advantages

  • Loose coupling
  • Better resilience
  • Services can process independently
  • Good for background work
  • Natural support for eventual consistency

Disadvantages

  • More complicated
  • Eventual consistency
  • Message duplication
  • Ordering issues
  • Dead-letter handling
  • Harder debugging

4. REST Between Microservices

You already know REST from the API topics.

Example:

OrderService
      ↓
HTTP POST
      ↓
PaymentService

In .NET, don't manually create a new HttpClient everywhere.

Instead, use:

IHttpClientFactory

Microsoft recommends IHttpClientFactory as a DI-friendly way to configure logical clients, manage underlying handlers, add outgoing middleware, and provide logging. Microsoft Learn

5. Typed HttpClient

This is especially useful for your interview.

Suppose:

OrderService
     ↓
PaymentService

Create:

public class PaymentClient
{
    private readonly HttpClient _httpClient;

    public PaymentClient(HttpClient httpClient)
    {
        _httpClient = httpClient;
    }

    public async Task<PaymentResponse?> ProcessPaymentAsync(
        PaymentRequest request,
        CancellationToken cancellationToken)
    {
        var response = await _httpClient.PostAsJsonAsync(
            "/api/payments",
            request,
            cancellationToken);

        response.EnsureSuccessStatusCode();

        return await response.Content
            .ReadFromJsonAsync<PaymentResponse>(
                cancellationToken);
    }
}

Register it:

builder.Services.AddHttpClient<PaymentClient>(client =>
{
    client.BaseAddress =
        new Uri("https://payment-service");
});

Then your service can simply inject:

private readonly PaymentClient _paymentClient;

Architecture:

OrderController
      ↓
OrderService
      ↓
PaymentClient
      ↓
HttpClient
      ↓
PaymentService

6. Why Use IHttpClientFactory?

Interview Question

Why don't you just create HttpClient directly?

Interview Answer

IHttpClientFactory gives us centralized configuration and proper management of the underlying HTTP handlers.

It also supports:

  • named clients
  • typed clients
  • delegating handlers
  • logging
  • resilience policies
  • authentication handlers
  • centralized configuration.

Microsoft specifically notes that the factory manages the lifetime/caching of underlying HttpClientHandler instances, helping avoid common DNS and connection-management problems. Microsoft Learn

7. Named vs Typed HttpClient

Named

builder.Services.AddHttpClient(
    "PaymentApi",
    client =>
    {
        client.BaseAddress =
            new Uri("https://payment-service");
    });

Usage:

var client = _factory.CreateClient("PaymentApi");

Typed

builder.Services.AddHttpClient<PaymentClient>(
    client =>
    {
        client.BaseAddress =
            new Uri("https://payment-service");
    });

Then:

public OrderService(PaymentClient paymentClient)

Which is easier to maintain?

For a strongly defined external/internal service client, typed clients are often easier to work with because the service-specific behavior is encapsulated in a class.

8. DelegatingHandler

A DelegatingHandler is essentially outgoing HTTP middleware.

Architecture:

OrderService
     ↓
PaymentClient
     ↓
LoggingHandler
     ↓
AuthenticationHandler
     ↓
Retry/Resilience
     ↓
HttpClient
     ↓
Payment Service

Example:

public class CorrelationHandler : DelegatingHandler
{
    protected override async Task<HttpResponseMessage> SendAsync(
        HttpRequestMessage request,
        CancellationToken cancellationToken)
    {
        request.Headers.Add(
            "X-Correlation-ID",
            Guid.NewGuid().ToString());

        return await base.SendAsync(
            request,
            cancellationToken);
    }
}

Then:

builder.Services
    .AddTransient<CorrelationHandler>();

builder.Services
    .AddHttpClient<PaymentClient>()
    .AddHttpMessageHandler<CorrelationHandler>();

This is useful for:

  • logging
  • correlation IDs
  • authentication
  • headers
  • telemetry
  • resilience behavior.

9. gRPC

gRPC is another important service-to-service communication technology.

Instead of:

JSON + HTTP REST

we generally use:

Protocol Buffers
+
HTTP/2
+
gRPC

A contract is typically defined using a .proto file.

Conceptually:

Order Service
      │
      │ gRPC
      ▼
Payment Service

Microsoft's current ASP.NET Core gRPC documentation shows .NET clients and servers communicating through generated contracts and supports unary and streaming calls. Microsoft Learn

10. Why Use gRPC?

gRPC is particularly useful for internal service-to-service communication where both sides are controlled by the organization.

Advantages include:

  • strongly typed contracts
  • generated client/server code
  • efficient binary serialization
  • HTTP/2
  • streaming support
  • good performance
  • language interoperability.

Example:

Order Service (.NET)
       │
       │ gRPC
       ▼
Payment Service (.NET)

11. gRPC Communication Types

gRPC supports:

1. Unary
2. Server streaming
3. Client streaming
4. Bidirectional streaming

Unary

Client ─────► Server
Client ◄───── Server

Normal request/response.

Server streaming

Client ─────► Server

Client ◄───── Response 1
Client ◄───── Response 2
Client ◄───── Response 3

Client streaming

Request 1 ──►
Request 2 ──► Server
Request 3 ──►

            ◄── Response

Bidirectional streaming

Client ─────► Server
Client ◄───── Server
Client ─────► Server
Client ◄───── Server

12. gRPC Client Factory

ASP.NET Core provides gRPC client-factory integration.

Example:

builder.Services.AddGrpcClient<
    Payment.PaymentClient>(options =>
{
    options.Address =
        new Uri("https://payment-service");
});

Then inject:

public class OrderService
{
    private readonly Payment.PaymentClient _paymentClient;

    public OrderService(
        Payment.PaymentClient paymentClient)
    {
        _paymentClient = paymentClient;
    }
}

Microsoft's gRPC client factory integration provides centralized configuration and manages the underlying HTTP handler lifetime. It also supports interceptors, credentials, named clients, and cancellation/deadline propagation. Microsoft Learn

13. REST vs gRPC

This is a very common interview question.

RESTgRPC
HTTP APIsRPC framework
Usually JSONProtocol Buffers
Human-readableBinary
Very browser/client friendlyBetter for controlled service-to-service communication
Simple debuggingStrong contracts
Common public APIsCommon internal APIs
HTTP/1.1 or HTTP/2HTTP/2
FlexibleStrongly typed
Easy with ReactUsually not directly the first choice for browsers

Interview answer

"For public APIs consumed by React, mobile apps, or third-party clients, I would generally prefer REST because it's simple and broadly supported. For internal microservice-to-microservice communication where I control both sides and need strong contracts, efficient serialization and high-performance communication, gRPC can be a good choice."

14. REST vs Messaging

Suppose Order Service needs to notify Notification Service.

REST

Order
  │
  │ HTTP POST
  ▼
Notification

Order waits for Notification.

Messaging

Order
  │
  │ OrderCreated
  ▼
Queue
  │
  ▼
Notification

Order doesn't need Notification Service to be available immediately.

Rule of thumb

Need immediate response?
        ↓
REST / gRPC

Can process later?
        ↓
Messaging

It's not an absolute rule, but it's a useful interview mental model.

15. Service Discovery

In microservices, services can run on dynamic instances.

You don't want:

https://192.168.1.25:5001

hardcoded everywhere.

Instead:

Order Service
     ↓
Payment Service
     ↓
Service Discovery
     ↓
Payment instance

Examples of infrastructure that can provide service discovery include:

  • Kubernetes DNS
  • cloud service discovery
  • Consul
  • service mesh platforms.

The important concept is:

The caller should be able to locate the current healthy instances of the target service without hardcoding individual instance addresses.

16. Load Balancing

Suppose Payment Service has three instances:

             Payment Service
             /      |      \
            ▼       ▼       ▼
        Instance 1  2       3

Requests can be distributed across them.

Order
  │
  ▼
Load Balancer
  │
  ├──► Payment #1
  ├──► Payment #2
  └──► Payment #3

This supports:

  • horizontal scaling
  • availability
  • traffic distribution.

17. Authentication Between Services

Microservices shouldn't blindly trust every internal request.

Example:

Order Service
      │
      │ authenticated request
      ▼
Payment Service

Possible approaches include:

  • OAuth 2.0 access tokens
  • JWT bearer tokens
  • mTLS
  • managed workload identities
  • service mesh identity.

For example:

Authorization: Bearer <access-token>

The Payment Service validates the caller's identity and permissions.

18. Timeout

Never assume a downstream service will respond quickly.

Bad:

Order
 ↓
Payment

(wait forever)

Better:

Order
 ↓
Payment
 ↓
Timeout: 3 seconds

If Payment doesn't respond:

Timeout
   ↓
Handle failure

And propagate:

await paymentClient.ProcessPaymentAsync(
    request,
    cancellationToken);

This connects directly to the CancellationToken topic we studied earlier.

19. Retry

Suppose:

Order → Payment

Payment temporarily fails because of a transient network issue.

A retry may help:

Attempt 1 ❌
     ↓
wait
     ↓
Attempt 2 ❌
     ↓
wait
     ↓
Attempt 3 ✅

But don't blindly retry everything.

For example:

POST /payments

could potentially create duplicate business effects.

Therefore:

Retry
 +
Idempotency

is often required.

20. Circuit Breaker

Suppose Payment Service is completely down.

Without a circuit breaker:

Order
 ↓
Payment ❌
 ↓
Retry ❌
 ↓
Retry ❌
 ↓
Retry ❌
 ↓
Retry ❌

Thousands of requests continue hitting an unhealthy service.

With a circuit breaker:

Payment failures
       ↓
Circuit opens
       ↓
Stop sending requests
       ↓
Wait
       ↓
Test recovery
       ↓
Close circuit

This protects both services.

We already covered this in Topic 42 — Resilience Patterns.

21. Correlation ID

Imagine:

React
 ↓
API Gateway
 ↓
Order Service
 ↓
Payment Service
 ↓
Notification Service

A single user request can cross multiple services.

You need to identify all logs belonging to the same request.

Example:

X-Correlation-ID:
abc-123

Then:

Order Service       abc-123
Payment Service     abc-123
Notification        abc-123

Now you can trace the request across the system.

This becomes particularly important when using distributed tracing and observability.

22. Real-World Example Using Your Stack

Imagine:

React
  │
  ▼
ASP.NET Core API Gateway
  │
  ▼
Order Service
  │
  ├──── REST/gRPC ────► Payment Service
  │
  └──── Event ────────► Message Broker
                            │
                            ├──► Notification Service
                            └──► Inventory Service

Inside Order Service:

Controller
    ↓
OrderService
    ↓
PaymentClient
    ↓
HttpClient / gRPC Client
    ↓
Payment Service

And asynchronous processing:

OrderService
    ↓
OrderCreated
    ↓
AWS SQS
    ↓
Background Worker / Lambda
    ↓
Notification

This is a very realistic architecture to discuss in a .NET interview.

23. How Do You Choose Between REST, gRPC and Messaging?

Use this mental table:

RequirementChoice
Public APIREST
React frontendREST
Third-party integrationREST
Internal high-performance communicationgRPC
Strong service contractsgRPC
Immediate response requiredREST/gRPC
Background processingMessaging
Loose couplingMessaging
Event notificationMessaging
Multiple consumersPub/Sub
Long-running operationMessaging
Eventually consistent workflowMessaging

24. Common Interview Questions

🔴 Must Know

1. How do microservices communicate?

REST, gRPC or asynchronous messaging.

2. REST vs gRPC?

REST is generally simpler and widely supported; gRPC provides strongly typed contracts, efficient binary serialization and streaming, making it attractive for controlled internal communication. Microsoft Learn

3. REST vs messaging?

REST is usually request/response; messaging decouples sender and consumer and is useful for asynchronous workflows.

4. Why use IHttpClientFactory?

Centralized HTTP client configuration, handler lifetime management, outgoing middleware and logging. Microsoft Learn

5. What is a typed HttpClient?

A dedicated class encapsulating communication with a particular HTTP service.

6. What is DelegatingHandler?

Outgoing HTTP middleware used for things such as logging, authentication, correlation IDs and resilience.

7. What is gRPC?

A strongly typed RPC framework commonly used for efficient service-to-service communication.

8. What is service discovery?

A mechanism that allows services to locate available instances of another service dynamically.

9. How do you handle a downstream service failure?

Use:

Timeout
+
Cancellation
+
Retry
+
Circuit Breaker
+
Fallback where appropriate
+
Idempotency

10. How do you prevent duplicate processing?

Use idempotency keys for HTTP operations and message IDs/deduplication mechanisms for asynchronous consumers.

🎯 Strong 60-Second Interview Answer

"In a microservices architecture, I choose the communication mechanism based on the business requirement. For public APIs or frontend communication, I generally use REST because it's simple and widely supported. For internal service-to-service communication where both services are controlled by us and strong contracts and efficient communication are important, I can use gRPC. For asynchronous workflows such as notifications, inventory updates or background processing, I use messaging through a broker such as SQS.

For REST communication in ASP.NET Core, I prefer IHttpClientFactory with typed clients so service-specific HTTP communication is encapsulated and the underlying handlers are managed correctly. I can also use DelegatingHandlers for correlation IDs, authentication and logging. For production communication, I propagate CancellationToken, configure timeouts, use retries only for appropriate transient failures, and use circuit breakers to prevent cascading failures. For operations that can be retried, I also consider idempotency to prevent duplicate business effects.

For larger deployments, service discovery and load balancing allow services to communicate with dynamic instances rather than hardcoded addresses. Finally, I use correlation IDs and distributed tracing so requests can be followed across multiple services."

🧠 Final Mental Model

           SERVICE-TO-SERVICE
                  │
      ┌───────────┼───────────┐
      ▼           ▼           ▼
    REST         gRPC      Messaging
      │           │           │
  Request/      Request/     Async
  Response      Response     Events
      │           │           │
      └───────────┼───────────┘
                  ▼
          Production Needs
                  │
      ┌───────────┼───────────┐
      ▼           ▼           ▼
   Timeout      Retry      Circuit Breaker
      │           │           │
      └───────────┼───────────┘
                  ▼
             Idempotency
                  │
                  ▼
             Observability

One-line memory trick

REST = simple API | gRPC = efficient internal RPC | Messaging = asynchronous decoupling.

46. API Gateway / BFF in ASP.NET Core

This is an important Senior .NET / Microservices interview topic because API Gateway sits between clients and your microservices and can centralize routing and cross-cutting concerns.

For .NET, YARP (Yet Another Reverse Proxy) is Microsoft's customizable reverse-proxy library. It supports routing, load balancing, health checks, authentication/authorization integration, session affinity and request/response transforms. Microsoft Learn

🔴 Priority: MUST MASTER

Focus on these:

  1. What is an API Gateway?
  1. Why do we need an API Gateway?
  1. API Gateway vs Reverse Proxy
  1. API Gateway vs Load Balancer
  1. API Gateway responsibilities
  1. Request routing
  1. Authentication/authorization at gateway
  1. Rate limiting
  1. Caching
  1. Request aggregation
  1. BFF — Backend for Frontend
  1. Gateway vs BFF
  1. Gateway single point of failure
  1. Gateway becoming a bottleneck
  1. YARP in ASP.NET Core
  1. Real-world .NET microservices gateway architecture

1. What is an API Gateway?

An API Gateway is a single entry point between clients and backend services.

Instead of React directly communicating with multiple microservices:

                    ┌──► Order Service
                    │
React ──────────────┼──► Product Service
                    │
                    ├──► Payment Service
                    │
                    └──► User Service

we introduce:

                       API Gateway
                           │
             ┌─────────────┼─────────────┐
             ▼             ▼             ▼
       Order Service  Product Service  Payment Service
             │             │             │
           DB            DB             DB

The client knows about the gateway rather than the internal service topology.

A reverse proxy can route requests to backend destinations and hide internal endpoints from external clients. Microsoft Learn

2. Why Do We Need an API Gateway?

Imagine your React application needs:

Products
Orders
Payments
Users
Notifications

Without a gateway:

React
 ├──► product.company.com
 ├──► order.company.com
 ├──► payment.company.com
 ├──► user.company.com
 └──► notification.company.com

The frontend needs to know:

  • service URLs
  • service versions
  • authentication details
  • routing
  • potentially different policies.

With a gateway:

React
  │
  ▼
api.company.com
  │
  ├── /products → Product Service
  ├── /orders   → Order Service
  ├── /payments → Payment Service
  └── /users    → User Service

The internal architecture can change without necessarily changing the public API structure.

Microsoft specifically identifies routing, security, caching, versioning and TLS termination as common reverse-proxy responsibilities. Microsoft Learn

3. API Gateway Responsibilities

A gateway can handle many cross-cutting concerns:

                     API Gateway
                          │
       ┌──────────────────┼──────────────────┐
       ▼                  ▼                  ▼
    Routing         Authentication      Rate Limiting
       │                  │                  │
       ▼                  ▼                  ▼
    Caching          Authorization       Logging
       │                  │                  │
       └──────────────────┼──────────────────┘
                          ▼
                    Microservices

Typical responsibilities:

  • request routing
  • authentication
  • authorization policies
  • rate limiting
  • TLS termination
  • caching
  • request aggregation
  • API version routing
  • correlation IDs
  • logging/telemetry
  • load balancing
  • health-aware routing
  • request/response transformation.

YARP supports route/cluster-based configuration, load balancing, transforms and proxy middleware. Microsoft Learn

4. API Gateway vs Reverse Proxy

These terms are related but not identical.

Reverse Proxy

Primarily forwards requests:

Client
  ↓
Reverse Proxy
  ↓
Backend

Example:

/api/products
      ↓
Product Service

API Gateway

A reverse proxy can be the foundation of an API Gateway, but the gateway commonly adds API-specific concerns:

                    API Gateway
                         │
       ┌─────────────────┼─────────────────┐
       ▼                 ▼                 ▼
   Routing          Authentication     Rate Limiting
       │                 │                 │
       └─────────────────┼─────────────────┘
                         ▼
                    Microservices

Interview answer

"A reverse proxy primarily forwards client requests to backend destinations. An API Gateway is a broader architectural component that can use reverse-proxy capabilities while also implementing API concerns such as authentication, authorization, rate limiting, aggregation, versioning and observability."

5. API Gateway vs Load Balancer

Another common interview question.

Load Balancer

Main goal:

Distribute traffic across healthy instances.
             Load Balancer
             /     |      \
            ▼      ▼       ▼
          API 1   API 2   API 3

API Gateway

Main goal:

Provide a controlled entry point and API-level policies.
                 API Gateway
                      │
          ┌───────────┼───────────┐
          ▼           ▼           ▼
       Orders      Products     Payments

A gateway can itself use load balancing to select among multiple healthy destinations. YARP provides built-in load-balancing policies for clusters with multiple destinations. Microsoft Learn

6. Routing

One of the gateway's primary responsibilities is routing.

Example:

/api/products/*
        ↓
Product Service

/api/orders/*
        ↓
Order Service

/api/payments/*
        ↓
Payment Service

Conceptually:

React
 │
 ▼
API Gateway
 │
 ├── /api/products → Product Service
 ├── /api/orders   → Order Service
 └── /api/payments → Payment Service

YARP models this using Routes, Clusters, and Destinations. Microsoft Learn

7. YARP in ASP.NET Core

For .NET interviews, know this name:

YARP — Yet Another Reverse Proxy

It's a Microsoft reverse-proxy library built on .NET.

A basic setup:

var builder = WebApplication.CreateBuilder(args);

builder.Services
    .AddReverseProxy()
    .LoadFromConfig(
        builder.Configuration.GetSection("ReverseProxy"));

var app = builder.Build();

app.MapReverseProxy();

app.Run();

This is the standard YARP configuration approach documented by Microsoft. Microsoft Learn

8. YARP Configuration

Conceptually:

{
  "ReverseProxy": {
    "Routes": {
      "products-route": {
        "ClusterId": "products-cluster",
        "Match": {
          "Path": "/api/products/{**catch-all}"
        }
      }
    },
    "Clusters": {
      "products-cluster": {
        "Destinations": {
          "products-1": {
            "Address": "https://product-service/"
          }
        }
      }
    }
  }
}

Think:

Route
  ↓
Which incoming request?

Cluster
  ↓
Which backend service?

Destination
  ↓
Which instance?

YARP can load route and cluster configuration through ASP.NET Core's IConfiguration, and configuration can be updated without restarting when the underlying configuration source supports reloads. Microsoft Learn

9. Route → Cluster → Destination

This is worth memorizing.

/api/products
       │
       ▼
     Route
       │
       ▼
    Cluster
       │
   ┌───┼────┐
   ▼   ▼    ▼
  P1   P2   P3

Route

Determines:

Which incoming request matches?

Cluster

Represents:

The group of backend destinations.

Destination

Represents:

An individual backend instance.

10. Authentication at the Gateway

The gateway can authenticate requests before forwarding them.

React
  │
  │ JWT
  ▼
API Gateway
  │
  ├── Validate authentication
  ├── Check policy
  │
  ▼
Order Service

YARP supports configuring authorization policies per route. Microsoft Learn

For example:

/api/products
     ↓
Anonymous allowed

/api/orders
     ↓
Authenticated users

/api/admin/*
     ↓
Admin policy

Important

Authentication at the gateway doesn't necessarily mean backend services can blindly trust the gateway.

For defense in depth, downstream services may also validate identity/authorization according to the architecture.

11. Rate Limiting at Gateway

Suppose a client sends:

10,000 requests/sec

The gateway can reject excessive traffic before it reaches your services.

Client
  │
  ▼
API Gateway
  │
  ├── Rate limit
  │
  ├── 429 if exceeded
  │
  ▼
Backend

This protects:

  • CPU
  • database
  • downstream services
  • network
  • application resources.

12. Caching at Gateway

Suppose:

GET /api/products

is requested frequently.

The gateway could cache appropriate responses:

Client
  │
  ▼
Gateway
  │
  ├── Cache HIT → Response
  │
  └── Cache MISS
           ↓
     Product Service

This can reduce backend traffic.

But caching must consider:

  • data freshness
  • invalidation
  • user-specific data
  • authorization
  • cache keys
  • sensitive information.

13. Request Aggregation

This is one of the most important gateway capabilities.

Suppose your React dashboard needs:

User
Orders
Recommendations
Notifications

Without aggregation:

React
 ├──► User Service
 ├──► Order Service
 ├──► Recommendation Service
 └──► Notification Service

With aggregation:

React
  │
  ▼
API Gateway
  │
  ├──► User Service
  ├──► Order Service
  ├──► Recommendation Service
  └──► Notification Service
          │
          ▼
    Combined Response
          │
          ▼
         React

For example:

{
  "user": {},
  "orders": [],
  "recommendations": [],
  "notifications": []
}

This can reduce frontend network calls.

But there is a trade-off

The gateway now depends on several services.

Gateway
 ├── User
 ├── Orders
 ├── Recommendations
 └── Notifications

If every gateway endpoint becomes a complex business workflow, the gateway can become a bottleneck or a new monolith.

14. What is BFF?

BFF = Backend for Frontend

A BFF is a backend specifically designed for a particular frontend/client.

Example:

                    API Gateway
                         │
              ┌──────────┴──────────┐
              ▼                     ▼
          Web BFF               Mobile BFF
              │                     │
              ▼                     ▼
        Microservices          Microservices

Maybe your React application needs:

User
Orders
Products

while mobile needs:

User
Orders

but with a completely different response shape.

Instead of forcing all clients to consume the same API contract:

React
  ↓
Web BFF

and:

Mobile
  ↓
Mobile BFF

Each BFF can optimize the API for its client.

15. API Gateway vs BFF

API GatewayBFF
General entry pointClient-specific backend
Shared across clientsUsually dedicated to a client
Routing/security/rate limitingClient-specific aggregation/orchestration
Common API policiesTailored response models
Often infrastructure-orientedMore application/client-oriented

Simple memory

Gateway = Where should this request go?

BFF = What does this particular client need?

16. BFF Example With React

Suppose React needs:

Dashboard

Instead of:

React
 ├── User API
 ├── Orders API
 ├── Product API
 └── Notification API

Use:

React
  │
  ▼
Dashboard BFF
  │
  ├──► User
  ├──► Orders
  ├──► Products
  └──► Notifications

BFF returns:

{
  "user": {
    "name": "Saurabh"
  },
  "recentOrders": [],
  "recommendedProducts": [],
  "unreadNotifications": 3
}

This gives the frontend a contract designed specifically for its screen/use case.

17. Request/Response Transformation

Sometimes the backend expects a different contract from the public API.

A gateway can transform requests/responses.

For example:

Client
/api/v1/products
       ↓
Gateway
       ↓
/internal/catalog/products

YARP supports request/response transforms for things such as paths, headers and other HTTP metadata. Microsoft Learn

For example:

/api/products
       ↓
/catalog-service/products

The client doesn't need to know the internal route.

18. TLS Termination

A gateway/reverse proxy can terminate HTTPS:

Client
   │
 HTTPS
   ▼
Gateway
   │
 HTTP/HTTPS
   ▼
Service

The gateway decrypts the incoming TLS connection and can then forward the request according to its configuration.

YARP operates as a Layer 7 HTTP proxy and supports TLS termination. Microsoft Learn

In production, whether the internal connection remains encrypted depends on your security and network architecture.

19. API Gateway as a Single Point of Failure

This is a classic interview trap.

You might have:

              Gateway
                 │
        ┌────────┼────────┐
        ▼        ▼        ▼
      Order   Product   Payment

If there's only one gateway instance:

Gateway ❌
   ↓
Everything unavailable

Therefore production architecture typically uses multiple gateway instances:

                 Load Balancer
                 /     |      \
                ▼      ▼       ▼
             Gateway Gateway Gateway
                │      │       │
                └──────┼───────┘
                       ▼
                  Microservices

The gateway itself should be horizontally scalable and preferably stateless where practical.

20. Can API Gateway Become a Bottleneck?

Yes.

For example:

10,000 requests/sec
        ↓
Single Gateway
        ↓
Limited CPU
        ↓
Bottleneck

Solutions include:

  • horizontal scaling
  • load balancing
  • efficient routing
  • avoiding expensive business logic
  • caching
  • rate limiting
  • appropriate timeouts
  • observability
  • keeping gateway responsibilities focused.

21. What Should NOT Go Into the Gateway?

Avoid putting core business logic there.

Bad architecture

API Gateway
 ├── Order business rules
 ├── Payment business rules
 ├── Inventory business rules
 ├── Database queries
 └── Everything else

Now:

API Gateway = Monolith

Better

Gateway
  ↓
Order Service
  ↓
Order business logic

The gateway should primarily handle cross-cutting and routing concerns, not own the core business domain.

22. Gateway vs Service-to-Service Communication

This distinction is very important.

Client → Gateway

React
 ↓
API Gateway
 ↓
Services

Service → Service

Order Service
 ↓
Payment Service

The Order service should generally communicate directly with Payment or through appropriate messaging infrastructure—not route every internal interaction back through the public gateway.

Bad:

Order
 ↓
API Gateway
 ↓
Payment

Better:

Order
 ↓
Payment

or:

Order
 ↓
Message Broker
 ↓
Payment

23. Real-World Architecture for Your Stack

A production-style architecture could look like:

                         React
                           │
                           ▼
                    Load Balancer
                           │
                           ▼
                    API Gateway
                     /         \
                    /           \
             Authentication    Rate Limit
                    │
                    ▼
        ┌───────────┼───────────────┐
        │           │               │
        ▼           ▼               ▼
   Order API    Product API    Payment API
        │           │               │
        ▼           ▼               ▼
   Order DB     Product DB      Payment DB
        │
        ▼
   Message Broker
        │
    ┌───┴───────────┐
    ▼               ▼
Inventory       Notification
 Service           Service

And each ASP.NET Core service could internally use:

Controller
    ↓
Application/Service Layer
    ↓
Domain
    ↓
EF Core / Dapper
    ↓
Service-owned Database

24. API Gateway + YARP Interview Question

Question

How would you implement an API Gateway using ASP.NET Core?

Strong Answer

"For a .NET-based solution, I can use YARP, Microsoft's reverse-proxy library. I would configure routes that map public API paths to internal service clusters and destinations. The gateway can handle cross-cutting concerns such as authentication and authorization policies, rate limiting, correlation IDs, logging and potentially caching or request aggregation. YARP supports load balancing across multiple destinations, health-aware routing and request/response transforms. I would keep business logic inside the individual microservices rather than putting domain logic into the gateway. For production, I would deploy multiple gateway instances behind a load balancer so the gateway itself doesn't become a single point of failure." Microsoft Learn

25. Common Interview Questions

🔴 Must Know

1. What is an API Gateway?

A single entry point between clients and backend services.

2. Why use an API Gateway?

To centralize routing and common API concerns and hide internal service topology.

3. Gateway vs reverse proxy?

A reverse proxy forwards traffic; an API Gateway typically adds API-specific capabilities such as auth, rate limiting, aggregation and versioning.

4. Gateway vs load balancer?

Load balancer distributes traffic; gateway provides API-level routing and policies.

5. What is BFF?

Backend for Frontend—a backend tailored to a specific client application.

6. What is YARP?

Microsoft's customizable reverse-proxy library for .NET. Microsoft Learn

7. What are YARP Routes, Clusters and Destinations?

Route → incoming request matching

Cluster → group of destinations

Destination → individual backend instance

8. Can gateway handle authentication?

Yes. YARP can apply authentication/authorization policies to proxy routes. Microsoft Learn

9. Can gateway perform load balancing?

Yes. YARP supports multiple destinations and load-balancing policies. Microsoft Learn

10. Can gateway aggregate requests?

Yes, but aggregation should be used carefully because it can create coupling and increase gateway complexity.

11. Can gateway cache responses?

Yes, where caching semantics are appropriate.

12. Should business logic be in the gateway?

Generally no. Business logic should remain in the owning service.

13. Can API Gateway become a bottleneck?

Yes. Scale it horizontally and keep gateway processing lightweight.

14. Can API Gateway be a single point of failure?

Yes, if deployed as a single instance. Use multiple instances and load balancing.

🎯 Strong 60-Second Interview Answer

"An API Gateway is a single entry point between clients such as React applications and backend microservices. Instead of exposing every microservice directly to the client, I can expose the gateway and route requests such as /api/orders or /api/products to the appropriate services.

The gateway can handle cross-cutting concerns such as authentication, authorization policies, rate limiting, TLS termination, logging, correlation IDs, caching and sometimes request aggregation. In a .NET environment, I can use YARP, which provides reverse-proxy functionality with routes, clusters, destinations, load balancing, health checks and request/response transforms.

For client-specific requirements, I can use a BFF, where the backend is tailored to a particular frontend such as a React web application or mobile application. I keep core business logic inside the microservices rather than putting it into the gateway. Finally, I would deploy multiple gateway instances behind a load balancer so the gateway doesn't become a single point of failure." Microsoft Learn

🧠 Final Mental Model

                         CLIENT
                           │
                           ▼
                    LOAD BALANCER
                           │
                           ▼
                    API GATEWAY
                           │
       ┌───────────────────┼───────────────────┐
       │                   │                   │
    ROUTING          AUTH / RATE LIMIT       CACHE
       │                   │                   │
       └───────────────────┼───────────────────┘
                           ▼
                ┌──────────┼──────────┐
                ▼          ▼          ▼
             ORDER      PRODUCT    PAYMENT
             SERVICE    SERVICE    SERVICE
                │          │          │
                ▼          ▼          ▼
               DB         DB         DB

One-line memory trick

API Gateway = Single entry point + routing + cross-cutting API concerns.

BFF = Gateway/backend tailored to a specific frontend.

YARP = .NET reverse-proxy building block for implementing this architecture.

47. Messaging & Event-Driven Architecture

This is a high-priority Senior .NET / Microservices topic because messaging is one of the main ways to decouple services.

Microsoft's .NET microservices guidance describes asynchronous messaging as important for propagating changes across microservices and supporting eventual consistency. It distinguishes point-to-point messaging from publish/subscribe event-driven communication. Microsoft Learn

🔴 Priority: MUST MASTER

Focus heavily on:

  1. What is messaging?
  1. Synchronous vs asynchronous communication
  1. Message broker
  1. Queue
  1. Topic / Pub-Sub
  1. Command vs Event
  1. Producer vs Consumer
  1. Point-to-point messaging
  1. Publish/Subscribe
  1. Event-driven architecture
  1. Message delivery guarantees
  1. At-most-once vs at-least-once
  1. Exactly-once vs effectively-once
  1. Message duplication
  1. Idempotent consumers
  1. Retry
  1. Dead-Letter Queue
  1. Message ordering
  1. Message acknowledgment
  1. Outbox Pattern
  1. SQS / RabbitMQ / Azure Service Bus / Kafka
  1. Real-world .NET implementation

1. What is Messaging?

Messaging means that services communicate by sending messages through a messaging infrastructure rather than directly calling each other.

Instead of:

Order Service
      │
      │ HTTP
      ▼
Notification Service

we can have:

Order Service
      │
      │ Message
      ▼
 Message Broker
      │
      ▼
Notification Service

The sender and receiver don't need to be available at exactly the same time.

A message typically contains metadata/header information and a body containing the actual data. Microsoft Learn

2. Why Use Messaging?

Imagine an order system:

Customer
   ↓
Create Order
   ↓
Order Service

After creating an order, we need to:

  • reserve inventory
  • send email
  • update analytics
  • generate invoice
  • notify shipping

Without messaging:

Order Service
   │
   ├──► Inventory
   ├──► Notification
   ├──► Analytics
   ├──► Invoice
