   └──► Shipping

The Order Service becomes tightly coupled to everything.

With messaging:

Order Service
      │
      ▼
  Message Broker
      │
 ┌────┼───────┬────────┐
 ▼    ▼       ▼        ▼
Inventory Notification Invoice Analytics

Now services can process the work independently.

Messaging can also buffer bursts and allow consumers to process work when they're available. Microsoft Learn

3. What is a Message Broker?

A message broker is infrastructure that receives, stores/routes, and delivers messages between producers and consumers.

Producer
   │
   ▼
┌────────────────┐
│ Message Broker │
└───────┬────────┘
        │
        ▼
    Consumer

Examples:

  • Amazon SQS/SNS
  • RabbitMQ
  • Azure Service Bus
  • Apache Kafka

Microsoft's architecture guidance identifies message brokers such as Azure Service Bus and Kafka as common infrastructure for asynchronous microservice communication. Microsoft Learn

4. Producer and Consumer

Producer

The service that sends the message.

Order Service
     ↓
Producer

Consumer

The service that receives/processes the message.

Message Broker
     ↓
Inventory Service
     ↓
Consumer

Complete flow:

Order Service
     ↓
Producer
     ↓
Message Broker
     ↓
Consumer
     ↓
Inventory Service

5. Queue

A queue generally represents point-to-point communication.

Producer
   │
   ▼
┌─────────────┐
│    Queue    │
└──────┬──────┘
       │
       ▼
   Consumer

Suppose there are three consumers:

             Queue
          /    |    \
         ▼     ▼     ▼
       C1     C2     C3

A message is generally processed by one consumer in the consumer group/competing-consumer model.

This is useful for workload distribution.

For example:

1000 Orders
     ↓
   Queue
     ↓
Workers process orders

Instead of one service trying to process all 1000 simultaneously.

6. Pub/Sub

Pub/Sub = Publish/Subscribe

A producer publishes an event, and multiple subscribers can independently receive it.

                  Publisher
                      │
                      ▼
                 Event Broker
                 /     |      \
                ▼      ▼       ▼
          Inventory Notification Analytics

For example:

OrderCreated

could be consumed by:

Inventory Service
Notification Service
Analytics Service

The publisher doesn't need to know all the consumers.

Microsoft describes publish/subscribe as a way to add subscribers without modifying the sending service. Microsoft Learn

7. Queue vs Pub/Sub

QueuePub/Sub
Point-to-pointOne-to-many
Usually one consumer processes each messageMultiple subscribers can receive event
Work distributionEvent broadcasting
Commands/jobsEvents/notifications
Good for background jobsGood for integration events

Memory trick

Queue = "Someone please do this."

Pub/Sub = "This happened; whoever cares can react."

8. Command vs Event

This is extremely important.

Command

A command asks someone to perform an action.

ProcessPayment
ReserveInventory
CreateInvoice
SendNotification

Conceptually:

"Please do this."

A command usually has a specific intended consumer.

Event

An event tells other components that something already happened.

OrderCreated
PaymentCompleted
InventoryReserved
OrderShipped

Conceptually:

"This happened."

Multiple services may react to the event.

Microsoft's messaging guidance explicitly distinguishes commands from events and describes events as notifications of something that occurred in a service's domain. Microsoft Learn

9. Command vs Event Example

Suppose an order is created.

Command

CreateOrderCommand
       ↓
Order Service

The sender is asking:

Create this order.

Event

After the order is successfully created:

OrderCreatedEvent
       ↓
Message Broker
       │
   ┌───┼────┐
   ▼   ▼    ▼
Inventory
Notification
Analytics

The event says:

The order has already been created.

10. Event-Driven Architecture

In an event-driven architecture, services react to events.

Example:

                 Order Service
                      │
                      │
                      ▼
                OrderCreated
                      │
                      ▼
                 Event Broker
                 /     |      \
                ▼      ▼       ▼
          Inventory  Email   Analytics
             │
             ▼
      InventoryReserved
             │
             ▼
        Other Services

The producer doesn't need to directly call every consumer.

This creates loose coupling.

Microsoft describes this pattern as asynchronous event-driven communication where services publish events and other services subscribe and react to them. Microsoft Learn

11. Synchronous vs Asynchronous

Synchronous

Order
  │
  │ HTTP
  ▼
Payment
  │
  │ Response
  ▼
Order

Order waits.

Asynchronous

Order
  │
  │ Message
  ▼
Broker
  │
  ▼
Payment

Order doesn't need to wait for Payment to finish.

Important

Asynchronous doesn't necessarily mean:

"The operation will never return a response."

It means the communication doesn't require the sender to wait synchronously for the receiver's processing.

12. When Should You Use Messaging?

Good scenarios:

Background processing

API
 ↓
Queue
 ↓
Worker

Notifications

OrderCreated
 ↓
Notification Service

Long-running workflows

Order
 ↓
Payment
 ↓
Inventory
 ↓
Shipping

Integration

Application
 ↓
Event
 ↓
External systems

Traffic bursts

10,000 requests
      ↓
    Queue
      ↓
Workers process gradually

This is sometimes called queue-based load leveling. Azure architecture guidance identifies buffering bursts and load leveling as important messaging use cases. Microsoft Learn

13. Message Delivery Guarantees

This is a common senior-level interview question.

There are three commonly discussed models:

At-most-once
At-least-once
Exactly-once

At-Most-Once

Message is delivered:

0 or 1 times

Possible:

Message
  ↓
Consumer ❌

The message may be lost.

Advantage:

  • no duplicates

Disadvantage:

  • possible message loss.

14. At-Least-Once

Message is delivered:

1 or more times

Example:

Message
  ↓
Consumer
  ↓
Processing succeeds
  ↓
ACK fails
  ↓
Broker thinks processing failed
  ↓
Message delivered again

Result:

Message processed twice

This is why idempotent consumers are extremely important.

Microsoft's Azure Service Bus guidance documents at-least-once delivery and dead-letter queues as part of its reliability features. Microsoft Learn

15. Exactly-Once

The theoretical goal:

Message processed exactly once

But true end-to-end exactly-once processing across distributed systems is difficult.

For interview purposes, say:

"Instead of assuming exactly-once processing, I design consumers to be idempotent so duplicate delivery produces the same intended business effect."

That's a much stronger distributed-systems answer.

16. Idempotent Consumer

Suppose:

PaymentCompleted

is delivered twice.

Bad:

Message 1 → Credit account
Message 2 → Credit account again

Good:

Message
   ↓
Check MessageId
   ↓
Already processed?
   ├── Yes → Ignore / return
   └── No
        ↓
    Process
        ↓
   Mark processed

Example:

MessageId = ABC123

Store:

ProcessedMessages

ABC123

If ABC123 arrives again:

Already processed
       ↓
Don't repeat business operation

17. Retry

Suppose consumer processing fails:

Message
  ↓
Consumer
  ↓
❌ Temporary DB failure

Retry:

Attempt 1 ❌
    ↓
wait
    ↓
Attempt 2 ❌
    ↓
wait
    ↓
Attempt 3 ✅

But retry only makes sense for retryable failures.

For example:

Temporary network issue → retry
Temporary database issue → potentially retry
Invalid message → don't blindly retry forever

18. Dead-Letter Queue

Suppose a message keeps failing:

Message
 ↓
Attempt 1 ❌
 ↓
Attempt 2 ❌
 ↓
Attempt 3 ❌
 ↓
Attempt 4 ❌

Don't keep retrying forever.

Move it to:

Dead-Letter Queue

Architecture:

                Main Queue
                    │
                    ▼
                 Consumer
                    │
              ┌─────┴─────┐
              │           │
            Success      Failure
              │           │
              ▼           ▼
             ACK       Retry
                          │
                    Max retries
                          │
                          ▼
                    Dead Letter

DLQ allows operations teams to inspect and reprocess problematic messages.

19. Message Acknowledgment

An acknowledgment tells the broker:

"I successfully processed this message."

Conceptually:

Broker
  ↓
Message
  ↓
Consumer
  ↓
Process
  ↓
ACK
  ↓
Broker removes/completes message

If processing fails before acknowledgment:

No ACK
  ↓
Message can be redelivered

For example, Azure Service Bus uses a peek-lock model where a consumer receives a locked message and then completes it after successful processing. Microsoft Learn

20. Message Ordering

Sometimes ordering matters.

Example:

OrderCreated
PaymentCompleted
OrderShipped

You shouldn't process:

OrderShipped
PaymentCompleted
OrderCreated

if the business workflow depends on ordering.

But distributed systems make ordering difficult, especially with:

  • multiple consumers
  • partitions
  • retries
  • parallel processing
  • multiple producers.

Therefore, if ordering matters, choose messaging infrastructure and partitioning/keying strategies that support the required ordering scope.

Don't simply say:

"Messages are always processed in order."

They aren't necessarily.

21. Message Duplication

Duplicates can happen because of:

  • retries
  • network failures
  • consumer crashes
  • acknowledgment failures
  • broker redelivery
  • application restarts.

Therefore:

Messaging
    ↓
Assume duplicate delivery is possible
    ↓
Idempotent consumer

This is one of the most important practical rules in messaging.

22. Message Schema

A message should have a well-defined contract.

For example:

{
  "messageId": "8f2...",
  "eventType": "OrderCreated",
  "occurredAt": "2026-10-02T12:30:00Z",
  "version": 1,
  "data": {
    "orderId": 12345,
    "customerId": 500,
    "totalAmount": 2500
  }
}

Useful metadata can include:

  • MessageId
  • EventType
  • CorrelationId
  • CausationId
  • Timestamp
  • Version
  • TenantId
  • Trace information

23. Thin vs Fat Events

Thin event

{
  "orderId": 123
}

Consumer can then retrieve details.

Fat event

{
  "orderId": 123,
  "customerId": 500,
  "total": 2500,
  "items": [...]
}

Consumer receives most required data directly.

Neither is universally correct.

The decision depends on:

  • coupling
  • payload size
  • consistency requirements
  • consumer needs
  • number of downstream calls.

Microsoft's guidance explicitly notes that deciding how much business data to include in integration events is an important design consideration. Microsoft Learn

24. Outbox Pattern

This is a very important Senior interview topic.

Problem:

Order Service
     │
     ├── Save Order → DB ✅
     │
     └── Publish Event → Broker ❌

Now:

Order exists
BUT
OrderCreated event wasn't published

The system becomes inconsistent.

Outbox Solution

Store the event in the same database transaction:

                SQL Server
              ┌──────────────┐
              │ Orders       │
              │ OutboxEvents │
              └──────┬───────┘
                     │
             Same transaction
                     │
                     ▼
                  COMMIT

Then a background process publishes the Outbox event:

Outbox Table
     ↓
Background Worker
     ↓
Message Broker
     ↓
Consumers

Microsoft's .NET microservices guidance identifies the Outbox pattern as one approach for reliably publishing integration events alongside a state change. Microsoft Learn

25. Outbox Flow

Create Order
     ↓
BEGIN TRANSACTION
     │
     ├── Insert Order
     │
     └── Insert OrderCreated into Outbox
     │
     ▼
COMMIT
     ↓
Background Publisher
     ↓
Message Broker
     ↓
Consumers

This avoids the dangerous gap between:

Database update

and:

Event publishing

26. Your AWS SQS Experience

This is particularly useful for your own interview answers, because you've worked with AWS Lambda + SQS/SNS.

A realistic architecture:

ASP.NET Core API
       │
       ▼
     SQS
       │
       ▼
AWS Lambda
       │
       ├── Process notification
       ├── Send email
       └── Update status

For fan-out:

Order Service
      │
      ▼
     SNS
      │
 ┌────┼─────┐
 ▼    ▼     ▼
SQS  SQS    SQS
 │    │      │
 ▼    ▼      ▼
Email Inventory Analytics

This gives you a strong practical example in interviews.

27. SQS vs SNS

SQS

Primarily a queue.

Producer
   ↓
SQS
   ↓
Consumer

Good for:

  • background jobs
  • workload distribution
  • decoupling
  • asynchronous processing.

SNS

Primarily publish/subscribe notification/fan-out.

Publisher
    ↓
   SNS
  / | \
 ▼  ▼  ▼
SQS SQS SQS

Good for:

  • broadcasting events
  • fan-out
  • multiple consumers.

28. RabbitMQ

RabbitMQ is a message broker commonly used for:

  • queues
  • routing
  • exchanges
  • pub/sub
  • acknowledgments
  • consumer management.

Conceptually:

Producer
    ↓
 Exchange
 /   |   \
▼    ▼    ▼
Queue Queue Queue
 │     │     │
 ▼     ▼     ▼
C1    C2    C3

Microsoft's .NET microservices guidance uses RabbitMQ as an example of a lightweight message broker and discusses Azure Service Bus as another production messaging option. Microsoft Learn

29. Kafka

Kafka is commonly used for:

  • high-throughput event streaming
  • event logs
  • analytics
  • distributed event processing
  • stream processing.

Conceptually:

Producer
    ↓
Kafka Topic
    │
 ┌──┼────┐
 ▼  ▼    ▼
C1  C2   C3

Kafka is particularly strong when you need durable event streams and high-throughput partitioned processing.

Don't simply say:

Kafka = queue.

A better answer is:

"Kafka is a distributed event-streaming platform built around durable, partitioned logs, whereas traditional queues are generally focused more directly on work distribution."

30. SQS vs RabbitMQ vs Kafka

For interview purposes:

TechnologyTypical Strength
SQSManaged queueing
SNSManaged pub/sub and fan-out
RabbitMQFlexible message broker/routing
Azure Service BusEnterprise queues/topics and messaging
KafkaHigh-throughput event streaming

The exact choice depends on requirements rather than one technology being universally better.

31. Eventual Consistency

Messaging often leads to:

Order DB
   ↓
OrderCreated
   ↓
Message Broker
   ↓
Inventory DB

There can be a delay.

Therefore:

T1:
Order = Created

T2:
Inventory = Pending

T3:
Inventory = Reserved

The system eventually becomes consistent.

Microsoft explicitly connects asynchronous event-driven communication with eventual consistency across distributed services. Microsoft Learn

32. Background Worker as Consumer

In ASP.NET Core/.NET, a consumer can be implemented using BackgroundService.

Conceptually:

public class OrderConsumer : BackgroundService
{
    protected override async Task ExecuteAsync(
        CancellationToken stoppingToken)
    {
        while (!stoppingToken.IsCancellationRequested)
        {
            // Receive message

            // Process message

            // Acknowledge message

            await Task.Delay(
                1000,
                stoppingToken);
        }
    }
}

For production systems, the actual broker SDK handles receiving, acknowledgment/settlement, retries and other broker-specific behavior.

ASP.NET Core supports hosted services and BackgroundService for long-running background processing. Microsoft Learn

33. Real-World Architecture

Let's combine everything:

                         React
                           │
                           ▼
                      API Gateway
                           │
                           ▼
                      Order API
                           │
                           ▼
                      Order Service
                           │
                 ┌─────────┴─────────┐
                 │                   │
                 ▼                   ▼
             SQL Server          Outbox
                                     │
                                     ▼
                              Message Publisher
                                     │
                                     ▼
                               Message Broker
                               /     |      \
                              ▼      ▼       ▼
                       Inventory  Notification Analytics
                          │           │
                          ▼           ▼
                       DB/SQS      Email/Lambda

34. Failure Scenario

Suppose:

Order created

but Notification Service is down.

With synchronous HTTP:

Order
 ↓
Notification ❌
 ↓
Order request may fail

With messaging:

Order
 ↓
OrderCreated
 ↓
Queue
 ↓
Notification Service ❌

The message remains available according to the broker's delivery/retention semantics.

When Notification Service recovers:

Queue
 ↓
Notification Service
 ↓
Process

That's one of the biggest benefits of asynchronous messaging.

35. Important Production Concerns

When designing messaging systems, think about:

Messaging
│
├── Delivery guarantee
├── Duplicate messages
├── Idempotency
├── Retry
├── Dead-letter queue
├── Ordering
├── Message schema/versioning
├── Observability
├── Correlation ID
├── Outbox
├── Consumer scaling
└── Failure recovery

36. Common Interview Questions

🔴 Must Know

1. What is a message broker?

Infrastructure that transports/routes messages between producers and consumers.

2. Queue vs Pub/Sub?

Queue distributes work; Pub/Sub allows multiple subscribers to react independently.

3. Command vs Event?

Command = request to perform an action.

Event = notification that something already happened.

4. What is event-driven architecture?

An architecture where services communicate/react through events, generally asynchronously.

5. What is at-least-once delivery?

A message may be delivered multiple times, so consumers must handle duplicates safely.

6. How do you handle duplicate messages?

Use idempotency/deduplication.

7. What is a DLQ?

A queue where messages that cannot be successfully processed after configured attempts are moved for inspection/reprocessing.

8. What is the Outbox Pattern?

Persist business state and the event in the same local DB transaction, then publish the outbox event asynchronously.

9. Why use messaging instead of REST?

To decouple services, support asynchronous processing, buffer workloads and improve resilience for appropriate workflows.

10. What is eventual consistency?

Different services may temporarily have different states, but their state converges through asynchronous propagation.

11. What is SQS?

A managed message queue service commonly used for asynchronous workload processing.

12. What is SNS?

A managed publish/subscribe service useful for fan-out notifications.

13. What is Kafka?

A distributed event-streaming platform designed for durable, partitioned, high-throughput event streams.

14. Why do messages get duplicated?

Retries, crashes, network failures, failed acknowledgments and broker redelivery can all cause duplicates.

15. How do you handle poison messages?

Retry a limited number of times and then move the message to a DLQ for investigation/reprocessing.

🎯 Strong 60-Second Interview Answer

"In a microservices architecture, I use asynchronous messaging when I want to decouple services or process work independently. A producer sends a command or event to a message broker, and one or more consumers process it. Queues are useful for point-to-point workload distribution, while publish/subscribe is useful when multiple services need to react to an event.

For example, after an OrderCreated event, Inventory, Notification and Analytics services can independently consume the event. This improves decoupling and allows services to continue operating even if one consumer is temporarily unavailable. The trade-off is that the system becomes eventually consistent and introduces concerns such as retries, duplicate messages, ordering and dead-letter handling.

I therefore design consumers to be idempotent, use retries for transient failures, move poison messages to a dead-letter queue, and include message IDs and correlation IDs for tracking. For reliable publishing, I can use the Outbox Pattern, where the business change and the outgoing event are stored in the same database transaction and a background publisher sends the event to the broker. In my experience, AWS SQS/SNS can be used for queueing and fan-out, and ASP.NET Core BackgroundService or Lambda can process asynchronous workloads."

🧠 Final Mental Model

                  MESSAGING
                      │
        ┌─────────────┴─────────────┐
        ▼                           ▼
      QUEUE                       PUB/SUB
        │                           │
   One consumer                Many consumers
        │                           │
     COMMAND                       EVENT
        │                           │
        └─────────────┬─────────────┘
                      ▼
                MESSAGE BROKER
                      │
          ┌───────────┼───────────┐
          ▼           ▼           ▼
        Retry      Idempotency    DLQ
          │           │           │
          └───────────┼───────────┘
                      ▼
              Eventual Consistency
                      │
                      ▼
                 OUTBOX

One-line memory trick

Queue = do this → Pub/Sub = this happened → Broker = transport → Consumer = process → Idempotency = handle duplicates → Retry = handle transient failure → DLQ = isolate poison messages → Outbox = reliably publish after DB change.

48. Eventual Consistency & Distributed Data

This topic is very important for senior .NET / microservices interviews, especially after you've covered messaging, Saga, CQRS, and distributed systems.

The key idea is: once each microservice owns its own database, keeping data consistent across services becomes an application-level problem. Microsoft’s guidance recommends defining the consistency requirement for each part of the system and using eventual consistency where strong consistency isn't necessary. Microsoft Learn

🔴 Must Master

Focus heavily on these:

  1. Strong consistency vs eventual consistency
  1. Why microservices use eventual consistency
  1. Database-per-Service
  1. Data ownership
  1. Single Source of Truth
  1. Distributed queries
  1. CQRS read models
  1. CAP theorem
  1. ACID vs BASE
  1. Cross-service transactions
  1. Saga + eventual consistency
  1. Handling stale data
  1. Data duplication / denormalization
  1. Event-driven synchronization
  1. Real-world e-commerce example

1. What is Data Consistency?

Data consistency means that different parts of the system have a correct and expected view of the data according to the consistency guarantees we've chosen.

For example:

Order Service
     ↓
Order DB
     ↓
Order = PAID

If another service has a copy:

Analytics Service
     ↓
Analytics DB
     ↓
Order = PENDING

then the two databases temporarily have different views.

The question becomes:

Is this temporary difference acceptable?

If yes → eventual consistency

If no → we need stronger consistency guarantees.

2. Strong Consistency

With strong consistency, after a successful update, subsequent reads see the latest committed value according to the system's consistency guarantee.

Example:

User changes address
        ↓
Database updated
        ↓
Immediately read address
        ↓
New address returned

Example

For a banking balance:

Balance = ₹10,000

Withdraw ₹2,000

Balance = ₹8,000

If another operation immediately reads the balance, it generally needs to see the correct current balance.

Strong consistency is appropriate when stale data could cause an unacceptable business result.

3. Eventual Consistency

Eventual consistency means different copies of data may temporarily have different values, but assuming updates are successfully propagated and no new conflicting changes occur, they eventually converge.

Example:

Order Service
     ↓
Order = PAID
     ↓
OrderPaid event
     ↓
Message Broker
     ↓
Analytics Service
     ↓
Analytics DB = PAID

There can be a small period:

Order DB       → PAID
Analytics DB   → PENDING

Then:

Order DB       → PAID
Analytics DB   → PAID

Microsoft specifically notes that asynchronous event-driven systems can have a measurable delay between a producer's state change and consumers reflecting that change. Microsoft Learn

4. Strong vs Eventual Consistency

Strong ConsistencyEventual Consistency
Latest state available according to guaranteeTemporary stale data possible
More coordinationLess coordination
Often higher latencyOften better availability/scalability
Easier business reasoningMore complex application logic
Useful for critical invariantsUseful for distributed workflows
Example: account balanceExample: analytics/read model

Interview answer

“Strong consistency means reads reflect the latest committed state according to the system's consistency guarantee. Eventual consistency allows temporary differences between distributed copies, with the expectation that they converge after updates propagate. In microservices, I use strong consistency where business invariants require it and eventual consistency where temporary stale data is acceptable.”

5. Why Does Microservices Architecture Create This Problem?

Imagine a monolith:

Application
     ↓
SQL Server
 ┌───────────────┐
 │ Orders        │
 │ Payments      │
 │ Inventory     │
 └───────────────┘

You can potentially use one database transaction:

BEGIN TRANSACTION

Create Order
Update Inventory
Create Payment

COMMIT

Everything happens inside one database boundary.

Now split it:

Order Service       → Order DB

Payment Service     → Payment DB

Inventory Service   → Inventory DB

Now:

Order DB
Payment DB
Inventory DB

are independent.

A normal SQL transaction cannot simply span all three databases/services.

Microsoft describes this as one of the fundamental data-management challenges of microservices. Microsoft Learn

6. Database-per-Service

This is one of the most important interview concepts.

Each microservice owns its data.

Order Service
     ↓
Order DB

Payment Service
     ↓
Payment DB

Inventory Service
     ↓
Inventory DB

Notification Service
     ↓
Notification DB

The other services should not directly access those databases.

Microsoft's current architecture guidance explicitly recommends private data stores for services rather than sharing schemas/tables between services. Microsoft Learn

7. Why Can't Services Share the Same Database?

Suppose:

Order Service ─────┐
                   ↓
              SQL Server
                   ↑
Payment Service ───┘

And both directly access:

Orders
Payments
Customers

Now the services are tightly coupled.

If the database schema changes:

Payments.Amount
        ↓
Payments.TotalAmount

multiple services may need to change simultaneously.

That destroys independent deployment.

Microsoft specifically identifies shared schemas/data stores as a source of tight coupling between microservices. Microsoft Learn

Better:

Order Service
     ↓
Order DB

Payment Service
     ↓
Payment DB

Services communicate through APIs/events instead of direct database access.

8. Does Database-per-Service Mean Different Physical Servers?

No.

This is a common interview trap.

You can have:

SQL Server Instance
│
├── OrderDatabase
├── PaymentDatabase
└── InventoryDatabase

The important concept is data ownership and isolation, not necessarily separate physical database servers.

Microsoft explicitly notes that services can safely share the same physical database server; the problem is sharing schemas or directly accessing each other's tables. Microsoft Learn

Interview answer

“Database-per-service doesn't necessarily mean a separate physical database server. The important principle is that each service owns its data and other services don't directly access its tables or schema.”

9. Data Ownership

Every important piece of business data should have a clear owner.

Example:

Customer data
      ↓
Customer Service

Order data
      ↓
Order Service

Payment data
      ↓
Payment Service

If another service needs customer information, it shouldn't directly query the Customer DB.

Instead:

Order Service
      ↓
Customer API

or:

CustomerUpdated event
      ↓
Message Broker
      ↓
Order Service's local copy

10. Single Source of Truth

Suppose:

Customer Service
      ↓
Customer DB

is the authoritative owner of:

CustomerAddress

The Order Service might store:

CustomerId
CustomerName

for its own use.

But if there is disagreement:

Customer Service → Mumbai

Order Service → Pune

the Customer Service's data is authoritative for the customer address.

Microsoft recommends using a single source of truth when strong consistency is required, while other services can maintain eventually consistent copies. Microsoft Learn

11. Why Duplicate Data?

You might ask:

“If services shouldn't access each other's databases, why duplicate data?”

Because sometimes we need performance and independence.

Example:

Customer Service
       ↓
Customer DB

Order Service
       ↓
Order DB
       ↓
CustomerName
CustomerEmail

The Order Service can display:

Order #123
Customer: Saurabh
Email: ...

without calling Customer Service for every order.

The copy isn't the source of truth.

It's a local read copy.

12. How Do We Synchronize Duplicate Data?

Usually through events.

Customer Service
      ↓
CustomerUpdated
      ↓
Message Broker
      ↓
Order Service
      ↓
Update local customer information

For example:

CustomerUpdated
{
    CustomerId: 101,
    Name: "Saurabh",
    Email: "..."
}

Order Service consumes the event and updates its local representation.

Now:

Customer DB
     ↓
Source of Truth

Order DB
     ↓
Eventually Consistent Copy

13. Distributed Queries

This is another very common senior interview question.

Suppose you want:

Order
+
Customer
+
Payment
+
Product

In a monolith:

SELECT ...
FROM Orders
JOIN Customers ...
JOIN Payments ...
JOIN Products ...

Easy.

In microservices:

Order DB
Customer DB
Payment DB
Product DB

You can't simply perform a normal SQL JOIN across service boundaries.

14. How Do You Handle Distributed Queries?

There are several approaches.

Approach 1 — API Composition

A service or gateway calls multiple services:

Client
   ↓
API Gateway
   ├── Order Service
   ├── Customer Service
   └── Payment Service

Then combines the results.

Example:

OrderService → Order
CustomerService → Customer
PaymentService → Payment

Gateway returns:

{
  "orderId": 123,
  "customer": "...",
  "paymentStatus": "Paid"
}

Problem

If you need 10 services:

Gateway
 ├── Service 1
 ├── Service 2
 ├── Service 3
 ...
 └── Service 10

latency and failure probability can increase.

15. Approach 2 — Local Read Model

For frequently queried data, create a denormalized read model.

Order Service
     ↓
OrderCreated
     ↓
Message Broker
     ↓
Order Read Model

The read model might contain:

OrderId
CustomerName
ProductName
PaymentStatus
ShippingStatus

Now:

GET /order-summary/123
        ↓
Read Model
        ↓
Fast response

This is closely related to CQRS.

Microsoft's cloud-native guidance describes CQRS read models as schemas optimized for queries, potentially physically separated from write models. Microsoft Learn

16. CQRS + Eventual Consistency

You already studied CQRS.

Now connect the concepts:

Command
   ↓
Write Model
   ↓
Database
   ↓
Event
   ↓
Message Broker
   ↓
Read Model

Example:

POST /orders
      ↓
Order Command
      ↓
Order DB
      ↓
OrderCreated
      ↓
Message Broker
      ↓
Order Read DB

Immediately after creating the order, there may be a short period where:

Write DB → Order exists

Read DB  → Order not yet visible

That's eventual consistency.

17. CAP Theorem

CAP is a classic interview question.

CAP stands for:

  • C — Consistency
  • A — Availability
  • P — Partition Tolerance

The important point:

CAP describes the trade-off during a network partition.

A distributed system can experience a network partition:

Service A
   X
Service B

They cannot communicate.

You must decide how the system behaves during that partition.

CP

Prefer consistency:

Partition
   ↓
Don't return potentially stale data

Availability may be sacrificed.

AP

Prefer availability:

Partition
   ↓
Continue serving requests
   ↓
Data may temporarily be stale

Eventually synchronize.

Important interview correction

Don't say:

“CAP means you can choose any two of the three whenever you want.”

A better answer is:

“CAP describes what happens when a network partition occurs. Since partition tolerance is generally necessary in distributed systems, the practical trade-off during a partition is usually between stronger consistency and availability.”

18. CAP vs ACID

These are not the same thing.

ACID

Database transaction properties:

Atomicity
Consistency
Isolation
Durability

CAP

Distributed-system behavior during network partition:

Consistency
Availability
Partition Tolerance

Don't confuse the two.

19. ACID vs BASE

Another common interview question.

ACID

Typically associated with strong transactional guarantees:

Atomic
Consistent
Isolated
Durable

BASE

Commonly associated with distributed/event-driven systems:

Basically Available
Soft State
Eventually Consistent

The important idea isn't that one is universally better.

The architecture should choose the consistency model based on the business requirement.

Microsoft's microservices guidance explicitly discusses the move from single-database ACID transactions toward BASE/eventual consistency across independent service data stores. Microsoft Learn

20. Real-World Example — E-Commerce Order

This is a very good interview scenario.

Suppose we have:

React
  ↓
Order Service
  ↓
Order DB

Payment Service
  ↓
Payment DB

Inventory Service
  ↓
Inventory DB

Notification Service
  ↓
Notification DB

User places order.

Step 1

POST /orders

Order Service creates:

Order = Pending

Step 2

Publish:

OrderCreated

Step 3

Inventory Service consumes:

OrderCreated

and reserves inventory.

Step 4

Payment Service processes payment.

Step 5

Payment Service publishes:

PaymentCompleted

Step 6

Order Service receives the event:

Order = Confirmed

During this process, the system might temporarily have:

Order DB       → Pending
Payment DB     → Paid
Inventory DB   → Reserved

That temporary inconsistency is expected.

Eventually:

Order DB       → Confirmed
Payment DB     → Paid
Inventory DB   → Reserved

21. What If Payment Fails?

Suppose:

Order created
↓
Inventory reserved
↓
Payment fails

We cannot simply execute:

ROLLBACK

across all services.

Instead, we can use a Saga.

OrderCreated
      ↓
Reserve Inventory
      ↓
Payment
      ↓
FAILED
      ↓
Release Inventory

The ReleaseInventory operation is a compensating transaction.

Saga coordinates local transactions across services and uses compensation when later steps fail. Microsoft Learn

22. How Do You Handle Stale Data?

Suppose:

Product Service
Price = ₹1,000

and another service has:

Price = ₹900

You need to decide whether stale data is acceptable.

If not acceptable

Use the source of truth:

Order Service
     ↓
Product Service
     ↓
Current Price

If acceptable

Maintain a local eventually consistent copy:

ProductUpdated
      ↓
Message
      ↓
Local Product Read Model

The important interview statement:

“I don't automatically choose eventual consistency. I first identify which business data requires strong consistency and which data can tolerate stale reads.”

23. What About Reporting and Analytics?

Analytics is a great candidate for eventual consistency.

Example:

Order Service
      ↓
OrderCreated
      ↓
Message Broker
      ↓
Analytics Service
      ↓
Analytics DB

It usually isn't necessary for a dashboard to reflect an order within the exact same database transaction as order creation.

A few seconds of delay may be acceptable.

24. Data Duplication Is Not Necessarily Bad

In traditional relational design:

Avoid duplication

because duplication can create consistency problems.

In distributed systems:

Controlled duplication
        +
Clear ownership
        +
Event synchronization

can be a useful architectural decision.

For example:

Customer Service
     ↓
Customer DB

Order Service
     ↓
CustomerName
CustomerEmail

The Order Service stores only the information it needs.

Microsoft recommends that a service store only the data it actually needs rather than trying to reproduce the complete domain entity. Microsoft Learn

25. Eventual Consistency Doesn't Mean "Eventually It Will Definitely Work"

This is an important nuance.

Bad implementation:

Publish event
   ↓
Hope consumer processes it

Production architecture needs:

Event
 ↓
Broker
 ↓
Consumer
 ↓
Retry
 ↓
Idempotency
 ↓
DLQ
 ↓
Monitoring

You also need to consider:

  • duplicate messages
  • consumer failures
  • message ordering
  • poison messages
  • schema evolution
  • observability

Event-driven architectures inherently introduce challenges around delivery, ordering and eventual consistency. Microsoft Learn

26. Outbox + Eventual Consistency

This connects directly with Topic 47.

Imagine:

Order DB

You need to do:

1. Save Order
2. Publish OrderCreated

Potential failure:

Save Order → SUCCESS

Publish Event → FAILED

Now the order exists but the event wasn't published.

Outbox helps:

BEGIN TRANSACTION

Save Order
Save Outbox Event

COMMIT

Then:

Outbox
   ↓
Background Publisher
   ↓
Message Broker
   ↓
Consumers

This provides a reliable bridge from local transaction to asynchronous event propagation. Microsoft's guidance describes the transactional outbox as a pattern for reliable messaging and idempotent processing. Microsoft Learn

27. Common Interview Questions

🔴 Must Know

  1. What is eventual consistency?
  1. Strong consistency vs eventual consistency?
  1. Why is eventual consistency common in microservices?
  1. What is database-per-service?
  1. Why shouldn't microservices share databases?
  1. Does database-per-service mean separate physical servers?
  1. What is data ownership?
  1. What is a single source of truth?
  1. How do you synchronize duplicated data?
  1. How do you perform joins across microservices?
  1. What is API composition?
  1. What is a read model?
  1. How does CQRS relate to eventual consistency?
  1. Explain CAP theorem.
  1. CAP vs ACID?
  1. ACID vs BASE?
  1. How do you maintain consistency across services?
  1. How does Saga help?
  1. What happens when an event consumer is unavailable?
  1. How do you handle stale data?
  1. Why is data duplication sometimes acceptable?
  1. What is distributed transaction?
  1. Why can't a normal SQL transaction span microservices?
  1. How does Outbox help?
  1. Design an e-commerce system with eventual consistency.

🎯 Strong 60-Second Interview Answer

“Eventual consistency is a consistency model commonly used in distributed systems where different services or data stores may temporarily have different versions of data, but they eventually converge after updates are propagated. In a microservices architecture, each service typically owns its own data, so we can't rely on a single database transaction across multiple services.

For example, in an e-commerce system, Order, Payment and Inventory can each have their own database. When an order is created, the Order Service publishes an event, and other services process it independently. During this process, the system can be temporarily inconsistent, which is acceptable if the business requirement allows it. For workflows that require coordination across services, I can use Saga with compensating transactions.

For frequently queried data, I can maintain a denormalized read model using CQRS and synchronize it through events. I also make consumers idempotent and use retries, dead-letter queues and an Outbox Pattern for reliable event publishing. The key is that I don't use eventual consistency everywhere—I first identify where strong consistency is required and use eventual consistency where temporary stale data is acceptable.”

🧠 Final Mental Model

Remember this flow:

             MICROSERVICES
                   │
                   ▼
        Database-per-Service
                   │
                   ▼
            Data Ownership
                   │
         ┌─────────┴─────────┐
         ▼                   ▼
 Strong Consistency    Eventual Consistency
         │                   │
         │                   ▼
         │              Events/Messaging
         │                   │
         │                   ▼
         │              Read Models
         │                   │
         │                   ▼
         │                 CQRS
         │
         ▼
   Local ACID Transaction

Cross-Service Transaction
         │
         ▼
       Saga
         │
         ▼
 Compensation

🔥 One-line memory

“Each service owns its data; use strong consistency for critical business invariants and eventual consistency with events/read models where temporary stale data is acceptable.”

Interview trap to remember

Database-per-service ≠ necessarily separate physical database server.

The important part is ownership and isolation of data, not physical infrastructure. Microsoft Learn

49. Advanced Distributed Transactions & Saga Patterns

This is a high-priority Senior .NET / Microservices interview topic because it combines several things you've already studied: microservices, database-per-service, messaging, eventual consistency, idempotency, retries, and compensation.

Microsoft describes Saga as a sequence of local transactions across services, where failures are handled through compensating transactions rather than relying on a single cross-service ACID transaction. Microsoft Learn

🔴 Must Master

Focus heavily on:

  1. What is a distributed transaction?
  1. Why normal DB transactions don't work across microservices
  1. Saga pattern
  1. Saga orchestration
  1. Saga choreography
  1. Orchestration vs choreography
  1. Local transaction
  1. Compensating transaction
  1. Retryable vs compensable transactions
  1. Pivot transaction
  1. Idempotency in Saga
  1. Saga state management
  1. Failure handling
  1. Saga + messaging
  1. Saga + Outbox
  1. Order → Payment → Inventory example
  1. Saga vs 2-Phase Commit
  1. Handling partial failures
  1. Observability/correlation IDs
  1. Real-world implementation in ASP.NET Core

1. What Is a Distributed Transaction?

A distributed transaction is a business transaction that involves multiple independently managed services or data stores.

Example:

Place Order
    │
    ├── Order Service
    │       ↓
    │    Order DB
    │
    ├── Payment Service
    │       ↓
    │    Payment DB
    │
    └── Inventory Service
            ↓
         Inventory DB

One business operation involves three different databases.

The challenge is:

How do we make sure the entire business operation reaches a consistent final state if one step fails?

A normal SQL transaction cannot simply span these independent service boundaries.

Microsoft notes that ACID transactions are straightforward within a single service/database but become considerably more complex across independently managed microservice data stores. Microsoft Learn

2. Why Not Just Use One Big SQL Transaction?

Suppose:

BEGIN TRANSACTION

Create Order
Reserve Inventory
Charge Payment

COMMIT

This works when everything is inside one database transaction boundary.

But with microservices:

Order Service
      ↓
Order DB

Payment Service
      ↓
Payment DB

Inventory Service
      ↓
Inventory DB

You cannot simply do:

BEGIN TRANSACTION

Order DB
Payment DB
Inventory DB

COMMIT

because these services own their databases independently.

You could consider distributed transaction protocols such as Two-Phase Commit, but they introduce coordination, availability and operational complexity and are often a poor fit for loosely coupled microservices. Microsoft specifically identifies Saga as a pattern for cases where traditional distributed transaction models are impractical. Microsoft Learn

3. What Is the Saga Pattern?

Interview definition

Saga is a pattern for managing a distributed business transaction by breaking it into a sequence of local transactions. If a later step fails, compensating transactions are executed to logically undo the effects of earlier successful steps.

Example:

Create Order
     ↓
Reserve Inventory
     ↓
Process Payment
     ↓
Confirm Order

If payment fails:

Create Order        ✓
Reserve Inventory   ✓
Process Payment     ✗
                     ↓
             Release Inventory
                     ↓
             Cancel Order

Notice something important:

We're not literally doing:

ROLLBACK

on all databases.

We're performing new business operations that compensate for previous operations.

4. Local Transaction

Each service still uses normal transactions inside its own database.

Example:

Inventory Service

BEGIN TRANSACTION

Reserve Product

COMMIT

This is a local ACID transaction.

Then the service publishes an event/message:

InventoryReserved

The next service processes its own local transaction.

So:

Service A
Local Transaction
      ↓
Event
      ↓
Service B
Local Transaction
      ↓
Event
      ↓
Service C

That's the fundamental Saga model. Microsoft Learn

5. Two Ways to Implement Saga

There are two major approaches:

Saga
 ├── Choreography
 └── Orchestration

This is extremely common in interviews.

6. Saga Choreography

There is no central coordinator.

Each service listens for events and decides what it needs to do next.

Example:

Order Service
     │
     │ OrderCreated
     ▼
 Message Broker
     │
     ▼
Inventory Service
     │
     │ InventoryReserved
     ▼
 Message Broker
     │
     ▼
Payment Service
     │
     │ PaymentCompleted
     ▼
 Message Broker
     │
     ▼
Order Service

Each service knows:

“When I receive this event, I perform my local operation and publish the next event.”

Microsoft describes choreography as decentralized workflow logic where services participate in the workflow through events/messages rather than relying on a central controller. Microsoft Learn

7. Choreography Example

Suppose an order is created.

Order Service

Create Order
     ↓
OrderCreated

Inventory Service

Receives:

OrderCreated

Then:

Reserve Inventory
     ↓
InventoryReserved

Payment Service

Receives:

InventoryReserved

Then:

Process Payment
     ↓
PaymentCompleted

Order Service

Receives:

PaymentCompleted

Then:

Order = Confirmed

8. What Happens If Payment Fails?

Payment Service publishes:

PaymentFailed

Inventory Service receives it:

Release Inventory
     ↓
InventoryReleased

Order Service receives it:

Order = Cancelled

So:

OrderCreated
     ↓
InventoryReserved
     ↓
PaymentFailed
     ↓
InventoryReleased
     ↓
OrderCancelled

This is compensation.

9. Advantages of Choreography

Benefits

Loose coupling

Services don't depend on a central coordinator.

No central orchestrator

There isn't one component controlling the entire workflow.

Good for simple workflows

Especially when there are only a few services and straightforward event relationships.

Easy to add event consumers

For example:

OrderCreated
     ↓
 ┌───┼──────────┐
 ↓   ↓          ↓
Email Analytics Fraud

Each service independently reacts to the event.

Microsoft identifies reduced central coordination and suitability for simpler, independently handled workflows as key benefits. Microsoft Learn

10. Disadvantages of Choreography

This is where senior-level understanding matters.

Suppose we eventually have:

Order
 ↓
Inventory
 ↓
Payment
 ↓
Shipping
 ↓
Notification
 ↓
Loyalty
 ↓
Analytics

Now it's difficult to answer:

“What is the complete state of Order #123?”

Because there isn't one component holding the entire workflow state.

You can end up with:

Event
 ↓
Service
 ↓
Event
 ↓
Service
 ↓
Event
 ↓
Service

This can become difficult to understand and debug.

Microsoft highlights workflow complexity and observability challenges as choreography grows. Microsoft Learn

11. Saga Orchestration

With orchestration, we introduce a central Saga Orchestrator.

             Saga Orchestrator
              /      |      \
             /       |       \
            ↓        ↓        ↓
       Order      Inventory  Payment
       Service     Service   Service

The orchestrator knows the workflow.

For example:

1. Create Order
2. Reserve Inventory
3. Process Payment
4. Confirm Order

It sends commands to each service.

12. Orchestration Example

Client
  ↓
Order API
  ↓
Saga Orchestrator
  │
  ├── CreateOrder
  │       ↓
  │   Order Service
  │
  ├── ReserveInventory
  │       ↓
  │   Inventory Service
  │
  ├── ProcessPayment
  │       ↓
  │   Payment Service
  │
  └── ConfirmOrder
          ↓
      Order Service

The orchestrator maintains the workflow state and determines what happens next.

Microsoft describes orchestration as a centralized controller that coordinates participants, tracks task state and manages failure recovery/compensation. Microsoft Learn

13. Orchestration — Payment Failure

Suppose:

Create Order      ✓
Reserve Inventory ✓
Process Payment   ✗

The orchestrator knows:

Completed:
✓ Order
✓ Inventory

Failed:
✗ Payment

So it executes:

ReleaseInventory
      ↓
CancelOrder

Final state:

Order       → Cancelled
Inventory   → Available
Payment     → Failed

14. Choreography vs Orchestration

ChoreographyOrchestration
No central coordinatorCentral orchestrator
Event-drivenCommand/workflow-driven
Services decide next stepOrchestrator decides next step
Less central couplingEasier centralized workflow control
Simple workflowsComplex workflows
Harder to visualize at scaleEasier to visualize
Distributed workflow stateCentral workflow state
Can become event spaghettiOrchestrator adds complexity

Interview answer

“In choreography, each service reacts to events and independently decides its next action, so there is no central workflow controller. In orchestration, a central Saga orchestrator knows the workflow, sends commands to participating services, tracks their state and performs compensation when required. I would generally consider choreography for simple, loosely coupled workflows and orchestration when the workflow is complex and requires explicit coordination and state tracking.”

15. What Is a Compensating Transaction?

A compensating transaction is a business operation that logically reverses the effect of a previous successful operation.

Example:

Reserve Inventory

Compensation:

Release Inventory

Another example:

Create Shipment

Compensation:

Cancel Shipment

Another:

Create Order

Compensation:

Cancel Order

Microsoft emphasizes that compensation is not necessarily a database rollback; it is a new operation that restores the desired business state. Microsoft Learn

16. Compensation Is NOT Always a Perfect Rollback

This is a very important interview point.

Suppose:

Payment = ₹1,000

Payment succeeds.

Then something fails.

You issue:

Refund ₹1,000

That's compensation.

But the original payment transaction isn't literally rolled back.

There could be:

Payment succeeded
      ↓
Refund requested
      ↓
Refund temporarily failed

Now you have another failure to handle.

Microsoft explicitly notes that compensating transactions themselves can fail and may not always restore the exact original state. Microsoft Learn

17. Retry vs Compensation

This distinction is extremely important.

Suppose:

Payment Service
     ↓
Timeout

Don't immediately compensate.

First determine:

Is this a transient failure?

If yes:

Retry
  ↓
Retry
  ↓
Success

If retries are exhausted:

Retry exhausted
       ↓
Compensation

Current Microsoft guidance for compensating transactions similarly emphasizes retrying transient faults before invoking compensation when forward progress is still possible. Microsoft Learn

18. Retryable vs Compensable Transactions

Saga documentation uses useful terminology here.

Compensable transaction

An operation whose effects can be undone.

Example:

Reserve Inventory

Compensation:

Release Inventory

Retryable transaction

An operation that can safely be retried.

Example:

Update Order Status

provided the operation is designed to be idempotent.

Pivot transaction

A point of no return in the Saga.

Microsoft's Saga guidance identifies compensable, pivot and retryable transactions as important Saga concepts. Microsoft Learn

19. What Is a Pivot Transaction?

Think:

Compensable steps
        ↓
     PIVOT
        ↓
Retryable steps

Before pivot:

Operation can potentially be compensated.

After pivot:

Operation is considered the point of no return.

The exact pivot depends on the business workflow.

For example:

Create Order
      ↓
Reserve Inventory
      ↓
Payment Authorization  ← Pivot
      ↓
Create Shipment
      ↓
Send Notification

Once the business process crosses the pivot, later steps need to complete through retry/recovery rather than assuming everything can simply be undone.

20. Idempotency in Saga

This is absolutely critical.

Imagine:

PaymentCompleted

is delivered twice:

PaymentCompleted
PaymentCompleted

If your consumer does:

Add ₹1,000 payment

twice:

₹1,000
+
₹1,000
=
₹2,000

That's a serious problem.

Instead:

MessageId = ABC123

Consumer checks:

AlreadyProcessed(ABC123)?

If yes:

Ignore / return existing result

If no:

Process
Save MessageId

Because distributed workflows commonly involve retries and duplicate delivery, Saga participants need idempotent operations. Microsoft explicitly calls out idempotence as a requirement for handling transient failures in Saga workflows. Microsoft Learn

21. Saga State

A Saga needs to know:

Which steps completed?
Which step failed?
Which compensations are pending?
What should happen next?

Example:

{
  "sagaId": "SAGA-123",
  "orderId": 1001,
  "status": "PaymentFailed",
  "steps": {
    "orderCreated": true,
    "inventoryReserved": true,
    "paymentCompleted": false,
    "inventoryReleased": false
  }
}

This is particularly important with orchestration.

The orchestrator can persist this state so that if it crashes, it can resume or recover the workflow.

22. Where Should Saga State Be Stored?

For production systems, don't rely only on:

private Dictionary<Guid, SagaState> _states;

because:

  • application can restart
  • multiple instances may exist
  • load balancer can send requests to different instances
  • state would be lost

Instead use durable/shared storage:

Saga Orchestrator
       ↓
Saga State Store
       ↓
SQL / Cosmos DB / Redis*
  • The appropriate choice depends on durability and consistency requirements.

23. Saga + Message Broker

A common architecture:

                ┌──────────────────┐
                │ Saga Orchestrator│
                └────────┬─────────┘
                         │
              Commands / Events
                         │
                         ▼
                  Message Broker
                 /       |       \
                ↓        ↓        ↓
            Order    Inventory  Payment
            Service   Service   Service
               │         │         │
               ↓         ↓         ↓
             DB        DB        DB

This gives us:

  • decoupling
  • asynchronous processing
  • retries
  • buffering
  • independent service availability

24. Saga + Outbox

This is a very strong senior interview combination.

Suppose Order Service performs:

Create Order
Publish OrderCreated

Potential failure:

Create Order → SUCCESS
Publish Event → FAILURE

Use Outbox:

BEGIN TRANSACTION

INSERT Order
INSERT OutboxEvent

COMMIT

Then:

Outbox
  ↓
Publisher
  ↓
Message Broker
  ↓
Saga

Now the local business state and outgoing event are committed atomically within the service's database transaction.

25. Real-World Order Saga

Let's design one.

Requirement

User places an order.

We need:

Order
Inventory
Payment
Shipping
Notification

Architecture:

React
  ↓
Order API
  ↓
Saga Orchestrator
  │
  ├──── Order Service
  │
  ├──── Inventory Service
  │
  ├──── Payment Service
  │
  ├──── Shipping Service
  │
  └──── Notification Service

Step 1 — Create Order

CreateOrder

Order Service:

Order = Pending

Returns:

OrderCreated

Step 2 — Reserve Inventory

ReserveInventory

Inventory Service:

Inventory = Reserved

Returns:

InventoryReserved

Step 3 — Process Payment

ProcessPayment

Payment Service:

Payment = Completed

Returns:

PaymentCompleted

Step 4 — Create Shipment

CreateShipment

Shipping Service:

Shipment = Created

Returns:

ShipmentCreated

Step 5 — Confirm Order

ConfirmOrder

Order Service:

Order = Confirmed

26. What If Inventory Fails?

Flow:

Create Order        ✓
Reserve Inventory   ✗

Compensation:

Cancel Order

Final:

Order = Cancelled

27. What If Payment Fails?

Create Order        ✓
Reserve Inventory   ✓
Payment             ✗

Compensation:

Release Inventory
       ↓
Cancel Order

28. What If Shipping Fails?

Create Order        ✓
Reserve Inventory   ✓
Payment             ✓
Shipping            ✗

Now it gets more interesting.

Possible compensation:

Cancel Shipment
Refund Payment
Release Inventory
Cancel Order

But compensation itself can fail.

Therefore:

Retry
  ↓
Retry
  ↓
DLQ / Recovery
  ↓
Manual intervention if necessary

This is why distributed transactions are significantly more complex than a local SQL transaction.

29. Saga vs Two-Phase Commit

Two-Phase Commit

Conceptually:

Coordinator
   │
   ├── Prepare Order DB
   ├── Prepare Payment DB
   └── Prepare Inventory DB

        ↓

   COMMIT ALL

The coordinator tries to get all participants to prepare and then commit.

Saga

Order transaction
      ↓
Inventory transaction
      ↓
Payment transaction

If something fails:

Compensation

Interview answer

“Two-Phase Commit tries to provide a distributed atomic transaction across participants, but it introduces tight coordination and can be expensive in distributed microservice architectures. Saga instead breaks the business transaction into local transactions and uses events or commands plus compensating actions to reach a consistent business state. Saga is generally more aligned with independently deployable microservices, but it introduces eventual consistency and more complex failure handling.”

Microsoft's architecture guidance describes Saga as an alternative when distributed transactions such as traditional two-phase commit are impractical in microservices. Microsoft Learn

30. How Do You Monitor a Saga?

This is a very good Senior Engineer question.

You need:

SagaId
CorrelationId
OrderId
MessageId
ServiceName
Step
Status
Timestamp

Example:

CorrelationId = ORD-1001

Order Service
    ↓
Inventory Service
    ↓
Payment Service
    ↓
Shipping Service

Every log should contain:

CorrelationId = ORD-1001

Then you can trace the entire workflow.

For choreography especially, Microsoft recommends distributed tracing and correlation identifiers because no single component necessarily has a complete view of the in-flight workflow. Microsoft Learn

31. What Happens When a Saga Service Is Down?

Suppose:

OrderCreated
     ↓
Inventory Service DOWN

The broker retains the message according to its delivery semantics.

When Inventory Service comes back:

Message
   ↓
Inventory Service
   ↓
Process

For transient failures:

Retry

For poison messages:

Retry exhausted
      ↓
DLQ

For business failures:

Compensation

For unrecoverable situations:

Manual remediation

32. Saga Failure Handling Mental Model

Remember this:

Failure
  │
  ├── Transient?
  │      ↓
  │    Retry
  │
  ├── Retry exhausted?
  │      ↓
  │   Compensation
  │
  ├── Poison message?
  │      ↓
  │     DLQ
  │
  └── Irrecoverable?
         ↓
    Manual Recovery

33. Common Interview Questions

🔴 Must Know

  1. What is a distributed transaction?
  1. Why can't we use a normal SQL transaction across microservices?
  1. What is Saga?
  1. How does Saga work?
  1. What is a local transaction?
  1. What is a compensating transaction?
  1. Saga choreography vs orchestration?
  1. When would you choose choreography?
  1. When would you choose orchestration?
  1. What are the disadvantages of choreography?
  1. What are the disadvantages of orchestration?
  1. What is a Saga orchestrator?
  1. How does Saga handle failures?
  1. What is a pivot transaction?
  1. What is a retryable transaction?
  1. What is a compensable transaction?
  1. Why is idempotency important in Saga?
  1. How do you handle duplicate events?
  1. How do you persist Saga state?
  1. What happens if the Saga orchestrator crashes?
  1. How does Outbox work with Saga?
  1. Saga vs Two-Phase Commit?
  1. How do you monitor a distributed transaction?
  1. What happens if compensation fails?
  1. Design an Order/Payment/Inventory Saga.

🎯 Strong 60-Second Interview Answer

“A Saga is a pattern I would use when a business transaction spans multiple microservices that each own their own database. Instead of trying to maintain one distributed ACID transaction, I break the workflow into a sequence of local transactions. For example, in an e-commerce system, creating an order, reserving inventory and processing payment can each be separate local transactions. If a later step fails, I use compensating transactions such as releasing inventory or cancelling the order to bring the system back to a valid business state.

There are two main approaches: choreography, where services communicate through events without a central coordinator, and orchestration, where a Saga orchestrator controls the workflow and tracks its state. I would generally use choreography for simpler workflows and orchestration when the workflow is complex and requires explicit coordination.

Because distributed messaging can involve retries and duplicate delivery, Saga operations need to be idempotent. I also use timeouts, retries, dead-letter queues, correlation IDs and distributed tracing. For reliable event publishing, I can combine Saga with the Outbox Pattern. The main trade-off is that Saga provides eventual consistency and failure recovery, but it is more complex than a normal local database transaction.”

🧠 Final Mental Model

                 DISTRIBUTED TRANSACTION
                          │
                          ▼
                 Multiple Services
                          │
                          ▼
                  Local Transactions
                          │
             ┌────────────┴────────────┐
             │                         │
       CHOREOGRAPHY              ORCHESTRATION
             │                         │
        Events only              Orchestrator
             │                         │
             └────────────┬────────────┘
                          ▼
                    Failure?
                          │
                ┌─────────┴─────────┐
                ▼                   ▼
             Retry              Compensation
                │                   │
                ▼                   ▼
           Idempotency          Undo Effect
                │                   │
                └─────────┬─────────┘
                          ▼
                     Eventual
                     Consistency
                          │
                          ▼
                Outbox + DLQ + Tracing

🔥 One-line memory

“Saga replaces one distributed transaction with multiple local transactions plus compensation, coordinated either through choreography or orchestration.”

Most important distinction

2PC
→ Try to make distributed work atomic

Saga
→ Accept distributed boundaries
→ Perform local transactions
→ Compensate when necessary
→ Eventually reach a consistent business state

That distinction is one of the most useful things to be able to explain clearly in a Senior .NET interview.

50. Event Sourcing & Event-Driven Data Architecture

This is the natural next step after Saga, eventual consistency, CQRS, and messaging.

The key idea is simple:

Instead of storing only the current state of an entity, Event Sourcing stores the sequence of business events that produced that state.

Microsoft's current .NET architecture guidance describes Event Sourcing as storing state changes as an append-only sequence of events and rebuilding current state by replaying those events. Microsoft Learn

🔴 Must Master

Focus heavily on:

  1. What is Event Sourcing?
  1. Event vs Event Sourcing
  1. Event Store
  1. Current state vs event history
  1. Event replay
  1. Rebuilding state
  1. Snapshots
  1. Event Sourcing + CQRS
  1. Event Sourcing + eventual consistency
  1. Event Sourcing vs traditional CRUD
  1. Event Sourcing vs database audit logs
  1. Event schema/versioning
  1. Immutable events
  1. Projections/read models
  1. Handling corrections
  1. Benefits and disadvantages
  1. When to use Event Sourcing
  1. When NOT to use it
  1. Real-world banking/order example
  1. Event Sourcing in .NET architecture

1. What Is Event Sourcing?

In a traditional application, we usually store the current state.

For example:

Customer
---------
Id       = 101
Name     = Saurabh
Balance  = ₹8,000

If the balance changes:

₹10,000 → ₹8,000

we update the row.

The previous state may no longer be directly available.

With Event Sourcing, instead of storing only:

Balance = ₹8,000

we store the sequence of events:

AccountCreated
MoneyDeposited ₹10,000
MoneyWithdrawn ₹2,000

Then:

Events
  ↓
Replay
  ↓
Current State
  ↓
Balance = ₹8,000

Microsoft describes this as an append-only event store that becomes the system of record, with current state reconstructed by replaying events. Microsoft Learn

2. Traditional CRUD vs Event Sourcing

Traditional CRUD

Database

Account
----------------
Id       Balance
101      8000

Update:

UPDATE Account
SET Balance = 8000
WHERE Id = 101

Previous value:

10000

may not be available unless you separately audit it.

Event Sourcing

Event Store

1. AccountCreated
2. MoneyDeposited 10000
3. MoneyWithdrawn 2000

Current state:

Replay events
     ↓
Balance = 8000

So:

CRUD
→ Store current state

Event Sourcing
→ Store state changes
→ Derive current state

3. What Is an Event?

An event represents something that already happened.

Examples:

OrderCreated
PaymentCompleted
InventoryReserved
CustomerRegistered
MoneyDeposited
MoneyWithdrawn
AddressChanged

Notice the naming:

OrderCreated

not:

CreateOrder

Why?

Because:

CreateOrder

is a command.

OrderCreated

is an event.

4. Command vs Event

This is an important interview question.

Command

A command says:

“Please perform this action.”

Example:

CreateOrder

Event

An event says:

“This action already happened.”

Example:

OrderCreated

Think:

Command
   ↓
Business Logic
   ↓
State Change
   ↓
Event

5. What Is an Event Store?

An event store is the persistent storage containing the sequence of events.

Example:

EventId | AggregateId | EventType          | Data
-----------------------------------------------------
1       | 101         | AccountCreated     | ...
2       | 101         | MoneyDeposited     | 10000
3       | 101         | MoneyWithdrawn     | 2000

The events are generally treated as immutable.

Instead of:

UPDATE Event

you append another event.

6. Why Immutable Events?

Suppose:

MoneyDeposited ₹10,000

happened yesterday.

You generally don't modify that historical event to:

MoneyDeposited ₹8,000

Instead, if there was a correction, you record another event.

For example:

MoneyDeposited 10000
CorrectionApplied -2000

The complete history remains available.

7. Event Replay

This is one of the most important concepts.

Suppose we have:

1. AccountCreated
2. MoneyDeposited 10000
3. MoneyWithdrawn 2000
4. MoneyDeposited 500

To calculate current balance:

0
↓
AccountCreated
↓
10000
↓
8000
↓
8500

Current state:

Balance = ₹8,500

This process is called event replay.

8. Why Is Event Replay Useful?

Imagine you discover that your business logic for calculating some derived state was wrong.

With traditional storage:

Current State
     ↓
Only latest value

Historical information may be unavailable.

With Event Sourcing:

Event History
      ↓
Replay
      ↓
New Projection

You can rebuild a new read model from the historical events.

Microsoft identifies this ability to reconstruct state and maintain historical information as a major benefit of Event Sourcing. Microsoft Learn

9. Event Sourcing + CQRS

These two concepts are related but not the same.

CQRS

Separates:

Commands
   ↓
Write Model

Queries
   ↓
Read Model

Event Sourcing

Stores:

State changes
   ↓
Events

They can be used independently.

But they work particularly well together.

10. Event Sourcing + CQRS Architecture

A common architecture:

                    Client
                      │
          ┌───────────┴───────────┐
          ▼                       ▼
      Command API             Query API
          │                       │
          ▼                       ▼
     Write Model             Read Model
          │                       ▲
          ▼                       │
     Event Store ───────► Projection
          │
          ▼
        Events

For example:

POST /orders
      ↓
Order Command
      ↓
Order Aggregate
      ↓
OrderCreated
      ↓
Event Store
      ↓
Projection
      ↓
Order Read Model

The query side can then use a database optimized specifically for reads.

Microsoft's CQRS guidance describes separate read/write stores and event-driven synchronization, while recommending Outbox when the database state change and event publication must be made reliable. Microsoft Learn

11. Event Sourcing Does NOT Require CQRS

Common interview trap:

“Does Event Sourcing always require CQRS?”

No.

You can have:

Event Sourcing

without CQRS.

And:

CQRS

without Event Sourcing.

For example:

CQRS
Write DB → SQL Server
Read DB  → Redis

No event store is required.

Similarly:

Event Sourcing
Event Store

can exist without physically separating read and write APIs.

12. Event Sourcing + Eventual Consistency

Suppose:

Order Service
      ↓
Event Store
      ↓
OrderCreated
      ↓
Projection
      ↓
Read Database

There may be a small delay between:

Event Store updated

and:

Read Model updated

Therefore:

Write side
→ latest

Read side
→ temporarily stale

This is eventual consistency.

Microsoft notes that CQRS implementations with separate read/write stores must synchronize those stores and can therefore have consistency delays. Microsoft Learn

13. What Is a Projection?

A projection consumes events and builds a representation optimized for queries.

Example events:

OrderCreated
ProductAdded
PaymentCompleted
OrderShipped

Projection:

OrderReadModel
-------------------------
OrderId
CustomerName
TotalAmount
PaymentStatus
ShippingStatus

The projection processes:

Events
  ↓
Projection Logic
  ↓
Read Model

14. Why Use Projections?

Different consumers may need different views of the same events.

For example:

Customer view

OrderId
Status
Total

Admin view

OrderId
Customer
Payment
Inventory
Shipment
Audit

Analytics view

Date
Product
Revenue
Region
CustomerSegment

All can be generated from the same event history.

                 Event Store
                      │
          ┌───────────┼───────────┐
          ▼           ▼           ▼
     Customer View  Admin View  Analytics

15. What Is a Snapshot?

Replay can become expensive.

Imagine an account has:

10 million events

Every time you need its state, replaying all 10 million events would be inefficient.

So you can periodically save a snapshot:

Events 1 → 100,000
       ↓
Snapshot
Balance = ₹50,000

Then:

Snapshot
   ↓
Events 100001 → 100500
   ↓
Current State

Instead of replaying:

1 → 100500

you replay:

100001 → 100500

16. Snapshot Example

Suppose:

Snapshot:
Balance = ₹50,000
Version = 1000

Then:

Event 1001 → Deposit 1000
Event 1002 → Withdraw 500
Event 1003 → Deposit 2000

Replay only:

50000
+1000
-500
+2000
=52500

Current state:

₹52,500

17. Event Sourcing vs Audit Logging

These are not the same thing.

Audit Log

You might have:

User updated order
Old status = Pending
New status = Confirmed
User = 101
Time = ...

The main database remains the source of truth.

The audit table records history.

Event Sourcing

The events themselves are the system of record.

OrderCreated
PaymentCompleted
OrderShipped

Current state is derived from those events.

Interview answer

“An audit log records historical changes alongside a traditional state-based system, while Event Sourcing makes the sequence of domain events the source of truth and derives current state from those events.”

18. Event Sourcing vs Traditional Database

Traditional CRUDEvent Sourcing
Stores current stateStores state changes
Updates existing recordsAppends events
History often requires auditingHistory is inherent
Simple queryingRead models/projections often required
Easier to understandMore complex
Normal relational modelingEvent-oriented storage
Current state is primaryEvent history is primary

19. Benefits of Event Sourcing

1. Complete history

You know:

What happened?
When?
In what order?

2. Rebuild state

Events
 ↓
Replay
 ↓
State

3. Multiple read models

Same events
    ↓
Multiple projections

4. Auditability

Useful for domains where historical business actions matter.

5. Temporal analysis

You can understand how state changed over time.

6. Decoupling

Events can feed other components and projections.

Microsoft highlights history, replayability, and materialized views as key benefits of Event Sourcing. Microsoft Learn

20. Disadvantages of Event Sourcing

This is equally important in interviews.

Complexity

You need:

Event Store
Projection
Replay
Versioning
Snapshots
Event handling

Event schema evolution

Old events may have an older schema.

Debugging

A bug could involve:

Event
 ↓
Consumer
 ↓
Projection
 ↓
Read Model

Storage growth

Events accumulate.

Eventual consistency

Read models may lag.

Replay complexity

Large event histories can require substantial processing.

Microsoft explicitly cautions that Event Sourcing increases architectural complexity and should be adopted strategically rather than automatically. Microsoft Learn

21. When Should You Use Event Sourcing?

Good candidates include domains where history itself is valuable.

Examples:

Banking
Financial transactions
Order history
Trading
Inventory movements
Audit-heavy systems
Workflow/state machines

For example:

Bank Account

Deposit 5000
Withdraw 1000
Deposit 2000
Withdraw 500

The transaction history is inherently meaningful.

22. When Should You NOT Use It?

Don't use Event Sourcing just because:

“We're building microservices.”

That's a bad architectural reason.

For simple CRUD:

Employee
Product
Category
Country

a normal relational model may be much simpler.

Example:

Products
----------------
Id
Name
Price
CategoryId

No need to introduce:

ProductCreated
ProductPriceChanged
ProductRenamed
ProductCategoryChanged
...

unless the business actually benefits from that model.

23. Event Schema Versioning

Suppose version 1:

{
  "orderId": 101,
  "amount": 1000
}

Later version 2:

{
  "orderId": 101,
  "totalAmount": 1000,
  "currency": "INR"
}

But your Event Store still contains old events.

Your application needs to understand historical event formats.

Common strategies include:

Versioned event types
Event upcasting
Backward-compatible schemas
Migration strategies

This is one of the operational complexities of Event Sourcing.

24. What Is Event Upcasting?

Suppose old event:

OrderCreatedV1
{
    orderId,
    amount
}

New application expects:

OrderCreatedV2
{
    orderId,
    amount,
    currency
}

An upcaster can transform:

V1
 ↓
V2

while replaying old events.

For example:

OrderCreatedV1
amount = 1000

      ↓

OrderCreatedV2
amount = 1000
currency = "INR"

This allows historical events to remain immutable.

25. What Happens If a Projection Fails?

Suppose:

OrderCreated
    ↓
Projection
    ↓
FAILED

The event remains in the event store.

You can retry projection processing:

Event Store
    ↓
Replay
    ↓
Projection
    ↓
Read DB

This is one of the powerful properties of event-based architecture.

You can potentially rebuild a corrupted or newly designed read model from the event history.

26. Real-World Banking Example

Imagine a bank account.

Traditional CRUD:

Account
---------
Balance = 8500

Event Sourcing:

1. AccountCreated
2. MoneyDeposited 10000
3. MoneyWithdrawn 2000
4. MoneyDeposited 1000
5. MoneyWithdrawn 500

Replay:

0
+10000
-2000
+1000
-500
------
8500

Current state:

Balance = ₹8,500

But now you also know the complete history.

27. Event Sourcing + ASP.NET Core

A possible .NET architecture:

React
  ↓
ASP.NET Core API
  ↓
Command Handler
  ↓
Domain Aggregate
  ↓
Generate Domain Events
  ↓
Event Store
  ↓
Outbox / Event Publisher
  ↓
Message Broker
  ↓
Projection Workers
  ↓
Read Database

For example:

POST /orders
      ↓
CreateOrderCommand
      ↓
OrderAggregate
      ↓
OrderCreatedEvent
      ↓
Event Store
      ↓
Order Read Model

Your React application can then query:

GET /orders/101

against the read model.

28. Event Sourcing + Outbox

There's an important relationship here.

If your system stores:

Business State
+
Events

in the same transactional boundary, you need reliable event publication.

The Transactional Outbox pattern can help ensure that state changes and outgoing events aren't separated by a failure window. Microsoft recommends the pattern for scenarios where database changes and event publication need reliable coordination. Microsoft Learn

Conceptually:

Transaction
 ├── Save business state
 └── Save event/outbox record
          ↓
       COMMIT
          ↓
 Background Publisher
          ↓
 Message Broker

29. Event Sourcing + Saga

These patterns solve different problems.

Event Sourcing

Answers:

How do I persist the history/state changes of an entity?

Saga

Answers:

How do I coordinate a business workflow across multiple services?

They can work together.

Saga
 ↓
Commands
 ↓
Services
 ↓
Local Events
 ↓
Event Stores

Don't say:

“Saga and Event Sourcing are the same.”

They are not.

30. Event Sourcing + Microservices

Imagine:

Order Service
     ↓
Order Event Store

Payment Service
     ↓
Payment Event Store

Inventory Service
     ↓
Inventory Event Store

Each service can maintain its own event history.

Other services don't directly access those stores.

Instead:

OrderCreated
     ↓
Message Broker
     ↓
Inventory / Payment / Analytics

This preserves service ownership and avoids shared database coupling. Microsoft recommends keeping data stores private to the owning service and communicating through well-defined APIs/events. Microsoft Learn

31. Event Sourcing Failure Scenario

Suppose:

OrderCreated
      ↓
Event Store ✓
      ↓
Projection ✗

What happens?

The source event still exists.

We can:

Retry
   ↓
Projection

or:

Rebuild projection
   ↓
Replay historical events
   ↓
New Read Model

That's one of the major reasons Event Sourcing can be valuable.

32. Common Interview Questions

🔴 Must Know

  1. What is Event Sourcing?
  1. How is Event Sourcing different from CRUD?
  1. What is an event store?
  1. What is event replay?
  1. Why are events immutable?
  1. What is a projection?
  1. What is a read model?
  1. What is a snapshot?
  1. Why do we need snapshots?
  1. Event Sourcing vs audit logging?
  1. Event vs command?
  1. Does Event Sourcing require CQRS?
  1. Does CQRS require Event Sourcing?
  1. How does CQRS work with Event Sourcing?
  1. What are the benefits of Event Sourcing?
  1. What are its disadvantages?
  1. When should you use Event Sourcing?
  1. When should you avoid it?
