62. Design Patterns in .NET 🎨

For your 3+ years .NET Full Stack / Senior Software Engineer interviews, you should focus less on memorizing 23 GoF patterns and more on knowing which pattern solves which problem and where you've used the idea in ASP.NET Core.

.NET itself uses many established patterns, and Microsoft's documentation specifically discusses patterns such as Factory, Strategy, Decorator, Adapter, Observer, Iterator and Template Method in the .NET/ASP.NET ecosystem. Microsoft Learn

🔴 Must Master

Prioritize these:

  1. What is a Design Pattern?
  1. Why use Design Patterns?
  1. Creational vs Structural vs Behavioral patterns
  1. Singleton
  1. Factory
  1. Abstract Factory
  1. Builder
  1. Prototype
  1. Adapter
  1. Decorator
  1. Facade
  1. Proxy
  1. Strategy
  1. Observer
  1. Template Method
  1. Chain of Responsibility
  1. Command
  1. Repository
  1. Unit of Work
  1. Dependency Injection
  1. Specification
  1. Mediator
  1. CQRS
  1. Which patterns are actually useful in ASP.NET Core?
  1. When should you not use a design pattern?

1. What is a Design Pattern?

A design pattern is a:

Reusable solution approach to a commonly occurring software design problem.

It isn't a ready-made piece of code.

For example:

Problem:
I need to create different payment providers.

Possible solution:
Factory Pattern

Instead of:

if (type == "Stripe")
{
    return new StripePayment();
}
else if (type == "PayPal")
{
    return new PayPalPayment();
}

we can encapsulate object creation in a factory.

2. Why use Design Patterns?

They help with:

  • Maintainability
  • Loose coupling
  • Reusability
  • Testability
  • Extensibility
  • Separation of responsibilities

But don't use patterns just because they exist.

Strong interview statement

"I use design patterns when they solve an actual design problem. I avoid introducing a pattern when it adds unnecessary abstraction or complexity."

That's an important senior-level answer.

3. Three Major Categories

The classic GoF patterns are commonly grouped into:

Design Patterns
│
├── Creational
│
├── Structural
│
└── Behavioral

Creational

Concerned with object creation.

Examples:

Singleton
Factory
Abstract Factory
Builder
Prototype

Structural

Concerned with how objects/classes are composed.

Examples:

Adapter
Decorator
Facade
Proxy
Composite

Behavioral

Concerned with communication and responsibilities.

Examples:

Strategy
Observer
Command
Mediator
Chain of Responsibility
Template Method

4. Singleton Pattern

Singleton ensures that a class has a single instance within a defined lifetime/context.

Classic implementation:

public sealed class Logger
{
    private static readonly Lazy<Logger> _instance =
        new(() => new Logger());

    private Logger()
    {
    }

    public static Logger Instance => _instance.Value;
}

Usage:

Logger.Instance.Log("Something happened");

But ASP.NET Core has an important distinction

In ASP.NET Core, you normally don't manually implement Singleton for application services.

You can register a service:

builder.Services.AddSingleton<IMyService, MyService>();

The built-in .NET DI container supports singleton, scoped and transient registrations. Microsoft Learn

Interview question

Should every Singleton be thread-safe?

Generally, yes, if it contains mutable shared state and can be accessed concurrently.

Microsoft's DI guidance specifically notes that singleton services should be thread-safe when they have shared mutable state. Microsoft Learn

5. Singleton vs Singleton DI Lifetime

Don't confuse:

Singleton Design Pattern

with:

AddSingleton()

Design Pattern

The class itself controls the single instance.

DI Lifetime

The dependency injection container controls how many instances are created within its service-provider lifetime.

For interviews:

"AddSingleton gives a service singleton lifetime through the DI container; it isn't the same thing as implementing the Singleton design pattern manually."

6. Factory Pattern ⭐

One of the most important patterns for you.

Factory encapsulates object creation.

Suppose:

Payment
├── CreditCardPayment
├── PayPalPayment
└── UpiPayment

Interface:

public interface IPayment
{
    void Pay(decimal amount);
}

Implementations:

public class CreditCardPayment : IPayment
{
    public void Pay(decimal amount)
    {
        Console.WriteLine("Credit Card");
    }
}

public class UpiPayment : IPayment
{
    public void Pay(decimal amount)
    {
        Console.WriteLine("UPI");
    }
}

Factory:

public class PaymentFactory
{
    public IPayment Create(string type)
    {
        return type switch
        {
            "card" => new CreditCardPayment(),
            "upi" => new UpiPayment(),
            _ => throw new ArgumentException("Invalid payment type")
        };
    }
}

Usage:

var payment = factory.Create("upi");

payment.Pay(1000);

7. Why use Factory?

Without factory:

Controller
   ↓
new CreditCardPayment()
new UpiPayment()
new PayPalPayment()

Now the controller knows implementation details.

With factory:

Controller
    ↓
PaymentFactory
    ↓
IPayment

The creation logic is centralized.

Interview answer

"I use Factory when object creation involves choosing between different implementations based on some input or configuration. It keeps creation logic out of controllers or business services and makes the calling code depend on abstractions."

8. Factory Pattern vs Dependency Injection

This is a very good interview question.

DI

DI provides dependencies to a class.

Service
 ↓
IPayment
 ↓
DI Container

Factory

Factory decides which object to create.

Service
 ↓
Factory
 ↓
Payment implementation

They can also work together.

For example:

public interface IPayment
{
    Task PayAsync(decimal amount);
}

Register multiple implementations and use a factory to select one.

Modern .NET also supports keyed services, which can sometimes remove the need for a custom factory for straightforward keyed resolution. Microsoft's current DI documentation includes keyed services. Microsoft Learn

9. Abstract Factory

Factory:

Creates one type of related object.

Abstract Factory:

Creates families of related objects.

Example:

UI Factory
│
├── Windows Button
├── Windows Checkbox
└── Windows TextBox

Another:

Mac UI Factory
│
├── Mac Button
├── Mac Checkbox
└── Mac TextBox

Use it when multiple related objects must be created consistently.

For typical ASP.NET Core interviews, know the concept, but Factory is more important.

10. Builder Pattern

Builder constructs a complex object step-by-step.

Example:

var request = new ReportRequestBuilder()
    .ForCustomer(100)
    .WithDateRange(start, end)
    .IncludeTransactions()
    .IncludeSummary()
    .Build();

Instead of:

new ReportRequest(
    customerId,
    startDate,
    endDate,
    true,
    true,
    false,
    ...
);

When useful?

When an object has:

  • Many optional parameters
  • Complex construction
  • Multiple construction steps

11. Adapter Pattern ⭐

Adapter makes incompatible interfaces work together.

Suppose your application expects:

public interface INotificationService
{
    Task SendAsync(string message);
}

But an external provider gives:

public class SmsProvider
{
    public void SendSms(string text)
    {
    }
}

Create an adapter:

public class SmsAdapter : INotificationService
{
    private readonly SmsProvider _provider;

    public SmsAdapter(SmsProvider provider)
    {
        _provider = provider;
    }

    public Task SendAsync(string message)
    {
        _provider.SendSms(message);
        return Task.CompletedTask;
    }
}

Now:

Application
    ↓
INotificationService
    ↓
SmsAdapter
    ↓
External SMS Provider

Interview answer

"Adapter is useful when I need to integrate an existing or third-party component whose interface doesn't match what my application expects."

12. Decorator Pattern ⭐

Decorator adds behavior without modifying the original class.

Suppose:

public interface IOrderService
{
    Task CreateOrderAsync();
}

Base implementation:

public class OrderService : IOrderService
{
    public Task CreateOrderAsync()
    {
        return Task.CompletedTask;
    }
}

Decorator:

public class LoggingOrderService : IOrderService
{
    private readonly IOrderService _inner;

    public LoggingOrderService(IOrderService inner)
    {
        _inner = inner;
    }

    public async Task CreateOrderAsync()
    {
        Console.WriteLine("Before");

        await _inner.CreateOrderAsync();

        Console.WriteLine("After");
    }
}

Architecture:

Controller
    ↓
LoggingOrderService
    ↓
OrderService

The original service doesn't need to know about logging.

13. Where do you see Decorator in .NET?

A strong example is middleware-like wrapping/delegation patterns.

You also see decorator concepts in:

HttpMessageHandler
DelegatingHandler
Streams
Logging
Caching
Authorization

For example:

HttpClient
   ↓
Logging Handler
   ↓
Retry Handler
   ↓
Auth Handler
   ↓
Actual HTTP Handler

Each layer adds behavior.

14. Facade Pattern ⭐

Facade provides a simple interface over a complex subsystem.

Suppose placing an order requires:

Inventory
Payment
Shipping
Notification

Without facade:

Controller
 ├── InventoryService
 ├── PaymentService
 ├── ShippingService
 └── NotificationService

With facade:

Controller
     ↓
OrderFacade
     ↓
 ┌───┼────┬──────────┐
 ↓   ↓    ↓          ↓
Inv Payment Shipping Notification

Interview answer

"Facade hides subsystem complexity behind a simpler interface. In an application, an application service or orchestration service can act like a facade when it coordinates several lower-level services."

15. Proxy Pattern

Proxy provides a substitute object that controls access to another object.

Conceptually:

Client
 ↓
Proxy
 ↓
Real Object

The proxy might add:

Caching
Authorization
Logging
Lazy loading
Remote communication

Example:

Client
 ↓
Caching Proxy
 ↓
Product Service

16. Strategy Pattern ⭐⭐⭐

Very important.

Strategy allows you to select an algorithm/behavior at runtime.

Example:

Discount
├── RegularDiscount
├── PremiumDiscount
└── FestivalDiscount

Interface:

public interface IDiscountStrategy
{
    decimal Calculate(decimal amount);
}

Implementations:

public class RegularDiscount : IDiscountStrategy
{
    public decimal Calculate(decimal amount)
        => amount * 0.05m;
}

public class PremiumDiscount : IDiscountStrategy
{
    public decimal Calculate(decimal amount)
        => amount * 0.15m;
}

Service:

public class DiscountService
{
    private readonly IDiscountStrategy _strategy;

    public DiscountService(IDiscountStrategy strategy)
    {
        _strategy = strategy;
    }

    public decimal Calculate(decimal amount)
    {
        return _strategy.Calculate(amount);
    }
}

17. Why Strategy?

Without Strategy:

if (customerType == "Regular")
{
    ...
}
else if (customerType == "Premium")
{
    ...
}
else if (customerType == "VIP")
{
    ...
}

As rules grow:

if
else if
else if
else if
...

becomes difficult to maintain.

Strategy gives:

DiscountService
      ↓
IDiscountStrategy
      ↓
Regular / Premium / VIP

Interview answer

"Strategy is useful when I have multiple interchangeable algorithms or business rules. Instead of putting many conditional branches into one class, I encapsulate each strategy behind an interface and select the appropriate implementation."

18. Observer Pattern

Observer allows one object to notify multiple subscribers when something changes.

Order Service
     ↓
Order Created
   / | \
  ↓  ↓  ↓
Email
SMS
Analytics

Conceptually:

Publisher
    ↓
Subscribers

.NET examples

You can see observer concepts through:

Events
IObservable<T>
Reactive programming

In your architecture, an event-driven notification system can also follow the same conceptual idea.

19. Template Method

Defines the overall algorithm structure while allowing subclasses to customize certain steps.

Example:

public abstract class ReportGenerator
{
    public void Generate()
    {
        LoadData();
        ProcessData();
        GenerateOutput();
    }

    protected abstract void LoadData();
    protected abstract void ProcessData();

    protected virtual void GenerateOutput()
    {
        Console.WriteLine("Generate PDF");
    }
}

Different reports can implement the individual steps.

Mental model

Fixed algorithm
      ↓
Variable steps

20. Chain of Responsibility ⭐

A request passes through a chain of handlers.

Request
  ↓
Authentication
  ↓
Authorization
  ↓
Validation
  ↓
Logging
  ↓
Controller

Each handler can:

  • Handle the request
  • Modify it
  • Reject it
  • Pass it forward

This is highly relevant to ASP.NET Core because the middleware pipeline has a chain-like structure.

For example:

Request
 ↓
Middleware A
 ↓
Middleware B
 ↓
Middleware C
 ↓
Endpoint

21. Command Pattern

Encapsulates an operation/request as an object.

public interface ICommand
{
    Task ExecuteAsync();
}

Example:

CreateOrderCommand
UpdateOrderCommand
CancelOrderCommand

This is especially relevant when discussing:

CQRS
MediatR
Background processing
Undo/redo
Message-based systems

22. Mediator Pattern ⭐

Mediator reduces direct communication between multiple objects.

Instead of:

Controller
 ↓
Service A
 ↓
Service B
 ↓
Service C

multiple components communicate through a mediator.

Conceptually:

Controller
    ↓
Mediator
 /   |   \
A    B    C

MediatR is a commonly used .NET library implementing mediator-style request/notification handling.

Important

Don't say:

"MediatR = CQRS."

Instead:

"MediatR is a mediator library. It can be used to implement CQRS-style command/query handlers, but CQRS is an architectural pattern and doesn't require MediatR."

23. Repository Pattern

Very important for .NET interviews.

Repository abstracts data access.

public interface IProductRepository
{
    Task<Product?> GetByIdAsync(int id);
    Task AddAsync(Product product);
}

Implementation:

public class ProductRepository : IProductRepository
{
    private readonly AppDbContext _context;

    public ProductRepository(AppDbContext context)
    {
        _context = context;
    }

    public Task<Product?> GetByIdAsync(int id)
    {
        return _context.Products
            .FirstOrDefaultAsync(x => x.Id == id);
    }
}

Architecture:

Controller
    ↓
Service
    ↓
Repository
    ↓
DbContext
    ↓
SQL Server

24. Is Repository Always Required with EF Core?

No.

This is a very important senior-level point.

EF Core's:

DbContext
DbSet

already provide many repository/unit-of-work-like capabilities.

So adding:

GenericRepository<T>

over every DbSet<T> may simply add another abstraction layer without much value.

Strong interview answer

"I don't automatically add a repository on top of EF Core. DbContext and DbSet already provide repository/unit-of-work-like behavior. I'd introduce a repository when it provides a meaningful abstraction, such as isolating complex persistence logic, supporting a particular domain boundary, or allowing different data-access implementations."

That's a much stronger answer than:

"Repository is always best practice."

25. Unit of Work

Unit of Work coordinates multiple changes as one logical transaction.

Conceptually:

Order
+
OrderItems
+
Payment
      ↓
Unit of Work
      ↓
Commit

In EF Core:

context.Orders.Add(order);
context.OrderItems.Add(item);

await context.SaveChangesAsync();

DbContext already provides unit-of-work-like behavior through change tracking and SaveChanges.

26. Specification Pattern

Specification encapsulates reusable business/query criteria.

Example:

public class ActiveCustomerSpecification
{
    public Expression<Func<Customer, bool>> Criteria =>
        c => c.IsActive && c.IsVerified;
}

Then:

Customer
   ↓
Specification
   ↓
IsActive
AND
IsVerified

Useful when complex filtering/business rules need to be composed and reused.

27. Dependency Injection as a Design Pattern ⭐⭐⭐

You've already studied DI extensively.

DI is itself a design pattern/technique for providing dependencies from outside a class rather than having the class construct them directly. .NET has built-in DI support. Microsoft Learn

Bad:

public class OrderService
{
    private readonly SqlOrderRepository _repository;

    public OrderService()
    {
        _repository = new SqlOrderRepository();
    }
}

Better:

public class OrderService
{
    private readonly IOrderRepository _repository;

    public OrderService(IOrderRepository repository)
    {
        _repository = repository;
    }
}

Now:

OrderService
     ↓
IOrderRepository
     ↓
DI Container
     ↓
SqlOrderRepository

This improves:

  • Loose coupling
  • Testability
  • Maintainability
  • Replaceability

Microsoft's current DI guidance also recommends avoiding direct instantiation of dependencies and designing small, testable services. Microsoft Learn

28. Patterns in YOUR ASP.NET Core Architecture

This is the part I want you to remember for interviews.

Your architecture can look like:

React
  ↓
ASP.NET Core Controller
  ↓
Application Service
  ↓
Strategy / Factory
  ↓
Repository / DbContext
  ↓
SQL Server

Cross-cutting:

Middleware
   ↓
Chain of Responsibility

DI
   ↓
Dependency Injection

HttpClientFactory
   ↓
DelegatingHandler / Decorator-like pipeline

CQRS
   ↓
Command / Query

MediatR
   ↓
Mediator

Redis
   ↓
Cache-aside

SQS/SNS
   ↓
Event-driven architecture

29. Which Patterns Should YOU Prioritize?

For your interviews:

🔴 Tier 1 — Must Master

Dependency Injection
Factory
Strategy
Decorator
Adapter
Facade
Repository
Unit of Work
Mediator
CQRS
Chain of Responsibility

🟡 Tier 2 — Know Well

Singleton
Builder
Observer
Command
Specification
Proxy
Template Method

🟢 Tier 3 — Know the concept

Abstract Factory
Prototype
Composite
Bridge
Flyweight
State
Visitor
Interpreter
Memento
Iterator

You don't need to spend equal preparation time on every GoF pattern.

30. Design Pattern vs Architecture

Very common conceptual question.

Design Pattern

Solves a localized design problem.

Example:

Strategy
Factory
Decorator
Adapter

Architecture

Defines the overall structure of the system.

Example:

Clean Architecture
Microservices
Layered Architecture
Event-Driven Architecture
CQRS

So:

Architecture
     ↓
contains/uses
     ↓
Design Patterns

31. Design Pattern vs SOLID

Another common question.

SOLID

Design principles.

SRP
OCP
LSP
ISP
DIP

Design Patterns

Reusable design approaches.

Factory
Strategy
Decorator
Adapter
...

They complement each other.

For example:

DIP
 ↓
Depend on abstraction
 ↓
Strategy Pattern
 ↓
Multiple implementations

32. When Should You NOT Use a Design Pattern?

This is a very good senior-level question.

Don't introduce a pattern simply because:

"It's a best practice."

Use it when it solves a real problem.

For example, if you have:

public class ProductService
{
    public Product Get(int id)
    {
        ...
    }
}

and nothing needs abstraction or multiple implementations, don't create:

ProductFactory
ProductBuilder
ProductStrategy
ProductRepositoryFactory
ProductServiceFacade
ProductMediator

just to make the architecture look sophisticated.

Strong answer

"Patterns are tools, not requirements. I use them when they reduce coupling, improve extensibility or solve a recurring design problem. If a pattern adds more abstraction than value, I prefer the simpler design."

33. Top Design Pattern Interview Questions

Make sure you can answer these:

🔴 Must Know

  1. What is a design pattern?
  1. Why do we need design patterns?
  1. What are the three categories?
  1. Explain Singleton.
  1. Singleton vs AddSingleton.
  1. Explain Factory.
  1. Factory vs DI.
  1. Explain Abstract Factory.
  1. Explain Builder.
  1. Explain Adapter.
  1. Explain Decorator.
  1. Explain Facade.
  1. Explain Proxy.
  1. Explain Strategy.
  1. Strategy vs Factory.
  1. Explain Observer.
  1. Explain Template Method.
  1. Explain Chain of Responsibility.
  1. How is ASP.NET Core middleware related to Chain of Responsibility?
  1. Explain Command.
  1. Explain Mediator.
  1. Mediator vs CQRS.
  1. Explain Repository.
  1. Is Repository required with EF Core?
  1. Explain Unit of Work.
  1. Does EF Core implement Unit of Work?
  1. Explain Specification.
  1. DI vs Factory.
  1. Design Patterns vs SOLID.
  1. Design Pattern vs Architecture.
  1. Which design patterns have you used in real projects?
  1. When should you avoid design patterns?

🎯 Strong 60-Second Interview Answer

If the interviewer asks:

"Which design patterns have you used in .NET?"

You can answer:

"In .NET applications, I mainly use patterns based on the problem rather than applying patterns everywhere. Dependency Injection is fundamental for loose coupling and testability. I've used Factory-style approaches when selecting between different implementations, Strategy when business behavior can vary, and Repository or data-access abstractions when they provide a meaningful persistence boundary. Middleware follows a chain-of-responsibility style, and Decorator concepts are useful for adding cross-cutting behavior such as logging or resilience. I've also worked with CQRS and mediator-style handlers for separating commands and queries. With EF Core, I don't automatically add a repository and unit-of-work abstraction because DbContext already provides many of those capabilities. My focus is choosing the simplest pattern that solves the actual design problem."

🧠 Final Mental Model

Remember:

CREATIONAL
───────────
Singleton → One instance
Factory → Create the right object
Builder → Build complex object
Abstract Factory → Create related objects


STRUCTURAL
───────────
Adapter → Make incompatible interfaces work
Decorator → Add behavior
Facade → Simplify complex subsystem
Proxy → Control access


BEHAVIORAL
───────────
Strategy → Select algorithm
Observer → Notify subscribers
Command → Encapsulate request
Mediator → Centralize communication
Chain → Pass request through handlers
Template → Fixed algorithm + customizable steps


ASP.NET CORE
────────────
DI → Dependency management
Middleware → Chain of Responsibility
HttpClient handlers → Delegation/Decorator-like pipeline
Repository → Data-access abstraction
Unit of Work → Coordinate persistence
CQRS → Separate reads/writes
Mediator → Decouple request handlers
Factory → Select implementation
Strategy → Business rules

One-line memory

Factory creates, Strategy chooses, Adapter translates, Decorator adds behavior, Facade simplifies, Proxy controls, Observer notifies, Mediator coordinates, Repository abstracts data access, and DI supplies dependencies.

63. Advanced C# / .NET Internals ⚙️

This topic is about the deeper C# and .NET concepts that interviewers use to distinguish someone who can write C# from someone who understands what happens under the hood.

For your experience level, focus especially on memory management, GC, value/reference types, boxing, delegates, generics, Span/Memory, threading, ThreadPool, JIT, reflection, IDisposable, and performance.

Microsoft's current advanced .NET documentation groups these areas around threading, parallel programming, async programming, native interop and memory management. Microsoft Learn

🔴 Must Master

Prioritize these:

  1. CLR, CTS and CLS
  1. Managed vs unmanaged code
  1. Stack vs heap
  1. Value types vs reference types
  1. Boxing and unboxing
  1. struct vs class
  1. readonly struct
  1. ref, in, out
  1. ref return / ref local
  1. Span<T>
  1. ReadOnlySpan<T>
  1. Memory<T> / ReadOnlyMemory<T>
  1. ref struct
  1. Garbage Collection
  1. Generations 0, 1 and 2
  1. Large Object Heap
  1. Finalizers
  1. IDisposable
  1. using / await using
  1. Memory leaks in managed code
  1. Delegates
  1. Events
  1. Func, Action, Predicate
  1. Lambda expressions
  1. Expression trees
  1. Generics
  1. Generic constraints
  1. Covariance / contravariance
  1. Reflection
  1. Attributes
  1. JIT compilation
  1. AOT vs JIT
  1. Thread vs Task
  1. ThreadPool
  1. Synchronization primitives
  1. lock
  1. Monitor
  1. SemaphoreSlim
  1. Interlocked
  1. volatile
  1. Race conditions
  1. Deadlocks
  1. IEnumerable vs IQueryable
  1. yield
  1. Exception handling internals
  1. Performance optimization

1. CLR

CLR = Common Language Runtime.

It provides the runtime environment for .NET applications.

Conceptually:

C# Code
   ↓
Compiler
   ↓
IL / CIL
   ↓
CLR
   ↓
JIT
   ↓
Native Machine Code

CLR handles things such as:

  • Garbage collection
  • JIT compilation
  • Exception handling
  • Type safety
  • Thread management
  • Interoperability

Interview answer

"CLR is the runtime environment that executes managed .NET code. It provides services such as garbage collection, JIT compilation, exception handling, type safety and thread management."

2. CTS and CLS

CTS — Common Type System

Defines how types work in .NET.

For example:

int
string
class
struct
interface
delegate

CLS — Common Language Specification

Defines rules that .NET languages can follow to interoperate.

Conceptually:

C#
 ↓
     .NET
 ↓
VB.NET
 ↓
F#

Easy memory

CTS defines types; CLS defines language interoperability rules.

3. Managed vs Unmanaged Code

Managed

Runs under CLR management.

Examples:

class Customer
{
}

CLR manages:

  • Memory
  • GC
  • Exceptions
  • Type safety

Unmanaged

Runs outside normal CLR memory management.

Examples:

Native C/C++
Operating system APIs
Native libraries

Interop can use:

P/Invoke
COM
Marshalling

4. Stack vs Heap

Very common interview question.

Stack

Generally stores:

  • Method call frames
  • Local execution state
  • Some value-type data

Example:

int x = 10;

Heap

Managed objects are allocated on the managed heap.

Example:

var customer = new Customer();

Conceptually:

Stack                 Heap
──────                ──────
customer reference →  Customer object
x = 10

But be careful:

Don't say "all value types are on the stack and all reference types are on the heap."

That's an oversimplification.

A value type can be embedded inside an object on the heap, and implementation details determine where storage resides.

5. Value Type vs Reference Type

Value type

Examples:

int
double
bool
struct
enum

Assignment copies the value.

int a = 10;
int b = a;

b = 20;

Result:

a = 10
b = 20

Reference type

Examples:

class
string
array
delegate

Assignment copies the reference.

var a = new Person();
var b = a;

b.Name = "John";

Both references point to the same object.

6. Boxing and Unboxing ⭐⭐⭐

Very common.

Boxing

Converts a value type to object or an implemented interface type.

int number = 10;

object obj = number;

Conceptually:

int
 ↓
boxing
 ↓
object on managed heap

Unboxing

Converts it back:

int number = (int)obj;

Why does boxing matter?

It can introduce:

  • Allocation
  • Copying
  • Runtime type checks
  • Performance overhead

Avoid unnecessary boxing in performance-sensitive code.

7. Struct vs Class

Class

Reference type.

public class Customer
{
    public int Id { get; set; }
}

Struct

Value type.

public struct Point
{
    public int X;
    public int Y;
}

Use a struct when the type is conceptually a small value and value semantics make sense.

Don't automatically use structs to "avoid the heap"; large structs can be expensive to copy.

8. readonly struct

A readonly struct expresses that the struct is immutable from the perspective of its instance members.

public readonly struct Point
{
    public int X { get; }
    public int Y { get; }

    public Point(int x, int y)
    {
        X = x;
        Y = y;
    }
}

Useful for small immutable value types.

9. ref, in, and out

ref

Passes an existing variable by reference.

void Increment(ref int x)
{
    x++;
}

out

Method must assign the value.

void GetValue(out int value)
{
    value = 10;
}

in

Passes a value by readonly reference.

void Print(in LargeStruct value)
{
}

Useful when you want to avoid copying a large value type while preventing modification.

10. ref return

A method can return a reference to existing storage when the lifetime rules permit it.

public ref int GetValue(int[] values)
{
    return ref values[0];
}

Then:

ref int value = ref GetValue(values);

value = 100;

The original array element is modified.

C# has compiler-enforced ref-safe-context rules so a reference can't escape the lifetime of the storage it refers to. Microsoft Learn

11. Span<T> ⭐⭐⭐

This is a high-value advanced C# interview topic, especially because you've specifically prepared ReadOnlySpan<T> before.

Span<T> provides a type-safe view over contiguous memory without requiring a new array allocation for every slice.

Example:

int[] numbers = { 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 };

Span<int> span = numbers;

var slice = span.Slice(1, 3);

Conceptually:

Array
┌───┬───┬───┬───┬───┐
│ 1 │ 2 │ 3 │ 4 │ 5 │
└───┴───┴───┴───┴───┘
    ↑───────────↑
       Span

It can work over:

  • Arrays
  • Stack memory
  • Unmanaged memory

12. Why is Span fast?

Instead of:

var copy = numbers[1..4];

creating a new collection in situations where a view is enough, Span<T> can represent a view over existing contiguous memory.

Microsoft describes Span<T> as a ref struct that holds a reference and length and avoids copying the underlying storage. Microsoft Learn

Mental model

Span = view over memory, not a new copy of the data.

13. ReadOnlySpan<T>

Same basic concept, but you can't modify the elements through the span.

ReadOnlySpan<char> text = "Hello".AsSpan();

Good for:

Parsing
String processing
High-performance APIs
Avoiding allocations

14. Why can't Span<T> be stored in a normal class?

Because Span<T> is a ref struct.

ref struct types are restricted so they cannot escape to the managed heap. They cannot, for example, be boxed, stored as fields in ordinary classes, or captured by lambdas. Microsoft Learn

Conceptually:

Span<T>
   ↓
ref struct
   ↓
stack-only lifetime constraints

This is why you can't simply do:

class MyClass
{
    Span<int> _span; // Not allowed
}

15. Span vs Memory ⭐⭐⭐

Very common senior question.

Span<T>

Fast synchronous memory access

Memory<T>

Memory that can safely participate in asynchronous workflows

Think:

Span<T>
 ↓
Synchronous processing

Memory<T>
 ↓
Can be stored/passed across async boundaries

Interview answer

"Span<T> is ideal for synchronous high-performance memory access because it's a ref struct. Memory<T> provides a heap-storable representation that can be used across asynchronous operations."

16. Garbage Collection ⭐⭐⭐

.NET uses a garbage collector to automatically manage managed memory.

Conceptually:

Application
   ↓
Allocate objects
   ↓
Managed Heap
   ↓
Objects become unreachable
   ↓
GC
   ↓
Memory reclaimed

Microsoft describes GC as the runtime mechanism that manages allocation and release of managed memory. Microsoft Learn

17. GC Generations

.NET GC uses generations.

Generation 0
Generation 1
Generation 2

Gen 0

Short-lived objects.

Temporary objects
Request allocations

Gen 1

Intermediate lifetime.

Gen 2

Long-lived objects.

Caches
Long-lived application state

Mental model

New object
   ↓
Gen 0
   ↓ survives
Gen 1
   ↓ survives
Gen 2

The goal is to make collection of short-lived objects cheap and frequent while preserving long-lived objects.

18. Large Object Heap

Large objects are handled differently from ordinary small allocations and are associated with the Large Object Heap.

Typical examples:

Large arrays
Large buffers
Large strings/data structures

Large allocations can create memory pressure and fragmentation.

So avoid unnecessarily creating huge temporary objects.

19. Server GC vs Workstation GC

For server applications such as ASP.NET Core, server GC is an important concept.

Server GC is designed for applications requiring high throughput and scalability and uses dedicated GC threads. Microsoft Learn

Conceptually:

ASP.NET Core
     ↓
Many requests
     ↓
Many allocations
     ↓
Server GC

Don't simply say:

"Server GC is always faster."

The correct answer depends on workload and resource usage.

20. What causes GC performance problems?

Suppose:

for (int i = 0; i < 1_000_000; i++)
{
    var data = new byte[10_000];
}

You're generating huge allocation pressure.

Possible result:

More allocations
      ↓
More GC work
      ↓
Higher CPU
      ↓
Lower throughput

Microsoft's GC performance guidance specifically points to allocation rate, object survival, heap fragmentation and collection duration as important areas when investigating GC performance. Microsoft Learn

21. Managed Memory Leak

People often say:

"There are no memory leaks in .NET."

That's incorrect.

GC only collects objects that are no longer reachable.

Example:

public static List<object> Cache = new();

public void Add()
{
    Cache.Add(new HugeObject());
}

If the list keeps references forever:

Cache
 ↓
Object
Object
Object
Object
...

GC cannot reclaim those objects.

Common causes

  • Static collections
  • Event subscriptions
  • Long-lived caches
  • Incorrect object lifetimes
  • Timers
  • Unreleased unmanaged resources

22. Finalizer

A finalizer provides a mechanism for cleanup before an object is reclaimed when finalization is involved.

Syntax:

~MyClass()
{
}

But don't use finalizers as your normal resource-management mechanism.

For deterministic cleanup:

IDisposable

is preferred.

23. IDisposable ⭐⭐⭐

Used for deterministic cleanup of resources.

public class FileService : IDisposable
{
    public void Dispose()
    {
        // release resources
    }
}

Usage:

using var service = new FileService();

At the end of the scope:

Dispose()

is called.

Typical resources:

File handles
Streams
Database connections
Native resources
Sockets

24. using vs finally

This:

using var stream = File.OpenRead(path);

is essentially compiler-supported resource cleanup around a try/finally pattern.

Conceptually:

var stream = File.OpenRead(path);

try
{
    // use stream
}
finally
{
    stream.Dispose();
}

25. IAsyncDisposable

For resources requiring asynchronous cleanup:

await using var resource = new MyAsyncResource();

The type implements:

IAsyncDisposable

and provides:

ValueTask DisposeAsync();

26. Delegates ⭐⭐⭐

A delegate represents a reference to a method with a compatible signature.

delegate int Calculator(int a, int b);

Usage:

int Add(int a, int b) => a + b;

Calculator calculator = Add;

int result = calculator(10, 20);

Think:

Delegate
   ↓
Reference to callable method

27. Func, Action and Predicate

Instead of declaring your own delegate:

Func

Returns a value.

Func<int, int, int> add =
    (a, b) => a + b;

Action

Returns nothing.

Action<string> log =
    message => Console.WriteLine(message);

Predicate

Returns bool.

Predicate<int> isEven =
    x => x % 2 == 0;

28. Events

Events provide a controlled publisher/subscriber mechanism.

public event EventHandler? OrderCreated;

Publisher:

OrderCreated?.Invoke(this, EventArgs.Empty);

Subscriber:

service.OrderCreated += Handler;

Mental model:

Publisher
   ↓
Event
   ↓
Subscribers

29. Delegates vs Events

Delegate

Can generally be invoked by whoever has access to the delegate variable.

Event

Restricts external code to subscribing/unsubscribing; only the declaring type can raise the event.

Easy answer

"A delegate represents a callable method reference, while an event provides a controlled publish-subscribe mechanism built around delegates."

30. Generics ⭐⭐⭐

Generics allow reusable type-safe code.

Without generics:

object value;

With generics:

public class Repository<T>
{
    public T Get(int id)
    {
        ...
    }
}

Benefits:

  • Type safety
  • Reusability
  • Less casting
  • Often better performance than object-based designs

31. Generic Constraints

Example:

public class Repository<T>
    where T : class
{
}

Other constraints:

where T : struct
where T : class
where T : new()
where T : BaseClass
where T : IInterface

Example:

public T Create<T>()
    where T : new()
{
    return new T();
}

32. Covariance and Contravariance ⭐⭐

Covariance — out

Allows a more derived type to be used where a base type is expected in supported generic interfaces/delegates.

Example:

IEnumerable<string> strings = ...;

IEnumerable<object> objects = strings;

IEnumerable<T> is covariant.

Contravariance — in

Works in the opposite direction for input types.

Example:

Action<object> objectAction = ...
Action<string> stringAction = objectAction;

Memory trick

out → output → covariance

in → input → contravariance

33. Reflection

Reflection lets you inspect types and members at runtime.

Example:

Type type = typeof(Customer);

var properties = type.GetProperties();

You can inspect:

Types
Methods
Properties
Fields
Attributes
Constructors

It is useful for:

Serialization
Dependency injection
Frameworks
ORMs
Plugin systems
Metadata-driven behavior

But reflection can be more expensive than direct calls, especially for operations such as invocation and dynamic member access. Microsoft Learn

34. Attributes

Attributes add metadata to code.

Example:

[Obsolete("Use NewMethod instead")]
public void OldMethod()
{
}

ASP.NET Core uses attributes heavily:

[Authorize]
[HttpGet]
[ApiController]
[Route("api/products")]

Conceptually:

Code
 +
Metadata
 ↓
Framework behavior

35. JIT Compilation ⭐⭐⭐

JIT = Just-In-Time compiler.

The runtime compiles IL into native machine code as needed.

C#
 ↓
IL
 ↓
JIT
 ↓
Machine Code
 ↓
CPU

JIT can perform runtime optimizations.

Modern .NET continues to improve JIT code generation and optimization. Microsoft Learn

36. JIT vs AOT

JIT

Compile IL → native code at runtime

AOT

Compile to native code ahead of execution

AOT can provide benefits such as:

  • Faster startup in suitable scenarios
  • Smaller deployment characteristics in some scenarios
  • Reduced runtime compilation requirements

But compatibility and reflection/dynamic-code considerations can affect whether AOT is appropriate.

37. Thread vs Task ⭐⭐⭐

Thread

An actual execution thread managed by the operating system/runtime.

var thread = new Thread(MyMethod);
thread.Start();

Task

Represents asynchronous work.

Task.Run(MyMethod);

A Task does not necessarily mean a new thread.

This is extremely important.

Task is an abstraction for asynchronous work; it is not synonymous with a thread.

38. ThreadPool

.NET maintains a pool of reusable worker threads.

Application
     ↓
ThreadPool
 ┌───┼────┬────┐
 T1  T2   T3   T4

This avoids creating a new OS thread for every small piece of work.

ASP.NET Core relies heavily on asynchronous programming and the ThreadPool to efficiently process concurrent requests.

39. ThreadPool Starvation ⭐⭐⭐

Suppose an ASP.NET Core endpoint does:

var result = SomeAsyncOperation().Result;

or:

SomeAsyncOperation().Wait();

Many requests can occupy ThreadPool threads while waiting.

Conceptually:

Requests
 ↓
ThreadPool threads
 ↓
Blocking
 ↓
Threads unavailable
 ↓
New requests wait
 ↓
Latency increases

That's why you should prefer:

await SomeAsyncOperation();

This connects directly to the async/await topic you already studied.

40. lock

Used for mutual exclusion.

private readonly object _lock = new();

lock (_lock)
{
    _counter++;
}

Only one thread can enter the protected section at a time for that lock object.

Important

lock is for in-process synchronization.

It doesn't coordinate multiple application servers.

41. Monitor

lock is implemented using Monitor-style synchronization semantics.

Conceptually:

Monitor.Enter(_lock);

try
{
    // critical section
}
finally
{
    Monitor.Exit(_lock);
}

Normally prefer lock because it is simpler and safer.

42. SemaphoreSlim

Allows a limited number of concurrent operations.

Example:

private readonly SemaphoreSlim _semaphore = new(5);

await _semaphore.WaitAsync();

try
{
    await DoWorkAsync();
}
finally
{
    _semaphore.Release();
}

This allows up to:

5 concurrent operations

Useful for limiting concurrency around:

  • External APIs
  • Expensive resources
  • Background processing

43. Interlocked

Used for atomic operations on certain primitive values.

Interlocked.Increment(ref counter);

Useful when you need simple atomic operations without taking a traditional lock.

44. volatile

volatile relates to memory visibility for certain fields between threads.

private volatile bool _stopped;

But:

volatile does not make arbitrary compound operations atomic.

For example:

counter++;

is not made safely atomic simply by declaring counter volatile.

Use:

Interlocked
lock
appropriate synchronization

depending on the problem.

45. Race Condition

A race condition occurs when correctness depends on the timing/interleaving of concurrent operations.

Example:

Thread A → read counter = 10
Thread B → read counter = 10
Thread A → write 11
Thread B → write 11

Expected:

12

Actual:

11

Solutions include:

lock
Interlocked
atomic operations
concurrent collections
database concurrency control

46. Deadlock ⭐⭐⭐

A deadlock occurs when threads wait indefinitely for resources held by each other.

Example:

Thread A
  ↓
Lock A
  ↓
waits for Lock B

Thread B
  ↓
Lock B
  ↓
waits for Lock A
A → B
↑   ↓
└───┘

Prevention

  • Consistent lock ordering
  • Smaller critical sections
  • Avoid nested locks where possible
  • Use async-compatible synchronization appropriately
  • Timeouts where applicable

47. IEnumerable vs IQueryable ⭐⭐⭐

Very important for EF Core.

IEnumerable<T>

Generally represents enumeration of objects in application memory.

var products = context.Products
    .AsEnumerable()
    .Where(x => x.Price > 100);

Filtering after AsEnumerable() occurs in memory.

IQueryable<T>

Represents a query that can be translated by a provider such as EF Core.

var products = context.Products
    .Where(x => x.Price > 100);

EF Core can translate the expression into SQL.

Conceptually:

IQueryable
   ↓
Expression Tree
   ↓
EF Core
   ↓
SQL Server

48. Why is calling ToList() too early bad?

Example:

var products = await context.Products
    .ToListAsync();

var result = products
    .Where(x => x.Price > 100);

Potentially:

SQL Server
   ↓
ALL products
   ↓
Application memory
   ↓
Filter

Better:

var result = await context.Products
    .Where(x => x.Price > 100)
    .ToListAsync();

Now:

SQL Server
   ↓
WHERE Price > 100
   ↓
Only required rows
   ↓
Application

This connects directly to your EF Core performance preparation.

49. yield return

yield allows lazy iteration.

Example:

public IEnumerable<int> GetNumbers()
{
    for (int i = 0; i < 5; i++)
    {
        yield return i;
    }
}

Values are generated as the sequence is enumerated rather than creating the entire collection upfront.

Mental model:

Normal collection
→ Build everything
→ Return

yield
→ Generate when requested
→ Generate next
→ Generate next

50. Expression Trees

An expression tree represents code as data.

Example:

Expression<Func<Product, bool>> filter =
    p => p.Price > 100;

Instead of simply executing the lambda, a provider can inspect its structure.

That's why EF Core can translate:

p => p.Price > 100

into something like:

WHERE Price > 100

Conceptually:

Lambda
 ↓
Expression Tree
 ↓
EF Core
 ↓
SQL

51. IEnumerable vs IQueryable vs Expression

A useful mental model:

IEnumerable<T>
    ↓
Execute/enumerate objects

IQueryable<T>
    ↓
Build provider-specific query

Expression<TDelegate>
    ↓
Represent executable logic as data

52. Exception Handling Internals

Basic flow:

try
{
    DoSomething();
}
catch (Exception ex)
{
    Log(ex);
}
finally
{
    Cleanup();
}

Important interview points

  • Don't use exceptions for normal control flow.
  • Preserve stack trace with throw;.
  • Avoid throw ex;.

Correct:

catch (Exception)
{
    throw;
}

Incorrect:

catch (Exception ex)
{
    throw ex;
}

throw ex resets the stack-trace origin in the rethrown exception context, making diagnosis harder.

53. Performance Optimization in .NET

When asked:

"How would you optimize a slow .NET application?"

Don't immediately say:

"Use Span."

Instead:

Measure
  ↓
Profile
  ↓
Identify bottleneck
  ↓
Optimize
  ↓
Measure again

Look at:

CPU
Memory
GC
Database
Network
Allocations
ThreadPool
Locks
External APIs

Microsoft's performance guidance emphasizes measurement and profiling rather than guessing, including allocation and GC analysis when memory is suspected. Microsoft Learn

54. Example: Your ASP.NET Core API is Slow

Suppose:

React
 ↓
ASP.NET Core API
 ↓
EF Core
 ↓
SQL Server

Response time:

2 seconds

Don't immediately optimize C#.

Measure:

API processing = 100ms
SQL query = 1.7 sec

Then:

Execution plan
 ↓
Missing index
 ↓
Add appropriate index
 ↓
Query = 100ms

Now total:

2 sec → ~200ms

This is much more valuable than micro-optimizing object allocations.

Say:

On the C# side, I'm comfortable with value versus reference types, boxing, generics, delegates, events, reflection, ref parameters and high-performance memory types such as Span and ReadOnlySpan. For concurrency, I understand Tasks, the ThreadPool, locks, SemaphoreSlim, Interlocked, race conditions and deadlocks. I also understand how IEnumerable, IQueryable and expression trees affect EF Core query execution. 64. React / Frontend Integration

This is an important topic for your profile specifically, because you can be interviewed as a .NET Full Stack Engineer, not just a backend developer. Your strongest story is:

React + TypeScript → ASP.NET Core Web API → JWT/Auth → Service Layer → EF Core/Dapper → SQL Server

Current React documentation lists React 19.3 as the latest version, and the core interview concepts below remain centered around components, state, Hooks, effects, context, refs, and performance. React

🔴 Must Master

For your interviews, prioritize these:

  1. React component architecture
  1. Props vs State
  1. React Hooks
  1. useState
  1. useEffect
  1. useMemo
  1. useCallback
  1. useRef
  1. useContext
  1. Controlled components
  1. API calls from React
  1. Loading/error/success states
  1. React + ASP.NET Core Web API integration
  1. JWT authentication flow
  1. Token handling
  1. CORS
  1. Axios/fetch interceptors
  1. Refresh-token flow
  1. Redux Toolkit
  1. Async Redux / API calls
  1. React performance optimization
  1. React.memo
  1. Pagination/filtering/sorting
  1. Debouncing
  1. TypeScript with React
  1. DTOs and frontend/backend contracts
  1. Environment configuration
  1. Production deployment
  1. SignalR integration
  1. Frontend error handling

1. What is React?

Interview answer

React is a JavaScript library for building user interfaces using reusable components. Instead of managing the entire UI manually, we describe what the UI should look like based on the current state and props, and React handles rendering and updating the DOM.

In your project

For example:

App
 ├── Login
 ├── Dashboard
 │    ├── Header
 │    ├── Sidebar
 │    └── AuditList
 │         └── AuditRow
 └── Reports

Each part can be a reusable React component.

2. What is a React component?

A component is a reusable piece of UI.

Example:

function UserCard({ name }: { name: string }) {
    return <div>Hello {name}</div>;
}

Usage:

<UserCard name="Saurabh" />

Interview point

Modern React primarily uses function components and Hooks.

3. Props vs State

This is extremely common.

PropsState
Passed from parentManaged by component
Read-onlyCan change
Used to configure componentRepresents changing data
Parent controlsComponent manages

Example:

function User({ name }: { name: string }) {
    return <h1>{name}</h1>;
}

name is a prop.

State:

const [count, setCount] = useState(0);

count is state.

Easy memory

Props come in. State lives inside.

4. What is useState?

useState allows a component to maintain state.

const [count, setCount] = useState(0);

When we update:

setCount(count + 1);

React schedules a re-render.

React's documentation describes useState as the Hook for declaring state variables. React

Better update when depending on previous state

setCount(prev => prev + 1);

This is preferable when the new value depends on the previous value.

5. What is useEffect?

useEffect is used to synchronize a component with an external system, such as network requests, browser APIs, subscriptions, timers, or non-React libraries. React

Example:

useEffect(() => {
    fetchUsers();
}, []);

The empty dependency array means the effect doesn't rerun because of changing dependencies.

With dependency:

useEffect(() => {
    fetchUser(userId);
}, [userId]);

When userId changes, the effect runs again.

Cleanup

useEffect(() => {

    const connection = createConnection();

    connection.connect();

    return () => {
        connection.disconnect();
    };

}, []);

The returned function performs cleanup.

Important interview point

Don't say:

"useEffect is used for everything after rendering."

A better answer is:

"useEffect is primarily used to synchronize React with external systems."

That's also how the current React documentation frames it. React

6. What is useMemo?

useMemo caches the result of an expensive calculation.

const filteredUsers = useMemo(() => {
    return users.filter(x => x.name.includes(search));
}, [users, search]);

It avoids recalculating unless dependencies change.

Don't overuse it

You shouldn't memoize every calculation.

Use it when:

  • calculation is expensive
  • unnecessary recalculation matters
  • profiling shows a performance problem

React documents useMemo as a way to cache calculation results. React

7. What is useCallback?

useCallback caches a function reference.

const handleDelete = useCallback((id: number) => {
    deleteUser(id);
}, []);

This becomes particularly useful when passing callbacks to memoized child components.

useMemo vs useCallback

useMemo
    ↓
caches a value

useCallback
    ↓
caches a function

8. What is useRef?

useRef stores a value that persists between renders without causing a re-render when changed.

Common example:

const inputRef = useRef<HTMLInputElement>(null);

inputRef.current?.focus();

React also documents refs as useful for holding DOM nodes or values such as timeout IDs that aren't used for rendering. React

Interview answer

"useRef is useful when I need to keep a mutable value across renders without triggering another render, or when I need direct access to a DOM element."

9. What is useContext?

Context allows data to be shared with deeply nested components without passing props through every level.

Example:

App
 ↓
Dashboard
 ↓
Header
 ↓
UserMenu

Instead of:

App → Dashboard → Header → UserMenu

passing user through every component, Context can provide it directly.

const UserContext = createContext(null);

Then:

const user = useContext(UserContext);

React describes Context as a way for components to receive information from distant parents without passing it through props. React

10. What are the Rules of Hooks?

Very common interview question.

Two major rules:

Rule 1

Call Hooks only at the top level.

Wrong:

if (isLoggedIn) {
    useEffect(() => {});
}

Correct:

useEffect(() => {

    if (isLoggedIn) {
        // logic
    }

}, [isLoggedIn]);

Rule 2

Call Hooks only from:

  • React function components
  • custom Hooks

Not from ordinary JavaScript functions.

Current React documentation explicitly defines these rules. React

11. What is a controlled component?

A controlled form element gets its value from React state.

const [email, setEmail] = useState("");

<input
    value={email}
    onChange={e => setEmail(e.target.value)}
/>

React controls the value.

Why useful?

You can easily perform:

  • validation
  • conditional UI
  • formatting
  • submission handling

12. What is an uncontrolled component?

The DOM maintains the value instead of React state.

Usually accessed through useRef.

const inputRef = useRef<HTMLInputElement>(null);

<input ref={inputRef} />

Easy interview answer

Controlled components keep form state in React, while uncontrolled components rely more on the DOM and refs.

13. How do you call ASP.NET Core APIs from React?

This is very important for you.

Typical architecture:

React
   ↓
fetch / Axios
   ↓
ASP.NET Core Web API
   ↓
Controller
   ↓
Service
   ↓
EF Core / Dapper
   ↓
SQL Server

Example:

const response = await fetch("/api/users");

if (!response.ok) {
    throw new Error("Failed to load users");
}

const data = await response.json();

Or Axios:

const response = await axios.get("/api/users");

const users = response.data;

14. How do you handle loading, success and error states?

A good production component shouldn't only have:

data

It should generally consider:

Loading
Success
Empty
Error

Example:

const [users, setUsers] = useState<User[]>([]);
const [loading, setLoading] = useState(false);
const [error, setError] = useState("");

Then:

setLoading(true);

try {
    const response = await getUsers();
    setUsers(response.data);
}
catch {
    setError("Unable to load users");
}
finally {
    setLoading(false);
}

Interview answer

I normally handle loading, success, empty and error states explicitly so the UI doesn't assume that an API call always succeeds.

15. How does React communicate with ASP.NET Core?

Example:

React
GET /api/audits?page=1&pageSize=20
        ↓
ASP.NET Core Controller
        ↓
AuditService
        ↓
EF Core
        ↓
SQL Server

Response:

{
  "items": [],
  "page": 1,
  "pageSize": 20,
  "totalCount": 150
}

React uses the response to render the UI.

16. How does JWT authentication work between React and ASP.NET Core?

Very important.

React Login
     ↓
POST /api/auth/login
     ↓
ASP.NET Core
     ↓
Identity Provider / Authentication
     ↓
Access Token
     ↓
React
     ↓
Authorization: Bearer <token>
     ↓
ASP.NET Core JWT Middleware
     ↓
ClaimsPrincipal
     ↓
[Authorize]
     ↓
Controller

ASP.NET Core's JWT bearer handler validates the token and extracts identity claims; Microsoft recommends validating the signature, issuer, audience and expiration. Microsoft Learn

17. Where should JWT tokens be stored?

This is a senior-level interview question because there isn't one universal answer.

Possible approaches include:

localStorage
sessionStorage
memory
secure HttpOnly cookie

Important tradeoff

Tokens in browser-accessible storage such as localStorage can be exposed if an XSS vulnerability allows malicious JavaScript to read them.

For cookie-based authentication, HttpOnly, Secure, SameSite, and CSRF protections become important depending on the architecture.

Interview answer

I don't treat token storage as a simple "always use localStorage" decision. I choose it based on the authentication architecture and security requirements. For browser applications, I consider XSS and CSRF risks and prefer a design where sensitive credentials aren't unnecessarily exposed to JavaScript.

18. What is an Axios interceptor?

An interceptor can process requests/responses centrally.

For example:

axios.interceptors.request.use(config => {

    const token = getToken();

    if (token) {
        config.headers.Authorization = `Bearer ${token}`;
    }

    return config;
});

Now individual API calls don't need to manually add the token every time.

19. How do you handle 401 responses?

Typical flow:

API request
    ↓
401
    ↓
Access token expired
    ↓
Refresh token
    ↓
Get new access token
    ↓
Retry original request

But you need to prevent infinite refresh loops.

A common production approach is:

401
 ↓
Check refresh state
 ↓
Refresh once
 ↓
Update token
 ↓
Retry queued requests

If refresh fails:

Clear authentication
      ↓
Redirect to login

20. What is CORS?

CORS stands for Cross-Origin Resource Sharing.

Suppose:

React
http://localhost:3000

ASP.NET Core
https://localhost:7001

These are different origins.

The browser applies same-origin restrictions, and the API must provide appropriate CORS headers for permitted browser requests. Microsoft specifically notes that CORS is a browser mechanism for relaxing the same-origin policy; it isn't itself an API security feature. Microsoft Learn

ASP.NET Core:

builder.Services.AddCors(options =>
{
    options.AddPolicy("ReactPolicy", policy =>
    {
        policy
            .WithOrigins("http://localhost:3000")
            .AllowAnyHeader()
            .AllowAnyMethod();
    });
});

Then:

app.UseCors("ReactPolicy");

21. What is a preflight request?

For certain cross-origin requests, the browser sends an OPTIONS request first.

Example:

Browser
   ↓
OPTIONS /api/orders
   ↓
ASP.NET Core
   ↓
CORS headers
   ↓
Browser
   ↓
Actual POST

This commonly happens when requests involve things such as certain methods or custom headers.

Interview scenario

"My React application works in Postman but fails in Chrome. Why?"

One possible cause is CORS.

Postman isn't enforcing browser CORS rules in the same way a browser does. Microsoft explicitly notes that CORS is enforced by the browser. Microsoft Learn

22. What is Redux?

Redux is a predictable state-management library.

Instead of keeping important shared state scattered across components:

Component A
Component B
Component C

you can have:

             Redux Store
          /      |       \
       A         B        C

For your experience, Redux Toolkit is the important modern approach.

23. What is Redux Toolkit?

Redux Toolkit simplifies Redux development.

Typical structure:

store
 ├── authSlice
 ├── userSlice
 ├── auditSlice
 └── reportSlice

Example:

const initialState = {
    users: [],
    loading: false
};

A slice contains:

state
reducers
actions

Interview answer

I use Redux Toolkit when state needs to be shared across multiple parts of the application. It reduces Redux boilerplate and provides a structured way to manage state through slices, reducers and actions.

24. Local state vs Redux

Don't put everything into Redux.

Local state

Use for:

Modal open/close
Form input
Selected tab
Dropdown
Temporary UI state

Redux

Useful for:

Logged-in user
Permissions
Shared application state
Cross-page state
Cached server data depending on architecture

Simple rule

Local UI state → component state. Shared application state → global state management.

25. How do you handle API calls with Redux?

One approach is an async thunk.

Conceptually:

Component
   ↓
dispatch(fetchUsers())
   ↓
API
   ↓
success/failure
   ↓
Redux state
   ↓
Component re-renders

For example:

dispatch(fetchUsers());

Then state might become:

loading = true

followed by:

loading = false
users = [...]

26. How do you optimize React performance?

This is another important senior question.

I would check:

1. Unnecessary renders

Use:

React.memo
useMemo
useCallback

where justified.

2. Large lists

Use:

pagination
virtualization

3. API calls

Avoid:

duplicate requests
unnecessary requests

4. Bundle size

Use:

lazy loading
code splitting

5. Expensive calculations

Use memoization when measurement shows it's useful.

React provides memo, useMemo, useCallback, lazy, and transition APIs for different performance scenarios. React

27. What is React.memo?

React.memo can skip re-rendering a component when its props haven't changed.

const UserCard = React.memo(function UserCard({ user }) {
    return <div>{user.name}</div>;
});

But if the parent creates a new object/function every render, the props may still appear changed.

That's where:

React.memo
+
useMemo
+
useCallback

can sometimes work together.

28. What are keys in React lists?

Example:

users.map(user => (
    <UserRow
        key={user.id}
        user={user}
    />
))

Keys help React identify which items changed.

Prefer:

key={user.id}

over:

key={index}

when the list can be reordered, inserted into, or deleted from.

29. How would you implement pagination?

Backend:

GET /api/audits?page=2&pageSize=20

Backend:

SQL Server
    ↓
WHERE
ORDER BY
OFFSET
FETCH

Response:

{
    "items": [...],
    "page": 2,
    "pageSize": 20,
    "totalCount": 200
}

Frontend:

Previous
1
2
3
4
Next

For large datasets, I'd also consider cursor/keyset pagination instead of relying only on large offset values.

30. How would you implement search with debouncing?

Without debounce:

S
Se
Sea
Sear
Searc
Search

could generate six API calls.

With debounce:

User types
    ↓
wait 300ms
    ↓
No new input?
    ↓
API call

Example:

useEffect(() => {

    const timer = setTimeout(() => {
        searchUsers(search);
    }, 300);

    return () => clearTimeout(timer);

}, [search]);

31. What is code splitting?

Instead of loading the entire application immediately:

Huge JS bundle
     ↓
Browser downloads everything

load parts when required:

Login
 ↓
Dashboard
 ↓
Reports

React supports lazy for deferring component code loading until it is first rendered. React

Conceptually:

const Reports = lazy(() => import("./Reports"));

32. What are Error Boundaries?

Error boundaries prevent a rendering error in one part of the React UI from taking down the entire visible application.

Typical architecture:

App
 └── ErrorBoundary
      ├── Header
      ├── Dashboard
      └── Reports

If a component fails during rendering, the boundary can show a fallback UI.

Important distinction

Error boundaries are for React rendering errors.

They aren't a replacement for API error handling.

API errors should still be handled explicitly.

33. How do you use TypeScript with React?

Example:

interface User {
    id: number;
    name: string;
    email: string;
}

interface UserProps {
    user: User;
}

Component:

function UserCard({ user }: UserProps) {
    return (
        <div>
            {user.name}
        </div>
    );
}

TypeScript provides compile-time checking for props, state, API models and functions. React's current TypeScript documentation also notes that Hook types are provided through React's type definitions and can often be inferred automatically. React

34. How should frontend DTOs relate to backend DTOs?

This is important for a full-stack developer.

ASP.NET Core:

public class UserDto
{
    public int Id { get; set; }
    public string Name { get; set; }
}

React:

interface UserDto {
    id: number;
    name: string;
}

The frontend should depend on the API contract, not on the backend's EF Core entity.

Good architecture

SQL Entity
    ↓
EF Core
    ↓
Backend DTO
    ↓
JSON
    ↓
Frontend TypeScript interface

Don't expose your EF entities directly just because it is convenient.

35. How do you handle environment-specific API URLs?

For example:

Development
    API = localhost

QA
    API = QA server

Production
    API = production API

The React build should use environment-specific configuration rather than hardcoding production URLs throughout components.

Conceptually:

Component
   ↓
API service
   ↓
configured API base URL

This keeps API configuration centralized.

This connects directly to your backend experience.

Architecture:

React

      ↓

      ↓

      ↓
UI updates immediately

Instead of:

wait

 ↓

39. Production scenario: API works in Postman but React gets CORS error

Your answer:

First I would check the browser Network tab and the OPTIONS preflight request. Then I would verify the ASP.NET Core CORS policy allows the React application's exact origin, required HTTP methods and headers. I would also verify middleware configuration and ordering. I wouldn't treat CORS as an authentication mechanism because CORS is primarily a browser enforcement mechanism. Microsoft Learn

40. Production scenario: React gets 401 after some time

Likely flow:

Login
 ↓
Access token
 ↓
API works
 ↓
Token expires
 ↓
401

I would check:

  1. token expiration
  1. Authorization header
  1. JWT validation
  1. refresh-token mechanism
  1. Axios interceptor
  1. whether refresh is looping
  1. logout behavior

ASP.NET Core should validate the JWT's signature, issuer, audience and expiration. Microsoft Learn

41. Production scenario: React page renders 10,000 records

I wouldn't simply render everything.

I'd consider:

Server-side pagination
        +
Filtering
        +
Sorting
        +
Projection
        +
Indexes
        +
Virtualization if necessary

Architecture:

React
 ↓
GET /api/audits?page=1&pageSize=50
 ↓
ASP.NET Core
 ↓
SQL Server
 ↓
Only required 50 records

This connects your frontend and SQL optimization knowledge.

42. Your 60-second interview answer

If they ask:

"Tell me about your React experience and how you integrate it with .NET."

Say:

"I've worked with React and TypeScript as part of full-stack .NET applications. I typically structure the frontend using reusable functional components and Hooks such as useState, useEffect, useMemo and useCallback, and I use Redux Toolkit when state needs to be shared across different parts of the application. For backend integration, React communicates with ASP.NET Core REST APIs through an API layer using fetch or Axios. We use DTO-based contracts between the frontend and backend, and authentication is handled using JWT bearer tokens. I also work with CORS, centralized API error handling, loading states, pagination, filtering and performance optimization. On the backend, the API flows through controllers and services to EF Core or Dapper and SQL Server. For real-time scenarios, SignalR can push updates from ASP.NET Core to the React application."

That's a very strong answer for your profile.

1. Tell me about yourself

This is probably the most important answer in the entire interview.

Don't start with:

Start technically.

Interview-ready answer

"I'm a Software Engineer with 3+ years of experience primarily working with C#, .NET Core, ASP.NET Core, SQL Server, React and TypeScript. My experience has been mainly in full-stack development, where I've worked on REST APIs, business logic, database integration and responsive React-based interfaces.

In my current role, I've worked on technical design discussions, code reviews and production development, and I've also mentored a team of developers. I've worked on performance optimization using asynchronous programming, SQL index tuning and EF Core optimization, and I've worked with automated testing using xUnit and Moq.

I've also worked with AWS services such as Lambda, SQS and SNS for asynchronous workflows, and Azure DevOps for CI/CD. I'm now looking for a role where I can work on larger-scale product problems, take more ownership of architecture and continue growing as a full-stack software engineer."

2. Explain your current project

For your experience, you can explain the healthcare project without unnecessarily revealing the client name.

Strong answer

"I'm currently working on a healthcare-related web application that supports audit and reporting workflows. The application has both backend and frontend components, with ASP.NET Core and SQL Server on the backend and React-based UI components on the frontend.

My responsibilities include developing REST APIs, implementing business logic, working with EF Core and SQL Server, building and enhancing React functionality, troubleshooting production issues and participating in technical design and code reviews.

I've also worked on performance optimization, automated testing and asynchronous workflows using AWS services such as Lambda, SQS and SNS."

Interview answer

"The frontend is built using React and TypeScript and communicates with ASP.NET Core REST APIs. The API layer handles authentication, validation and HTTP concerns, while controllers remain relatively thin and delegate business logic to services. Data access is handled using EF Core and, where appropriate, Dapper, with SQL Server as the primary database. 4. Explain one feature end-to-end

This is a very common senior interview technique.

Suppose they ask:

"Walk me through a feature you developed."

Use this structure:

Requirement
   ↓
UI
   ↓
API
   ↓
Business logic
   ↓
Database
   ↓
Response
   ↓
UI update

Example

"Let's say we have an audit listing feature. The React component sends a request with pagination and filtering parameters to the ASP.NET Core API. The controller validates the request and passes it to the service layer. The service applies the business rules and calls the data-access layer. EF Core or Dapper executes the required SQL query against SQL Server. We return a DTO rather than exposing the database entity directly. React then handles the response and updates the table, loading state or error state accordingly."

That's much stronger than simply saying:

"I created an API."

Interviewers often want to distinguish:

team work vs your work.

6. Explain your 35% performance improvement

This should be one of your strongest project stories.

Structure

Problem
 ↓
Investigation
 ↓
Root cause
 ↓
Change
 ↓
Measurement
 ↓
Result

Interview answer

"We had a performance issue in one of the application workflows. Instead of optimizing based on assumptions, I first looked at where the time was being spent. The main areas were asynchronous processing and database query performance.

I improved the implementation using async/await for I/O-bound operations and optimized the SQL queries, including index-related improvements. I also reviewed EF Core query behavior to reduce unnecessary database work.

After testing the changes against the relevant workload, we observed roughly a 35% improvement in performance."

If they ask:

"How did you measure 35%?"

Be honest.

If you have exact before/after numbers, give them.

For example:

Before: 5 seconds
After: 3.25 seconds
Improvement: 35%

If you don't remember the exact measurement, don't invent one.

Say:

"The measured improvement was approximately 35% based on the performance comparison we performed."

7. How did you optimize SQL?

Your answer should demonstrate the SQL knowledge we've covered.

"I first identify the slow query and inspect its execution plan rather than immediately adding indexes. I look for scans, expensive joins, key lookups, incorrect cardinality estimates and other bottlenecks. Then I review filtering, projections and indexes, make a targeted change and measure the result again."

That is a senior-level answer.

Mental model

Slow query
   ↓
Execution plan
   ↓
Find bottleneck
   ↓
SQL/index/statistics change
   ↓
Measure again

8. How do you troubleshoot a slow API?

Don't immediately blame the backend.

Use:

React
 ↓
Network
 ↓
API latency
 ↓
Middleware
 ↓
Controller
 ↓
Service
 ↓
Database / external API

Interview answer

"I first determine whether the latency is actually coming from the frontend, API, database or an external dependency. I check the browser network timing, API logs and traces, then look at service and database timings. If the database is responsible, I inspect the SQL query and execution plan. If an external API is involved, I check timeout and downstream latency. I prefer measuring each layer before making an optimization."

.NET provides diagnostics through logs, metrics, traces, profilers and other diagnostic tools, which supports this measurement-first approach. Microsoft Learn

9. How do you handle exceptions?

Architecture:

Controller
   ↓
Service
   ↓
Exception
   ↓
Global Exception Middleware
   ↓
ProblemDetails
   ↓
React

Answer

"I prefer centralized exception handling rather than putting repetitive try-catch blocks in every controller. Unexpected exceptions are logged centrally with useful contextual information, while the API returns a consistent error response such as Problem Details without exposing internal implementation details."

10. How do you approach logging?

ASP.NET Core provides structured logging through ILogger, with configurable providers and log levels. Microsoft Learn

Answer

"I use structured logging and choose the log level based on the event. Information is useful for normal application flow, Warning for unexpected conditions that don't necessarily fail the operation, Error for operation failures and Critical for serious application-wide problems. I also avoid logging sensitive information such as tokens or passwords."

Remember

Information → normal flow
Warning     → abnormal condition
Error       → operation failed
Critical    → serious system failure

11. How do you handle 10k+ daily transactions?

Don't say:

"The API can handle 10k transactions."

Instead explain the design.

"For that type of workload, I focus on keeping APIs stateless so they can scale horizontally. On the application side, I use asynchronous I/O, efficient database queries, pagination and caching where appropriate. At the database level, I focus on proper indexing and avoiding unnecessary queries. For work that doesn't need to block the HTTP request, I can use asynchronous messaging or background processing. Monitoring latency, errors and resource utilization is also important."

12. Why use async/await?

Strong answer

"For I/O-bound operations such as database calls and HTTP calls, async/await allows the application thread to return to the ThreadPool while the I/O operation is waiting. This improves scalability because threads aren't unnecessarily blocked. In my APIs, I use asynchronous EF Core and HTTP operations and propagate CancellationToken where appropriate."

Don't say:

"async creates a new thread."

It doesn't.

13. EF Core vs Dapper

Interview answer

"EF Core is a full ORM and provides features such as LINQ, change tracking, relationships, migrations and database abstraction. Dapper is a lightweight micro-ORM where I have more direct control over SQL and mapping. I would use EF Core when its ORM capabilities provide value, and Dapper for scenarios where direct SQL control and lightweight mapping are more appropriate. I don't claim that one is always faster; the actual query and workload matter."

Excellent senior-level answer.

14. Why use both EF Core and Dapper?

Possible answer:

"They can coexist if there is a clear reason. For example, EF Core can handle normal transactional domain operations while Dapper can be useful for complex read-heavy queries where I want precise SQL control. I would keep both behind clear data-access boundaries rather than mixing them randomly."

15. Why React?

Don't say:

"Because React is popular."

Instead:

"React provides a component-based approach that makes UI functionality reusable and easier to compose. Hooks make state and side-effect management straightforward, and TypeScript gives stronger typing for frontend contracts. It also integrates cleanly with REST APIs, which fits well with our ASP.NET Core backend."

16. How does JWT authentication work?

React
 ↓
Login
 ↓

 ↓

 ↓
ASP.NET Core JWT middleware

 ↓

Answer

"The client obtains an access token and sends it with API requests using the Authorization Bearer scheme. ASP.NET Core's JWT bearer handler validates the token, including its signature and relevant issuer, audience and expiration requirements. After successful authentication, the user's claims are available through HttpContext.User and authorization policies determine whether the endpoint can be accessed."

Very important.

but not authorized

19. What happens if the API suddenly gets 10× traffic?

Answer:

"First I'd identify whether the bottleneck is CPU, memory, database, external dependencies or request concurrency. Since the API should ideally be stateless, I could horizontally scale instances behind a load balancer. I'd also review database capacity, caching, rate limiting and connection pools. For non-critical synchronous work, I'd consider moving processing to a queue and background worker. Monitoring would guide the actual scaling decision."

23. Why did you use SignalR?

Answer

"SignalR is useful when the server needs to push real-time information to connected clients. For example, after a backend process completes, instead of having React continuously poll the API, the server can push a notification to the client. I would still use REST APIs for normal CRUD operations and SignalR specifically for real-time communication."

25. What happens when a deployment fails?

Don't say:

 ↓

Senior answer

"First I determine whether the deployment itself failed or the application became unhealthy after deployment. I check pipeline logs, application logs, health checks and monitoring. If production impact is significant, I'd restore the last known-good version using the deployment strategy available, then investigate the root cause separately."

Good answer

This is much better than:

31. What is the biggest technical mistake you have made?

Don't say:

32. What if requirements change after development?

Answer:

"First I understand exactly what changed and whether it affects the API contract, database model, frontend behavior or existing consumers. Then I estimate the impact, discuss trade-offs with the team and implement the change in a way that minimizes breaking existing functionality. For APIs, backward compatibility and versioning become especially important when the contract changes."

34. How would you design for failure?

This is a very senior question.

Think:

Timeout
Retry
Backoff + Jitter
Circuit Breaker
Bulkhead
Idempotency
Dead Letter Queue
Health Checks
Logging
Tracing

Answer

"I assume external dependencies can fail. I use appropriate timeouts, retry only transient failures with bounded exponential backoff and jitter, circuit breakers to prevent repeatedly calling unhealthy dependencies, and idempotency when operations can be retried. For asynchronous processing, I also use retries and dead-letter handling."

35. Why shouldn't every application be microservices?

Excellent senior answer:

"Microservices provide independent deployment and scaling, but they also introduce distributed-system complexity such as network failures, eventual consistency, service discovery, observability and operational overhead. For a smaller system, a modular monolith can provide strong separation without introducing those distributed-system costs. I would choose microservices when the business and scaling requirements justify them."

36. Why not put business logic in controllers?

Because controllers should primarily handle HTTP concerns.

Controller
   ↓
Validate/request handling
   ↓
Service
   ↓
Business logic

Answer

"Keeping business logic out of controllers improves testability, reuse and separation of concerns. Controllers should primarily translate HTTP requests into application operations and return HTTP responses."

39. What happens when the database is unavailable?

Good answer:

"I wouldn't allow the API to keep repeatedly hammering the unavailable database. I'd first detect the failure through health monitoring and logs. Requests that genuinely require the database should fail gracefully with an appropriate response. For asynchronous operations, messages can remain queued for later processing depending on the reliability requirements. I'd also verify connection configuration, database health, connection pool behavior and whether the failure is transient or persistent."

I've worked on API development, database optimization, frontend development, testing, production troubleshooting and technical design discussions. I've also had experience mentoring developers and participating in code reviews.

At this stage, I'm looking for an opportunity where I can use that experience on larger and more challenging product problems while taking greater ownership of technical decisions and continuing to grow as a software engineer."

🎯 The interview formula

For almost any technical/project question, think:

Requirement → Design → Implementation → Trade-off → Testing → Production → Result

And for troubleshooting:

Symptom → Measure → Root Cause → Fix → Validate → Monitor

That is the mindset that will make your answers sound much more experienced than simply listing technologies.
